Instead of studying Dedekind rings next, I'm going to take a break from 200c notes to study point set topology. In particular, I want to learn about uniform spaces. So, I shall be reading \textit{Topological and Uniform Spaces} by Ioan James (see \inLinkRap{Sixth Citation}{citation 6} in my bibliography).\newpage

Here are some conventions for relations on $X$ (i.e. subsets of $X \times X$).
\begin{itemize}
	\item If $R \subseteq X \times X$ then we shorthand $(a,b) \in R$ as $aRb$.
	\item We write $\Delta X \coloneqq \{(a, a) : a \in X\}$. Note that $\Delta X \subseteq R$ if and only if $R$ is a reflexive relation.
	\item Given $R \subseteq X \times X$ we define $R^{-1} \coloneqq \{(a, b) : (b, a) \in R\}$. Note that $R^{-1} \subseteq R$ if and only if $R$ is a symmetric relation.
	\item Given $R, S \subseteq X \times X$, we define $R \circ S \subseteq X \times X$ where $aR \circ S b$ iff there exists\\ $c \in X$ such that $aRc$ and $cSb$. Note that $R \circ R \subseteq R$ if and only if $R$ is a transitive relation.\retTwo
\end{itemize}

\exTwo\ul{Remark 1:} If $R_1, R_2, R_3 \subseteq X \times X$, then $(R_1 \circ R_2) \circ R_3 = R_1 \circ (R_2 \circ R_3)$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	If $a(R_1 \circ R_2) \circ R_3 b$ then there exists $c$ with $a(R_1 \circ R_2)c$ and $cR_3 b$. Next, there exists $d$ with $aR_1 d$ and $dR_2 c$. But now $dR_2 \circ R_3 b$. So, $aR_1 \circ (R_2 \circ R_3)b$. This proves that $(R_1 \circ R_2) \circ R_3 \subseteq R_1 \circ (R_2 \circ R_3)$. Mirror reasoning shows the other inclusion. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\exTwo\ul{Remark 2:} If $R, S \subseteq X \times X$ then $(R \circ S)^{-1} = S^{-1} \circ R^{-1}$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:
	$a(R \circ S)^{-1} b$ iff $bR \circ Sa$. But that happens iff there exists $c$ such that $bRc$ and $cSa$, and that happens iff there exists $c$ such that $aS^{-1}c$ and $cR^{-1}b$. That is equivalent to saying that $aS^{-1} \circ R^{-1}b$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\exTwo\ul{Remark 3:} If $S, R \subseteq X \times X$ with $\Delta X \subseteq S$ then $R \subseteq R \circ S$ and $R \subseteq S \circ R$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Why?\\
	If $aRb$ then $aSa$ implies that $aS \circ Rb$. Similarly $bSb$ implies that $aR \circ Sb$.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\exTwo\ul{Remark 4:} If $R, R^\prime, S \subseteq X \times X$ and $R \subseteq R^\prime$ then $S \circ R \subseteq S \circ R^\prime$ and $R \circ S \subseteq R^\prime \circ S$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Hopefully this is obvious.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo For our purposes here, the relations on $X$ that we will care about will be relations giving a way of describing when any two elements $a$ and $b$ in $X$ are "close" to each other.\retTwo

A \udefine{uniform structure} on a set $X$ is a filter $\mathscr{U}$ on $X \times X$ satisfying that:
\begin{itemize}
	\item $\Delta X \subseteq D$ for all $D \in \mathscr{U}$
	\item $D \in \mathscr{U} \Longrightarrow D^{-1} \in \mathscr{U}$
	\item If $D \in \mathscr{U}$ then there exsts $D^\prime \in \mathscr{U}$ with $D^\prime \circ D^\prime \subseteq D$.\retTwo
\end{itemize}

A \udefine{uniform space} $(X, \mathscr{U})$ is a set $X$ equipped with a uniform structure $\mathscr{U}$.\retTwo

\begin{myIndent}\mySepThree\end{myIndent}

Two trivial uniform structures are as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
	\item[1.] The \udefine{discrete uniform structure} on a set $X$ is the filter consisting of all sets containing $\Delta X$.\newpage
	\item[2.] The \udefine{indiscrete uniform structure} on a set $X$ is the filter whose only element is $X \times X$.\retTwo
\end{enumerate}

In order to get more interesting uniform structures, we consider uniform structures\\ generated by collections of sets. Unfortunately, the third bullet point in the definition of a uniform structure makes it so that an intersection of many uniform structures may not be a uniform structure. Hence, we can't always define a "smallest" uniform structure generated by some collection of sets in the same way that we can for topologies. Something we can do though is consider a filterbase for a uniform structure. Then a smallest uniform structure containing that filterbase is guarenteed to exist as we will see.\retTwo

We say a \udefine{uniformity base} on a set $X$ is a filterbase $\mathscr{B}$ on $X \times X$ satisfying that:
\begin{itemize}
	\item $\Delta X \subseteq E$ for all $E \in \mathscr{B}$
	\item $E \in \mathscr{B} \Longrightarrow E^{-1} \in \mathscr{B}$
	\item If $E \in \mathscr{B}$ then there exsts $E^\prime \in \mathscr{B}$ with $E^\prime \circ E^\prime \subseteq E$.\retTwo
\end{itemize}

\exTwo\ul{Claim:} The filter $\mathscr{U}$ generated by a uniformity base $\mathscr{B}$ is a uniform structure.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Let $D \in \mathscr{U}$. Then there exists $E \in \mathscr{B}$ with $E \subseteq D$. Since $\Delta X \subseteq E$, we can conclude $\Delta X \subseteq D$ as well. Also, note that $E \subseteq D \implies E^{-1} \subseteq D^{-1}$. And since $E^{-1} \in \mathscr{B}$ we know $D^{-1} \in \mathscr{U}$. Finally, let $E^\prime \in \mathscr{B}$ satisfy that $E^\prime \circ E^\prime \subseteq E$. Then we also have that $E^\prime \in \mathscr{U}$ and $E^\prime \circ E^\prime \subseteq D$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo Here are two* important uniform structures defined using uniformity bases.
\begin{itemize}
	\item[1.] Suppose $(X, \rho)$ is a metric space. Then we define $\mathscr{B} \coloneqq \{D_\varepsilon : \varepsilon > 0\}$ where\\ $D_\varepsilon \coloneqq \{(x, y) \in X \times X : \rho(x, y) < \varepsilon\}$. Next, we let the \udefine{metric uniform structure} $\mathscr{U}$ be generated $\mathscr{B}$.
	
	\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
		$\mathscr{B}$ is trivially directed by inclusion since we can make a stronger statment that $\{D_\varepsilon\}_{\varepsilon > 0}$ is ordered by inclusion. Thus, $\mathscr{B}$ is a filterbase. Furthermore, $\rho(x, x) = 0$ for all $x \in X$ guarentees that $\Delta X \subseteq D_\varepsilon$ for all $\varepsilon$. Similarly, $\rho(x, y) = \rho(y, x)$ guarentees that $D_\varepsilon = D_\varepsilon^{-1}$ for all $\varepsilon$.\retTwo

		Finally, let $C \geq 1$ satisfy that $\rho(x, z) \leq C(\rho(x, y) + \rho(y, z))$ for all $x, y, z \in X$. Then we can see that $D_{\frac{\varepsilon}{2C}} \circ D_{\frac{\varepsilon}{2C}} \subseteq D_\varepsilon$.
		\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
			I used an arbitrary constant $C$ instead of just setting $C = 1$ cause I wanted to show that this construction also works for certain \udefine{semimetrics} (such as\\ quasinorms).\retTwo
		\end{myIndent}
	\end{myIndent}

	\item [2.] Suppose $(G, \mathcal{T})$ is a topological group. We define the \udefine{left uniform structure} $\mathscr{U}_{\ell}$ to be generated by the collection $\mathscr{B}$ of sets of the form $L_N \coloneqq \{(x, y) \in G \times G : x^{-1}y \in N\}$ where $N$ is a neighborhood of the identity element $e$ of $G$.
	\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
		\begin{myIndent}\myComment
			In other words, $x L_N y$ iff $y \in xN$.\retTwo
		\end{myIndent}

		To see why $\mathscr{B}$ is a filterbase, first note $G \times G \in \mathscr{B}$ always. Hence, $\mathscr{B}$ is nonempty.\\ Also, since $N$ is a neighborhood of the identity, we know that $x = xe \in xN$ for\newpage all $x \in G$. Hence, $\Delta X \subseteq L_N$ for all neighborhoods $N$ of the identity. This also means $\emptyset \notin \mathscr{B}$. Finally, consider $L_{N_1}$ and $L_{N_2}$ in $\mathscr{B}$. Then $N \coloneqq N_1 \cap N_2$ is still a neighborhood of $e$. Also, $y \in xN \Longrightarrow y \in xN_1$ and $y \in xN_2$. So, $L_N \subseteq L_{N_1} \cap L_{N_2}$. And this proves that $\mathscr{B}$ is directed by inclusion.\retTwo

		As for additionally showing that $\mathscr{B}$ is a uniformity base, note that if $N$ is an open neighborhood of $e$ then so is $N^{-1}$. Also $y \in xN$ iff $x^{-1}y \in N$ iff $y^{-1}x \in N^{-1}$ iff $x \in yN^{-1}$. So $L_N^{-1} = L_{N^{-1}} \in \mathscr{B}$.\retTwo

		Finally, suppose $N$ is a neighborhood of $e$. Then recall from \inLinkRap{placeholder}{page 333} that we can\\ find a neighborhood $N^\prime$ of $e$ with $N^\prime N^\prime \subseteq N$. But now if $y \in xN^\prime$ and $z \in yN^\prime$,\\ we have that $z \in xN^\prime N^\prime \subseteq xN$. So $L_{N^\prime} \circ L_{N^\prime} \subseteq L_N$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Similarly, we define the \udefine{right uniform structure} $\mathscr{U}_r$ to be generated by the collection $\mathscr{B}$ of sets of the form $R_N \coloneqq \{(x, y) : yx^{-1} \in N\}$ where $N$ is a neighborhood of the identity element $e$.
	\begin{myDindent}\myComment
		In other words, $x R_N y$ iff $y \in Nx$.
	\end{myDindent}
\end{itemize}
\begin{myIndent}\mySepThree\end{myIndent}

Let $(X, \mathscr{U})$ be a uniform space. Then we define a relation $R \coloneqq \bigcap_{D \in \mathscr{U}}D$. 
\begin{itemize}
	\item Note that $R$ is reflexive since $\Delta X \subseteq D$ for all $D \in \mathscr{U}$. 
	\item Also note that if $xRy$ then $xDy$ for all $D \in \mathscr{U}$. Yet we also know $D \in \mathscr{U}$ implies that $D^{-1} \in \mathscr{U}$ So, $xRy \in R \implies xD^{-1}y$ for all $D \in \mathscr{U}$. So, $yDx$ for all $D \in \mathscr{U}$. In other words, $xRy$ implies $yRx$. So $R$ is symmetric.
	\item Finally, suppose $xRy$ and $yRz$. Then for any fixed $D \in \mathscr{U}$ we can pick $D^\prime \in \mathscr{U}$ with $D^\prime \circ D^\prime \subseteq D$. Yet now note that $xD^\prime y$ and $yD^\prime z$. So, $xDz$. And since $D$ was arbitrary, we've shown that $xRz$. So, $R$ is transitive.\retTwo
\end{itemize}

As a result of the prior reasoning, we know $R$ is an equivalence relation on $X$. We say $(X, \mathscr{U})$ is a \udefine{separated uniform space} if $\Delta X = R$.
\begin{myIndent}\myComment
	Intuitively, $(X, \mathscr{U})$ is separated iff for all distinct $x, y \in X$ we can find some measure of "closeness" in $\mathscr{U}$ for which $x$ is not close to $y$. As we will see once we connect uniform structures to topology, a uniform space being separated is equivalent to it being Hausdorff as a topological space.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\begin{myIndent}\mySepThree\end{myIndent}

Let $\phi: X \to Y$ be a map between two uniform spaces $(X, \mathscr{U}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathscr{U}_Y)$. We denote $\phi \times \phi: X \times X \to Y \times Y$ to be the map $(x_1, x_2) \mapsto (\phi(x_1), \phi(x_2))$. Then, we say $\phi$ is \udefine{uniformly continuous} if $(\phi \times \phi)^{-1}(E) \in \mathscr{U}_X$ for all $E \in \mathscr{U}_Y$.\retTwo

\myComment\ul{Remark 1:} Let $\phi: X \to Y$ and $\psi: Y \to Z$ be uniformly continuous maps between uniform spaces. Then $\psi \circ \phi$ is a uniformly continuous map from $X$ to $Z$.\newpage

\ul{Remark 2:} Any constant function on a uniform space $X$ is uniformly continuous. Similary,\\ $\myId_X : X \to X$ is always uniformly continuous.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Both remarks are trivial to verify.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\exTwo\ul{Proposition:} \hypertarget{top of page 996}{If} $\phi: (X, \mathscr{U}_X) \to (Y, \mathscr{U}_Y)$ is a map between uniform spaces and $\mathscr{B}_Y$ is a uniformity base for $\mathscr{U}_Y$, then $\phi: X \to Y$ is uniformly continuous iff $(\phi \times \phi)^{-1}(E) \in \mathscr{U}_X$ for all $E \in \mathscr{B}_Y$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	$(\implies)$\\
	This direction is trivial from the fact that $\mathscr{B}_Y \subseteq \mathscr{U}_Y$.\retTwo

	$(\impliedby)$\\
	Consider any $D \in \mathscr{U}_Y$ and then pick $E \in \mathscr{B}_Y$ with $E \subseteq D$. Then\\ $ (\phi \times \phi)^{-1}(D) \supseteq (\phi \times \phi)^{-1}(E) \in \mathscr{U}_X$. So, $(\phi \times \phi)^{-1}(D) \in \mathscr{U}_X$ since $\mathscr{U}_X$ is a filter. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\exTwo\ul{Corollary:} If $(X, \rho_X)$ and $(Y, \rho_Y)$ are metric spaces equipped with their metric uniform structures, then our new definition of uniform continuity agrees with our old definition.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Why?\\
	Let $\mathscr{U}_X$ and $\mathscr{U}_Y$ denote the uniform structures on $X$ and $Y$ respectively, and suppose\\ $\phi: X \to Y$ is a map. Now for any $E_\varepsilon$ in the standard uniformity base for $\mathscr{U}_Y$ we have that $(\phi \times \phi)^{-1}(E_\varepsilon) \in \mathscr{U}_X$ iff there exists $D_\delta$ in the standard uniformity base for $\mathscr{U}_X$ such that $D_\delta \subseteq (\phi \times \phi)^{-1}(E_\varepsilon)$. Equivalently this means that $\phi$ is uniformly continuous according to our new definition iff for all $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $\delta > 0$ with $\rho_X(x, y) < \delta \Longrightarrow \rho_Y(\phi(x), \phi(y)) < \varepsilon$.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo One related headache to mention is as follows:\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Corollary 2:} Let $G$ be a topological group equipped with the left uniform structure $\mathscr{U}_L$, and also let $\mathbb{R}$ be equipped with the (Euclidean) metric uniform structure. Then left uniform continuity by our new definition is equivalent to Folland's notion of right uniform continuity (see \inLinkRap{placeholder}{page 334}).
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	$(\Longrightarrow)$\\
	Let $\phi: G \to \mathbb{R}$ be a map. Then for any $\varepsilon > 0$ we know that $E_\varepsilon \coloneqq \{(x, y) : |x - y| < \varepsilon\}$ satisfies that $(\phi \times \phi)^{-1}(E_\varepsilon) \in \mathscr{U}_\ell$ Hence, there exists a filter $L_N \in \mathscr{U}_\ell$ satisfying that $L_N \subseteq (\phi \times \phi)^{-1}(E_\varepsilon)$. In other words, if $z \in xN$ then $|f(x) - f(z)| < \varepsilon$. Yet this is equivalent to saying that for all $x \in G$ and $y \in N$, we have that $|f(xy) - f(x)| < \varepsilon$.\retTwo

	$(\Longleftarrow)$\\
	Just reverse all the steps in the prior direction. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

Similarly, right uniform continuity by our new definition is equivalent to Folland's notion of left uniform continuity.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	The proof is almost entirely identical to the one before except for an additional step where you shrink your neighborhood $N$ to a symmetric neighborhood.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo Unfortunately, both James and Folland's notions  of left vs right make sense in the context of what they were thinking about. Thus for the time being, I'm going to stick to James's convention.\newpage

A \udefine{uniform equivalence} $\phi: X \to Y$ (where both $X$ and $Y$ are uniform spaces) is a bijective function such that both $\phi$ and $\phi^{-1}$ are uniformly continuous.\retTwo

\pracOne\ul{Example:} Suppose $\phi : G \to H$ is a continuous group homomorphism between topological groups. Then $\phi$ is uniformly continuous if $G$ and $H$ are both equipped with the left uniform structure, and also if $G$ and $H$ are both equipped with the right uniform structures.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	I'll only show this for the left uniform structure.
	Suppose $N$ is any neighorhood of the identity $e_H$ of $H$. Then let $N^\prime = \phi^{-1}(N)$. Because $\phi$ is continuous, we also know that $N^\prime$ is a neighborhood of the identity $e_G$ of $G$. But now if $y \in xN^\prime$, we know that $\phi(y) \in \phi(x)N$ since $\phi$ is a group homomorphism. Hence, $L_{N^\prime}$ in the uniform structure on $G$ satisfies that $L_{N^\prime} \subseteq (\phi \times \phi)^{-1}(L_{N})$. And since the $L_N$ generate the left uniform structure on $H$, we've proven that $\phi$ is uniformly continuous. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

As a consequence, we can also say that if $\phi: G \to H$ is a topological group isomorphism (i.e. a homeomorphism and group isomorphism), then $\phi$ is a left and right uniform\\ equivalence.\retTwo

\hTwo One reason to care about uniform equivalences is that we can study properties that are invariant under uniform equivalences.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Proposition:} If $(X, \mathscr{U}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathscr{U}_Y)$ are uniform spaces, $X$ is separated, and $\phi: X \to Y$ is a bijective map such that $\phi^{-1}$ is uniformly continuous, then $Y$ is separated as well.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Let $R_Y \coloneqq \bigcap_{E \in \mathscr{U}_Y} E$. We want to prove $R_Y = \Delta Y$. So consider any $(y_1, y_2) \in Y \times Y$ such that $y_1 \neq y_2$. Since $\phi$ is bijective, we know that there exists unique distinct elements $x_1, x_2 \in X$ such that $\phi(x_1) = y_1$ and $\phi(x_2) = y_2$. And now since $X$ is separated, we can find some $D \in \mathscr{U}_X$ such that $(x_1, x_2) \notin D$.\retTwo

	But now set $E = (\phi \times \phi)(D)$. Since $\phi^{-1}$ is uniformly continuous, we know that\\ $(\phi \times \phi)(D) \in \mathscr{U}_Y$. Furthermore, $(\phi \times \phi)^{-1}(\{(y_1, y_2)\}) = \{(x_1, x_2)\} \not\subseteq D$. So\\ $(y_1, y_2) \notin E$. And with that, we've shown that $(y_1, y_2) \notin \Delta Y \Longrightarrow (y_1, y_2) \notin R_Y$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\exTwo\ul{Corollary:} If $(X, \mathscr{U}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathscr{U}_Y)$ are uniform spaces and $\phi: X \to Y$ is a uniform\\ equivalence, then $X$ is separated iff $Y$ is separated.\retTwo

I have more to go over from \textit{Topological and Uniform Spaces} today. For the time being I'll still be working with uniform structures as a thing defined separately from topological spaces.\retTwo

Firstly, here's another convention of James for relations on a set $X$. Suppose $R \subseteq X \times X$. If $a R b$ we say that $a$ is \udefine{$R$-related} to $b$. Then, we define $R[a] \coloneqq \{b \in X : aRb\}$. In other words, $R[a]$ denotes the set of elements that $a$ is $R$-related to.\retTwo

Similarly, if $S \subseteq X$ then we define $R[S] \coloneqq \bigcup_{a \in S}R[a]$.\newpage

Suppose $(X, \mathscr{U})$ is a uniform space. We say that $X$ is \udefine{totally bounded} if for all $D \in \mathscr{U}$ there exists a finite set $S \subseteq X$ such that $X = D[S]$.
\begin{myIndent}\myComment
	Remark: If $\mathscr{B}$ is a filterbase for $\mathscr{U}$ then $X$ is totally bounded iff for all $D \in \mathscr{B}$ we can find a finite set $S \subseteq X$ such that $X = D[S]$. From this observation, hopefully it is clear how this definition of total boundedness agrees with the metric space definition when we equip our metric space with the metric uniform structure.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\exTwo\ul{Proposition:} Suppose $(X, \mathscr{U}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathscr{U}_Y)$ are uniform spaces and $\phi: X \to Y$ is a\\ uniformly continuous surjection. If $X$ is totally bounded then so is $Y$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Consider any $E \in \mathscr{U}_Y$ and then let $D \coloneqq (\phi \times \phi)^{-1}(E) \in \mathscr{U}_X$. Since $X$ is totally bounded, we can find a finite set $S \subseteq X$ with $D[S] = X$. In turn, we have that $Y = E[\phi(S)]$. After all, suppose $y \in Y$. Since $\phi$ is surjective, there exists $x \in X$ such that $\phi(x) = y$. Yet now pick $s \in S$ such that $s D x$. Then $\phi(s) E y$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\exTwo\ul{Corollary:} If $X$ and $Y$ are uniform spaces, and $\phi: X \to Y$ is a uniform equivalence, then $X$ is totally bounded iff $Y$ is totally bounded.\retTwo

\hTwo
\begin{myIndent}\mySepThree\end{myIndent}

One of the main reasons for caring about uniform spaces is that they let us define what it means for a sequence to be Cauchy.\retTwo

Suppose $(X, \mathscr{U})$ is a uniform space and $\{x_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is a sequence in $X$. Then we say $\{x_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is a \udefine{Cauchy sequence} if:

{\centering $\forall D \in \mathscr{U}, \hspace{0.3em} \exists N \in \mathbb{N} \suchthat \forall n, m \geq N, \hspace{0.3em} x_n D x_m$ \retTwo\par}

\begin{myIndent}\myComment
	Remark: Like with total boundedness, if $\mathscr{B}$ is a filterbase for $\mathscr{U}$ then it suffices to check the condition for a sequence being Cauchy only for the elements in $\mathscr{B}$. With this in mind, hopefully it is clear how this definition of a sequence being Cauchy agrees with the metric space definition when we equip out metric space with the metric uniform structure.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

Similarly, we say a net $\langle x_\alpha\rangle_{\alpha \in A}$ is \udefine{Cauchy} if:

{\centering $\forall D \in \mathscr{U}, \hspace{0.3em} \exists \alpha \in A \suchthat \forall \beta, \gamma \geq \alpha, \hspace{0.3em} \beta D \gamma$ \retTwo\par}

Once we define a topology associated with a uniform structure, we'll be able to discuss whether a uniform space is \udefine{complete} or not (i.e. if all Cauchy sequences and nets converge or not). Furthermore, we'll be able to discuss taking completions of uniform spaces.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Proposition:} Suppose $(X, \mathscr{U}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathscr{U}_Y)$ are uniform spaces, $\langle x_\alpha\rangle_{\alpha \in A}$ is a Cauchy net in $X$, and $\phi: X \to Y$ is a uniformly continuous map. Then $\langle \phi(x_\alpha)\rangle_{\alpha \in A}$ is a Cauchy net in $Y$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Let $E$ be a relation in $\mathscr{U}_Y$.
	\begin{myIndent}\myComment
		By the way, something I've not mentioned before is that a relation in $\mathscr{U}_Y$ would\\ normally be called an \udefine{entourage}. The reason I wasn't using that terminology before\newpage is that the word "entourage" makes my mind immediately think of a neighborhood in $Y$ as opposed to a subset of $Y \times Y$. That said, it would be helpful to not have to keep explicitely naming the uniform structure of $X$ and $Y$. So, I'm going to start calling relations in uniform structures "entourages".\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Since $\phi$ is uniformly continuous, we know that $D \coloneqq (\phi \times \phi)^{-1}(E)$ is an entourage on $X$. In turn, as $\langle x_\alpha\rangle_{\alpha \in A}$ is a Cauchy net, we know there exists $\alpha_0 \in A$ with $x_\beta D x_\gamma$ for all $\beta, \gamma \geq \alpha_0$. And now $\phi(x_\beta) E \phi(x_\gamma)$ for all $\beta, \gamma \geq \alpha_0$. Since $E$ was arbitrary, we can conclude that $\langle \phi(x_\alpha)\rangle_{\alpha \in A}$ is a Cauchy net in $Y$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\pracOne\mySepTwo

I would mostly rather work with nets if possible since they along with sequences are\\ much more natural to think about then filters are (at least when it comes to things like\\ convergence). That said, I think it is unavoidable that I need to introduce some facts about them here.\retTwo

Suppose $\mathscr{F}$ is a filter. We say another filter $\mathscr{F}^\prime$ \udefine{refines} $\mathscr{F}$ if $\mathscr{F} \subseteq \mathscr{F}^\prime$.\\ [-6pt]
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Note that we can let $\mathcal{F}$ be the collection of all filters $\mathscr{F}^\prime$ refining $\mathscr{F}$. Importantly, $\mathcal{F}$ is nonempty since $\mathscr{F} \in \mathcal{F}$. Next, we can partially order $\mathcal{F}$ via inclusion. Then suppose we are given a chain of filters $\{\mathscr{F}^\prime_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ contained in $\mathcal{F}$. By defining $\mathscr{F}^\prime \coloneqq \bigcup_{\alpha \in A}\mathscr{F}^\prime_\alpha$, we get another filter in $\mathcal{F}$ which is an upper bound to our chain. With that, we can conclude by Zorn's lemma that $\mathcal{F}$ has a maximal element.\retTwo

	So, we've shown for any filter that there is a maximal filter refining our original filter.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

If $\mathscr{F}$ is a maximal filter (meaning that for any filter $\mathscr{G}$ refining $\mathscr{F}$ we have that $\mathscr{F} = \mathscr{G}$), then we call $\mathscr{F}$ an \udefine{ultrafilter}.\retTwo

\ul{Proposition:} Let $\mathscr{F}$ be a filter on a set $X$. Then $\mathscr{F}$ is an ultrafilter if and only if whenever $A \cup B \in \mathscr{F}$ where $A, B \subseteq X$ then $A \in \mathscr{F}$ or $B \in \mathscr{F}$.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo 
	$(\Longrightarrow)$\\
	Suppose that $A$ and $B$ are subsets of $X$ such that $A \cup B \in \mathscr{F}$ but $A \notin \mathscr{F}$ and $B \notin \mathscr{F}$. Then we can define another filter $\mathscr{G} \coloneqq \{B^\prime \subseteq X : A \cup B^\prime \in \mathscr{F}\}$.\retTwo
	
	To see that $\mathscr{G}$ is a filter, first note that $\emptyset \notin \mathscr{G}$ since $A = A \cup \emptyset \notin \mathscr{F}$. Meanwhile, $X \in \mathscr{G}$\\ since $X = A \cup X \in \mathscr{F}$. Next, suppose $B^\prime \in \mathscr{G}$ and $B^\prime \subseteq C^\prime \subseteq X$. Then note that\\ $A \cup C^\prime \supseteq A \cup B^\prime \in \mathscr{F}$. So, $A \cup C^\prime \in \mathscr{F}$ and this proves that $C^\prime \in \mathscr{G}$. Finally, suppose $B_1^\prime, B_2^\prime \in \mathscr{G}$. Then $(A \cup B_1^\prime) \cap (A \cup B_2^\prime) = A \cup (B_1^\prime \cap B_2^\prime) \in \mathscr{F}$. So, $B_1^\prime \cap B_2^\prime \in \mathscr{G}$.\retTwo

	Yet now note that $\mathscr{G}$ refines $\mathscr{F}$. After all, if $B^\prime \in \mathscr{F}$ then:
	
	{\centering $A \cup B^\prime \subseteq B^\prime \Longrightarrow A \cup B^\prime \in \mathscr{F} \Longrightarrow B^\prime \in \mathscr{G}$.\retTwo\par}

	At the same time, $B \in \mathscr{G} - \mathscr{F}$. This proves that $\mathscr{F}$ is not an ultrafilter since $\mathscr{G}$ properly contains $\mathscr{F}$.\retTwo

	$(\Longleftarrow)$\\
	Suppose $\mathscr{F}$ is not an ultrafilter and let $\mathscr{G}$ be a filter properly containing $\mathscr{F}$. In turn, we know that there exists a set $A \in \mathscr{G} - \mathscr{F}$. But now consider that $X - A \notin \mathscr{G}$ since otherwise\newpage $\emptyset = (X - A) \cap A$ would be in $\mathscr{G}$. Since $\mathscr{F} \subseteq \mathscr{G}$, we can also thus conclude that\\ $X - A \notin \mathscr{F}$. Simultanously though, we know $X \in \mathscr{F}$. So $X = A \cup (X - A) \in \mathscr{F}$\\ but $A$ and $X - A$ are both not in $\mathscr{F}$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo

	\begin{myIndent}\myComment
		\ul{Remark 1:}, we can more strongly conclude from the reasoning of the prior proof that $\mathscr{F}$ is an ultrafilter on $X$ if and only if for all $A \subseteq X$ we have that $A \in \mathscr{F}$ or $X - A \in \mathscr{F}$.\retTwo

		\ul{Remark 2:} If $\mathscr{F}$ is an ultrafilter and $\bigcup_{i=1}^n A_i \in \mathscr{F}$, then we can easily now conclude by induction that at least one $A_i$ is in $\mathscr{F}$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
\end{myIndent}

A useful application of ultrafilters is as follows. We say a net $\langle x_\alpha\rangle_{\alpha \in A}$ on a set $X$ is\\ an \udefine{ultra-net} if and only if for all $E \subseteq X$ we have that $x_\alpha$ is eventually in $E$ or $x_\alpha$ is\\ eventually in $X - E$. Importantly, every net $\langle x_\alpha\rangle_{\alpha \in A}$ has an ultra-subnet.\\ [-6pt]
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Proof:\\
	For all $\alpha \in A$ we let $T_\alpha \coloneqq \{x_\beta : \beta \in A \text{ with } \beta \geq \alpha\}$. Importantly, the collection of all $T_\alpha$ constitutes a filterbase. In turn, we can find some ultrafilter $\mathscr{F}$ containing each of the $T_\alpha$.\retTwo

	Next, let $B \subseteq A \times \mathscr{F}$ be defined to be the set of all pairs $(\alpha, F) \in A \times \mathscr{F}$ with $x_\alpha \in F$. Importantly, $B$ is a directed set when we define $(\alpha_1, F_1) \lesssim (\alpha_2, F_2)$ if $\alpha_1 \leq \alpha_2$ and $F_1 \supseteq F_2$.
	\begin{myIndent}
		Why?\\
		The only nonobvious thing to prove is that if $(\alpha_1, F_1), (\alpha_2, F_2) \in B$ then there\\ exists $(\alpha^\prime, F^\prime) \in B$ such that $(\alpha^\prime, F^\prime) \gtrsim(\alpha_1, F_1)$ and $(\alpha^\prime, F^\prime) \gtrsim(\alpha_2, F_2)$.\\ Fortunately, note that $A$ being a directed set means that there exists $\beta \in A$\\ with $\beta \gtrsim \alpha_1$ and $\beta \gtrsim \alpha_2$. Next, as $\mathscr{F}$ is a filter containing $F_1$, $F_2$, and $T_\beta$, we\\ know that $F^\prime \coloneqq F_1 \cap F_2 \in \mathscr{F}$ and $F^\prime \cap T_\beta \in \mathscr{F}$. In particular, this means\\ that $F^\prime \cap T_\beta \neq \emptyset$. So, there exists $\alpha^\prime \in A$ such that $x_{\alpha^\prime} \in F^\prime$ and $\alpha^\prime \geq \beta$.\\ And with that, we've now show that $(\alpha^\prime, F^\prime) \in B$. Also, this element is clearly\\ an upper bound to our original two elements of $B$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Now for any $(\alpha, F) \in B$ we define $y_{(\alpha, F)} = x_\alpha$. Then we consider the net $\langle y_{(\alpha, F)}\rangle_{(\alpha, F) \in B}$.
	\begin{myIndent}
		To see that this is a subnet of $\langle x_\alpha\rangle_{\alpha \in A}$, suppose that $\alpha_0 \in A$ and then pick any\\ $F \in \mathscr{F}$. Since $T_{\alpha_0} \in \mathscr{F}$ we know that $F \cap T_{\alpha_0} \in \mathscr{F}$. In particular, this means that $F \cap T_{\alpha_0} \neq \emptyset$. So, we can find $\alpha_1 \in A$ with $(\alpha_1, F) \in B$ and $\alpha_1 \geq \alpha_0$. Now it is easy to see that if $(\alpha^\prime, F^\prime) \in B$ satisfies that $(\alpha^\prime, F^\prime) \gtrsim (\alpha_1, F)$ then $\alpha^\prime \geq \alpha_0$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Finally, I claim that $\langle y_{(\alpha, F)}\rangle_{(\alpha, F) \in B}$ is an ultra-net.
	\begin{myIndent}
		After all, suppose $E \subseteq X$ is any set. Since $\mathscr{F}$ is an ultrafilter, we know that either $E \in \mathscr{F}$ or $X - E \in \mathscr{F}$.
		\begin{itemize}
			\item Suppose $E \in \mathscr{F}$. Then we can pick some $\alpha_0 \in A$ with $x_{\alpha_0} \in E$. (This is because $E \cap T_\alpha \in \mathscr{F}$ and thus $E \cap T_\alpha \neq \emptyset$ for all $\alpha \in A$.) But now if $(\alpha, F) \in B$\\ satisfies that $(\alpha, F) \gtrsim (\alpha_0, E)$, we know $y_{(\alpha, F)} = x_\alpha \in E$. So, our subnet\\ is eventually in $E$.\retTwo

			\item Meanwhile, the case where $X - E \in \mathscr{F}$ can be dealt with using analogous reasoning. (Just replace $E$ with $X - E$.)\newpage
		\end{itemize}
	\end{myIndent}
\end{myIndent}

One other note I want to make is that if $\langle x_\alpha\rangle_{\alpha \in A}$ is an ultra-net and $X = \bigcup_{i=1}^n E_i$, then\\ we can conclude that there is at least one $E_i$ such that $x_\alpha$ is eventually in $E_i$.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Proof:\\
	We proceed by induction on $n$. For our base case, suppose $X = E_1 \cup E_2$. Then if $x_\alpha$ is not eventually in $E_1$, we know that $x_\alpha$ is eventually in $X - E_1$. And since $X - E_1 \subseteq E_2$, we can conclude that $x_\alpha$ is eventually in $E_2$.\retTwo

	Now suppose $n > 2$ and that $X = \bigcup_{i=1}^n E_i$. Then by writing:
	
	{\centering$X = (E_1 \cup E_2) \cup E_3 \cup \cdots \cup E_n$,\\ [4pt]\par}
	
	we can conclude by induction that either there exists $i \geq 3$ with $x_\alpha$ eventually in $E_i$, or\\ we have that $x_\alpha$ is eventually in $E_1 \cup E_2$. We're trivially done in the former case. So assume the latter case is what happens.\retTwo

	Next, write $X = E_1 \cup (E_2 \cup E_3) \cup E_4 \cup \cdots \cup E_n$. Then we know from our induction hypothesis that either there exists $i \neq 2, 3$ with $x_\alpha$ eventually in $E_i$ or we have that $x_\alpha$ is eventually in $E_2 \cup E_3$. We assume the former case doesn't happen since otherwise we'd be trivially done. In particular, this means that $x_\alpha$ is not eventually in $E_1$.\retTwo

	But now we have that $x_\alpha$ is eventually in $(E_1 \cup E_2)$, and yet at the same time since $\langle x_\alpha\rangle_{\alpha \in A}$ is an ultrafilter, we can conclude that $x_\alpha$ is eventually in $X - E_1$. In turn, we can conclude that $x_\alpha$ is eventually in $(E_1 \cup E_2) \cap (X - E_1) = E_2 - E_1 \subseteq E_2$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\mySepTwo

\exTwo\ul{Proposition:} Suppose $X$ is a uniform space. Then $X$ is totally bounded if and only if every net $\langle x_\alpha\rangle_{\alpha \in A}$ in $X$ admits a Cauchy subnet.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	$(\Longrightarrow)$\\
	Let $\langle x_{\alpha_\beta}\rangle_{\beta \in B}$ be an ultra-subnet of $\langle x_\alpha\rangle_{\alpha \in A}$. Then I claim that $\langle x_{\alpha_\beta}\rangle_{\beta \in B}$ is Cauchy since more generally, any ultra-net $\langle y_\gamma\rangle_{\gamma \in C}$ is Cauchy in a totally bounded space.\\ [-6pt]
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		To see why, let $\{y_\gamma\}_{\gamma \in C}$ be an ultra-net. Then suppose $E$ is any entourage of $X$. Firstly, we find an entourage $E^\prime$ such that $E^\prime = (E^\prime)^{-1}$ and $E^\prime \circ E^\prime \subseteq E$. Next,\\ note that since $X$ is totally bounded, there exists $x_1, \ldots, x_n \in X$ such that\\ $X = \bigcup_{i=1}^n E^\prime[x_i]$. Since $\{y_\gamma\}_{\gamma \in C}$ is an ultra-net, we know there must exist some\\ $x_i$ such that $y_\gamma$ is eventually in $E^\prime[x_i]$.\retTwo

		But now let $\gamma_0 \in C$ be such that $y_\gamma \in E^\prime[x_i]$ for all $\gamma \geq \gamma_0$. Then for all\\ $\gamma_1, \gamma_2 \geq \gamma_0$ in $C$ we have that $x_i E^\prime y_{\gamma_1}$ and $x_i E^\prime y_{\gamma_2}$. This implies that $y_{\gamma_1} E y_{\gamma_2}$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	$(\Longleftarrow)$\\
	Suppose that $X$ is not a totally bounded space. Thus, we know there exists an entourage $E$ such that $E[S]$ is a proper subset of $X$ for all finite subsets $S$ of $X$.\retTwo

	Let $\mathcal{S}$ be the collection of all finite subsets of $X$. This becomes a directed set when\\ partially ordered by inclusion. Next, for every $S \in \mathcal{S}$ let $x_S$ be an element of $X - E[S]$. Then, we can consider the net $\langle x_S\rangle_{S \in \mathcal{S}}$.\newpage

	I claim that $\langle x_S\rangle_{S \in \mathcal{S}}$ has no Cauchy subnets. To see why, suppose that $\langle x_{S_\beta}\rangle_{\beta \in B}$ is any subnet of $\langle x_S\rangle_{S \in \mathcal{S}}$. Then consider any fixed $\beta_0 \in B$. It suffices to show that there exists\\ [2pt] $\beta_1, \beta_2 \geq \beta_0$ in $B$ such that $(x_{S_{\beta_1}}, x_{S_{\beta_2}}) \notin E$. Fortunately, just let $\beta_1 = \beta_0$ and then let $\beta_2 \in B$ be such that $\beta_2 \geq \beta_0$ and $S_{\beta_2} \supseteq S_{\beta_0} \cup \{x_{S_{\beta_0}}\}$. Then we know $(x_{S_{\beta_1}}, x_{S_{\beta_2}}) \notin E$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo Before wrapping up for the day, I also want to translate the prior result into a result about Cauchy sequences. I think this is especially worth doing since the constructions in this simpler case are less set-theoretic.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Proposition:} Suppose $X$ is a uniform space whose uniform structure is generated by a countable filterbase $\{E_k\}_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$. Then $X$ being totally bounded implies every sequence $\{x_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ in $X$ admits a Cauchy subsequence.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	For each $k$ we can pick $E_k^\prime$ such that $E_k^\prime = (E_k^\prime)^{-1}$ and $E_k^\prime \circ E_k^\prime \subseteq E_k$. Then because $X$ is totally bounded, we know for each $k$ that there exists $y_1^{(k)}, \ldots, y_{m(k)}^{(k)} \in X$ such that $X = \bigcup_{j=1}^{m(k)} E^\prime_k[y_j^{(k)}]$.\retTwo
	
	But now suppose $\{x_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is any sequence in $X$. Then there exists some $y_j^{(1)}$ as well as\\ [-2pt] some subsequence $\{x_{n_i^{(1)}}\}_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that $x_{n_i^{(1)}} \in E^\prime_1[y_j^{(1)}]$ for all $i$. Next, there exists a\\ [-4pt] subsequence $\{x_{n_i^{(2)}}\}_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ of $\{x_{n_i^{(1)}}\}_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ as well as some $y_j^{(2)}$ with $x_{n_i^{(2)}} \in E^\prime_2[y_j^{(2)}]$ for all $i$. Continuing on in this manner, for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$ we can find a sequence $\{x_{n_i^{(k)}}\}_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ which is\\ [-2pt] a subsequence of $\{x_{n_i^{(k^\prime)}}\}_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ for all $k^\prime < k$ and which also satisfies that there exists\\ [-2pt] $y^{(k)} \in X$ with $x_{n_i^{(k)}} \in E_k^\prime[y^{(k)}]$ for all $i$.\retTwo

	To finish off, we now do a diagonal argument on all of the previous sequences we\\ constructed. Namely, consider the sequence $\{z_k\}_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ where $z_k \coloneqq x_{n_k^{(k)}}$. This is a\\ [-4pt] subsequence of $\{x_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$. Also I claim it is Cauchy. 
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP 
		After all, suppose $D$ is an entourage of $X$. Then we can find an entourage $E_k$ such that $E_k \subseteq D$. Next, note for all $k_1, k_2 \geq k$ that $y^{(k)} E_k^\prime z_{k_1}$ and $y^{(k)} E_k^\prime z_{k_2}$. Hence, we know that $z_{k_1} E_k z_{k_2}$. So, $(z_{k_1}, z_{k_2}) \in E_k \subseteq D$ for all $k_1, k_2 \geq k$.  \exThreeP $\blacksquare$\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
\end{myIndent}

\ul{Proposition:} Suppose $X$ is a uniform space. If every sequence $\{x_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ in $X$ admits a Cauchy subsequence then $X$ is totally bounded.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Suppose $X$ is not totally bounded and let $E$ be an entourage such that $E[S] \neq X$ for all finite subsets $S$ of $X$. By shrinking $E$, we can without loss of generality assume that $E$ is symmetric (i.e. $E = E^{-1}$). Now pick any $x_1 \in X$. We can find $x_2 \in X - E[x_1]$. Next, we can find $x_3 \in X- E[x_1, x_2]$. And continuing on in this fashion, we can find $x_n \in X - \bigcup_{i=1}^{n-1} E[x_i]$. Then we consider the sequence $\{x_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$.\retTwo

	Trivially, no subsequence (or even any subnet I now realize) of $\{x_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ will be Cauchy since $(x_{n_1}, x_{n_2}) \notin E$ whenever $n_1 \neq n_2$. $\blacksquare$
\end{myIndent}
\hTwo\mySepTwo\newpage

\dispDate{6/23/2026}

Today I want to start tying the theory of uniform spaces to the theory of topology. So, I'll continue loosely following the book I was following before.\retTwo

Let $(X, \mathscr{U})$ be a uniform space. Then taking inspiration from \inLinkRap{Page 798 theorem 4-3-5}{pages 798-800} as well as from how the metric space topology is defined, we'll define that a set $U \subseteq X$ is open in the uniform topology if for all $x \in U$ there exists an entourage $E \in \mathscr{U}$ with $E[x] \subseteq U$.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Proposition:} The uniform topology is a well-defined topology. 
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	To start off, we trivially have that $\emptyset$ and $X$ are open sets in the uniform topology.\retTwo

	Next suppose $U_1$ and $U_2$ are open sets in the uniform topology, and consider any\\ $x \in U_1 \cap U_2$. Since $U_1$ and $U_2$ are open, we can find entourages $E_1$ and $E_2$ such that $E_1[x] \subseteq U_1$ and $E_2[x] \subseteq U_2$. So, we then consider the entourage $E \coloneqq E_1 \cap E_2$. Now $E[x] \subseteq U_1 \cap U_2$. And since $x$ was arbitrary, we've proven that $U_1 \cap U_2$ is an open set in the uniform topology.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		(By induction we can in turn conclude that any finite intersection of open sets is open in the uniform topology.)\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Finally, suppose $\{U_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ is an arbitrary collection of open sets in the uniform topology. Then for any $x \in \bigcup_{\alpha \in A}U_\alpha$ we know that there exists $\alpha_0 \in A$ with $x \in U_{\alpha_0}$. Next, since $U_{\alpha_0}$ is open we know that there exist an entourage $E$ such that $E[x] \subseteq U_{\alpha_0}$. And now $E[x] \subseteq \bigcup_{\alpha \in A}U_\alpha$. This proves that $\bigcup_{\alpha \in A}U_\alpha$ is open. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\exTwo\ul{Proposition:} Suppose $\mathscr{B}$ is a filterbase for $\mathscr{U}$. Then for any $x \in X$ we have that\\ $\{E[x] : E \in \mathscr{B}\}$ is a local base of neighborhoods of $x$. {\color{red} (See \inLinkRap{local base of neighborhoods definition}{page 796} for the definition\\ of a local base of neighborhoods.)}
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	To start off, suppose $N$ is any neighborhood of $x$. Then we know there is an open set $U$ such that $x \in U \subseteq N$. But now since $U$ is open, we know there exists some entourage $D \in \mathscr{U}$ such that $D[x] \subseteq U$. And finally, since $\mathscr{B}$ is a filterbase for $\mathscr{U}$ we know that there exists another entourage $E \in \mathscr{B}$ with $E \subseteq D$. In turn, $E[x] \subseteq D[x]$. And with that, we've proven that for all neighborhoods $N$ of $x$ there exists $E \in \mathscr{B}$ with $x \in E[x] \subseteq N$.\retTwo
	
	Meanwhile, we also need to show that $E[x]$ is a neighborhood of $x$ for all $E \in \mathscr{B}$. So, having fixed our entourage $E$, let $U \coloneqq \{y \in X : \exists D \in \mathscr{U} \text{ s.t. } D[y] \subseteq E[x]\}$. Note that:
	\begin{itemize}
		\item $x \in U$ since $E \in \mathscr{U}$ and $E[x] \subseteq E[x]$.
		\item Also since $y \in D[y]$ for all entourages $D \in \mathscr{U}$ and $y \in X$, we know that $U \subseteq E[x]$.
		\item Finally, $U$ is open. After all, consider any $y \in U$ and let $D \in \mathscr{B}$ be such that\\ $D[y] \subseteq E[x]$. But now since $\mathscr{U}$ is a uniform structure, we can find some $D^\prime \in \mathscr{U}$\\ such that $D^\prime \circ D^\prime \subseteq D$. And now I claim that $D^\prime[y] \subseteq U$.
		\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
			After all, suppose $z \in D^\prime[y]$. Then for any $w \in D^\prime[z]$ we have that $y D^\prime z$ and $z D^\prime w$. It follows that $y D^\prime \circ D^\prime w$. So, $w \in D[y] \subseteq E[x]$. And this proves that\newpage $D^\prime[z] \subseteq E[x]$. In turn, by the definition of $U$ we know that $z \in U$. And since $z$ was arbitrary, this proves that $D^\prime[y] \subseteq U$.\retTwo
		\end{myIndent}
	\end{itemize}

	With that, we can conclude that $E[x]$ is a neighborhood of $x$ for every entourage $E \in \mathscr{B}$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\exTwo\ul{Corollary:} If $(X, \rho)$ is a metric space, then the uniform topology associated with the metric uniform structure is precisely the standard metric topology.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Let $\{D_\varepsilon\}_{\varepsilon > 0}$ be the standard uniformity base for the metric uniform structure. Then we can see for all $x \in X$ that $D_\varepsilon[x]$ is just the ball of radius $\varepsilon$ centered at $x$. Hence, for any $x \in X$ we have that $\{D_\varepsilon[x], \varepsilon > 0\}$ is a local base of neighborhoods of $x$ in both the standard metric topology and in the uniform topology. It follows that convergence in both topologies are equivalent, and in turn the topologies are equal to each other. $\blacksquare$\retTwo 
\end{myIndent}

\ul{Corollary 2:} Let $G$ be a topological group. Then the uniform topologies associated with the left uniform structure and the right uniform structure are both equivalent to the original topology on $G$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Just show like in the prior corollary that either of the uniform topologies on $G$ admits\\ a local base of neighborhoods at any $x \in G$ which is also a local base of neighborhoods\\ of $x$ in the original topology. After all given any neighborhood $N$ of the identity element\\ $e \in G$ we have that $L_N[x] = xN$ and $R_N[x] = Nx$.\retTwo

	\begin{myIndent}\myComment
		As a side note, since the left and right uniform structures on a topological group are generally not the same, this corollary also demonstrates that while we can speak of a single canonical topology associated with a uniform space, we generally can't speak of a single canonical uniform structure whose associated topology is some desired topology.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo\begin{myIndent}\mySepThree\end{myIndent}

There are two propertes of the uniform topology which had better be true. Namely,\\ uniform continuity should be stronger than continuity, and also every convergent net\\ should be Cauchy. I'll prove these facts below.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Proposition:} Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are uniform spaces and $\phi: X \to Y$ is uniformly continuous. Then $\phi$ is continuous when $X$ and $Y$ are equipped with the uniform topologies.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Consider any $x \in X$ and then consider any neighborhood $N$ of $\phi(x)$ in $Y$. We\\ know there exists an entourage $E$ of $Y$ with $E[\phi(x)] \subseteq N$. Yet also note that\\ $D \coloneqq (\phi \times \phi)^{-1}(E)$ is an entourage of $X$ since $\phi$ is uniformly continuous. And\\ now I claim that $D[x]$ is a neighborhood of $x \in X$ satisfying that $\phi(D[x]) \subseteq N$.\\ After all, if $y \in D[x]$ then $\phi(y) \in E[\phi(x)] \subseteq N$. This proves that $\phi$ is continuous\\ at $x$. And since $x$ was arbitrary, we can conclude that $\phi$ is continuous everywhere. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\exTwo\ul{Proposition:} Suppose $X$ is a uniform space and that the net $\langle x_\alpha\rangle_{\alpha \in A}$ converges with\\ respect to the uniform topology to a point $x \in X$. Then $\langle x_\alpha\rangle_{\alpha \in A}$ is a Cauchy net.\newpage
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Let $E$ be any entourage of $X$ and then pick a symmetric entourage $E^\prime$ of $X$ such\\ that $E^\prime \circ E^\prime \subseteq E$. Since $x_\alpha \to x$ in the uniform topology, we know that the $x_\alpha$ are\\ eventually in $E^\prime[x]$. But now let $\alpha_0 \in A$ satisfy that $x_\alpha \in E^\prime[x]$ for all $\alpha \geq \alpha_0$. Then\\ for all $\alpha, \beta \geq \alpha_0$ we have that $xE^\prime x_\alpha$ and $xE^\prime x_\beta$ implies that $x_\alpha E^\prime \circ E^\prime x_\beta$. So,\\ $x_\alpha E x_\beta$ for all $\alpha, \beta \geq \alpha_0$. And this proves that our net is Cauchy. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo Next I want to prove another useful fact about uniform the uniform topology.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Proposition:} Suppose $X$ is a uniform space. Then the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
	\item[(a)] $X$ is a separated uniform space,
	\item[(b)] the uniform topology on $X$ is $T_0$, 
	\item[(c)] the uniform topology on $X$ is $T_1$,
	\item[(d)] the uniform topology on $X$ is Hausdorff.
\end{enumerate}
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	$(a \Longrightarrow d)$\\
	Let $x$ and $y$ be two distinct points in $X$. Since $X$ is separated, we know that there exists an entourage $E$ such that $y \notin E[x]$. Next, we pick a symmetric entourage $E^\prime$ such that $E^\prime \circ E^\prime \subseteq E$. And I claim that $E^\prime[x]$ and $E^\prime[y]$ are disjoint neighborhoods of $x$ and $y$ respectively.\retTwo

	To see why they are disjoint, suppose $z \in E^\prime[x]$. Then we know that $z \notin E^\prime[y]$ since otherwise $xE^\prime z$ and $y E^\prime z$ would imply that $xEy$ (a contradiction). So, $E^\prime[x] \cap E^\prime[y] = \emptyset$. This proves that $X$ is Hausdorff.\retTwo

	$(d \Longrightarrow c)$ and $(c \Longrightarrow b)$\\
	This is obvious.\retTwo

	$(b \Longrightarrow a)$\\
	Suppose $X$ is $T_0$ and let $x$ and $y$ be distinct elements of $X$. Without loss of generality we can assume there exists an open set $U$ such that $x \in U$ and $y \notin U$. In turn, we can find an entourage $E[x]$ such that $x \in E[x] \subseteq U$. And now we know $(x, y) \notin E$. This proves that $X$ is separated. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo\begin{myIndent}\mySepThree\end{myIndent}

A particularly important thing we ought to be able to do is consider uniform structures on product spaces. After all, multi-variable functions ought to be able to be jointly continuous.\retTwo

Suppose $\{X_\alpha, \mathscr{U}_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ is a collection of uniform spaces and let us write $X = \prod_{\alpha \in A} X_\alpha$. We can identify $X \times X$ with $\prod_{\alpha \in A} X_\alpha \times X_\alpha$ via the obvious map. And now, we let the collection of $\prod_{\alpha \in A}D_\alpha$ form a uniformity base for $X$ (where each $D_\alpha \in \mathscr{U}_\alpha$ and for all but finitely many $\alpha$ we have that $D_\alpha = X_\alpha \times X_\alpha$).\\ [-6pt]
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	First, I want to justify that this is in fact a uniformity base for $X$.\newpage
	\begin{itemize}
		\item To start off, note that $X \times X$ is always in this base. Hence our base is nonempty.\\ [-6pt]
		\item Also note that $\Delta X = \prod_{\alpha \in A}\Delta X_\alpha$ is a subset of very entourage in our base.\\ [-6pt]
		\item Our base is a directed collection of sets. After all, suppose $\prod_{\alpha \in A}D_\alpha$ and $\prod_{\alpha \in A}E_\alpha$ are both entourages in our base. Then we have that $\prod_{\alpha \in A}(D_\alpha \cap E_\alpha)$ is also an entourage in our base contained in both of the original entourages.
		\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
			You check if you aren't convinced!!\\ [-6pt]
		\end{myIndent}
		\item Suppose $\prod_{\alpha \in A}D_\alpha$ is an entourage in our base. Then we can see that\\ $(\prod_{\alpha \in A}D_\alpha)^{-1} = \prod_{\alpha \in A}(D_\alpha^{-1})$ is also in our base.
		\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
			Again, you check if you aren't convinced!!\\ [-6pt]
		\end{myIndent}
		\item Finally, suppose $\prod_{\alpha \in A}D_\alpha$ is an entourage in our base. Then for each $\alpha$ such that $D_\alpha \neq X_\alpha \times X_\alpha$, we can pick an entourage $D^\prime_\alpha$ of $X_\alpha$ such that $D^\prime_\alpha \circ D^\prime_\alpha \subseteq D_\alpha$. Meanwhile, if $D_\alpha = X_\alpha \times X_\alpha$ then we trivially set $D_\alpha^\prime = D_\alpha$ and observe that $D^\prime_\alpha \circ D^\prime_\alpha \subseteq D_\alpha$. But now:
		
		{\centering$(\prod_{\alpha \in A}D_\alpha^\prime) \circ (\prod_{\alpha \in A}D_\alpha^\prime) = \prod_{\alpha \in A}(D_\alpha^\prime \circ D_\alpha^\prime) \subseteq \prod_{\alpha \in A}D_\alpha$.\retTwo\par}

		\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
			I'll show that $(\prod_{\alpha \in A}D_\alpha^\prime) \circ (\prod_{\alpha \in A}D_\alpha^\prime) = \prod_{\alpha \in A}(D_\alpha^\prime \circ D_\alpha^\prime)$ just to prove I know how to.\retTwo

			Let $f, g: A \to \bigcup_{\alpha \in A}X_\alpha$ be elements of $\prod_{\alpha \in A}X_\alpha$. Then\\ $(f, g) \in (\prod_{\alpha \in A}D_\alpha^\prime) \circ (\prod_{\alpha \in A}D_\alpha^\prime)$ iff there exists $h: A \to \bigcup_{\alpha \in A}X_\alpha$\\ such that $(f, h) \in \prod_{\alpha \in A}D_\alpha^\prime$ and $(h, g) \in \prod_{\alpha \in A}D_\alpha^\prime$. Yet now note that the\\ latter is possible iff for every $\alpha$ there exsts $h(\alpha) \in X_\alpha$ such that $f(\alpha) D^\prime_\alpha h(\alpha)$ and $h(\alpha) D^\prime_\alpha g(\alpha)$ for all $\alpha$, and that's equivalent to saying $f(\alpha) D^\prime_\alpha \circ D^\prime_\alpha g(\alpha)$ for all $\alpha$. Or in other words, $(f, g) \in \prod_{\alpha \in A}(D_\alpha^\prime \circ D_\alpha^\prime)$.\retTwo
		\end{myIndent}

		Also note that $\prod_{\alpha \in A}D_\alpha^\prime$ is in our base.\retTwo
	\end{itemize}

	\mySepFour

	Next, I want to justify why this is the natural definition for a uniformity base on $X$. For each $\alpha$ let $\pi_\alpha : X \to X_\alpha$ be the projection map. Then for any entourage $D_\alpha$ of $X_\alpha$ we have that:

	{\centering $(\pi_\alpha \times \pi_\alpha)^{-1}(D_\alpha) = D_\alpha \times \left(\prod_{\alpha^\prime \in A - \{\alpha\}} X_{\alpha^\prime} \times X_{\alpha^\prime}\right)$. \retTwo\par}

	It follows that $\pi_\alpha$ is uniformly continuous for every $\alpha \in A$ when $X$ is equipped with the \udefine{product uniform structure} (i.e. the structure generated by the uniformity base described priorly). More generally, by taking finite intersections we can also see that every uniform structure on $X$ satisfying that $\pi_\alpha: X \to X_\alpha$ is uniformly continuous for all $\alpha$ will\\ contain our uniformity base. So, the product uniform structure on $X$ is the smallest\\ uniform strucure such that all the $\pi_\alpha$ are uniformly continuous.\retTwo

	\mySepFour \newpage

	Finally, if all the $X_\alpha$ are equipped with their corresponding uniform topologies, then the uniform topology associated with $X$ (given the product uniform structure) is precisely the same as the product topology on $X = \prod_{\alpha \in A}X_\alpha$.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		Why?\\
		Note that $(\prod_{\alpha \in A}D_\alpha)[(x_\alpha)_{\alpha \in A}] = \prod_{\alpha \in A}D_\alpha[x_\alpha]$. Hence, we can see that both topologies have identical local bases of neighborhoods at any $(x_\alpha)_{\alpha \in A}$ in $X$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
\end{myIndent}

\exTwo\ul{Proposition:} Let $\{X_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ be a collection of uniform spaces and then let $X \coloneqq \prod_{\alpha \in A}X_\alpha$ be equipped with the product uniform structure. Next suppose $A$ is another uniform space and $\phi: A \to X$ is a map. Then $\phi$ is uniformly continuous if and only if for all $\alpha \in A$ we have that $\phi_\alpha \coloneqq \pi_\alpha \circ \phi:A \to X_\alpha$ is uniformly continuous.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	$(\Longrightarrow)$\\
	This direction is clear from the fact that compositions of uniformly continuous functions are uniformly continuous and $\pi_\alpha$ is uniformly continuous for all $\alpha$.\retTwo

	$(\Longleftarrow)$\\
	It suffices to show that $(\phi \times \phi)^{-1}(\prod_{\alpha \in A}D_\alpha)$ is an entourage of $A$ for any collection of entourages $\{D_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ with $D_\alpha = X_\alpha \times X_\alpha$ for all but finitely many $\alpha$. (After all, see the proposition at the top of \inLinkRap{top of page 996}{page 996}).\retTwo

	Fortunately, upon letting $B \subseteq A$ be the set of all $\alpha \in A$ with $D_\alpha \neq X_\alpha \times X_\alpha$, we can say that:
	
	{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
		$(\phi \times \phi)^{-1}(\prod_{\alpha \in A}D_\alpha) = (\phi \times \phi)^{-1}(\bigcap_{\alpha \in B}(\pi_\alpha \times \pi_\alpha)^{-1}(D_\alpha))$\\ [4pt]
		$\phantom{(\phi \times \phi)^{-1}(\prod_{\alpha \in A}D_\alpha)} = \bigcap_{\alpha \in B} (\phi \times \phi)^{-1}((\pi_\alpha \times \pi_\alpha)^{-1}(D_\alpha))$\\ [4pt]
		$\phantom{(\phi \times \phi)^{-1}(\prod_{\alpha \in A}D_\alpha)} = \bigcap_{\alpha \in B} ((\pi_\alpha \circ \phi) \times (\pi_\alpha \circ \phi))^{-1}(D_\alpha)$.
	\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

	Since the latter is a finite intersection of entourages of $A$ (since $\pi_\alpha \circ \phi$ is uniformly\\ continuous), we can conclude that $(\phi \times \phi)^{-1}(\prod_{\alpha \in A}D_\alpha)$ is an entourage of $A$. So, $\phi$ is uniformly continuous. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo\mySepTwo

\dispDate{6/25/2026}

I'm feeling burnt out talking about uniform spaces. So I'm going to take a break from that and instead study manifolds. I'll return to talking about uniform spaces on \inLinkRap{idk reference 5}{page \_\_\_\_}.\retTwo

My first goal for today is to give some proofs for some important facts about topological manifolds. An algebraic purist might not like the proofs I'm following to get these results. That said, my attempts to study manifolds prior to this point have been incredibly\\ hampered by not having these results.\retTwo

First is a proof that I'm getting from Terence Tao's blog (see \inLinkRap{Seventh Citation}{citation 7}).\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Theorem (Invariance of Domain):} \hypertarget{Invariance of Domain Theorem}{Suppose} $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is open and $f: U \to \mathbb{R}^n$ is an injective continuous function. Then $f(U)$ is an open set.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	To start off, for any $x \in U$ we can find a closed ball $\overline{B_r(x)}$ centered at $x$ and contained in $U$. And now to prove that $f(U)$ is an open set, it suffices to prove that $f(x)$ is an interior point of $f(\overline{B_r(x)})$. But now by scaling and translated our domain, we can without loss of generality assume that $r = 1$ and $x = 0$. So having denoted $B^n \coloneqq \overline{B_1(0)}$, we are left with the task of showing that:\\ [-6pt]
	\begin{myIndent}
		If $f: B^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ is a continuous injective function then $f(0)$ lies in the interior of $f(B^n)$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Fortunately, note that $f: B^n \to f(B^n)$ is a continuous bijection from a compact set to a Hausdorff space. So, the inverse map $f^{-1}: f(B^n) \to B^n$ must also be continuous. Furthermore, since $f(B^n)$ is a compact (and thus closed subset) of $\mathbb{R}^n$, we can apply a corollary of the Tietze Extension theorem to find a continuous function $G: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ with $G|_{F(B^n)} = f^{-1}$.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		See Folland corollary 4.17 in my math 240b notes.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Now $G(f(x)) = x$ for all $x \in B^n$. In particular this means that $G(f(0)) = 0$. So, $G$ has a zero on $f(B^n)$. As it turns out, this remains true when we perturb $G$.\retTwo

	\ul{Lemma:} Let $\widetilde{G}: f(B^n) \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be a continuous function with $|G(y) - \widetilde{G}(y)| \leq 1$ for all $y \in f(B^n)$. Then $\widetilde{G}$ has at least one zero.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		Why?\\
		Consider the function $h: B^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ given by:
		
		{\centering$h(x) = x - \widetilde{G}(f(x)) = G(f(x)) - \widetilde{G}(f(x))$.\retTwo\par}
		
		By our assumpion that $|G(y) - \widetilde{G}(y)| \leq 1$  for all $y \in f(B^n)$ we know that $h$ maps $B^n$ into $B^n$. So by Brouwer's fixed point theorem (see \inLinkRap{placeholder}{pages 324-326}), there must exist $x \in B^n$ with $x = h(x) = x - \widetilde{G}(f(x))$. But now we have that $\widetilde{G}(f(x)) = 0$.\retTwo 
	\end{myIndent}

	The rest of the proof will now be spent showing that if $f(0)$ is not an interior point of\\ $f(B^n)$ then we can find a perturbed $\widetilde{G}$ contradicting our lemma.\retTwo

	Fix $\varepsilon > 0$ with $|G(y)| < \frac{1}{3}$ if $|y - f(0)| \leq 2\varepsilon$. (We can do this since $G$ is continuous and $G(f(0)) = 0$.) Then supposing for the sake of contradiction that $f(0)$ is not an interior point of $f(B^n)$, we can find some $c \in \mathbb{R}^n - f(B^n)$ with $|c - f(0)| < \varepsilon$. By translating our codomain, we can assume without loss of generality that $c = 0$. So, we have that:
	
	{\centering $0 \notin f(B^n)$, $|f(0)| < \varepsilon$, and $|G(y)| < \frac{1}{3}$ if $|y| < \varepsilon$.\retTwo\par}

	Next let $\Sigma \coloneqq \Sigma_1 \cup \Sigma_2$ where:
	
	{\centering$\Sigma_1 \coloneqq \{y \in f(B^n) : |y| \geq \varepsilon\}$ and $\Sigma_2 \coloneqq \{y \in \mathbb{R}^n : |y| = \varepsilon\}$.\retTwo\par}
	
	Since $0 \notin f(B^n)$, we can define a continuous function $\Phi: f(B^n) \to \Sigma$ given by\\ [2pt] $\Phi(y) \coloneqq \max(\frac{\varepsilon}{|y|}, 1)y$. Also note that since $\Sigma_1$ is compact and $G$ is nonzero on $\Sigma_1$, we\\ [-1pt] can find some $0 < \delta < \frac{1}{3}$ with $|G(y)| \geq \delta$ for all $y \in \Sigma_1$. Also because $\Sigma$ is compact,\\ [2pt] we can conclude by the Stone Weierstrass theorem that there is a smooth function (even\\ [2pt] a polynomial) $P: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ with $|P(y) - G(y)| < \frac{\delta}{2}$ for all $y \in \Sigma$.\newpage

	In particular, since $|P(y) - G(y)| < \frac{\delta}{2}$ and $|G(y)| \geq \delta$ for all $y \in \Sigma_1$, we can conclude that $P$ is nonzero on $\Sigma_1$. That said, it may be the case that $P$ has a zero on $\Sigma_2$. So, we want to modify $P$ such that $P$ is nowhere zero on $\Sigma_2$.\retTwo

	Fortunately, note that $\Sigma_2$ has measure zero. It then follows that $P(\Sigma_2)$ also has measure zero. After all, consider the following lemma:\retTwo

	\ul{Lemma:} \hypertarget{Lemma page 1009}{Let} $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be an open set. If $g: U \to \mathbb{R}^n$ is a Lipschitz continuous function and $N \subseteq U$ has Lebesgue measure zero, then $g(N)$ is Lebesgue measurable and has Lebsgue measure zero.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		Proof:\\
		Let $C > 0$ be such that $|g(y_1) - g(y_2)| \leq C|y_1 - y_1|$ for all $y_1, y_2 \in U$.\\ Then importantly, for any closed ball $\overline{B_r(y)}$ contained in $U$ we have that $g(\overline{B_r(y)})$\\ is measurable (since it is a compact set) and also $g(\overline{B_r(y)}) \subseteq \overline{B_{rC}(g(y))}$.\retTwo
		
		Hence, we can say that $m(g(\overline{B_r(y)})) \leq m(\overline{B_{rC}(g(y))}) = C^n m(\overline{B_r(y)})$.
		\begin{myIndent}\color{orange}
			As a side note, this is the exact sentence of the lemma where we use that\\ $g$ is mapping $U$ into $\mathbb{R}^n$ as opposed to $\mathbb{R}^\ell$ where $\ell \neq n$. After all, let $V_n$ be the volume of the unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and let $V_\ell$ be the unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^\ell$. Then $m(B_{rC}(g(y))) = r^\ell C^\ell V_\ell$. Meanwhile $m(\overline{B_r(y)}) = r^n V_n$. We want to say that $r^\ell C^\ell V_\ell = C^n r^n V_n$ for all $r > 0$. Yet this is equivalent to asking that $r^{\ell - n} = C^{n-\ell} V_n / V_\ell$ for all $r > 0$. And if $\ell - n \neq 0$ this doesn't work.\retTwo
		\end{myIndent}

		But now since $N$ is a null set, for any $\varepsilon > 0$, we can find a cover of closed balls $\{B_k\}_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ contained in $U$, covering $N$, and satisfying that $\sum_{k=1}^\infty m(B_k) < \varepsilon$. In turn, we have that:
		
		{\centering$m(\bigcup_{k\in \mathbb{N}} g(B_k)) \leq \sum_{k \in \mathbb{N}} m(g(B_k)) \leq C^n\sum_{k=1}^\infty m(B_k) < C^n\varepsilon$\retTwo\par}

		Then by taking $\varepsilon \to 0$, we can show that that $g(N)$ is contained in a countable\\ intersection of measurable sets and that that intersection has measure $0$. Therefore since the $\sigma$-algebra of Lebesgue measurable sets is complete, we know that $g(N)$ is also measurable with a measure of $0$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Since $\Sigma_2$ is compact, we know it is bounded and can find $0 < r < R$ such that $\Sigma_2 \subseteq B_r(0)$. Then as $P$ is smooth on $B_{R + 1}(0)$ we know that $P$ is Lipschitz continuous on $\overline{B_r(0)}$ (see \inLinkRap{placeholder}{page 291}). In particular, we can find a Lipschitz constant for $P$ on $B_r(0)$ and apply the prior lemma to the null set $\Sigma_2$ contained in $B_r(0)$ to get that $P(\Sigma_2)$ is a null set.\retTwo

	Since $B_{\delta / 2}(0)$ doesn't have measure zero, we know that $B_{\delta/2}(0) - P(\Sigma_2) \neq \emptyset$. Hence, there must exist a constant $a \in B_{\delta/2}(0) - P(\Sigma_2)$. And by defining $Q(y) \coloneqq P(y) - a$, we have that $Q(y)$ is nowhere zero on $\Sigma_2$. Plus, $|Q(y) - G(y)| < \delta$ for all $y \in \Sigma$. Hence, we still don't have that $P = 0$ anywhere on $\Sigma_1$.\retTwo

	To finish off, let $\widetilde{G}: f(B^n) \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be defined as $\widetilde{G}(y) \coloneqq Q(\Phi(y))$. Then $Q$ is continuous and nowhere zero. Also note that if $|y| \geq \varepsilon$ then $|\widetilde{G}(y) - G(y)| < \delta < 1$. Meanwhile, if $|y| < \varepsilon$ then $|\Phi(y) - f(0)| \leq |\Phi(y)| + |f(0)| < 2\varepsilon$ implies that $|G(\Phi(y))| < \frac{1}{3}$. Since $|y| < \varepsilon$ also implies $|G(y)| < \varepsilon$, we can conclude that:\newpage

	{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
		$|\widetilde{G}(y) - G(y)| \leq |Q(\Phi(y)) - G(\Phi(y))| + |G(\Phi(y)) - 0| + |G(y) - 0|$\\ [4pt]
		$\phantom{|\widetilde{G}(y) - G(y)|} < \delta + \frac{2}{3} < 1$.
	\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

	This contradicts the lemma on the prior page. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo The invariance of domain theorem has far reaching consequences for the study of\\ manifolds. Now that I've received my bazooka from Terrance Tao, these next results will be easy to show on my own.\retTwo

In the statements of the below proposiions, $H^n \coloneqq \{(x_1, \ldots, x_n) \in \mathbb{R}^n : x_n \geq 0\}$.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Proposition:} If $m < n$ and $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is an open set, then there is no continuous injective function $f: U \to \mathbb{R}^m$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Let $i: \mathbb{R}^m \hookrightarrow \mathbb{R}^n$ be the obvious embedding. Then if such a function $f$ did exist, we'd\\ have that $i \circ f$ is an injective continuous function from $\mathbb{R}^n$ into $\mathbb{R}^n$. Yet we'd also have that $i \circ f(U)$ is contained in an $m$-dimensional hyperplane and thus has an empty interior. This contradicts the invariance of domain theorem. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\exTwo\ul{Corollary:} Suppose that $n$ and $m$ are positive integers, that $M$ is an $n$-dimensional\\ topological manifold, and that for some nonempty open set $U \subseteq M$ and some nonempty open set $V \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ or $H^m$ there is a homeomorphism $\varphi: U \to V$. Then, we must have that $m = n$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	To start off, by shrinking $U$ and $V$ if necessary, we can without loss of generality assume $V$ is an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^m$. Next, pick a point $p \in U$ and then pick a chart $(W, \psi)$ such that $p \in W$ and $\psi$ maps $W$ homeomorphically to an open set $\psi(W)$ of $H^n$ or $\mathbb{R}^n$. Again, by shrinking $W$ and maybe shifting $p$, we can assume with loss of generality that $W \subseteq U$ and $\psi(W)$ is open in $\mathbb{R}^n$.\retTwo

	But now we have homeomorphisms $\varphi|_W: W \to \varphi(W)$ and $\psi: W \to \psi(W)$ where $\varphi(W)$ is an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^m$ and $\psi(W)$ is an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$.
	\begin{itemize}
		\item If $n < m$ then $\psi \circ \varphi^{-1}$ contradicts our prior proposition.
		\item Meanwhile if $m < n$ then $\varphi \circ \psi^{-1}$ contradicts our prior proposition.\retTwo
	\end{itemize}

	It follows that $m = n$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo Based on the prior corollary, we can now easily conclude that the dimension of a\\ topological manifold is uniquely defined. In fact, we can make an even stronger statement that if $M$ is an $n$-dimensional topological manifold and $N$ is an $m$-dimensional topological manifold, then $M$ being homeomorphic to $N$ implies that $m = n$. Thus, the dimension of a topological manifold is invariant under homeomorphisms.\retTwo 

\exTwo\ul{Proposition:} \hypertarget{Proposition page 1010}{Suppose} $M$ is an $n$-dimensional topological manifold. Then $x$ is a boundary point of $M$ if and only if there is a chart $(U, \varphi)$ on $M$ such that $x \in U$, $\varphi(U)$ is open in $H^n$, and $\varphi(x) \in \partial H^n$.\newpage
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	$(\Longrightarrow)$\\
	The definition of a boundary point that I gave on \inLinkRap{placeholder}{page 146} is that there are no charts\\ $(V, \psi)$ on $M$ with $x \in V$ and $\psi(V)$ open in $\mathbb{R}^n$. So suppose $x$ is a boundary point. By the definition of a topological manifold there must exist a chart $(U, \varphi)$ on $M$ with $x \in U$. But since $x$ is a boundary point, we know that $\varphi(U)$ is not open in $\mathbb{R}^n$. Hence, we know that $\varphi(U)$ is only open in $H^n$. Furthermore, by intersecting $\varphi(U)$ with balls of decreasing radius around $\varphi(x)$, we can't be able to get a restricted chart whose image is open in $\mathbb{R}^n$. Hence, it follows that $\varphi(x) \in \partial H^n$.\retTwo

	$(\Longleftarrow)$\\
	Suppose $x \in M$ and $(U, \varphi)$ is a chart on $M$ such that $x \in U$, $\varphi(U)$ is open in $H^n$, and $\varphi(x) \in \partial H^n$. Then suppose for the sake of contradiction that $(V, \psi)$ is another chart on $M$ such that $x \in V$ and $\psi(V)$ is open in $\mathbb{R}^n$.\retTwo

	Let $W \coloneqq U \cap V$. Then we must have that $\varphi \circ \psi^{-1}$ is a continuous function mapping the open subset $\psi(W) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ into $\mathbb{R}^n$. So by the invariance of domain theorem, we must have that $\varphi(W)$ is an open subset $\mathbb{R}^n$. Yet simultaneously note that $\varphi(W)$ is a subset of $H^n$ containing $\varphi(x) \in \partial H^n$. Thus, we can't have that $\varphi(W)$ is open in $\mathbb{R}^n$ since $x$ is not an interior point of $\varphi(W)$ (considered as a subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ instead of $H^n$). This is a contradiction. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo Anyways, hopefully the prior results were enlightening.\retTwo
