\blect{Math 220c Notes:}\retTwo

Let $M$ be a $2$-dimensional topological manifold (without boundary). We identify $\mathbb{R}^2$ with $\mathbb{C}$.\retTwo

Next, suppose we have an atlas $\mathcal{A}$ on $M$ such that for all charts $(U, \varphi)$ and $(V, \psi)$ satisfying that $U \cap V \neq \emptyset$ we have that $\psi \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is a biholomorphic function from $\varphi(U \cap V)$ to $\psi(U \cap V)$. We call such an atlas a \udefine{complex atlas}. By identical reasoning as on \inLinkRap{placeholder}{pages 142-143}, we can find a maximal complex atlas containing an initial complex atlas. We call this maximal atlas a \udefine{complex structure on $M$}.\retTwo

Now a \udefine{Riemann surface} is defined as a $2$-dimensional topological manifold $M$ without boundary and equipped with a complex structure. I will refer to all the charts in the\\ complex structure on $M$ as \udefine{complex charts}.\retTwo

For some standard examples:\newpage
\begin{itemize}
	\item Any open subset $U$ of $\mathbb{C}$ equipped with the standard structure (i.e. the one generated by the chart $(U, \myId_{U})$) is a Riemann surface.\\ [-6pt]
	\item The Riemann sphere (i.e. $\mathbb{C}_\infty$) is a Riemann surface.
	\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
		We specifically equip it with the structure generated by the charts $(\mathbb{C}, z \mapsto z)$ and\\ $(\mathbb{C}_\infty - \{0\}, z \mapsto \frac{1}{z})$. Proving these charts are homeomorphisms into $\mathbb{C}$ is easy enough. Also, both of our transition maps are given by $z \mapsto \frac{1}{z}$ (defined on $\mathbb{C} - \{0\}$).\\ [-6pt]
	\end{myIndent}
	\item Let $\omega_1, \omega_2 \in \mathbb{C} - \{0\}$ satisfy that $\omega_1/ \omega_2 \notin \mathbb{R}$. Then let:
	
	{\centering$\Lambda \coloneqq \{n\omega_1 + m\omega_2 : n, m \in \mathbb{Z}\}$ be a lattice in $\mathbb{C}$.\retTwo\par}
	
	We know that $\Lambda$ is a subgroup of $\mathbb{C}$ (when considered a group equipped with\\ addition). Therefore, we now consider the topological group $X \coloneqq \mathbb{C}/\Lambda$ equipped with the quotient topology. Also, we let $\pi: \mathbb{C} \to X$ be the projection map. All that I want to say about $X$ as a Riemann surface is long enough that I'm going to go on a separate tangent first.
\end{itemize}

\pracOne\mySepTwo 

Let $X$ and $Y$ be topological spaces. We say a map $p: X \to Y$ is locally injective if every $x \in X$ has a neighborhood $N$ such that $p|_N : N \to Y$ is an injective function.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	For example, let $\pi: \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}/\Lambda$ be the quotient map from before. Then note that\\ $\pi(z) = \pi(w)$ if and only if $z = w + n\omega_1 + m\omega_2$ for some $n, m \in \mathbb{Z}$. But now note that if $n \neq 0 \neq m$ (which happens iff $z \neq w$), then $z - w \in \Lambda - \{0\}$. At the same time, recall from \inLinkRap{placeholder}{pages 582-583} that there exists $c > 0$ with $|n\omega_1 + m\omega_2| \geq c(|n| + |m|)$ for all $n,m \in \mathbb{Z}$. In turn, we can see that $\pi(z) = \pi(w)$ where $z \neq w$ implies that $|z - w| \geq c$. Or alternatively, we can see that if $U\subseteq \mathbb{C}$ satisfies that $\diam(U) < c$, then $\pi$ is injective on $U$.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

Also recall from \inLinkRap{placeholder}{page 121} the definition of a covering map.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	We can go a step further and say that the map $\pi: \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}/\Lambda$ from before is a\\ covering map. To see why, let $c$ be the constant from the prior paragraph such that\\ $|n\omega_1 + m\omega_2| \geq c(|n| + |m|)$. Next, consider any $z + \Lambda \in \mathbb{C}/\Lambda$. Then $B_{c/3}(z) + \Lambda$\\ is a union of the collection of disjoint open sets: $\{B_{c/3}(z) + n\omega_1 + m\omega_2 : n, m\in \mathbb{Z}\}$.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		As for why these sets are disjoint, note that if they weren't all disjoint then we could find $n_1, n_2, m_1, m_2 \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $|n_1 - n_2| + |m_1 - m_2| \geq 1$ as well as $w_1, w_2 \in \mathbb{C}$ with $|w_i| < c/3$ for both $i$, all satisfying that:
		
		{\centering$z + w_1 + n_1\omega_1 + m_1\omega_2 = z + w_2 + n_2\omega_1 + m_2\omega_2$\retTwo\par}

		By moving terms, we can see that $w_1 - w_2 = (n_2 - n_1)\omega_1 + (m_2 - m_1)\omega_2 \in \Lambda - \{0\}$. So, $|w_1 - w_2| \geq c$. But this contradicts that $|w_1| < c/3$ and $|w_2| < c/3$ implies that $|w_1 - w_2| < c$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Now note that $\pi^{-1}(\pi(B_{c/3}(z) + \Lambda)) = B_{c/3}(z) + \Lambda$. Since $\pi$ is a quotient map, it follows that $\frac{B_{c/3}(z) + \Lambda}{\Lambda}$ is an open subset of $\mathbb{C}/\Lambda$. Plus, it contains $z + \Lambda$.\newpage

	To finish off, I need to show that $B_{c/3}(z) + n\omega_1 + m\omega_2$ is homeomorphically mapped by $\pi$ to $\frac{B_{c/3}(z) + \Lambda}{\Lambda}$ for all integers $n$ and $m$. Fortunately since translation on $\mathbb{C}$ is a homeomoprhism, it already suffices to assume that $n = m = 0$. So, we just need to show that $B_{c/3}(z)$ is homeomorphically mapped by $\pi$ to $\frac{B_{c/3}(z) + \Lambda}{\Lambda}$.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		Yet since $\diam(B_{c/3}(z)) < c$, we know that $\pi$ is injective on $B_{c/3}(z)$. Also note that, $\pi$ maps $B_{c/3}(z)$ surjectively onto $\frac{B_{c/3}(z) + \Lambda}{\Lambda}$.\retTwo
		
		We trivially know that $\pi$ is continuous. And on \inLinkRap{placeholder}{page 350} I proved that if $G$ is a\\ topological group and $H \lhd G$, then the quotient map $G \mapsto G/H$ is an open map. This shows that $\pi$ is a homeomorphism from $B_{c/3}(z)$ to $\frac{B_{c/3}(z) + \Lambda}{\Lambda}$.
	\end{myIndent}
	\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

One last important observation is that if $X$ and $Y$ are topological spaces, $p: X \to Y$ is an open, surjective, continuous map, and $X$ is second countable, then $Y$ is also second countable.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	To see why, let $\{U_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a countable base for $X$. Then suppose $y \in Y$ and $V \subseteq Y$ is an open set containing $y$. Since $p$ is surjective, we can find $x \in X$ with $p(x) = y$. Next, as $p$ is continuous we know that $p^{-1}(V)$ is an open subset of $X$ containing $x$. Hence, we can find an open set $U_n$ in our base such that $x \in U_n \subseteq p^{-1}(V)$. And finally since $p$ is an open map, we know that $p(U_n)$ is an open subset of $Y$ containing $y = p(x)$ and which also satisfies that $p(U_n) \subseteq V$. This proves that $\{p(U_n)\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is also a countable base for $Y$.\retTwo

	(And since $\pi: \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}/\Lambda$ is an open, surjective, and continuous map, the prior result applies.)\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

Based on all the prior reasoning, we can now easily see that $\mathbb{C}/\Lambda$ is a topological\\ manifold. We define a complex structure generated by the maps $\pi|_V: V \to \mathbb{C}/\Lambda$ where $V \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ is an open set such that $\pi$ is an injection from $V$ into $\mathbb{C}/\Lambda$. The transition maps between the charts corresponding to these maps will all have the form $z \mapsto z + n\omega_1 + m\omega_2$ for some $n, m \in \mathbb{Z}$. So this is a well-defined complex structure.\retTwo 

One other note I'd like to make is that by the universal property of quotient maps, we have that any function on $\mathbb{C}/\Lambda$ is associated with a doubly periodic function on $\mathbb{C}$ (i.e. $f(z) = f(z + \omega_1) = f(z + \omega_2)$). Also, any continuous function on $\mathbb{C}/\Lambda$ is associated with a continuous doubly periodic function on $\mathbb{C}$.\retTwo

\mySepTwo

\hTwo Among the two example complex manifolds I gave before, I already know that $\mathbb{C}_\infty$ is\\ compact. I can also show that $\mathbb{C}/\Lambda$ is compact.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Let $\Lambda = \{n\omega_1 + m\omega_2 : n, m \in \mathbb{Z}\}$ where $\omega_1, \omega_2 \in \mathbb{C} - \{0\}$ with $\omega_1 / \omega_2 \notin \mathbb{R}$. Next, let $K$ be the fundamental parallelogram $\{x\omega_1 + y\omega_2 : x, y \in [0, 1]\}$. Note that $K$ is a compact subset of $\mathbb{C}$. Also if $\pi: \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}/\Lambda$ is the quotient map, then we can see that $\pi(K) = \mathbb{C}/\Lambda$.\retTwo
	
	Next let $\{U_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ be any open cover of $\mathbb{C}/\Lambda$. Then we have that $\{\pi^{-1}(U_\alpha)\}_{\alpha \in A}$ is an\\ open cover of $\mathbb{C}$ and in turn also of $K$. Since $K$ is compact, we can find $\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n$ with\newpage $K \subseteq \bigcup_{j=1}^n \pi^{-1}(U_{\alpha_j}) = \pi^{-1}(\bigcup_{j=1}^n U_{\alpha_j})$. And finally since $\pi$ is surjective, we have that $\pi(\pi^{-1}(\bigcup_{j=1}^n U_{\alpha_j})) = \bigcup_{j=1}^n U_{\alpha_j}$. So, $\mathbb{C}/\Lambda = \pi(K) \subseteq \bigcup_{j=1}^n U_{\alpha_j}$.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

Knowing a Riemann surface is compact will be relevant once I define holomorphic functions on and between Riemann surfaces.\retTwo

Recalling the definition of a differentiable map between manifolds on \inLinkRap{placeholder}{page 147}, we make the following definition:
\begin{myIndent}
	Suppose $M$ and $N$ are Riemann surfaces. Then a map $F: M \to N$ is \udefine{holomorphic} if for all $p \in M$ there is a complex chart $(U, \varphi)$ on $M$ and a complex chart $(V, \psi)$ on $N$ such that $p \in U$, $F(U) \subseteq V$, and $\psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is a holomorphic function (in the complex analytic sense) from $\varphi(U)$.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\myComment Note by identical reasoning as on \inLinkRap{placeholder}{pages 147-148}, we can see that a holomorphic function between Riemann surfaces $M$ and $N$ is continuous.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Proposition:} If $M$ and $N$ are Riemann surfaces and $F: M \to N$ is a holomorphic function, then for any complex charts $(U, \varphi)$ on $M$ and $(V, \psi)$ on $M$ we have that $\psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is a holomorphic function (in the complex analytic sense) on $\varphi(U \cap F^{-1}(V))$
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Because $F$ is continuous, we know that $U \cap F^{-1}(V)$ is an open subset of $M$. Now we have nothing to show if $U \cap F^{-1}(V) = \emptyset$. So, we can assume $U \cap F^{-1}(V)$ is nonempty. Then by shrinking $U$, we can without loss of generality just say that $U \subseteq F^{-1}(V)$. That way, our problem becomes showing that $\psi \circ f \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is a holomorphic function (in the\\ complex analytic sense) from $\varphi(U)$ into $\psi(V) \subseteq \mathbb{C}$.\retTwo

	Fortunately let $x = \varphi(p) \in \varphi(U)$. Then we know there exists complex charts $(U^\prime, \varphi^\prime)$ on $M$ and $(V^\prime, \psi^\prime)$ on $N$ with $p \in U^\prime$, $F(U^\prime) \subseteq V^\prime$, and $\psi^\prime \circ F \circ (\varphi^\prime)^{-1}$ a holomorphic function (in the complex analytic sense) from $\varphi^\prime(U^\prime)$.\retTwo

	But now $\psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1} = (\psi \circ (\psi^\prime)^{-1}) \circ (\psi^\prime \circ F \circ (\varphi^\prime)^{-1}) \circ (\varphi^\prime \circ \varphi^{-1})$ is a holomorphic function from $\varphi(U \cap U^\prime)$ to $\psi(V \cap V^\prime)$. Since $\varphi(U \cap U^\prime)$ is an open set containing $x$ (since $U \cap U^\prime$ is an open set containing $p$), we've proven that $\psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is holomorphic\\ at $x \in \varphi(U)$. And since $x$ was arbitrary, we can conclude that $\psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is a\\ holomorphic function from $\varphi(U)$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo Having shown the prior proposition, we can now conclude two other results really easily.\retTwo

Firstly, if $U, V \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ are open sets, then a function $f: U \to V$ is holomorphic in the complex analytic sense if and only if it is holomorphic in the Riemann surface sense.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	$(\Longrightarrow)$\\
	Just consider the complex charts $(U, \myId_U)$ and $(V, \myId_V)$ on $U$ and $V$ respectively.\\ Then any $p \in U$ is trivially contained in our chart on $U$, $f(U)$ is contained in $V$, and\\ $f = \myId_V \circ f \circ \myId_V^{-1}$ is a holomorphic function (in the complex analytic sense). So,\\ $f$ is holomorphic in the Riemann surface sense.\newpage

	$(\Longleftarrow)$\\
	If $f$ is holomorphic in the Riemann surface sense, then we know the complex charts $(U, \myId_U)$ and $(V, \myId_V)$ satisfy that $f = \myId_V \circ f \circ \myId_U^{-1}$ is holomorphic by our prior proposition.  $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

Secondly, suppose $M$ is any Riemann surface. Also suppose $V \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ is an open set. Then the following are equivalent:
\begin{itemize}
	\item $f: M \to V$ is holomorphic in the Riemann surface sense
	\item For any complex chart $(U, \varphi)$ on $M$ we have that $f \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is a holomorphic function (in the complex analytic sense) from $\varphi(U)$.
	\item For all $p \in M$ there exists a complex chart $(U, \varphi)$ of $M$ with $p \in U$ and $f \circ \varphi^{-1}$ a holomorphic function (in the complex analytic sense) from $\varphi(U)$.
	\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
		The proof of this fact is mostly identical to the prior proof.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
\end{itemize}

Given any Riemann surfaces $M$ and $N$ we let $O(M, N)$ denote the set of holomorphic functions from $M$ to $N$. In the special case that $N = \mathbb{C}$, we can now easily see from the second result prior that $O(M, \mathbb{C})$ is a complex algebra.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Theorem (Identity Principle):} \hypertarget{Identity Principle for Riemann surfaces}{Suppose} $M$ and $N$  are Riemann surfaces with $M$ connected. Also suppose $F: M \to N$ and $G: M \to N$ are two holomorphic functions. If\\ $S \coloneqq \{x \in M : F(x) = G(x)\}$ has an accumulation point in $M$ then $S = M$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Let $A = \mathrm{acc}(S) \subseteq M$ be the set of accumulation points of $S$ in $M$. By assumption we know that $A$ is nonempty. I also immediately claim that $A$ is a closed set. 
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		To see why, note that $\overline{A} = A \cup \mathrm{acc}(A)$. So $A$ is closed iff $\overline{A} = A$ iff $\mathrm{acc}(A) \subseteq A$. To prove the last statement does in fact hold, suppose $x \in \mathrm{acc}(A)$ and that $U \subseteq M$ is any open set containing $x$. We have that $(U - \{x\}) \cap A \neq \emptyset$. Hence, we can find a point $y \in U \cap A$ such that $y \neq x$. Next, since $M$ is Hausdorff (and thus $T_1$), we know that $U - \{x\}$ is an open set containing $y$. Hence since $y \in \mathrm{acc}(S)$, we can find $z \in (U - \{x, y\}) \cap S$. But this proves that $S \cap (U - \{x\}) \neq \emptyset$. Since $U$ was arbitrary, we've proven that $x \in \mathrm{acc}(S) = A$. And since $x$ was arbitrary, we can conclude $\mathrm{acc}(A) \subseteq A$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	But now by the identity principle for holomorphic functions (in the complex analytic sense), we can also conclude that $A$ is also an open set.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		To see why, first note that $F$ and $G$ being continuous implies that $A \subseteq S$. After all, if $x \in A = \mathrm{acc}(S)$ then we know that there is a net $\langle x_\beta\rangle_{\beta \in B}$ in $S - \{x\}$ converging to $x$ in the topology of $M$.
		\begin{myIndent}\color{orange}
			Technically as $M$ is by definition second countable, we can work with sequences instead of nets. However, it doesn't really matter.\retTwo
		\end{myIndent}

		Since $F$ and $G$ are continuous, we thus know $F(x_\beta) \to F(x)$ and $G(x_\beta) \to G(x)$ in the topology on $N$. Yet also note that since $x_\beta \in S$ for all $\beta$, we know that $F(x_\beta) = G(x_\beta)$ for all $\beta$. Therefore, we can actually conclude that $F(x_\beta)$ converges to both $F(x)$ and $G(x)$. Finally, since $N$ is Hausdorff by definition, we must have that $F(x) = G(x)$. So, $x \in S$. And since $x$ was arbitrary, we've proven that $A \subseteq S$.\newpage
		
		Next, we prove that every $x \in A$ is an interior point of $A$. To do this, first note that since $F$ is holomorphic, we can find a complex chart $(U, \varphi)$ on $M$ and a complex chart $(V, \psi)$ on $N$ such that $x \in U$, $F(U) \subseteq V$ and $\psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is a holomorphic function from $\varphi(U)$. Next, since $x \in A \subseteq S$, we know that $G(x) = F(x) \in V$. So, $G^{-1}(V) \cap U$ is a nonempty set containing $x$. Also as $G$ is holomorphic (and thus continuous), we know that $U \cap G^{-1}(V)$ is an open set of $M$.\retTwo

		In turn, we can shrink $U$ in order to without loss of generality have that $x \in U$, $U \subseteq M$ is open, $F(U) \subseteq V$, and $G(U) \subseteq V$. Additionally, note that since $\varphi(U)$ is locally connected (since its an open subset of $\mathbb{C}$), we can shrink $U$ one more time in order to guarentee without loss of generality that $\varphi(U)$ is connected.\retTwo

		So to summarize, we've shown there exists complex charts $(U, \varphi)$ on $M$ and $(V, \psi)$ on $N$ such that:
		\begin{itemize}
			\item $x \in U$,
			\item $\varphi(U)$ is connected, 
			\item $F(U) \subseteq V$ and $G(U) \subseteq V$,
			\item $f \coloneqq \psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1} \in O(\varphi(U), \mathbb{C})$ and $g \coloneqq \psi \circ G \circ \varphi^{-1} \in O(\varphi(U), \mathbb{C})$.\retTwo
		\end{itemize}

		But now $S \cap U$ has $x$ as a limit point inside $U$. In turn, we also know that\\ $\varphi(S \cap U)$ has $\varphi(x)$ as a limit point inside $\varphi(U)$. And since $\varphi(U)$ is an open\\ connected set and $f = g$ on $\varphi(S \cap U)$, we can conclude by the identity principle (from math 220a) that $f = g$ everywhere on $\varphi(U)$. In turn $F = \psi^{-1} \circ f \circ \varphi$ and $G = \psi^{-1} \circ g \circ \varphi$ must equal each other everywhere on $U$. In other words, $U \subseteq S$.\retTwo
		
		To finish off, its easy to see that every point of $\varphi(U)$ is a limit point of $\varphi(U)$ in the topology on $\mathbb{C}$. (This is just a property of open subsets in the Euclidean topology on $\mathbb{R}^n$.) In turn, we can also see that every point of $U$ is a limit point of $U \subseteq S$. So, we have shown that $U \subseteq A$. And this proves that $x \in A$ is an interior point. Also, since $x$ was arbitrary we can conclude that $A$ is an open set.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Since $M$ is connected, the only way for $A$ to be a nonempty clopen set is if $A = M$. Then since $A \subseteq S \subseteq M$, we can also conclude that $S = M$. So, $F = G$ on $M$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo\mySepTwo

\dispDate{6/27/2026}

Today I'm going to continue introducing Riemann surfaces. Although, the first result I want to introduce actually applies to more general topological manifolds and is an application of the invariance of domain theorem.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Theorem:} Suppose $M$ and $N$ are both $n$-dimensional topological manifolds (without\\ boundary) and suppose $U \subseteq M$ is an open set. Then $U$ is also an $n$-dimensional\\ topological manifold when equipped with the subspace topology. If $F: U \to N$ is a\\ locally injective continuous function then $F(U)$ is an open subset of $N$.\newpage
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Consider any $p \in U$ and let $W_1 \subseteq U$ be an open neighborhood of $p$ on which $F$ is injective. Next let $(W_2, \varphi)$ be a chart containing $p$. Thirdly, let $(V, \psi)$ be a chart on $N$ containing $F(p)$. Since $F$ is continuous, we know that $W_3 = F^{-1}(V)$ is an open set containing $p$. So now by setting $W = W_1 \cap W_2 \cap W_3$, we get that $p \in W$, $W$ is an open subset of $U$, $\varphi$ is a homeomorphism between $W$ and some open set $\varphi(W)\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, $F(W) \subseteq V$, and $\psi$ is a homeomorphism between $V$ and some open set $\psi(V) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.\retTwo

	Now to show that $F(U)$ is an open set, it suffices to show that $F(p)$ is in the interior of $F(U)$. Yet also note that $W \subseteq U \Longrightarrow F(W) \subseteq F(U)$. Plus, we know that $F(p) \in F(W)$. So if we can conclude that $F(W)$ is an open subset of $N$, then we will have successfully shown that $F(p)$ is an interior point of $F(U)$.\retTwo

	Fortunately, note that $f \coloneqq \psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is a continuous injective function from the open set $\varphi(W) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ into $\psi(V) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$. By the invariance of domain theorem, we can conclude that $(\psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1})(\varphi(W))$ is an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$. Then since $\psi$ is continuous, we in\\ turn know that $\psi^{-1}((\psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1})(\varphi(W))) = F(W)$ is an open subset of $V \subseteq N$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\exTwo\ul{Corollary:} Any bijective continuous function between topological manifolds is\\ automatically a homeomorphism.\retTwo

\hTwo\begin{myIndent}\mySepThree\end{myIndent}

Returning to the topic of Riemann surfaces, we have the following result for holomorphic functions:\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Open Mapping Theorem:} Suppose $M$ and $N$ are Riemann surfaces with $M$ connected, and also that $F: M \to N$ is a nonconstant holomorphic function. Then $F$ is an open map.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP 
	Proof:\\
	Let $U \subseteq M$ be any open set. To show that $F(U)$ is an open set, it suffices to prove that if $p \in U$ then $F(p)$ is an interior point of $F(U)$. Fortunately, as $F$ is holomorphic we know that there exists complex charts $(W, \varphi)$ on $M$ and $(V, \psi)$ on $N$ such that $p \in W$, $F(W) \subseteq V$, and $\psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is a holomorphic function from $\varphi(W)$. By shrinking $W$ if necessary, we can assume without loss of generality that $W \subseteq U$. Also because $\mathbb{C}$ is locally connected, we can additionally shrink $W$ and $\varphi(W)$ in order to guarentee without loss of generality that $\varphi(W)$ is a connected open subset of $\mathbb{C}$.\retTwo

	By the identity principle proven on the prior two pages, we know that $F$ cannot be constant on $W$ or else we'd be able to also show that $F$ is contant on all of $M$. So to avoid any contradictions, we must have that $F$ is nonconstant on $W$. In turn, $f \coloneqq \psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1}$ must also be nonconstant on the set $\varphi(W)$. So by the open mapping theorem proven in math 220a (see \inLinkRap{placeholder}{page 429}), we can conclude that $f$ is an open map.\retTwo

	With that we've shown $f(\varphi(W))$ is an open subset of $\psi(V) \subseteq \mathbb{C}$. Then since $\psi$ is\\ continuous, we can conclude that $F(W) = (\psi^{-1} \circ f \circ \varphi)(W)$ is also an open subset\\ of $V \subseteq N$. Finally, since $p \in W$ and $W \subseteq U$, we know $F(p) \in F(W)$ and\\ $F(W) \subseteq F(U)$. This proves that $F(p)$ is an interior point of $F(U)$. $\blacksquare$\newpage
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo Here's one more pair of results to justify why we will care about meromorphic functions a lot once we define them in a second.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Maximum Modulus Theorem:} Suppose $M$ is a connected Riemann surface and\\ $F: M \to \mathbb{C}$ is a holomorphic function. If $|F|$ attains a local maximum on $M$ then $F$\\ is a constant function.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Suppose $|F|$ has a local maximum at $p \in M$. Then let $(U, \varphi)$ be a complex chart containing $p$. By shrinking $U$ if necessary, we can also without loss of generality assume $\varphi(U)$ is a connected set. But now  $F \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is a holomorphic function on the region $\varphi(U)$ of $\mathbb{C}$ which also satisfies that $|F \circ \varphi^{-1}|$ attains a local maximum at $\varphi(p)$. It follows by the maximum modulus principle from complex analysis (see \inLinkRap{placeholder}{page 384}) that $F \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is a constant function on $\varphi(U)$. In turn $F \circ \varphi^{-1} \circ \varphi = F$ is also a constant function on $U$. And by the identity principle, we can then conclude that $F$ is constant on $M$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo

	\begin{myIndent}\myComment
		As a side note since I realize that I never showed this, any constant function between Riemann surfaces is automatically holomorphic. To see why, suppose $M$ and $N$ are Riemann surfaces, and $F: M \to N$ satisfies that $F(p) = q \in N$ for all $p \in M$. Then having picked a complex chart $(V, \psi)$ in $N$ containing $Q$, we have for every complex chart $(U, \varphi)$ in $M$ that $F(U) \subseteq V$ and $\psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is a constant function from $\varphi(U) \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ into $\mathbb{C}$. So, $\psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is trivially holomorphic.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
\end{myIndent}

\ul{Corollary:} If $M$ is a compact Riemann surface then $O(M, \mathbb{C})$ consists entirely of locally constant functions. In particular, if $M$ is connected then $O(M, \mathbb{C})$ consists only of constant functions. 
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Note that every connected component of $M$ is closed. And since closed subsets of compact sets are compact, we can thus conclude that every connected component of $M$ is compact.\retTwo
	
	Also note that since $M$ is locally connected, we know that every connected component of $M$ is open. Therefore every connected component of $M$ (equipped with the subspace topology) can sill still be viewed as a Riemann surface where $F$ restricted to each\\ component is holomorphic.\retTwo

	Finally, suppose $F \in O(M, \mathbb{C})$ and let $N$ be any connected component of $M$. Then $F$ being continuous on $N$ plus $N$ being compact implies that $|F|$ attains a local maximum on $N$. Yet also note that $F$ being holomorphic on $N$ as a Riemann surface means that the maximum modulus theorem applies. So, we must have that $F$ is constant on $N$. $\blacksquare$.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo Since a lot of the Riemann surfaces we actually care about are compact and connected, we thus can see that $O(M, \mathbb{C})$ is often not the collection of functions we want to study on a Riemann surface. Hence, we will instead often consider $O(M, \mathbb{C}_\infty)$.

\begin{myIndent}\mySepThree\end{myIndent}

To motivate the next bit, observe that if $U \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ is an open set then any meromorphic function $f: U \to \mathbb{C}$ extends to a holomorphic function from $U$ into $\mathbb{C}_\infty$ (in the Riemann surface sense).\newpage
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	If you squint you can see that this is just my comment from \inLinkRap{placeholder}{page 467}. After all, $z \mapsto f(z)$ is a holomorphic function from $U - f^{-1}(\{\infty\})$ into $\mathbb{C}$ and $z \mapsto 1/f(z)$ is a holomorphic function from $U - f^{-1}(\{0\})$ into $\mathbb{C}$.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

Conversely, suppose $G \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ is a region and $f: G \to \mathbb{C}_\infty$ is a holomorphic function (in the Riemann surface sense) satisfying that there exists $z \in G$  with $f(z) \neq \infty$. Since $f$ is not the constant $\infty$-valued function, we know by the identity principle that $f^{-1}(\{\infty\})$ can't have any limit points. This also means every $a \in f^{-1}(\{\infty\})$ must be an isolated point of $G$.\retTwo

Let $\Omega \coloneqq G - f^{-1}(\{\infty\})$. Since $f$ is continuous, we can conclude that $\Omega$ is an open subset of $G$. So, we consider the chart $(\Omega, \myId_{\Omega})$. Next, we consider the chart $(\mathbb{C}, \myId_\mathbb{C})$ in the standard structure on $\mathbb{C}_\infty$. So, $\myId_{\mathbb{C}} \circ f \circ \myId_{\Omega} = f$ is a holomorphic function from $\Omega$ into $\mathbb{C}$ (in the complex analytic sense).\retTwo

But now $f|_\Omega$ has singularities at every $a \in f^{-1}(\{\infty\})$. Also by the continuity of $f$ on $G$, we know that $|f(z)| \to \infty$ as $z \to a$. Therefore, we can conclude that $f|_{\Omega}$ has poles at all $a \in G - \Omega$. Or in other words, $f$ is a meromorphic function on $G$ (in the complex analytic sense).\retTwo

All in all, we can conclude that if $U \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ is an open set, then the set of meromorphic\\ functions on $U$ is precisely equal to $O(U, \mathbb{C}_\infty) - \mathcal{F}$ where $\mathcal{F}$ is the collection of\\ holomorphic functions that are constantly $\infty$ on any neighborhood. For the time\\ being, I'm going to denote the set of meromorphic functions on $U$ as $\mathcalli{M}(U)$.

\begin{myIndent}\myComment
	I realize that $\mathcalli{M}$ and $M$ look similar. So, I'll probably start denoting Riemann surfaces\\ by $X$ and $Y$ instead.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\begin{myIndent}\mySepThree\end{myIndent}

\exTwo\ul{Proposition:} Let $X$ be a connected Riemann surface. And suppose $f: X \to \mathbb{C}_\infty$ is a function such that $f \not\equiv \infty$ on $X$. Then the following are equivalent.
\begin{itemize}
	\item[(a)] $f: X \to \mathbb{C}_\infty$ is a holomorphic function.
	\item[(b)] For all complex charts $(U, \varphi)$ on $X$ we have that $f \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is a meromorphic function on $\varphi(U)$.
	\item[(c)] For every $p \in X$ there exists a complex chart $(U, \varphi)$ on $X$ with $p \in U$ and $f \circ \varphi^{-1}$ a meromorphic function on $\varphi(U)$.  
\end{itemize}

\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	$(a \Longrightarrow b)$\\
	Let $(U, \varphi)$ be any complex chart on $X$. Since $f$ is continuous and $f \not\equiv \infty$ on $X$, we know that $f^{-1}(\{\infty\}) \cap U$ must be a closed set (relative to $U$) with no limit points in $U$. In other words, $\Omega \coloneqq U - f^{-1}(\{\infty\})$ is an open set with $f(\Omega) \subseteq \mathbb{C}_\infty - \{\infty\}$. If we now consider\newpage the charts $(\Omega, \varphi|_\Omega)$ and $(\mathbb{C}, \myId)$, we know that $\myId \circ f \circ \varphi^{-1} = f \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is a holomorphic map from $\varphi(\Omega) = \varphi(U) - \varphi(f^{-1}(\{\infty\}))$ into $\mathbb{C}$ since $f$ is holomorphic in the Riemann surface sense. Furthermore, we know every $a \in \varphi(U - \Omega)$ has a neigborhood $N$ where $f \circ \varphi^{-1}(z) \neq \infty$ for any $z \in N - \{a\}$. Plus by the continuity of $f \circ \varphi^{-1}$, we know that $f \circ \varphi^{-1}(z) \to \infty$ as $z \to a$. So, every $a \in \varphi(U - \Omega)$ is a pole. And this finishes showing that $f \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is meromorphic on $\varphi(U)$.\retTwo

	$(b \Longrightarrow c)$\\
	This is obvious.\retTwo

	$(c \Longrightarrow a)$\\
	Suppose $p \in X$ and let $(U, \varphi)$ be a complex chart on $X$ such that $p \in U$ and $f \circ \varphi^{-1}$\\ a meromorphic function on $\varphi(U)$. If $f(p) \neq \infty$ then by shrinking $U$ and $\varphi(U)$ to a\\ coordinate ball around $p$, we can assume $f \neq \infty$ anywhere on $B$. And now $f(U) \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ and $\myId \circ f \circ \varphi^{-1} = f \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is a holomomorphic function on $\varphi(U)$.\retTwo

	Meanwhile, if $f(p) = \infty$ then we know $\varphi(p)$ is a pole of $f \circ \varphi^{-1}$. So, we can shrink $U$ and $\varphi(U)$ to a coordinate ball so that $f \neq 0$ anywhere on $U$. Next, $f(U) \subseteq \mathbb{C}_\infty - \{0\}$ and $z \mapsto 1/f(\varphi^{-1}(z))$ is a holomorphic function on $\varphi(U)$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo Given a Riemann surface $X$, we say $f: X \to \mathbb{C}_\infty$ is \udefine{meromorphic} if $f \in O(X, \mathbb{C}_\infty)$ and $f \not\equiv \infty$ on any neighborhood in $X$. We denote the set of meromorphic functions on $X$ as $\mathcalli{M}(X)$.\retTwo

\pracOne Example: What are the meromorphic functions on $\mathbb{C}_\infty$?
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Suppose $f: \mathbb{C}_\infty \to \mathbb{C}_\infty$ is meromorphic. Since $\mathbb{C}_\infty$ is compact, we know that $f$ has only finitely many \udefine{poles} (i.e. points in the set $f^{-1}(\{\infty\})$). So, we can let $p_1, \ldots, p_n$ be the poles of $f$ in $\mathbb{C}$ (repeated according to multiplicity). Then $g(z) \coloneqq f(z)\prod_{i=1}^n (z - p_i)$ is a well-defined entire function on $\mathbb{C}$.\retTwo

	Next, let $g(z) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty c_k z^k$ be the Taylor expansion of $g$ about $0$. Since $g$ is an entire function, we know this power series has an infinite radius of convergence. In turn, we also know $g(\frac{1}{z}) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty c_k z^{-k}$ is absolutely convergent for all $z \in \mathbb{C} - \{0\}$. Yet also note $g(\frac{1}{z}) = f(\frac{1}{z})\prod_{i=1}^n (\frac{1}{z} - p_i)$. And since $f$ is meromorphic, we know that $h(z) \coloneqq f(\frac{1}{z})$ has either a removable singularity or pole at $z = 0$. It follows that $z \mapsto g(\frac{1}{z})$ has a pole or removable singularity at $z = 0$ as well.\retTwo

	Yet now we can conclude there exists $K \in \mathbb{N}$ with $c_k = 0$ for all $k \geq K$. (If not then $z \mapsto g(\frac{1}{z})$ would have an essential singularity.) So, we've proven there exists a polynomial $P(z) \in \mathbb{C}[z]$ with $P(z) = f(z)\prod_{i=1}^n (z - p_i)$. Finally, by rearranging our expression and factoring $P(z)$, we can conclude that there exists $\lambda \in \mathbb{C}$ as well as $a_1, \ldots, a_m \in \mathbb{C}$ such that:

	{\centering $f(z) = \lambda\frac{(z - a_1)\cdots (z - a_m)}{(z - p_1)\cdots(z - p_n)}$ \retTwo\par}

	So, $\mathcalli{M}(\mathbb{C}_\infty) \subseteq \mathbb{C}(z)$ (where $\mathbb{C}(z)$ is the field of rational functions in $\mathbb{C}$). Conversely, it's easy to show every rational function is a holomorphic map from $\mathbb{C}_\infty$ into $\mathbb{C}_\infty$. $\blacksquare$\newpage
\end{myIndent}

Here's another interesting observation that the prior example brought to mind.\retTwo

\ul{Lemma:} Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are connected Riemann surface with $X$ also compact. Then any nonconstant holomorphic function $F \in O(X, Y)$ must be surjective.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Proof:\\
	Since $F$ is continuous and $X$ is compact, we know that $F(X)$ must be a compact subset of $Y$. In turn, since $Y$ is Hausdorff we also know that $F(X)$ is a closed subset of $Y$.\\ Meanwhile, since $F$ is a nonconstant holomorphic function and $X$ is connected, we know $F$ is an open map. In turn, as $X$ is open we must have that $F(X)$ is an open subset of\\ $Y$. Finally, we trivially know that $F(X) \neq \emptyset$. So, we can conclude from the connectedness\\ of $Y$ that $F(X) = Y$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

As a result of this lemma, any nonconstant rational function in $\mathbb{C}(z)$ must define a\\ surjective map from $\mathbb{C}_\infty$ into $\mathbb{C}_\infty$. In particular, this means that every nonconstant\\ meromorphic function on $\mathbb{C}_\infty$ will have both poles and zeros.

Suppose $\mcateg{I}$ is category (which we can think of as an indexing category). Next, we consider a functor $F: \mcateg{I} \to \mcateg{C}$. The \udefine{limit} of $F$ (if it exists) is defined to be an object $L$ in $\mcateg{C}$ along with a class of morphisms $\pi_I \in \Hom_{\mcateg{C}}(L, F(I))$ such that:

		\arrow["{\pi_J}", from=1-2, to=2-3]
		\arrow["{F(f)}"', from=2-1, to=2-3]
	\end{tikzcd}\]
	\item[2.] If $M \in \Obj(\mcateg{C})$ and $\eta_I \in \Hom_{\mcateg{C}}(M, F(I))$ is any other object and collection of\\ morphisms satisfying the prior commuting diagram, then there exists a unique\\ morphism $g: M \to L$ such that:\\ [-18pt]
	% https://q.uiver.app/#
	\[\begin{tikzcd}
		& M & \\

		\arrow["{\eta_J}", curve={height=-12pt}, from=1-2, to=3-3]
		\arrow["{\pi_I}"', from=2-2, to=3-1]
		\arrow["{\pi_J}", from=2-2, to=3-3]
		\arrow["{F(f)}"', from=3-1, to=3-3]
	\end{tikzcd}\]
\end{enumerate}

		% https://q.uiver.app/#q=WzAsMyxbMiwwLCJQIl0sWzAsMCwiTV9JIl0sWzEsMSwiXFxiaWdvcGx1c197SV5cXHByaW1lIFxcaW4gXFxPYmooXFxtY2F0ZWd7SX0pfU1fe0leXFxwcmltZX0iXSxbMSwwLCJcXGV0YV9JIl0sWzEsMiwial9JIiwyXSxbMiwwLCJoIiwyLHsic3R5bGUiOnsiYm9keSI6eyJuYW1lIjoiZGFzaGVkIn19fV1d

As a result, $N \subseteq \ker(h)$ and in turn we can define a module homomorphism $g: C \to P$ by $g((x_I)_{I \in \Obj(\mcateg{I})} + N) = h((x_I)_{I \in \Obj(\mcateg{I})})$. Since $A$-$\mcateg{mod}$ has a limit and colimit respectively for all functors $F$ going into $A$-$\mcateg{mod}$\\ from a small category, we say $A$-$\mcateg{mod}$ is \udefine{complete} and \udefine{cocomplete} respectively. Since\\ $A$-$\mcateg{mod}$ is \textit{both} complete \textit{and} cocomplete, we also call $A$-$\mcateg{mod}$ a \udefine{bicomplete} category.\retTwo

\hypertarget{Page 1024 reference}{One} more colimit I want to construct is as follows. Suppose $(I, \lesssim)$ is a directed set (see my math 240b notes to recall what that means). We can turn $I$ into a small category $\mcateg{I}$ whose objects are just the elements of $I$ and whose morphisms are just the relations $i \lesssim j$. Now suppose $F: \mcateg{I} \to \mcateg{Set}$ is a functor. Then we can construct $\lim\limits_{\longrightarrow}(F)$ as follows.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Let $S_i \coloneqq F(i)$ for all $i \in I$. Also, for reasons that will become apparent later, denote $F(i \lesssim j)$ as $r^{i}_j$. To construct the colimit of $F$, first let $S \coloneqq \bigcup_{i \in I}(\{i\} \times S_i)$. Next, we use the fact that $I$ is a directed set to define an equivalence relation. Namely, we say that $(i, x) \sim (j, y)$ if there is an element $k \in I$ with $i \lesssim k$ and $j \lesssim k$, and there exists $z \in S_k$ with $r^i_k(x) = z = r^j_k(y)$.\newpage

	I claim that $\sim$ is an equivalence relation. After all, since $i \lesssim i$ and $r_i^i = \myId_{S_i}$ for all $i \in I$, we know that $(i, x) \sim (i, x)$ for all $i \in I$ and $x \in S_i$. Also, its obvious from our definition that $(i, x) \sim (j, y)$ iff $(j, y) \sim (i, x)$. Finally, suppose $(i_1, x_1) \sim (i_2, x_2) \sim (i_3, x_3)$. Then we know there exists $(j, y)$ such that $r_{j}^{i_1}(x_1) = y = r_j^{i_2}(x_2)$. Similarly, we know there exists $(j^\prime, y^\prime)$ such that $r_{j^\prime}^{i_1}(x_2) = y^\prime = r_{j^\prime}^{i_2}(x_3)$. And finally, we let $k \in I$ be any element with $j \lesssim k$ and $j^\prime \lesssim k$. Note that $r^{j}_k \circ r_j^{i_2} = r_k^{i_2} = r^{j^\prime}_k \circ r_{j^\prime}^{i_2}$, and also that $r_k^{i_1} = r^{j}_k \circ r_j^{i_1}$ and $r_k^{i_3} = r^{j^\prime}_k \circ r_{j^\prime}^{i_3}$. Thus:

	{\centering $r_k^{i_1}(x_1) = r^{j}_k \circ r_j^{i_1}(x_1) = r^{j}_k \circ r_j^{i_2}(x_2) = r^{j^\prime}_k \circ r_{j^\prime}^{i_2}(x_2) = r^{j^\prime}_k \circ r_{j^\prime}^{i_3}(x_3) = r_k^{i_3}(x_3)$ \retTwo\par}

	And this proves that $(i_1, x_1) \sim (i_3, x_3)$.\retTwo

	We now let $C \coloneqq S/_\sim$. Also for every $i \in I$ we define $\iota_i: S_i \to C$ by $x \mapsto [(i, x_i)]$. I claim that $C$ along with the $\iota_i$ forms a colimit.
	\begin{itemize}
		\item Note that $(i, x) \sim (j, r_j^i(x))$ for all $j \in I$ with $i \lesssim j$. Hence, the following diagram holds for all $i, j \in I$ with $i \lesssim j$:\\ [-18pt]
		% https://q.uiver.app/#
		\[\begin{tikzcd}
			{} &&&& {} \\
			& {S_i} && {S_j} \\
			&& C \\
			& {} && {}
			\arrow[""{name=0, anchor=center, inner sep=0}, "x"{description}, color={rgb,255:red,92;green,92;blue,214}, draw=none, from=2-2, to=1-1]
			\arrow["{r^{i}_j}", from=2-2, to=2-4]
			\arrow["{\iota_i}"', from=2-2, to=3-3]
			\arrow[""{name=1, anchor=center, inner sep=0}, "{r_j^i(x)}"{description}, color={rgb,255:red,92;green,92;blue,214}, draw=none, from=2-4, to=1-5]
			\arrow["{\iota_j}", from=2-4, to=3-3]
			\arrow[""{name=2, anchor=center, inner sep=0}, "{[(i, x)]}"{description}, color={rgb,255:red,92;green,92;blue,214}, draw=none, from=3-3, to=4-2]
			\arrow[""{name=3, anchor=center, inner sep=0}, "{[(j, r_j^i(x))]}"{description}, color={rgb,255:red,92;green,92;blue,214}, draw=none, from=3-3, to=4-4]
			\arrow[draw={rgb,255:red,92;green,92;blue,214}, between={0.1}{0.85}, maps to, from=0, to=1]
			\arrow[draw={rgb,255:red,92;green,92;blue,214}, between={0.1}{0.9}, maps to, from=0, to=2]
			\arrow[draw={rgb,255:red,92;green,92;blue,214}, between={0.2}{0.9}, maps to, from=1, to=3]
			\arrow[color={rgb,255:red,92;green,92;blue,214}, between={0.2}{0.65}, equals, from=2, to=3]
		\end{tikzcd}\]

		\item Next, suppose a set $M$ and functions $\eta_i$ also satisfy for all $i \lesssim j$ that:\\ [-14pt]
		% https://q.uiver.app/#q=WzAsMyxbMCwwLCJTX2kiXSxbMiwwLCJTX2oiXSxbMSwxLCJNIl0sWzAsMSwicl5pX2oiXSxbMCwyLCJcXGV0YV9pIiwyXSxbMSwyLCJcXGV0YV9qIl1d
		\[\begin{tikzcd}
			{S_i} && {S_j} \\
			& M
			\arrow["{r^i_j}"', from=1-1, to=1-3]
			\arrow["{\eta_i}"', from=1-1, to=2-2]
			\arrow["{\eta_j}", from=1-3, to=2-2]
		\end{tikzcd}\]

		Then by the universal property of disjoint unions of sets (i.e. that they are categorical coproducts of sets), we know that there is a unique function $h: S \to M$ such that the following diagram holds for all $i \in I$:\\ [-14pt]
		% https://q.uiver.app/#
		\[\begin{tikzcd}
			& {S_i} && M \\
			{} && S \\
			& {}
			\arrow["{\eta_i}"', from=1-2, to=1-4]
			\arrow[hook, from=1-2, to=2-3]
			\arrow[""{name=0, anchor=center, inner sep=0}, draw=none, from=2-1, to=1-2]
			\arrow["{\exists! h}"', dashed, from=2-3, to=1-4]
			\arrow[""{name=1, anchor=center, inner sep=0}, draw=none, from=3-2, to=2-3]
			\arrow[""{name=2, anchor=center, inner sep=0}, "x"{description}, color={rgb,255:red,92;green,92;blue,214}, draw=none, from=0, to=1-2]
			\arrow[""{name=3, anchor=center, inner sep=0}, "{(i, x)}"{description}, color={rgb,255:red,92;green,92;blue,214}, draw=none, from=1, to=2-3]
			\arrow[color={rgb,255:red,92;green,92;blue,214}, between={0.2}{0.8}, maps to, from=2, to=3]
		\end{tikzcd}\]
		\phantom{.}\\ [-20pt]
		
		In other words, $h(i, x) = \eta_i(x)$ for all $(i, x) \in S$. Yet now suppose $(i, x) \sim (j, y)$. Thus, there exists $k \in I$ with $i \lesssim k$, $j \lesssim k$, and $r^{i}_k(x) = r^j_k(y)$. Since we also know that $\eta_k \circ r_k^i = \eta_i$ and $\eta_k \circ r_k^j = \eta_j$, we can say that:

		{\centering $h(i, x) = \eta_i(x) = \eta_k \circ r_k^i(x)= \eta_k \circ r_k^j(y) = \eta_j(y) = h(j, y)$ \newpage\par}

		It follows that we can define a function $g: C \to M$ by $g([(i, x)]) \coloneqq h(i, x)$. And since $h$ was uniquely determined, we also know $g$ is uniquely determined. This finishes showing that $C$ is a colimit.
	\end{itemize}
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo\dispDate{7/3/2026}

\hypertarget{Page 1026 reference}{Today} I want to try and take some notes on presheaves, stalks, and germs. I will be loosely following \textit{Differential Analysis on Complex Manifolds} by Raymond Wells. (See \inLinkRap{Ninth Citation}{citation 9}\dots)\retTwo

To start off, suppose $\mcateg{C}$ is a category. Then a \udefine{presheaf} is just a functor $F: \mcateg{C}^{\mathrm{op}} \to \mcateg{Set}$. If we replace the category $\mcateg{Set}$ with a different category $\mcateg{D}$ (say $A$-$\mcateg{mod}$), we just say our presheaf is \udefine{$\mcateg{D}$-valued}.\retTwo

A morphism between presheaves $F_1$ and $F_2$ is just a natural transformation between the two functors. In the special case that the natural transformation $\eta: F_1 \to F_2$ consists of only injective functions, then we say $F_1$ is a \udefine{subpresheaf} of $F_2$.\retTwo

Given a topological $X$, a relevant category for us to define is the category $\mcateg{Op}(X)$ of\\ nonempty open subsets of $X$. The objects of this category are open subsets, and the\\ morphisms are given by set inclusions. Clearly this is a small category. Using this category,\\ we now define a \udefine{presheaf} $\mathcalli{F}$ \textit{over a topological space} $X$ to be:
\begin{itemize}
	\item An assignment to every nonempty open set $U \subseteq X$ some other set $\mathcalli{F}(U)$,
	\item A collection of homomorphisms $r_{V}^U : \mathcalli{F}(U) \to \mathcalli{F}(V)$ (called \udefine{restriction\\ homomorphisms}) for each pair of nonempty open sets $V \subseteq U \subseteq X$ such that:
	\begin{itemize}
		\item[$\circ$] $r_U^U = \myId_{\mathcalli{F}(U)}$,
		\item[$\circ$] If $W \subseteq V \subseteq U$ then $r_W^U = r_W^V \circ r_V^U$. 
	\end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\begin{myDindent}\myComment
	As a side note, we call the objects $\mathcalli{F}(U)$ \udefine{sections} of the presheaf $\mathcalli{F}$.\retTwo
\end{myDindent}

The subpresheafs in this case that we care about are when we restrict the domain of $\mathcalli{F}$ to only open sets containing some arbitrary point $x \in X$.\retTwo

Let $\mcateg{D}$ denote either $\mcateg{Set}$, $\mcateg{Ab}$, $\mcateg{CRing}$, or $A$-$\mcateg{mod}$ or $\mcateg{CAlg}_A$ (where $A$ is some unital\\ commutative ring). Then let $\mathcalli{F}$ be a  $\mcateg{D}$-valued presheaf over a topological space $X$.\\ Given any $x \in X$ we define the \udefine{stalk of $\mathcalli{F}$ at $x$} to be the direct limit (i.e. colimit) of\\ $\mathcalli{F}$ restricted to the open sets containing $x$:

$$\mathcalli{F}_x \coloneqq \hspace{-1em}\lim\limits_{\substack{\longrightarrow\\ x \in U \in \Obj(\mcateg{Op}(X))}}\hspace{-2em}\mathcalli{F}(U)$$


Then, an element of $\mathcalli{F}_x$ is called a \udefine{germ}.\newpage
\begin{myIndent}\myComment
	The intuition for this naming scheme is that in agriculture, a sheaf refers to a bundle of wheat, then each stalk is a single wheat strand, and finally the germs are the seeds at end of the stalk. Similarly in the math sense, a sheaf (which will be a presheaf equipped with a few more assumptions) is a structure encoding local data on an entire topological space, each stalk is a structure encoding local data at a specific point, and the germs are all the possible configurations of local data at a given point.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\pracOne Here are three examples of presheaves over a topological space $X$:
\begin{itemize}
	\item Suppose $Y$ is another topological space and then for every $U \in \Obj(\mcateg{Op}(X))$ define:

	{\centering$\mathcalli{F}(U) = C(U, Y) \coloneqq \{(f: U \to Y) : f \text{ is continuous}\}$.\retTwo\par}

	Also if $V \subseteq U \subseteq X$ let $r^U_V(f) \coloneqq f|_V$. This is easily checked to be a presheaf which we denote $\mathscr{C}_{X,Y}$. Also if $Y = k$ (where $k = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$) then this presheaf is $(\mcateg{CAlg}_k)$-valued.\retTwo

	\item Suppose that $X$ in particular is a topological manifold equipped with a $C^r$ structure (where $r \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1} \cup \{\infty\}$). Then for every $U \in \Obj(\mcateg{Op}(X))$ let $\mathscr{C}_X^r(U)$ denote the space of real-valued $C^r$ functions from $U$ to $\mathbb{R}$. Also for $V \subseteq U \subseteq X$ let $r^U_V(f) \coloneqq f|_V$. This is also easily checked to be a $(\mcateg{CAlg}_\mathbb{R})$-valued presheaf.
	
	\item Meanwhile, suppose that $X$ is a topological manifold equipped with a complex\\ structure. Then for every $U \in \Obj(\mcateg{Op}(X))$ let $\mathcalli{O}_X$ denote the space of holomorphic functions from $U$. Also for $V \subseteq U \subseteq X$ let $r^U_V(f) \coloneqq f|_V$. This is also easily checked to be a $(\mcateg{CAlg}_\mathbb{C})$-valued presheaf.\retTwo
\end{itemize}

\hTwo Now a presheaf $\mathcalli{F}$ over a topological space $X$ is called a \udefine{sheaf} if for every collection of open sets $\{U_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ with $U \coloneqq \bigcup_{\alpha \in A}U_\alpha$ the following two axioms are satisfied:
\begin{enumerate}
	\item[1.] If $s, t \in \mathcalli{F}(U)$ satisfy that $r_{U_\alpha}^U(s) = r^{U}_{U_\alpha}(t)$ for all $\alpha \in A$ then $s = t$.
	\item[2.] Suppose there exists $s_\alpha \in \mathcalli{F}(U_\alpha)$ for all $\alpha \in A$ satisfying that if $\beta \in A$ and\\ $U_\alpha \cap U_\beta \neq \emptyset$ then $r_{U_\alpha \cap U_\beta}^{U_\alpha}(s_\alpha) =  r_{U_\alpha \cap U_\beta}^{U_\beta}(s_\beta)$. Then there exists an $s \in \mathcalli{F}(U)$\\ such that $r^U_{U_\alpha}(s) = s_\alpha$ for all $\alpha \in A$.\retTwo
\end{enumerate}

\pracOne Hopefully it is clear why all three examples of presheaves I just gave are also sheaves. The first bullet point is satisfied because because functions are uniquely determined by their values at each point. Meanwhile, the second bullet point is satisfied because we can glue compatible continuous, smooth, or holomorphic functions together.\retTwo

Firstly, I want to generalize the notes about tangent planes on \inLinkRap{page 926 tangent plane definition}{pages 926 and 927} to\\ abstract differentiable manifolds.\retTwo

Let $M$ be a $C^\infty$ manifold with or without boundary  and consider any $p \in M$. A linear map $v: C^\infty(M, \mathbb{R}) \to \mathbb{R}$ is a \udefine{derivation at $p$} if

{\centering$v(fg) = f(p)v(g) + g(p)v(f)$ for all $f, g \in C^\infty(M, \mathbb{R})$.\retTwo\par}

\begin{myIndent}\myComment
	It will be clear later why we require our functions to be $C^\infty$ as opposed to just $C^1$.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

Also, we let $T_p M$ be the set of all derivations at $p$. Importantly, we can see that $T_p M$ is a real vector space. So, we say an element of $T_p M$ is a \udefine{tangent vector at $p$}.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Lemma:} \hypertarget{lemma page 1028}{Suppose} $v \in T_p M$.
\begin{itemize}
	\item If $f \equiv C$ where $C \in \mathbb{R}$ then $v(f) = 0$.
	\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
		Why?\\
		$v(f) = \frac{1}{c} v(cf) = \frac{1}{c}v(f^2) = \frac{1}{c}(2f(p)v(f)) = 2v(f)$. By subtracting $v(f)$\\ from both sides we then get that $0 = v(f)$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	\item If $f, g \in C^\infty(M, \mathbb{R})$, $f(p) = 0$, and $g(p) = 0$ then $v(fg) = 0$.
	
	\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
		Hopefully this is obvious.
	\end{myIndent}
\end{itemize}

\hypertarget{Page 1028 intuition}{I'd} like to give some intuition on why derivations should be called "tangent vectors". For now, suppose we have a $k$-dimensional $C^r$ manifold $M \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ (where $r \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1} \cup \{\infty\}$), and for the sake of convenience assume $M$ has no boundary. (Here I'm taking $M$ to be a manifold as was studied on \inLinkRap{placeholder}{pages 77-99} as opposed to a general abstract manifold as covered by John Lee. As a side note, $M$ would also be an abstract manifold and its $C^r$ structure would be generated by all full rank bijective $C^r$ maps from open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^k$ to open subsets of $M$ which also have continuous inverses.)\retTwo

Next, consider any $p \in M$ and let $\phi$ be a $C^r$ diffeomorphism from an open set $U$ of $\mathbb{R}^k$ to an open set $V^\prime$ of $M$ containing $p$. Also let $q = \phi^{-1}(p)$. Then recalling \inLinkRap{page 926 tangent plane definition}{pages 926 and 927}, we define the "geometric tangent plane" based at $p$ as:

{\centering$\widetilde{T_p M} \coloneqq \{(p, \mVecAst{y}) : \mVecAst{y} \in \myIm(\Df \phi(q) : \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}^n)\}$\retTwo\par}

\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Importantly, $\widetilde{T_p M}$ is an $k$-dimensional vector space. Also suppose that\\ $\mVecAst{v}_p = (p, \mVecAst{v}) \in \widetilde{T_p M}$.\newpage

	\hypertarget{Reconciling different definitions page 1029}{I} realize I have two diffent definitions for what it means for a function $f: M \to \mathbb{R}$\\ to be a $C^s$ function (where $s \leq r$). So I want to quickly rectify that.
	\begin{itemize}
		\item Definition 1: $f: M \to \mathbb{R}$ is a $C^s$ map if there is an open set $W \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ containing $M$ and a $C^s$ function $g: W \to \mathbb{R}$ with $g|_M = f$.
		\item Definition 2: $f$ is a $C^s$ function in the manifold sense. Equivalently, this means for any open sets $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^k$ and $V \subseteq M$ as well as any bijective $C^\infty$ function $\varphi: U \to V$ such that $\Df \varphi(x)$ has full rank for all $x \in U$ and $\varphi^{-1}$ is continuous, we have that $f \circ \varphi$ is a $C^s$ map. (Note: this is equivalent to the manifold definition because the  $\varphi$ form a\\ $C^r$ subatlas of the $C^r$ structure of $M$).
	\end{itemize}

	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		$(1 \Longrightarrow 2)$\\
		This is hopefully obvious.\retTwo

		$(2 \Longrightarrow 1)$\\
		Recall from lemma 23.1 on \inLinkRap{placeholder}{page 83} that by passing to a partition of unity, it suffices to show definition 1 only locally. In other words, we must show for any $p \in M$ that there exists a $C^s$ function $g: W \to \mathbb{R}$ for some open set $W \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ containing $p$ such that $g|_{M \cap V} = f|_{M \cap V}$.\retTwo

		Fortunately, we can find open sets $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^k$ and $V \subseteq M$ and a homeomorphism $\varphi: U \to V$ such that $p \in V$, $\varphi$ is a $C^r$ function, and $\Df \varphi(x)$ has full rank for all $x \in U$. Next, note from theorem 24.1 on \inLinkRap{placeholder}{page 87} that $\varphi^{-1}$ can be extended to a\\ $C^r$ function $\psi: W \to \mathbb{R}^k$ such that $W \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is open and $\psi|_V = \varphi^{-1}$. But now as\\ $\psi$ is continuous and $\psi(V) = \varphi^{-1}(V) = U$, we know that $\psi^{-1}(U)$ is an open subset of $W$ containing $V$. Plus, $p \in V \subseteq \psi^{-1}(U)$. In other words, we can without loss of generality shrink $W$ so that $\psi(W) \subseteq U$ and still have that $p \in W$. And finally, $(f \circ \varphi) \circ \psi = f$ on $M$ and $(f \circ \varphi) \circ \psi$ is a composition of a $C^s$ map and a $C^r$ map on $W$. Hence, we've proven that definition 1 holds locally for $f$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Next, suppose $f \in C^1(M, \mathbb{R})$. We define its \udefine{directional derivative} $\Df_{\mVecAst{v}}|_p f$ in the direction of $\mVecAst{v}$ as follows:\retTwo

	Let $\gamma: [-1, 1] \to M$ be any $C^1$-path such that $\gamma(0) = p$ and $\gamma^\prime(0) = \mVecAst{v}$.
	\begin{myIndent}\color{VioletRed}
		As for how we know such a path $\gamma$ exists, recall that $\mVecAst{v} \in \Df \phi(q)$. Hence, there exists $w \in \mathbb{R}^k$ such that $(\Df \phi(q))\mVecAst{w} = \mVecAst{v}$. Let $\widetilde{\gamma} : [-1, 1] \to U$ be a $C^1$-path such that $\widetilde{\gamma}(0) = q$ and $\widetilde{\gamma}^\prime(0) = \mVecAst{w}$. Then let $\gamma \coloneqq \phi \circ \widetilde{\gamma}$. Clearly $\gamma(0) = p$ and $\gamma([-1, 1])$ is contained in $M$. Also by chain rule we have that:
		
		{\centering$\gamma^\prime(0) = (\Df \phi(q))\widetilde{\gamma}^\prime(0) = (\Df \phi(q))\mVecAst{w} = \mVecAst{v}$.\retTwo\par}
	\end{myIndent}

	Now we define $\Df_{\mVecAst{v}}|_p f = (f \circ \gamma)^\prime(0)$. I claim this definition is independent of the specific path $\gamma$ chosen. After all:
	\begin{myIndent}\color{VioletRed}
		Suppose $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$ are two distinct $C^1$-paths such that $\gamma_i(0) = p$ and $\gamma_i^\prime(0) = \mVecAst{v}$ for both $i$. Then after extending $f$ to a $C^r$ function on an open set $V \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ with $V^\prime = V \cap M$ (which we can do since $f \in C^r(M, \mathbb{R})$), we know that:
		
		{\centering$(f \circ \gamma_1)^\prime(0) = \nabla f(p)\cdot \gamma_1^\prime(0) = \nabla f(p) \cdot \mVecAst{v} = \nabla f(p) \cdot \gamma_2^\prime(0) = (f \circ \gamma_2)^\prime(0)$.\retTwo\par}
	\end{myIndent}

	It's also easy to see when $M$ is a $C^\infty$ manifold that the directional derivative $\Df_{\mVecAst{v}}|_p$ restricted to $C^\infty$ functions is a derivation at $p$. After all, we can just apply the product rule to the gradiant operator and also note that taking a dot product against a fixed vector $\mVecAst{v}$ defines\newpage a linear functional.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

Now supposing that $M$ is a $C^\infty$ manifold, we can consider the function $\widetilde{T_p M}$ to $T_p M$ given by $(p, \mVecAst{v}) \mapsto \Df_{\mVecAst{v}}|_p$. We can see from the fact that taking a dot product against a fixed vector $\nabla f(p)$ defines a linear functional that our mapping $(p, \mVecAst{v}) \mapsto \Df_{\mVecAst{v}}|_p$ is actually a linear map between vector spaces.\retTwo

Furthermore, I claim that our linear map is injective. After all, suppose $(p, \mVecAst{v})$ maps\\ to the zero derivation (i.e. the derivation mapping every $C^\infty$ function to $0$). Then let\\ $(p, u_1), \ldots, (p, u_k)$ be an orthonormal $\mathbb{R}$-basis for the vector space $\widetilde{T_p M}$. We can uniquely\\ express $\mVecAst{v} = c_1 u_1 + \ldots + c_k u_k$ where $c_1, \ldots, c_k \in \mathbb{R}$. And now for any $f \in C^\infty(M ,\mathbb{R})$ we\\ have that:

{\centering $\Df_{\mVecAst{v}}|_p f = \sum_{j=1}^k c_j \Df_{u_j}|_p f$ \retTwo\par}

To finish off, we can define $f_i \in C^\infty(M, \mathbb{R})$ by $f_i(x) = x \cdot u_i$ for all $x \in M \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$. This is a $C^\infty$ map because it more strongly extends to a smooth map on all of $\mathbb{R}^n$. Furthermore, note that $\nabla f_i(p) = u_i$. So, $\Df_{u_j}|_p f = u_i \cdot u_j$. And this equals $1$ if $i = j$ and $0$ otherwise. So, we can conclude for all $i$ that:

{\centering $0 = \Df_{\mVecAst{v}}|_p f_i = \sum_{j=1}^k c_j \Df_{u_j}|_p f_i = c_i$\retTwo\par}

In other words $\mVecAst{v} = 0u_1 + \ldots + 0u_k = 0$. And with that we've proven that $(p, \mVecAst{v}) \mapsto \Df_{\mVecAst{v}}|_p$ has a trivial kernel.\retTwo

Now to finish off, note that $\widetilde{T_p M}$ is $k$-dimensional. We'll also soon show for a general\\ abstract $C^\infty$ $k$-dimensional manifold that $T_p M$ is $k$-dimensional. Hence, our injective\\ linear map must also be surjective. And thus, we've proven that our linear map $\widetilde{T_p M}$\\ to $T_p M$ given by $(p, \mVecAst{v}) \mapsto \Df_{\mVecAst{v}}|_p$ is a bijection.\retTwo

The T.L.D.R. to all of this is that you should think of a tangent plane as being isomorphic to a vector space of directional derivative operators. Also, derivations are a generalization of directional derivatives.

\mySepTwo

\hTwo Suppose $M$ and $N$ are $C^\infty$ manifolds with or without boundary, and $F: M \to N$ is a\\ $C^\infty$ map. We define a map $\df F_p : T_p M \to F_{F(p)}N$ called the \udefine{differential of $F$ at $p$} such\\ that $\df F_p(v)f \coloneqq v(f \circ F)$ for all $v \in T_p M$ and $f \in C^\infty(N, \mathbb{R})$.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	To see that this map is well-defined, suppose $v \in T_p M$ and let $f, g \in C^\infty(N, \mathbb{R})$. Also suppose $c \in \mathbb{R}$. Then $\df F_p(v)(cf) = v(cf \circ F) = cv(f \circ F) = c\df F_p(v)f$. Similarly,

	{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
		$\df F_p(v)(f + g) = v((f + g) \circ F)$\\ [4pt]
		$\phantom{\df F_p(v)(f + g)} = v((f \circ F) + (g \circ F)) = v((f \circ F)) + v((g \circ F))$\\ [4pt]
		$\phantom{\df F_p(v)(f + g)= v((f \circ F) + (g \circ F))} = \df F_p(v)f + \df F_p(v)g$
	\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

	Thus, we've shown that $\df F_p(v)$ is a linear map on $C^\infty(N, \mathbb{R})$. As for additionally showing that $\df F_p(v)$ is a derivation at $F(p)$, note that:\newpage

	{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
		$\df F_p(v)(fg) = v((fg) \circ F)$\\ [4pt]
		$\phantom{\df F_p(v)(fg)} = v((f \circ F)(g \circ F)) = (f \circ F)(p)v(g \circ F) + (g \circ F)(p)v(f \circ F)$\\ [4pt]
		$\phantom{\df F_p(v)(fg) = v((f \circ F)(g \circ F))} = f(F(p))\df F_p(v)g + g(F(p))\df F_p(v)f$
	\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}
\end{myIndent}

\exTwo\ul{Proposition 3.6:} \hypertarget{Proposition 3.6 page 1031}{Let} $M$, $N$, and $P$ be $C^\infty$ manifolds with or without boundary. Also let\\ $F: M \to N$ and $G: N \to P$ be $C^\infty$ maps, and let $p \in M$.
\begin{enumerate}
	\item[(a)] $\df F_p: T_p M \to T_{F(p)}N$ is a linear map.
	\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
		Proof:\\
		Suppose $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ and $v, w \in T_p M$. Then for any $f \in C^1(N)$ we have that:
		
		{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
			$\df F_p(av + bw)f = (av + bw)(f \circ F)$\\ [4pt]
			$\phantom{\df F_p(av + bw)f} = av(f \circ F) + bw(f \circ F) = a\df F_p(v)f + b\df F_p(w)f$
		\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}
	\end{myIndent}

	\item[(b)] $\df (G \circ F)_p = \df G_{F(p)} \circ \df F_p$.
	\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
		Proof:\\
		Let $v \in T_p M$ and $f \in C^1(P, \mathbb{R})$. Then:

		{\centering $\df(G \circ F)_p(v)f = v(f \circ G \circ F) = (\df F_p(v))(f \circ G) = (\df G_{F(p)}(\df F_p(v)))f$.\retTwo\par}

		Thus $\df(G \circ F)_p(v) = \df G_{F(p)}(\df F_p(v))$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	\item[(c)] $\df (\myId_M)_p = \myId_{T_p M}$.
	\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
		Proof:\\
		Let $v \in T_p M$ and $f \in C^1(M, \mathbb{R})$. Then:

		{\centering $(\df (\myId_M)_p (v))f = v(f \circ \myId_M) = v(f)$.\retTwo\par}

		As a result, $\df (\myId_M)_p v = v$. In other words, $\df (\myId_M)_p = \myId_{T_p M}$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	\item[(d)] If $F$ is a $C^\infty$-diffeomorphism from $M$ to $N$ (i.e. a bijection such that $F$ and $F^{-1}$ are $C^\infty$ maps) then $\df F_p: T_p M \to T_{F(p)} N$ is an isomorphism and $(\df F_p)^{-1} = \df (F^{-1})_{F(p)}$.
	\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
		Why?\\
		From parts (b) and (c) we know that:
		\begin{itemize}
			\item $\myId_{T_pM} = \df (\myId_{M})_p = \df (F^{-1} \circ F)_p = \df (F^{-1})_{F(P)} \circ \df F_p$,
			\item $\myId_{T_{F(p)}N} = \df (\myId_{N})_{F(p)} = \df (F \circ F^{-1})_{F(p)} = \df F_p \circ \df (F^{-1})_{F(p)}$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
		\end{itemize}
	\end{myIndent}
\end{enumerate}

\hTwo\mySepTwo

\dispDate{7/13/2026}

In order to get anywhere studying differentials of $C^\infty$ maps, we will want to be able study differentials as being a local property as opposed to a global property. Hence, we shall first prove the following results.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Lemma (Existence of Bump Functions):} \hypertarget{page 1031 lemma}{Suppose} $(U, \varphi)$ is a chart on a $C^r$ manifold $M$ with or without boundary (where $r \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\})$. Then for any compact set $K \subseteq U$ we can find a compactly supported function $\phi \in C^r(M, [0, 1])$ with $\phi \equiv 1$ on $K$ and $\supp(\phi) \subseteq K$.\newpage
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	The proposition doesn't specify if $\varphi(U)$ is open in $\mathbb{R}^n$ or in $H^n$. That said, it will still be the case no matter what that $K^\prime \coloneqq \varphi(K)$ is compact in $\mathbb{R}^n$. Now if $\varphi(U)$ is open in $H^n$ but not $\mathbb{R}^n$ then let $V^\prime$ be an open set in $\mathbb{R}^n$ with $V^\prime \cap H^n = \varphi(U)$. Otherwise just set $V^\prime = U$.\retTwo

	By the $C^\infty$-Urysohn lemma for functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$, we can find a compactly supported smooth function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to [0, 1]$ such that $\supp(f) \subseteq V^\prime$ and $f \equiv 1$ on $K^\prime$. And then if we define $\widetilde{f}: U \to \mathbb{R}$ by $f \circ \varphi$, we have that $\widetilde{f}$ is a $C^r$ function, $\widetilde{f} \equiv 1$ on $K$, and $\supp(\widetilde{f})$ is a compact subset of $U$.\retTwo

	Next define $\widetilde{g}: M - \supp(f)$ to be the constant zero function. This will be a $C^r$ map.\retTwo

	Finally, by the gluing lemma (on \inLinkRap{placeholder}{page 150}) (since $\widetilde{f}$ and $\widetilde{g}$ agree on their shared domains), we know there is a unique $C^r$ map $\phi: M \to [0, 1]$ such that $\phi|_U = \widetilde{f}$ (and thus $\widetilde{f} \equiv 1$ on $K$), and also $\supp(\phi) = \supp(\widetilde{f}) \subseteq U$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\ul{Proposition (Existence of Partitions of Unity):} \hypertarget{Existence of Partitions of Unity}{Suppose} $M$ is a $C^r$ manifold with or without boundary. Then for any open cover $\mathcal{U} = \{U_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ of $M$ there is partition of unity $\{\phi_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ specifically satisfying that $\supp(\phi_\alpha) \subseteq U_\alpha$ and $\phi_\alpha \in C^r(M, [0, 1])$ for all $\alpha$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	For every $p \in M$ let $(V_p, \varphi_p)_{p \in M}$ be a smooth chart containing $p$ such that $V_p \subseteq U_\alpha$\\ for some $\alpha$. Then $\mathcal{V} \coloneqq \{V_p\}_{p \in M}$ is a refinement of $\mathcal{U}$. Next, by the exercise on \inLinkRap{placeholder}{page 138}, we can find two locally finite refinements $\mathcal{W} \coloneqq \{W_m\}_{m \in \mathbb{N}}$ and $\mathcal{X} \coloneqq \{X_m\}_{m \in \mathbb{N}}$ of $\mathcal{V}$ such that $\overline{W_m}$ is compact and $\overline{X_m} \subseteq W_m$ for all $m$. And then by the prior lemma, we can pick a compactly supported function $f_m \in C^r(M, [0, 1])$ with $f_m \equiv 1$ on $\overline{X_m}$ and $\supp(f_m) \subseteq W_m \subseteq V_{p}$ for some $p \in M$.\retTwo

	If we set $f = \sum_{m=1}^\infty f_m$, we have that $f$ is finite and a $C^r$ map on all of $M$ because each $p \in M$ has a neighborhood which intercepts only finitely many $W_m$ (and hence locally $f$ is only a sum of finitely many $C^r$ functions). Furthermore, we know $f(p) \geq 1$ for all $p \in M$ since every $p$ is contained in some $X_m$. Therefore, we can set $\psi_m = f_m / f$. Again, it is easily checked that since both $f_m$ and $f$ are $C^r$ maps and $f$ is nowhere zero, $\psi_m$ is also a $C^r$ map. Also, $\psi_m(M) \subseteq [0, 1]$ and $\supp(\psi_m)$ is contained in $W_m$ which in turn is contained in some $V_{p}$ which is contained in some $U_\alpha$. Also $\sum_{m\in \mathbb{N}}\psi_m = 1$. And for identical reasons as with the $f_m$, we know that every $p \in M$ has a neighborhood that intersects only finitely many of the supports of the $\psi_m$.\retTwo

	To finish off, let $h: \mathbb{N} \to A$ be a function such that $W_m \subseteq U_{h(m)}$ for all $m \in \mathbb{N}$. Then upon taking the convention that $\sum_{m \in \emptyset}\phi_m \equiv 0$, for every $\alpha \in A$ let $\phi_\alpha \coloneqq \sum_{m \in h^{-1}(\alpha)} \psi_m$. Each $\phi_\alpha$ will be a $C^r$ map for the same reason $f$ was a $C^r$ map. Furthermore, we will still have that $\sum_{\alpha \in A} \phi_\alpha \equiv 1$ (where every $p$ has a neighborhood on which only finitely many $\phi_\alpha$ are nonzero). And since all the $\phi_\alpha$ are nonnegative, we can conclude that $\phi_\alpha(M) \subseteq [0, 1]$.\retTwo

	Finally, for every $m$ let $K_m \coloneqq \supp(\psi_m)$ and note that each $K_m$ is a closed subset of $W_m$. Also, $\{K_m\}_{m \in \mathbb{N}}$ is a locally finite collection of sets since $\mathcalli{W}$ is. Hence by an exercise on\\ \inLinkRap{placeholder}{pages 139-140}:
	
	{\centering $\supp(\phi_\alpha) \subseteq \overline{\bigcup_{m \in h^{-1}(\alpha)}K_m} = \bigcup_{m \in h^{-1}(\alpha)} K_m \subseteq \bigcup_{m \in h^{-1}(\alpha)} W_m \subseteq U_\alpha$. $\blacksquare$\newpage\par}
\end{myIndent}

\exTwo\ul{Corollary (Urysohn's Lemma for $C^r$ manifolds):} Let $M$ be a $C^r$ manifold\\ with or without boundary. Then for any disjoint closed sets $A, B \subseteq M$ there exists\\ a function $\phi \in C^r(M, [0, 1])$ such that $\phi \equiv 1$ on $A$ and $\phi \equiv 0$ on $B$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Let $U_0 = M - A$ and $U_1 = M - B$. Because $A$ and $B$ are disjoint closed sets, $\{U_0, U_1\}$ is an open cover of $M$. So by the prior proposition, we can find two $C^r$ maps $\phi_0, \phi_1$ in $C^r(M, [0, 1])$ such that $\phi_0 + \phi_1 \equiv 1$, $\supp(\phi_0) \subseteq U_0$, and $\supp(\phi_1) \subseteq U_1$. But now since $\phi_0 \equiv 0$ on $A = M - U_0$ and $\phi_0 + \phi_1 \equiv 1$, we must have that $\phi_1 \equiv 1$ on $A$. Also, $\phi_1 \equiv 0$ on $B = M - U_1$. So, $\phi_1$ is our desired function. $\blacksquare$\retTwo

	\begin{myIndent}\myComment
		Another way of stating this lemma is that if $A \subseteq M$ is a closed set and $U \subseteq M$ is an open set such that $A \subseteq U$, then there exists $\phi \in C^r(M, [0, 1])$ such that $\phi \equiv 1$ on $A$ and $\supp(\phi) \subseteq U$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo \hypertarget{page 1033 reference}{Now} that we have the ability to construct all the bump functions we need, we can go back to studying the differential of a $C^\infty$ map between $C^\infty$ manifolds.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Proposition 3.8:} Let $M$ be a $C^\infty$ manifold with or without boundary, $p \in M$, and $v \in T_p M$. If $f, g \in C^\infty(M, \mathbb{R})$ agree on some neighborhood of $p$, then $v(f) = v(g)$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Let $h = f - g$ and note that $h \in C^\infty(M, \mathbb{R})$ with $h \equiv 0$ on some neighborhood $U$ of $p$. Next, by the prior corollary let $\phi: M \to [0, 1]$ be a $C^\infty$ map such that $\phi \equiv 1$ on $\supp(h)$ and $\supp(\phi) \subseteq M - \{p\}$. Since $\phi \equiv 1$ everywhere that $h \neq 0$, we know that $h = h\phi $. Hence:

	{\centering $v(f) - v(g) = v(h) = v(h\phi) = v(h)\phi(p) + v(\phi)h(p) = 0 + 0 = 0$ $\blacksquare$ \retTwo\par}
\end{myIndent}

\exTwo\ul{Proposition 3.9:} Let $M$ be a $C^\infty$ manifold with or without boundary, let $U \subseteq M$ be an open subset, and let $\iota: U \hookrightarrow M$ be the inclusion map. For every $p \in U$ the differential $\df \iota_p : T_pU \to T_p M$ is a vector space isomorphism. 
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	First we show injectivity. Suppose $v \in T_p U$ satisfies that $\df \iota_p (v) = 0 \in T_p M$. Then let $V$ be a precompact open set such that $p \in V \subseteq \overline{V} \subseteq U$. By Urysohn's lemma for $C^\infty$ manifolds, we know there is a $C^\infty$ function $\phi: M \to [0, 1]$ such that $\phi \equiv 1$ on $\overline{V}$ and $\supp(\phi) \subseteq U$.\retTwo

	Now suppose $f \in C^\infty(U, \mathbb{R})$. We can define a function $\widetilde{f} \in C^\infty(M, \mathbb{R})$ by setting\\ $\widetilde{f} \coloneqq \phi f$ on $U$ and $\widetilde{f} = 0$ outside of $U$. Note that $\widetilde{f}$ is a $C^\infty$ map by the gluing lemma\\ (see \inLinkRap{placeholder}{page 150}). But also by our prior proposition we know that:
	
	{\centering$v(f) = v(\widetilde{f}|_U) = v(\widetilde{f} \circ \iota) = \df \iota_p(v)\widetilde{f} = 0$.\retTwo\par}

	So, we've proven that $v(f) = 0$. And since $f$ was arbitrary, we've proven that $v$ is the zero derivation at $p$. This finishes proves that $\df \iota_p$ has a trivial kernel and is thus injective.\retTwo

	Next we show surjectivity. Suppose $w \in T_p M$ is arbitrary. Then we define $v \in T_p U$ by $v(f) = w(\widetilde{f})$ where $\widetilde{f} \in C^\infty(M, \mathbb{R})$ is any function such that $f = \widetilde{f}$ on the neighborhood $V$ of $p$ from before.\newpage
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		Note that such a function $\widetilde{f}$ exists by the reasoning given before. Also, $v$ is a well-defined function from $C^\infty(U, \mathbb{R})$ to $C^\infty(M, \mathbb{R})$ simply due to proposition 3.8. Also if $\widetilde{f}$ and $\widetilde{g}$ are $C^\infty$ maps on $M$ agreeing with $f$ and $g$ respectively on $V$, then $\widetilde{f}\widetilde{g}$ agrees with $fg$ on $V$ and $\widetilde{f} + \widetilde{g}$ agrees with $f + g$ on $V$. Thus, it's straightforward to also see that $v$ is a derivation.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Now I claim that $\df \iota_p(v) = w$. After all, let $f$ be any function in $C^\infty(M, \mathbb{R})$. Then since $f$ agrees with $f|_{U} = f \circ \iota$ on $V$, we have that $\df \iota_p(v)f = v(f \circ \iota) = w(f)$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\pracOne\mySepTwo 

\hypertarget{Page 1034 note}{We} now have two different cases where we know the differential of a function is a vector space isomorphism. Those two cases are when we are working with diffeomorphisms or with inclusion maps. Yet even just these two cases are useful. After all, suppose $M$ is a $C^\infty$ manifold, $p \in M$ and $(U, \varphi)$ is a smooth chart containing $p$.\retTwo

\ul{Lemma:} Suppose $M$ is a $C^r$ manifold and $(U, \varphi)$ is a smooth chart on $M$. Let $\widehat{U} = \varphi(U)$ and equip $\widehat{U}$ with the standard $C^r$ structure. Then $\varphi: U \to \widehat{U}$ is a $C^r$-diffeomorphism.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Why?\\
	Obviously $\varphi$ is a bijection. Also note that $\varphi$ is a $C^r$ map since the chart $(U, \varphi)$ trivially covers all of $U$ and also $\varphi \circ \varphi^{-1} = \myId_{\widehat{U}}$ is trivially a smooth function. Similarly, $\varphi^{-1}$ is a $C^r$ function since $\varphi \circ \varphi^{-1} \circ \myId_{\widehat{U}} = \myId_{\widehat{U}}$ is trivially a smooth map. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

As a result if $\iota: U \hookrightarrow M$ is the inclusion map, we have the following vector space\\ isomorphisms:
% https://q.uiver.app/#
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	{T_pM} && {T_pU} && {T_{\varphi(p)} \widehat{U}}
	\arrow["\sim", tail reversed, from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow["{\df \iota_p}"', draw=none, from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow["\sim", tail reversed, from=1-3, to=1-5]
	\arrow["{\df \varphi_p}"', draw=none, from=1-3, to=1-5]
\end{tikzcd}\]

This is especially nice because $T_{\varphi(p)} \widehat{U}$ is easy to describe.\retTwo 

\mySepTwo

\hTwo First we describe the tangent space of $\mathbb{R}^n$. Note that $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a parametrized $C^\infty$ manifold via the chart $(\mathbb{R}^n, \myId)$. Therefore, we can apply the observations on \inLinkRap{Page 1028 intuition}{pages 1028-1030}. In particular, note that $\Df (\myId)(a): \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ has full rank and hence the "geometric tangent plane" based at any $a \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is just $\widetilde{T_a M} \coloneqq \{(a, \mVecAst{y}) : \mVecAst{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n\}$. Furthermore, we have an injective linear map $\widetilde{T_a \mathbb{R}^n}$ to $T_a \mathbb{R}^n$ given by $(a, \mVecAst{y}) \mapsto \Df_{\mVecAst{y}}|_p$.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Lemma 3.2:} \hypertarget{Page 1035 lemma}{The} map described above is surjective.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Let $w \in T_a \mathbb{R}^n$ be any derivation. Then  having let $e_1, \ldots, e_n$ be the standard basis, for all $1 \leq i \leq n$ let $c_i \coloneqq w(x \mapsto x \cdot e_i)$. I claim $w = \Df_{v}|_a$ where $v = c_1 e_1 + \ldots + c_n e_n$.\retTwo

	\hypertarget{Page 1035 reference}{To} see why, let $f$ be any $C^\infty$ function on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Next for any $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ let\\ $h(t) \coloneqq f(a + t(x - a))$. If we say $a = (a_1, \ldots, a_n)$ and $x = (x_1, \ldots, x_n)$,\\ then note that:
	
	{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
		$f(x) - f(a) = h(1) - h(0) = \int_0^1 \frac{\df h}{\df t}(s)\df s$\\ [6pt]
		$\phantom{f(x) - f(a) = h(1) - h(0)} = \int_0^1 (x - a) \cdot \nabla f(a + s(x - a))\df s$\\ [6pt]
		$\phantom{f(x) - f(a) = h(1) - h(0)} = \sum_{i=1}^n  (x_i - a_i) \int_0^1 \frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}f(a + s(x - a))\df s$.
	\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

	In particular, we set $h_{i}(x) \coloneqq \int_0^1 \frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}f(a + s(x - a))\df s$. By Leibniz's rule applied $h_i$ (which we can apply to $x$ in bounded subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$ since $f$ is a $C^\infty$ function), we know $h_i$ is also a $C^\infty$ function on $\mathbb{R}^n$.
	\begin{myIndent}\myComment
		As a side note, if $f$ were only finitely many times differentiable then this paragraph would not work. This hints at how we need an alternate definition of tangent vectors for when we are working on $C^r$ manifolds where $r < \infty$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	And now we have that $w(f) = w\left(f(a) + \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - a_i)g_i(x)\right)$. Yet $w(f(a)) = 0$ since $f(a)$ is a constant. Meanwhile:
	
	{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
		$w((x_i - a_i)g_i(x)) = (a_i - a_i)w(g_i) + g_i(a)w(x_i - a_i)$\\ [6pt]
		$\phantom{w((x_i - a_i)g_i(x))} = 0 + (w(x \mapsto x \cdot e_i) - w(a_i))\int_0^1 \frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}f(a)\df s = (c_i - 0)\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}f(a)$.
	\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

	So, $w(f) = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i \frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}f(a) = D_v|_a f$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo

	\begin{myIndent}\myComment
		\hypertarget{Side note page 1035}{As} a side note, if we consider "derivations" whose domain is the vector space\\ $C^k(M, \mathbb{R})$ where $M$ is a $C^r$ manifold and $k < \min(r + 1, \infty)$, then we can ask\\ about "exotic derivations" which aren't described by directional derivatives.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
\end{myIndent}

\exTwo\ul{Corollary 3.3:} A vector space basis for $T_a \mathbb{R}^n$ is given by the partial derivative operators $\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}$ at $a$.\retTwo

\hTwo\mySepTwo

\dispDate{7/15/2026}

\exTwo\ul{Lemma 3.11:} \hypertarget{lemma 3.11 page 1035}{Suppose} $\iota: H^n \hookrightarrow \mathbb{R}^n$ is the inclusion map. (Hopefully it is obvious that this is a $C^\infty$-map.) For any $a \in \partial H^n$ the differential $\df \iota_a: T_a H^n \to T_a \mathbb{R}^n$ is an isomorphism.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	First I shall show injectivity. Suppose $v \in T_a H^n$ and $\df \iota_a(v) = 0 \in T_a \mathbb{R}^n$. Then consider any smooth function $f: H^n \to \mathbb{R}$. By definition we know that $f$ extends to a smooth function $g: U \to \mathbb{R}$ where $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is open and contains $H^n$. Furthermore, $H^n$ is a closed subset of $U$. Thus by identical reasoning as in the proof of proposition 3.9, we can find a smooth function $\widetilde{f}: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $\widetilde{f}|_{H^n} = g|_{H^n} = f$.\retTwo

	But now $v(f) = v(\widetilde{f}|_{H^n}) = v(\widetilde{f}\circ \iota) = \df \iota_a(v)\widetilde{f} = 0$. And since $f$ was arbitrary, we've proven that $v = 0$. So, $\df \iota_a$ has a trivial kernel and is thus injective.\retTwo

	Next we show surjectivity. Suppose $w \in T_a \mathbb{R}^n$ and then define $v \in T_a H^n$ by\\ $v(f) \coloneqq w(\widetilde{f})$ where $\widetilde{f}$ is any smooth extension of $f$ to all of $\mathbb{R}^n$.\newpage
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		To see that $v$ is well-defined, note by the prior corollary that $w = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i \frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}|_{a}$\\ for some $c_1, \ldots, c_n \in \mathbb{R}$. Yet since $\widetilde{f}$ has a continuous derivative, $\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\widetilde{f}(a)$ is\\ uniquely determined by $\widetilde{f}$'s restriction to $H^n$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Now its easy to check that $v$ is a derivation and that $\df \iota_a(v) = w$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\exTwo\ul{Proposition 3.12:} Given any $n$-dimensional $C^\infty$ manifold $M$ with or without boundary, for all $p \in M$ we have that $T_p M$ is an $n$-dimensional vector space.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	We already know from \inLinkRap{Page 1034 note}{page 1034} that $T_p M$ is isomorphic to $T_a \widehat{U}$ where $\widehat{U}$ is some\\ open subset of $H^n$ or $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $a \in \mathbb{R}^n$. But now it's straightforward to prove that $T_a \widehat{U}$ is\\ isomorphic to $T_a \mathbb{R}^n$ by just chaining together the isomorphisms induced by varying\\ inclusion functions. And finally, \inLinkRap{Page 1035 lemma}{lemma 3.2} tells us that $T_a \mathbb{R}^n$ is $n$-dimensional.\\ Thus, $T_p M$ is also $n$-dimensional. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo\mySepTwo

I want to switch to covering some category theory related notes about manifolds.\retTwo Firstly, we let $\mcateg{Man}$ be the category whose objects are topological manifolds without\\ boundaries and whose morphisms are continuous maps. If we want to allow our manifolds to have a boundary, we instead consider the category $\mcateg{Man}_b$.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Proposition:} Suppose $M_1, \ldots, M_{k-1}$ are topological manifolds without boundary and $M_k$ is a topological manifold with boundary. Also suppose each $M_i$ has dimension $n_i$. Then the topological product space $M \coloneqq M_1 \times \cdots \times M_k$ is an $n_1 + \ldots + n_k$ dimensional topological manifold with boundary. 
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Countable products of second countable topological spaces are still second countable. Hence $M$ is second countable.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		This is easy to verify.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
	
	Also arbitrary products of Hausdorff spaces are still Hausdorff. Hence, $M$ is Haudorff.\retTwo

	Finally, to show $M$ is locally Euclidean, let $(p_1, \ldots, p_k) \in M$. Then for each $1 \leq i \leq k$ we can pick a chart $(U_i, \varphi_i)$ on $M_i$ containing $p_i$. Now we identify $\mathbb{R}^{n_1} \times \cdots \times \mathbb{R}^{n_k}$ with $\mathbb{R}^{n_1 + \ldots + n_k}$ in the obvious way. Then we consider the chart $(U_1 \times \ldots \times U_k, \varphi_1 \times \cdots \times \varphi_k)$.
