\Hstatement\blab{Exercise 4-2:} \hypertarget{Exercise 4-2 page 1057}{Suppose} $M$ is a $C^r$ manifold (without a boundary) and $N$ is a $C^r$ manifold with\\ a boundary. Also let $\Int(N)$ denote the set of interior / non-boundary points of $N$. Then if\\ $F: N \to M$ is a $C^k$ map (where $k \leq r$), $p \in M$, and $\df F_p$ is bijective, we must have that\\ $F(p) \in \Int(N)$.
\begin{myIndent}\HexOne
	Proof:\\
	Once again, the fact that $\df F_p$ is injective means that there exists an integer $n$ with\\ $\dim(M) = n = \dim(N)$. Now let $(U, \varphi)$ be a smooth chart on $M$ containing $p$ and $(V, \psi)$ be a smooth chart on $N$ with $F(U) \subseteq V$. Since $M$ has no boundary, we know that $\widehat{U} \coloneqq \varphi(U)$ is open in $\mathbb{R}^n$.\retTwo

	Yet now note that $\widehat{F} \coloneqq \psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is a $C^k$ map from $\widehat{U}$ into $\mathbb{R}$ such that $\Df \widehat{F}(\varphi(p))$ is invertible. It follows by the inverse function theorem in my math 140c notes that there are open sets $\widehat{U}_0$ and $\widehat{V}_0$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ such that $\varphi(p) \in \widehat{U}_0 \subseteq \widehat{U}$ and $\widehat{F}$ is a bijection from $\widehat{U}_0$ to $\widehat{V}_0$. So $(\psi|_{\psi^{-1}(\widehat{V}_0)}, \psi^{-1}(\widehat{V}_0))$ is an interior chart on $N$ containing $F(p)$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\pracOne\mySepTwo

\hTwo\dispDate{7/23/2026}

\pracOne \hypertarget{page 1057 tangent}{To} start off, it's been bugging me for several days that I don't have a way of talking about tangent spaces to corner points of $C^r$ manifolds (where $r < \infty$). So I'm going to bodge a solution. I am not getting this construction from any resources though so I'm sorry if my construction disagrees with a better solution.\retTwo

Let $M$ be a $C^r$ manifold with a corner point $p$. Then we define $\mathcalli{C}(M, p)$ and $\mathcalli{V}_p M$ as on \inLinkRap{Page 1046 reference}{page 1046}. Also, we let $\mathcalli{D}_p M$ denote the space of derivations at $p$ from $C^1(M, \mathbb{R})$ to $\mathbb{R}$. Now for any $\gamma \in \mathcalli{C}(M, p)$ we know $D_\gamma: C^1(M, \mathbb{R}) \to \mathbb{R}$ given by $D_\gamma(f) \coloneqq (f \circ \gamma)^\prime(0)$ is a well-defined derivation at $p$. Also, we know by the definition of the equivalence classes in $\mathcalli{V}_p(M)$ that $[\gamma_1] = [\gamma_2]$ in $\mathcalli{V}_p$ if and only if $D_{\gamma_1} = D_{\gamma_2}$.\retTwo
\begin{myIndent}
	\ul{Lemma:} Let $S \coloneqq \{D_\gamma : [\gamma] \in \mathcalli{V}_p M\}$. Then let $T_p M$ be the subspace of $\mathcalli{D}_p M$ spanned by $S$.
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item[(a)] If $M$ is an $n$-dimensional manifold then $T_p M$ is also $n$-dimensional.
		\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
			Proof:\\
			Let $(U, \varphi)$ be a smooth chart on $M$ containing $p$, and then recall for any\\ $f \in C^1(M, \mathbb{R})$ and $[\gamma] \in \mathcalli{V}_p M$ that:

			{\centering $\Df_\gamma(f) = (f \circ \gamma)^\prime(0) = \nabla(f \circ \varphi^{-1})(\varphi(p)) \cdot (\varphi \circ \gamma)^\prime(0)$ \retTwo\par}

			Now suppose $\gamma_1, \ldots, \gamma_{n+1}$ are all in $\mathcalli{C}(M, p)$. Then for any $c_1, \ldots, c_{n+1}$\\ we have that:

			{\centering $\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n+1} c_i D_{\gamma_i}\right)(f) = \nabla(f \circ \varphi^{-1})(\varphi(p)) \cdot \left( \sum_{i=1}^{n+1} c_i(\varphi \circ \gamma_i)^\prime(0)\right)$ \retTwo\par}

			Yet because $\mathbb{R}^n$ is an $n$-dimensional vector space, we know there exists\\ $c_1, \ldots, c_{n+1}$ which aren't all zero such that $\sum_{i=1}^{n+1} c_i(\varphi \circ \gamma_i)^\prime(0) = 0 \in \mathbb{R}^n$.\newpage And then we'll have $\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n+1} c_i D_{\gamma_i}\right)(f) = \nabla(f \circ \varphi^{-1})(\varphi(p)) \cdot 0 = 0$ for all $f \in C^1(M, \mathbb{R})$. This proves that $\dim(T_p M) \leq n$.\retTwo

			As for the other inequality, note that because $\varphi(U)$ is open in $(\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0})^n$, we can guarentee if $e_1, \ldots, e_n$ is the standard basis for $\mathbb{R}^n$ then there exists $R > 0$ with $\varphi(p) + te_i \in \varphi(U)$ for all $t \in [0, R]$ and each $i$. So, I define $\gamma_i: [0, R] \to M$ by $\gamma(t) \coloneqq \varphi^{-1}(\varphi(p) + te_i)$. Then for any $c_1, \ldots, c_n$ we have that:

			{\centering $\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i D_{\gamma_i}\right)(f) = \nabla(f \circ \varphi^{-1})(\varphi(p)) \cdot (c_1, \ldots, c_n)$ \retTwo\par}

			At last, we just need to show that if $\mVecAst{c} \coloneqq (c_1, \ldots, c_n) \neq 0$ then there exists some $f \in C^1(M, \mathbb{R})$ with $\nabla(f \circ \varphi^{-1})(\varphi(p)) \cdot \mVecAst{c} \neq 0$. Fortunately, we know from the proof of the lemma on \inLinkRap{Lemma page 1047}{page 1047} how to go a step further and find $f \in C^r(M, \mathbb{R})$ with $\nabla(f \circ \varphi^{-1})(\varphi(p)) \cdot \mVecAst{c} \neq 0$. Therefore:
			\begin{itemize}
				\item $D_{\gamma_1}, \ldots, D_{\gamma_n}$ is a collection of linearly independent vectors in $S \subseteq \mathcalli{D}_p M$.
				\item If we restrict the domains of all the derivations in $T_p M$ to just $C^r(M, \mathbb{R})$ then we still have that $D_{\gamma_1}, \ldots, D_{\gamma_n}$ are linearly independent vectors.\retTwo
			\end{itemize}
		\end{myIndent}

		\item[(b)] Let $F: M \to N$ be a $C^1$ map. Then let $S^\prime \coloneqq \{D_\gamma : [\gamma] \in \mathcalli{V}_{F(p)} N\}$ and let $T_{F(p)} N$ be the subspace of $\mathcalli{D}_{F(p)} N$ spanned by $S^\prime$.
		\begin{myIndent}\color{red}
			[Note that if $F(p)$ is not a corner point of $N$, then this definition agress with our definition from \inLinkRap{Page 1051 reference}{page 1051} because $T_{F(p)}N$ would equal $S^\prime$].\retTwo
		\end{myIndent}
		
		Now define $\df F_p : \mathcalli{D}_p M \to \mathcalli{D}_{F(p)}N$ by $\df F_p(v)f \coloneqq v(f \circ F)$. Then we have that $\df F_p(T_p M) \subseteq T_{F(p)}N$.
		\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
			Proof:\\
			It suffices to show that $\df F_p(S) \subseteq S^\prime$. Fortunately, given any $D_\gamma \in S$ we have that $\df F_p (D_{\gamma})f = D_\gamma(f \circ F) = (f \circ F \circ \gamma)^\prime(0) = D_{F \circ \gamma} f$. Therefore\\ $\df F_p (D_{\gamma}) = D_{F \circ \gamma} \in S^\prime$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
		\end{myIndent}
	\end{enumerate}
\end{myIndent}

Based on the prior lemma, we now have a way of defining $T_p M$ when $p$ is a corner point. Also by part (b), we know that the differential of $F: M \to N$ at $p$ gives a well defined linear map $T_p M \to T_{F(p)}N$.\retTwo

The proofs for propositions 3.6, 3.8, and 3.9 on pages \inLinkRap{Proposition 3.6 page 1031}{1031} and \inLinkRap{page 1033 reference}{1033-1034} can now be repeated verbatim for our modified definition of $T_p M$ for when $p$ is a corner chart and $M$ is a $C^r$ manifold with $r \neq \infty$ necessarily. Similarly, nothing on \inLinkRap{page 1051-1053 reference}{pages 1051-1053} breaks down with our definition for this special case either. Finally, proposition 4.1 on \inLinkRap{Proposition 4.1 pages 1054-1056}{pages\\ 1054-1056} as well as exercise 4-2 on the prior page still work by identical reasoning.\retTwo

And with that I'll now allow my manifolds to have corners again by default.\retTwo

\mySepTwo 

\hTwo Next, I want to talk about product manifolds. Let $M_1, \ldots, M_k$ be $C^r$-manifolds of\\ dimensions $n_1, \ldots, n_k$ respectively. Then let $M \coloneqq M_1 \times \cdots \times M_k$ be their product\\ manifold, and for each $i$ let $\pi_i: M \to M_i$ be the projection map $(p_1, \ldots, p_k) \mapsto p_i$.\newpage
\begin{myIndent}\myComment
	Remark: Given any finite collection of $C^r$ manifolds $M_1, \ldots, M_k$ with corners, the standard product $C^r$-structure on $M \coloneqq M_1 \times \cdots \times M_k$ defined on \inLinkRap{proposition bottom of page 1038}{page 1038} is still well-defined. Furthermore, the proof of the proposition on \inLinkRap{proposition on page 1039}{page 1039} still works verbatim. Thus the category of $C^r$ manifolds with corners (which I'll denote $\mcateg{Diff}^r_c$) does admit products over any finite collection of objects. In particular, we can see that $(p_1, \ldots, p_k)$ is a corner point of $M$ if at least one $p_i$ is a corner point of $M_i$ or there are two components $p_i$ and $p_j$ which are boundary points of $M_i$ and $M_j$ respectively.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\exTwo\ul{Proposition 3.14:} \hypertarget{Proposition 3.14 page 1059}{Let} $p = (p_1, \ldots, p_k) \in M$. Then the map $\alpha: T_p M \to \bigoplus_{i=1}^k T_{p_i}M_i$ defined by $\alpha(v) \coloneqq (\df (\pi_1)_p (v), \ldots, \df (\pi_k)_p (v))$ is an isomorphism.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	For each $i$ let us define $\iota_i: M_i \to M$ by $\iota_i(q) \coloneqq (p_1, \ldots, p_{i-1}, q, p_{i+1}, \ldots, p_k)$. Then, we define $\beta: \bigoplus_{i=1}^k T_{p_i}M_i \to T_p M$ by $\beta(v_1, \ldots, v_k) \coloneqq \sum_{i=1}^k \df (\iota_i)_{p_i}(v_i)$. I claim that\\ $\beta = \alpha^{-1}$. To see why, first note that:

	{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
		$(\alpha \circ \beta)(v_1, \ldots, v_k) = \alpha\left(\sum\limits_{i=1}^k \df (\iota_i)_{p_i}(v_i)\right)$\\ [12pt]
		$\phantom{(\alpha \circ \beta)(v_1, \ldots, v_k)} = \left(\df (\pi_1)_p\left(\sum\limits_{i=1}^k \df (\iota_i)_{p_i}(v_i)\right), \ldots, \df (\pi_k)_p\left(\sum\limits_{i=1}^k \df (\iota_i)_{p_i}(v_i)\right)\right)$\\ [16pt]
		$\phantom{(\alpha \circ \beta)(v_1, \ldots, v_k)} = \left(\sum\limits_{i=1}^k\df (\pi_1)_p(\df (\iota_i)_{p_i}(v_i)), \ldots, \sum\limits_{i=1}^k\df (\pi_k)_p(\df (\iota_i)_{p_i}(v_i))\right)$\\ [16pt]
		$\phantom{(\alpha \circ \beta)(v_1, \ldots, v_k)} = \left(\sum\limits_{i=1}^k\df (\pi_1 \circ \iota_i)_{p_i}(v_i), \ldots, \sum\limits_{i=1}^k\df (\pi_k \circ \iota_i)_{p_i}(v_i)\right)$
	\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

	But now $\pi_j \circ \iota_i$ is a constant map if $j \neq i$. As a result, if $v \in T_{p_i}M_i$ and $f \in C^1(M_j, \mathbb{R})$ then $f \circ \pi_j \circ \iota_i$ is a constant function from $M_i$ to $\mathbb{R}$ and in turn:
	
	{\centering$\df (\pi_j \circ \iota_i)_{p_i}(v_i)f = v_i(f \circ \pi_j \circ \iota_i) = 0$.\retTwo\par}
	
	Since $f$ was arbitrary, this shows that if $j \neq i$ then $\df (\pi_j \circ \iota_i)_{p_i}(v)$ is the zero map. And since $v$ was arbitary, we can conclude $\df (\pi_j \circ \iota_i)_{p_i}$ is also the zero map. Meanwhile, $\pi_i \circ \iota_i = \myId_{M_i}$. Hence, we can conclude that:

	{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
		$\left(\sum\limits_{i=1}^k\df (\pi_1 \circ \iota_i)_{p_i}(v_i), \ldots, \sum\limits_{i=1}^k\df (\pi_k \circ \iota_i)_{p_i}(v_i)\right) = (\df (\myId_{M_1})_{p_1}(v_1), \ldots, \df (\myId_{M_k})_{p_k}(v_k))$\\ [6pt]
		$\phantom{\left(\sum\limits_{i=1}^k\df (\pi_1 \circ \iota_i)_{p_i}(v_i), \ldots, \sum\limits_{i=1}^k\df (\pi_k \circ \iota_i)_{p_i}(v_i)\right)} = (v_1, \ldots, v_k)$.
	\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

	With that, we've proven that $\beta$ is a right inverse of $\alpha$. Based on the fact that $\alpha$ has a right inverse, we know that $\alpha$ is a surjective linear map. And since $T_p M$ and $\bigoplus_{i=1}^k T_{p_i}M_i$ are both $(n_1 + \ldots + n_k)$-dimensional vector spaces and $\alpha$ is a linear map, we can conclude more strongly that $\alpha$ must be a bijection. And finally, any right inverse of a bijective function must also be a left inverse. Therefore, $\beta = \alpha^{-1}$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo The map $\alpha$ in the prior proposition is taken to define a standard identification between $T_p M$ and $\bigoplus_{i=1}^k T_{p_i}M_i$.\retTwo

\mySepTwo\newpage

\dispDate{7/24/2026}

\exTwo\ul{Proposition 4.6 (Properties of local $C^k$-diffeomorphisms):}
\begin{enumerate}
	\item[(a)] \hypertarget{Properties of local $C^k$-diffeomorphisms page 1060}{Let} $M, N, P$ be $C^r$ manifolds and suppose $k \leq r$. If $F: M \to N$ and $G: N \to P$ are local $C^k$-diffeomorphisms, then so is $G \circ F: M \to P$.
	\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
		Why?\\
		Consider any $p \in M$. Since $F$ is a local $C^k$-diffeomorphism, we know there exists an open set $U \subseteq M$ containing $p$ and an open set $V \subseteq N$ such that $F|_U$ is a $C^k$-diffeomorphism from $U$ to $V$. Next, since $G$ is a local $C^k$-diffeomorphism, we know that there is an open set $V^\prime \subseteq N$ containing $F(p)$ and an open set $W^\prime \subseteq P$ such that $G|_{V^\prime}$ is a $C^k$-diffeomorphism from $V^\prime$ to $W^\prime$. And now we set $V_0 \coloneqq V \cap V^\prime$, $W_0 \coloneqq G(V_0)$, and $U_0 \coloneqq F^{-1}(V_0) \cap U$. We know that $U_0$ and $W_0$ are open sets in $M$ and $P$ respectively, that $p \in U_0$, and that $(G \circ F)$ is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism from $U_0$ to $W_0$.
	\end{myIndent}

	\item[(b)] Suppose $M_1, \ldots, M_k$ are $C^r$ manifolds with $M \coloneqq M_1 \times \cdots \times M_k$, $N_1, \ldots, N_k$ are also $C^r$ manifolds with $N \coloneqq N_1 \times \cdots \times N_k$, and $F_i : M_i \to N_i$ is a local $C^s$ diffeomorphism for all $1 \leq i \leq k$ (where $s \leq r$). Then $F_1 \times \cdots \times F_k : M \to N$ is a local $C^s$ diffeomorphism.
	\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
		Why?\\
		Let $(p_1, \ldots, p_k)$ be any point in $M$. For each $i$ we can pick open sets $U_i \subseteq M_i$\\ containing $p$ and $V_i \subseteq N_i$ such that $F|_{U_i}: U_i \to V_i$ is a $C^s$ diffeomorphism.\\ And now $U \coloneqq U_1 \times \cdots \times U_k$ is an open subset of $M$ containing $(p_1, \ldots, p_k)$\\ and $V \coloneqq V_1 \times \cdots V_k$ is an open subset of $N$. I claim $F \coloneqq F_1 \times \cdots \times F_k$ is a\\ $C^s$ diffeomorphism from $U$ to $V$. This is because of the following lemma.\retTwo

		\ul{Lemma:} Suppose $M_1, \ldots, M_k$ are $C^r$ manifolds with $M \coloneqq M_1 \times \cdots \times M_k$,\\ $N_1, \ldots, N_k$ are also $C^r$ manifolds with $N \coloneqq N_1 \times \cdots \times N_k$, and $F_i : M_i \to N_i$ is a $C^s$ diffeomorphism for all $1 \leq i \leq k$. Then $F_1 \times \cdots \times F_k : M \to N$ is a $C^s$ diffeomorphism.
		\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
			Proof:\\
			It's incredibly straightforward to show that $F_1 \times \cdots \times F_k$ is a $C^s$ map. Also, for each $i$ let $G_i$ be the inverse map of $F_i$. Then as each $G_i$ is $C^s$, we can conclude by identical reasoning that $G_1 \times \cdots \times G_k: N \to M$ is a $C^s$ map. And also it is easy to check that 
			
			{\centering$G_1 \times \cdots \times G_k = (F_1 \times \cdots \times F_k)^{-1}$.\retTwo\par}
		\end{myIndent}
	\end{myIndent}

	\item[(c)] Let $M$ and $N$ be $C^r$ manifolds, and suppose $F: M \to N$ is a local $C^k$ diffeomorphism (where $k \leq r$). Then $F$ is a local homeomorphism and an open map.
	\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
		Proof:\\
		Since diffeomorphisms are homeomorphisms, the first claim should be obvious. Next suppose $U \subseteq M$ is any open set. Then for any $p \in U$ we need to prove that $F(p)$ is in the interior of $F(U)$. Fortunately, as $F$ is a local diffeomorphism we know there exists an open set $U_p \subseteq M$ containing $p$ and an open set $V_p \subseteq N$ such that $F|_{U_p}: U_p \to V_p$\newpage is a diffeomorphism. Next, as $U \cap U_p$ is an open subset of $U_p$, we know $F|_{U_p}(U \cap U_p)$ must be an open subset of $V_p$. So, $V \coloneqq V_p \cap F(U \cap U_p)$ is an open set in $N$ which is contained in $F(U)$. Also, $F(p) \in V$. $\blacksquare$
	\end{myIndent}
\end{enumerate}

\hTwo I'm bored and don't want to prove anymore parts of the prior proposition. So I'm moving on.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Proposition 4.8:} \hypertarget{Proposition 4.8 page 1061}{Suppose} $M$ is $C^r$ manifold without a boundary, $N$ is any other $C^r$\\ manifold, and $F: M \to N$ is a $C^k$ function (where $k \leq r$).
\begin{enumerate}
	\item[(a)] $F$ is a local $C^k$-diffeomorphism if and only if it is both an immersion and submersion.
	\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
		$(\Longrightarrow)$\\
		Given any $p \in M$, there is an open set $U \subseteq M$ containing $p$ such that $F(U)$ is an open set and $F$ is a $C^k$-diffeomorphism from $U$ to $F(U)$. But then in turn we must have that $\df (F|_{U})_p : T_p U \to T_{F(p)}(F(U))$ is an invertible map. Equivalently, this means that $\df F_p : T_p M \to T_p N$ is invertible. And since was $p$ was arbitrary, we can conclude that $\mRank(F) = \dim(M) = \dim(N)$. This shows that $F$ is an immersion and a submersion.\retTwo

		$(\Longleftarrow)$\\
		Conversely, suppose $F$ is an immersion and a submersion. Then we must have that $\df F_p$ is invertible for all $p \in M$. By the inverse function theorem for manifolds as well as exercise 4-2 on \inLinkRap{Theorem 4.5 page 1056}{pages 1056-1057}, we thus know that $F(M) \subseteq \Int(N)$ and $F$ is a local $C^k$-diffeomorphism.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	\item[(b)] If $\dim(M) = \dim(N)$ and $F$ is either an immersion or submersion, then $F$ is a local $C^k$-diffeomorphism. 
	\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
		Why?\\
		If $\dim(M) = \dim(N)$ then $F$ is an immersion if and only if $F$ is a submersion. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
\end{enumerate}

\Hstatement\ul{Exercise 4.10:} \hypertarget{Exercise 4.10 page 1061}{Suppose} $M$, $N$, and $P$ are $C^r$ manifolds and $F: M \to N$ is a local $C^k$\\ diffeomorphism.
\begin{enumerate}
	\item[(a)] If $G: P \to M$ is a continuous map then $G$ is $C^k$ if and only if $F \circ G$ is $C^k$.
	\begin{myIndent}\HexOne
		$(\Longrightarrow)$\\
		This is obvious.\retTwo

		$(\Longleftarrow)$\\
		Let $p \in P$. Since $F \circ G$ is $C^k$, we know that there are smooth charts $(U, \varphi)$ on $P$\\ [1pt]containing $p$ and $(V, \psi)$ on $N$ with $(F \circ G)(U) \subseteq V$ and $\psi \circ F \circ G \circ \varphi^{-1}$ a $C^k$\\ map. Next, because $F$ is a local $C^k$ diffeomorphism we know that there are open\\ [2pt] sets $W^\prime \subseteq M$ containing $G(p)$ and $V^\prime \subseteq N$ such that $F$ is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism\\ [1pt] from $W^\prime$ to $V^\prime$. By shrinking $W^\prime$ and $V^\prime$, we can assume without loss of generality\\ [2pt] that $V^\prime \subseteq V$ and that there is a smooth chart $(W^\prime, \eta)$ on $M$. Finally, because $G$\\ is continuous, we know that $U^\prime \coloneqq G^{-1}(W^\prime)$ is an open set of $P$. So, we set\\ $U_0 \coloneqq U \cap U^\prime$.\newpage

		Let $H = (F|_{W^\prime})^{-1}$. Then $(U_0, \varphi)$ is a smooth chart on $P$ containing $p$, $(W^\prime, \eta)$ is a smooth chart on $M$ with $G(U_0) \subseteq W^\prime$, and:
		
		{\centering$\eta \circ G \circ \varphi^{-1} = (\eta \circ H \circ \psi^{-1}) \circ (\psi \circ F \circ G \circ \varphi^{-1})$ is a $C^k$ map.\retTwo\par}
	\end{myIndent}

	\item[(b)] If $F$ is surjective and $G: N \to P$ is any map, then $G$ is $C^k$ if and only if $G \circ F$ is $C^k$.
	\begin{myIndent}\HexOne
		$(\Longrightarrow)$\\
		Again this is obvious.\retTwo

		$(\Longleftarrow)$\\
		Consider any $p \in N$. Since $F$ is surjective, we know there exists $q \in M$ such that\\ [2pt] $F(q) = p$. Next, since $G \circ F$ is a $C^k$ map, we know there is a smooth chart $(U, \varphi)$\\ [2pt] on $M$ containing $q$ and a smooth chart $(V, \psi)$ on $P$ such that $(G \circ F)(U) \subseteq V$ and $\psi \circ G \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is a $C^k$ map. But now as $F$ is a local $C^k$ diffomorphism, we can\\ [2pt] find an open set $U^\prime \subseteq M$ containing $q$ and an open set $W^\prime \subseteq N$ such that $F$ is a $C^k$\\ [2pt] diffeomorphism from $U^\prime$ to $W^\prime$. Finally, by shrinking $U^\prime$ and $W^\prime$, we can assume that\\ [2pt] $U^\prime \subseteq U$ and that there is a smooth chart $(W^\prime, \eta)$ on $N$.\retTwo

		Now $W^\prime$ is an open set containing $p = F(q)$ with $G(W^\prime) = (G \circ F)(U^\prime)$\\ $\subseteq (G \circ F)(U) \subseteq V$. Also let $H = (F|_{U^\prime})^{-1}$. Then:

		{\centering $\psi \circ G \circ \eta^{-1} = (\psi \circ G \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1}) \circ (\varphi \circ H \circ \eta^{-1})$ is a $C^k$ map. $\blacksquare$\retTwo\par}
	\end{myIndent}
\end{enumerate}

\exTwo\ul{Theorem 4.12 (The Rank Theorem):} \hypertarget{The Rank Theorem}{Suppose} $M$ and $N$ are $C^k$ manifolds \textit{without}\\ \textit{boundaries} of dimension $m$ and $n$ respectively, and also suppose $F: M \to N$ is a $C^k$ map of constant rank $r$. Then for each $p \in M$ there exists a smooth chart $(U, \varphi)$ on $M$ with $p \in U$ as well as a smooth chart $(V, \psi)$ on $N$ with $F(U) \subseteq V$ such that $\varphi(p) = 0$ and $\widehat{F} \coloneqq \psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1}$ has the form $\widehat{F}(x_1, \ldots, x_r, x_{r+1}, \ldots, x_m) = (x_1, \ldots, x_r,\hspace{-0.5em} \underbrace{0, \ldots, 0}_{n-r \text{ many zeros}}\hspace{-0.5em})$.\retTwo
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	\begin{myIndent}\myComment
		As a side note, if $k_1 > k_2$ in $\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1} \cup \{\infty\}$ then every $C^{k_1}$ structure on a manifold $M$ is contained in a unique $C^{k_2}$ structure. Therefore, it's not too too restrictive to assume $F$ is as smooth a map as the structure on the manifold is smooth. That said, if I didn't make this restriction clear than one might falsely think that this theorem proves every constant rank $C^1$ map between $C^k$ manifolds without boundaries is actually a $C^k$ map.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Proof:\\
	\ul{(Step 0: Simplying our notation)}\\
	Firstly, by choosing local coordinates around $p$ it suffices to assume $M$ is an open set\\ $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ and $N$ is an open set $V \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.\newpage 
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		To see why, consider picking smooth charts $(\widetilde{U}, \widetilde{\varphi})$ on $M$ containing $p$ and $(\widetilde{V}, \widetilde{\psi})$ on $N$ such that $F(\widetilde{U}) \subseteq \widetilde{V}$. Then set $U \coloneqq  \widetilde{\varphi}(\widetilde{U})$ and $V \coloneqq \widetilde{\psi}(\widetilde{V})$ and note that $U$ and $V$ are open in $\mathbb{R}^m$ and $\mathbb{R}^n$ respectively. Once we've shown that the theorem holds for $\widetilde{\psi} \circ F \circ (\widetilde{\varphi})^{-1}: U \to V$, then we can just find two $C^k$ diffeomorphisms\\ [2pt] $\varphi: U_0 \to \varphi(U_0)$ and $\psi: V_0 \to \psi(V_0)$ such that $\widetilde{\varphi}(p) \subseteq U_0 \subseteq U$, $V_0 \subseteq V$, $\varphi(\widetilde{\varphi}(p)) = 0$,  and $\widetilde{\psi} \circ F \circ (\widetilde{\varphi})^{-1}(U_0) \subseteq V_0$, and $(\psi \circ \widetilde{\psi}) \circ F \circ ((\widetilde{\varphi})^{-1} \circ \varphi^{-1})$ has the desired form. And since $(\widetilde{\varphi}^{-1}(U_0), \varphi \circ \widetilde{\varphi})$ is a smooth chart on $M$, $(\widetilde{\psi}^{-1}(V_0), \psi \circ \widetilde{\psi})$ is a smooth chart on $N$, we'll have shown our theorem holds at $p$ for the map $F$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Next, note that since $\Df F(p)$ has rank $r$, we know the Jacobian matrix has some\\ $r \times r$ invertible submatrix. By reordering our coordinates, we can assume without loss\\ of generality that the $r \times r$ invertible submatrix makes up the top left portion of $\Df F(p)$.\\ So, let us rename the standard coordinates on $\mathbb{R}^m$ and $\mathbb{R}^n$ as:
	
	{\centering$(x, y) \coloneqq (x_1, \ldots, x_r, y_{r+1}, \ldots, y_m)$ and $(v, w) \coloneqq (v_1, \ldots, v_r, w_{r+1}, \ldots, w_n)$.\retTwo\par}

	By applying a translation to the open sets $U$ and $V$, we can without loss of generality\\ assume $p = (0, 0)$ and $F(p) = (0, 0)$. Also, we write $F(x, y) \coloneqq (Q(x, y), R(x, y))$\\ where $Q: U \to \mathbb{R}^r$ and $R: U \to \mathbb{R}^{n - r}$ are $C^k$ functions. Therefore:

	$$\Df F(0, 0) = \begin{bmatrix} \left[\frac{\partial Q_i}{\partial x_j}(0, 0)\right]_{\substack{1 \leq i \leq r \\ 1 \leq j \leq r}}\phantom{1} & \left[\frac{\partial Q_i}{\partial y_j}(0, 0)\right]_{\substack{1 \leq i \leq r \\ r+1 \leq j \leq m}} \\ 
	\left[\frac{\partial R_i}{\partial x_j}(0, 0)\right]_{\substack{1 \leq i \leq n - r \\ 1 \leq j \leq r}} & \left[\frac{\partial R_i}{\partial y_j}(0, 0)\right]_{\substack{1 \leq i \leq n - r \\ r+1 \leq j \leq m}}\end{bmatrix}$$ 

	where $\left[\frac{\partial Q_i}{\partial x_j}(0, 0)\right]_{\substack{1 \leq i \leq r \\ 1 \leq j \leq r}}$ is an invertible matrix.\retTwo 

	\ul{(Step 1: Getting $\varphi$)}\\
	Now define $\varphi: U \to \mathbb{R}^m$ by $\varphi(x, y) = (Q(x, y), y)$. This will be $C^k$ map whose total derivative is given by:

	$$\Df \varphi(x, y) = \begin{bmatrix} \left[\frac{\partial Q_i}{\partial x_j}(x, y)\right]_{\substack{1 \leq i \leq r \\ 1 \leq j \leq r}} & \left[\frac{\partial Q_i}{\partial y_j}(x, y)\right]_{\substack{1 \leq i \leq r \\ r+1 \leq j \leq m}} \\ \mMat{0} & \mMat{I}_{m - r} \end{bmatrix}$$ 

	where $\mMat{I}_{m - r}$ is the $(m - r) \times (m - r)$ identity matrix. Importantly, we can specifically see that all the columns of $\Df \varphi(0, 0)$ are linearly independent. Hence, $\Df \varphi(0, 0)$ is invertible. And by the inverse function theorem we know there are connected open sets $U_0 \subseteq U$ and $\widehat{U}_0 \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ satisfying that $(0, 0) \in U_0$, $\varphi(0, 0) = (0, 0) \in \widehat{U}_0$, and $\varphi: U_0 \to \widehat{U}_0$ is a\\ $C^k$-diffeomorphism. By shrinking $U_0$ and $\widehat{U}_0$ we can without loss of generality assume\\ that $\widehat{U}_0 = (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)^{m}$ for some $\varepsilon > 0$.\retTwo

	Now we write the inverse map $\varphi^{-1}: \widehat{U}_0 \to U_0$ as $\varphi^{-1}(x, y) = (A(x, y), B(x, y))$ where $A: \widehat{U}_0 \to \mathbb{R}^r$ and $B: \widehat{U}_0 \to \mathbb{R}^{m-r}$ are $C^k$ maps. Importantly, we know that:
	
	{\center$(x, y) = \varphi(A(x, y), B(x, y)) = (Q(A(x, y), B(x, y)),\hspace{0.2em} B(x, y))$\retTwo\par}

	By comparing $y$-components we can see that $B(x, y) = y$. Hence, $\varphi^{-1}$ has the form\newpage $\varphi^{-1}(x, y) = (A(x, y),\hspace{0.2em} y)$. Meanwhile, by comparing $x$-components we can see that\\ $x = Q(A(x, y), \hspace{0.2em} y)$. Therefore, upon letting $\widetilde{R}(x, y) \coloneqq R(A(x, y), y)$ then we have\\ that:

	{\centering $(F \circ \varphi^{-1})(x, y) = (x,\hspace{0.2em} \widetilde{R}(x, y))$ \retTwo\par}

	\ul{(Step 2: Simplifying $\widetilde{R}$)}\\
	Consider that the Jacobian matrix of $F \circ \varphi^{-1}$ at any $(x, y) \in \widehat{U}_0 = (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)^m$ is given by:

	$$\Df (F \circ \varphi^{-1})(x, y) = \begin{bmatrix} \mMat{I}_r & \mMat{0} \\ \left[\frac{\partial \widetilde{R}_i}{\partial x_j}(x, y)\right]_{\substack{1 \leq i \leq n - r \\ 1 \leq j \leq r}} & \left[\frac{\partial \widetilde{R}_i}{\partial y_j}(x, y)\right]_{\substack{1 \leq i \leq n - r \\ r+1 \leq j \leq m}}\end{bmatrix}$$

	\phantom{.}\\
	Yet we also have that $\Df (F \circ \varphi^{-1})(x, y) = \Df F(\varphi^{-1}(x, y)) \Df (\varphi^{-1})(x, y)$. By assumption, we know that $\mRank(\Df F(\varphi^{-1}(x, y))) = r$ for all $(x, y) \in \widehat{U}_0$. Meanwhile, since $\varphi^{-1}$ is\\ a diffeomorphism, we know that $\Df (\varphi^{-1})(x, y)$ defines a bijective linear map for all\\ $(x, y) \in \widehat{U}_0$. It follows that $\mRank(\Df (F \circ \varphi^{-1})(x, y))$ will still equal $r$ for all $(x, y) \in \widehat{U}_0$.\retTwo

	Yet the only way this matrix:
	$$\begin{bmatrix} \mMat{I}_r & \mMat{0} \\ \left[\frac{\partial \widetilde{R}_i}{\partial x_j}(x, y)\right]_{\substack{1 \leq i \leq n - r \\ 1 \leq j \leq r}} & \left[\frac{\partial \widetilde{R}_i}{\partial y_j}(x, y)\right]_{\substack{1 \leq i \leq n - r \\ r+1 \leq j \leq m}}\end{bmatrix}\textit{,}$$
	can ever have rank $r$ is if $\left[\frac{\partial \widetilde{R}_i}{\partial y_j}(x, y)\right]_{\substack{1 \leq i \leq n - r \\ r+1 \leq j \leq m}} = \mMat{0}$.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		This is because the first $r$ columns are already linearly independent, and the\\ intersection of their span with the span of the last $m - r$ columns is just the\\ trivial subspace $\{0\}$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Consequently, we know that $\widetilde{R}$ must be constant with respect to $y$. In other words, there exists some $C^k$ map $S: (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)^r \to \mathbb{R}^{n - r}$ such that $\widetilde{R}(x, y) = S(x)$. And with that, we can write:

	{\centering $(F \circ \varphi^{-1})(x, y) = (x, S(x))$\retTwo\par}

	\ul{(Step 3: Getting $\psi$)}\\
	Let $V_0 \coloneqq \{(v, w) \in V : (v, 0) \in \widehat{U}_0\}$. Then $V_0$ will be an open subset of $V$ containing $F(0, 0) = (0, 0)$. Also because $\widehat{U}_0$ is a cube and $(F \circ \varphi^{-1})(x, y) = (x, S(x))$, we can see that $(F \circ \varphi^{-1})(\widehat{U}_0) \subseteq V_0$. (And this also implies $F(U_0) \subseteq V_0$).\retTwo

	To finish off, define $\psi: V_0 \to \mathbb{R}^n$ by $\psi(v, w) = (v, w - S(v))$. Then $\psi$ is a $C^k$ map which is also a diffeomorphism onto its image. After all, by the invariance of domain theorem we know its image is an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$. Also, its inverse map is precisely given by $\psi(v, w) = (v, w + S(v))$.\retTwo

	And now just note that $(\psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1})(x, y) = \psi(x, S(x)) = (x, S(x) - S(x)) = (x, 0)$. $\blacksquare$\newpage
\end{myIndent}

\exTwo\ul{Corollary 4.13:} Let $M$ and $N$ be $C^k$ manifolds without boundaries and let $F: M \to N$ be a $C^k$ map. Also suppose $M$ is connected. The following are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}
	\item[(a)] For each $p \in M$ there exists smooth charts $(U, \varphi)$ on $M$ and $(V, \psi)$ on $N$ with $p \in U$, $F(U) \subseteq V$, and $\widehat{F} \coloneqq \psi \circ F \circ \varphi$ a linear map.
	\item[(b)] $F$ has constant rank.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Firstly suppose (a) holds and for every $r \leq N \coloneqq \min(\dim(M), \dim(N))$ let $A_r \subseteq M$ be the set of all $p \in M$ at which $F$ has rank $r$. Trivially each $A_r$ is disjoint with $\bigcup_{r=0}^N A_r = M$. By (a) we also know each $A_r$ is an open set. By the connectedness of $M$ we can thus conclude there exists a single $r$ with $A_r = M$. So, $F$ has constant rank on $M$.\retTwo

	Conversely, if (b) is true than the rank theorem tells us how to find the smooth charts\\ described in (a). $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\ul{Theorem 4.14:} Let $M, N$ be $C^k$ manifolds without boundaries and let $F: M \to N$ be a $C^1$ map of constant rank.
\begin{enumerate}
	\item[(a)] If $F$ is surjective then $F$ is a submersion.
	\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
		Proof:\\
		Let $m = \dim(M)$ and $n = \dim(N)$, and suppose $F$ has constant rank $r$. We'll\\ suppose to the contrary that $F$ is \textit{not} a submersion. Thus $r < n$.\retTwo

		Now without loss of generality we can assume $k = 1$ (i.e. that $M$ and $N$ are $C^1$ manifolds).
		\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
			This is because the $C^k$ structures $\mathcal{A}_M$ and $\mathcal{A}_N$ that $M$ and $N$ are equipped\\ with are both contained in unique $C^1$ structures $\mathcalli{B}_M$ and $\mathcalli{B}_N$ respectively.\\ Furthemore, a map $f: M \to \mathbb{R}$ is $C^1$ with respect to $\mathcal{A}_M$ if and only if\\ it is $C^1$ with respect to $\mathcal{B}_M$. And a similar story holds for any $f: N \to \mathbb{R}$.\\ It follows that the tangents spaces to $M$ and $N$ stay identical when each is\\ equipped with either structure. In turn $F: (M, \mathcal{A}_M) \to (N, \mathcal{A}_N)$ is a\\ submersion if and only if $F: (M, \mathcal{B}_M) \to (N, \mathcal{B}_N)$ is a submersion.\retTwo
		\end{myIndent}

		Due to the prior reasoning, the rank theorem now applies. So, for all $p \in M$ there exists a smooth chart $(U_p, \varphi_p)$ on $M$ containing $p$ and a smooth chart $(V_p, \psi_p)$ on $N$ with $F(U_p) \subseteq V_p$ and $\widehat{F}_p: \psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1}$ having the form:
		
		{\centering$\widehat{F}_p(x_1, \ldots, x_r, x_{r+1}, \ldots, x_m) = (x_1, \ldots, x_r, \hspace{-0.75em}\underbrace{0, \ldots, 0}_{\text{nonzero }\#\text{ of zeros}}\hspace{-0.75em})$.\retTwo\par}

		Since $M$ is an LCH space, we can for each $p$ pick a precompact open set $W_p \subseteq M$\\ such that $p \in W_p \subseteq \overline{W_p} \subseteq U_p$. Then as $\overline{W_p}$ is compact and $N$ is Hausdorff, we\\ know that $F(\overline{W_p})$ is a closed subset of $N$ containing $F(W_p)$. Moreover, $F(\overline{W_p})$ has an empty interior. After all, let $\widehat{U}_{p} \coloneqq \varphi_{p}(U_p)$ and $\widehat{V}_{p} \coloneqq \psi_{p}(V_p)$. Then we have that $(\psi \circ F)(\overline{W_p}) \subseteq \widehat{F}_p(\widehat{U}_p) \subseteq (\text{ a hyperplane }) \cap \widehat{V}_p$. Since the latter set has an empty interior relative to $\widehat{V}_p$, we can conclude that $(\psi \circ F)(\overline{W_p})$ has an empty interior\newpage relative to $\widehat{V}_p$ as well. Then since $\psi$ is a homeomorphism from $V_p$ to $\widehat{V}_p$, we can\\ conclude that $F(\overline{W_p})$ has an empty interior relative to $V_p$. And since $F(\overline{W_p})$ is a closed subset of $N$ containing $F(W_p)$ and contained in $V_p$, we can finally conclude that $F(W_p)$ is nowhere dense.\retTwo
		
		But now to get our contradiction, note that because $M$ is second countable there must be a sequence $\{p_\ell\}_{\ell \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that $M = \bigcup_{\ell \in \mathbb{N}} W_{p_\ell}$. Since $F$ is surjective, we in turn know that $N = F(M) = \bigcup_{\ell \in \mathbb{N}}F(W_{p_\ell})$. So, we've proven that $N$ is a countable union of nowhere dense sets. In other words $N$ is meager. Yet $N$ is an LCH space and so this contradicts the Baire category theorem. [See \inLinkRap{placeholder}{pages 540-541}.]\retTwo 
	\end{myIndent}

	\item[(b)] If $F$ is injective then $F$ is an immersion.
	\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
		Proof:\\
		Let $m$, $n$, and $r$ be as in the prior proof, and this time suppose to the contrary that\\ $F$ is \textit{not} an immersion. For identical reasons as in the last proof, we can assume\\ without loss of generality that $k = 1$ (i.e. that $M$ and $N$ are $C^1$ manifolds). And this is important because it lets us apply the rank theorem.\retTwo 

		Consider any $p \in M$ and let $(U, \varphi)$ and $(V, \psi)$ be smooth charts on $M$ such that $p \in U$, $F(U) \subseteq V$, and $\widehat{F} \coloneqq \psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1}$ has the form:

		{\centering$\widehat{F}(x_1, \ldots, x_r, \hspace{-0.75em}\underbrace{x_{r+1}, \ldots, x_m}_{\text{nonzero }\#\text{ of coordinates}}\hspace{-0.5em}) = (x_1, \ldots, x_r, \hspace{-0.5em}\underbrace{0, \ldots, 0}_{n - r \text{ many zeros}}\hspace{-0.5em})$.\retTwo\par}

		But now $F$ being injective implies that $\widehat{F}$ is also injective. Simultaneously, write\\ $\varphi(p) = (p_1, \ldots, p_r, p_{r+1}, \ldots, p_m)$. Since $\varphi(U)$ is open in $\mathbb{R}^n$ we know for some\\ small enough $\varepsilon > 0$ that $\widehat{q} \coloneqq (p_1, \ldots, p_r, p_{r+1} + \varepsilon, \ldots, p_m) \in \varphi(U)$. But now if we let $q = \varphi^{-1}(q)$ we have that $(\psi \circ F)(p) = \widehat{F}(\varphi(p)) = \widehat{F}(\varphi(q)) = (\psi \circ F)(q)$. Since $\psi$ is injective, we in turn have that $F(p) = F(q)$. Yet $p \neq q$ since $\varphi^{-1}$ is injective. So, this all contradicts that $F$ is injective. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
\end{enumerate}

\exTwo\ul{Corollary:} \hypertarget{page 1066 corollary}{Let} $M, N$ be $C^r$ manifolds without boundaries and let $F: M \to N$ be a $C^k$ map of constant rank (where $k \leq r$). If $F$ is a bijection then $F$ is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	By the prior theorem, $F$ being a bijection means that $F$ is both a submersion and an\\ immersion. It then follows by proposition 4.8 on \inLinkRap{Proposition 4.8 page 1061}{page 1061} that $F$ is a local $C^k$\\ diffeomorphism. Yet finally, we can easily see by the pasting lemma that any local\\ $C^k$ diffeomorphism that is also bijective is a (global) $C^k$ diffeomorphism. So, $F$ is a $C^k$\\ diffeomorphism. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hypertarget{page 1066-1067 note}{I} mentioned a few days ago that my construction of the tangent space to a corner point might not be optimal. After talking to a colleague, I can now say that while nothing I've\newpage written is wrong, there is a cleaner equivalent way of defining the tangent space. This improved way will also be the way that generalizes to analytic and complex manifolds. So, it wouldn't hurt to go over it now.\retTwo

\pracOne\mySepTwo
\hypertarget{idk reference 6}{Firstly,} I'm going to fix an oversight I priorly made on \inLinkRap{page 1024 correction}{page 1024}. I already deleted the false statement on that page but I did leave a note explaining where my deleted remark went wrong.\retTwo

Firstly, since it will make my life easier and serve as a good review, I want to generalize the universal property of tensor products of module. Note that this will only use knowledge from math 200B.\retTwo

Given a collection of $A$-modules $M_1, \ldots, M_k$, we say their tensor product $\bigotimes_{i=1}^k M_i$ is an\\ $A$-module equipped with a $k$-linear map $\iota: \prod_{i=1}^k M_i \to \bigotimes_{i=1}^k M_i$ such that for any $k$-linear map $T: \prod_{i=1}^k M_i \to N$ the following diagram holds:\\ [-24pt]
% https://q.uiver.app/#
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	&&& {} \\
	&& {\bigotimes_{i=1}^k M_i} \\
	{} & {\prod_{i=1}^k M_i} & N \\
	{} &&& {}
	\arrow[""{name=0, anchor=center, inner sep=0}, "{m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_k \coloneqq \iota(m_1, \ldots, m_k)}"{description}, color={rgb,255:red,92;green,92;blue,214}, draw=none, from=2-3, to=1-4]
	\arrow["{\exists !f_T}", dashed, from=2-3, to=3-3]
	\arrow["\iota", from=3-2, to=2-3]
	\arrow["T"', from=3-2, to=3-3]
	\arrow[""{name=1, anchor=center, inner sep=0}, "{T(m_1, \ldots, m_k)}"{description}, color={rgb,255:red,92;green,92;blue,214}, draw=none, from=3-3, to=4-4]
	\arrow[""{name=2, anchor=center, inner sep=0}, "{(m_1, \ldots, m_k)}"{description}, color={rgb,255:red,92;green,92;blue,214}, draw=none, from=4-1, to=3-1]
	\arrow[draw={rgb,255:red,92;green,92;blue,214}, between={0.1}{0.9}, maps to, from=0, to=1]
	\arrow[draw={rgb,255:red,92;green,92;blue,214}, curve={height=-24pt}, between={0.1}{0.8}, maps to, from=2, to=0]
	\arrow[draw={rgb,255:red,92;green,92;blue,214}, between={0.2}{0.7}, maps to, from=2, to=1]
\end{tikzcd}\]

In math 200b I learned how to construct tensor products of $2$ modules and I also showed that $M_1 \otimes (M_2 \otimes M_3) \cong (M_1 \otimes M_2) \otimes M_3$. But for the sake of better notation and easier thinking, I want to be able to talk about tensor products of any finite number of modules. Fortunately, by standard reasoning we can see that any two $A$-modules satisfying the universal property in the above diagram are isomorphic.\retTwo

\ul{Lemma A:} \hypertarget{Page 1067 Lemma A}{Let} $k \geq 2$ and suppose $M_1, \ldots, M_k$ are all $A$-modules. Then there exists a\\ module $\bigotimes_{i=1}^k M_i$ and a $k$-linear map $\iota: \prod_{i=1}^k M_i \to \bigotimes_{i=1}^k M_i$ fulfilling the above universal property. Furthermore, $\iota(\prod_{i=1}^k M_i)$ is a generating / spanning set for $\bigotimes_{i=1}^k M_i$.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Proof:\\
	Our base case of $k = 2$ is already covered. So let us now proceed by induction and assume that we've already defined $\bigotimes_{i=2}^{k} M_i$ and $\overline{\iota}: \prod_{i=2}^{k} M_i \to \bigotimes_{i=2}^{k} M_i$. Then let's define\\ $M \coloneqq M_1 \otimes (\bigotimes_{i=2}^{k} M_i)$ and $\iota: \prod_{i=1}^k M_i \to M$ by:
	
	{\centering$\iota(m_1, \ldots, m_k) \coloneqq m_1 \otimes \overline{\iota}(m_2, \ldots, m_k)$.\retTwo\par}

	It's easy to see that $\iota$ is a $k$-linear map. Furthemore, suppose $T: \prod_{i=1}^k M_i \to N$ is any $k$-linear map. Then for any fixed $m_1 \in M_1$, we can see that $T_{m_1}: \prod_{i=2}^k M_i \to N$ defined by $T_{m_1}(m_2,\ldots, m_k) \coloneqq T(m_1, \ldots, m_k)$ is a well-defined $(k-1)$-linear map. So by the universal property of $\bigotimes_{i=2}^{k} M_i$ and $\overline{\iota}: \prod_{i=2}^{k} M_i \to \bigotimes_{i=2}^{k} M_i$, we know that there exists a unique $A$-module homomorphism $f_{m_1}: \bigotimes_{i=2}^{k} M_i \to N$ such that $f_{m_1} \circ \overline{\iota} = T_{m_1}$.\newpage

	Next, we define $S: M_1 \times (\bigotimes_{i=2}^{k} M_i) \to N$ by $S(m_1, t) \coloneqq f_{m_1}(t)$. Since each $f_{m_1}$ is $A$-linear, we know that $S$ is $A$-linear in its second variable. Meanwhile, note that:
	
	{\center\begin{tabular}{l}
		$f_{am_1 + a^\prime m_1^\prime}(\overline{\iota}(m_2, \ldots, m_k)) = T(am_1 + a^\prime m_1^\prime, m_2, \ldots, m_k)$\\ [3pt]
		$\phantom{f_{am_1 + a^\prime m_1^\prime}(\overline{\iota}(m_2, \ldots, m_k))} = aT(m_1, m_2, \ldots, m_k) + a^\prime T(m_1^\prime, m_2, \ldots, m_k)$\\ [3pt]
		$\phantom{f_{am_1 + a^\prime m_1^\prime}(\overline{\iota}(m_2, \ldots, m_k))} = af_{m_1}(\overline{\iota}(m_2, \ldots, m_k)) + a^\prime f_{m_1^\prime}(\overline{\iota}(m_2, \ldots, m_k))$.
	\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

	It follows $S$ is $A$-linear in its first variable if its second variable is contained in $\overline{\iota}(\prod_{i=2}^{k} M_i)$. And since $S$ is a $A$ linear in its second variable and $\overline{\iota}(\prod_{i=2}^{k} M_i)$ spans all of $\bigotimes_{i=2}^{k} M_i$, we\\ can in turn conclude that $S$ is $A$-linear in its first variable regardless of the value of its second variable. And with that we've shown $S$ is a bilinear map.\retTwo

	By the universal property of tensor products, we know there is a unique $A$-module\\ homomorphism $f_T: M_1 \otimes (\bigotimes_{i=2}^{k} M_i) \to N$ such that the below diagram commutes:\\ [-10pt]
	% https://q.uiver.app/#
	\[\begin{tikzcd}
		&&& {} & \\
		&& {M_1 \otimes (\bigotimes_{i=2}^k M_i)} \\
		{} & {M_1 \times (\bigotimes_{i=2}^k M_i)} & N \\
		{} &&&& {}
		\arrow[""{name=0, anchor=center, inner sep=0}, "{m_1 \otimes t}"{description}, color={rgb,255:red,92;green,92;blue,214}, draw=none, from=2-3, to=1-4]
		\arrow["{\exists !f_T}", dashed, from=2-3, to=3-3]
		\arrow[from=3-2, to=2-3]
		\arrow["S"', from=3-2, to=3-3]
		\arrow[""{name=1, anchor=center, inner sep=0}, "{f_{m_1}(t)}"{description}, color={rgb,255:red,92;green,92;blue,214}, draw=none, from=3-3, to=4-5]
		\arrow[""{name=2, anchor=center, inner sep=0}, "{(m_1, t)}"{description}, color={rgb,255:red,92;green,92;blue,214}, draw=none, from=4-1, to=3-1]
		\arrow[draw={rgb,255:red,92;green,92;blue,214}, between={0.1}{0.9}, maps to, from=0, to=1]
		\arrow[draw={rgb,255:red,92;green,92;blue,214}, curve={height=-30pt}, between={0.1}{0.9}, maps to, from=2, to=0]
		\arrow[draw={rgb,255:red,92;green,92;blue,214}, between={0.1}{0.9}, maps to, from=2, to=1]
	\end{tikzcd}\]

	I further claim that $f_T$ is the unique $A$-module homomorphism making this diagram\\ commute:
	% https://q.uiver.app/#q=WzAsMyxbMCwxLCJcXHByb2Rfe2k9MX1eayBNX2kiXSxbMSwwLCJNIl0sWzEsMSwiTiJdLFswLDIsIlQiLDJdLFswLDEsIlxcaW90YSJdLFsxLDIsImZfVCIsMCx7InN0eWxlIjp7ImJvZHkiOnsibmFtZSI6ImRhc2hlZCJ9fX1dXQ==
	\[\begin{tikzcd}
		& M \\
		{\prod_{i=1}^k M_i} & N
		\arrow["{f_T}", dashed, from=1-2, to=2-2]
		\arrow["\iota", from=2-1, to=1-2]
		\arrow["T"', from=2-1, to=2-2]
	\end{tikzcd}\]

	After all, the fact that this diagram commutes is simply because:

	{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
		$f_T(\iota(m_1, \ldots, m_k)) = f_T(m_1 \otimes \overline{\iota}(m_2, \ldots, m_k))$\\ [4pt]
		$\phantom{f_T(\iota(m_1, \ldots, m_k))} = S(m_1, \overline{\iota}(m_2, \ldots, m_k)) = f_{m_1}(\overline{\iota}(m_2, \ldots, m_k))$\\ [4pt]
		$\phantom{f_T(\iota(m_1, \ldots, m_k)) = S(m_1, \overline{\iota}(m_2, \ldots, m_k))} = T(m_1, m_2, \ldots, m_k)$.
	\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

	Meanwhile, if $g$ was another $A$-module homomorphism making the diagram commute, we'd similarly be able to say that:

	{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
		$g(m_1 \otimes \overline{\iota}(m_2, \ldots, m_k)) = g((\iota(m_1, \ldots, m_k)))$\\ [4pt]
		$\phantom{g(m_1 \otimes \overline{\iota}(m_2, \ldots, m_k))} = T(m_1, m_2, \ldots, m_k) = f_{m_1}(\overline{\iota}(m_2, \ldots, m_k))$\\ [4pt]
		$\phantom{g(m_1 \otimes \overline{\iota}(m_2, \ldots, m_k)) = T(m_1, m_2, \ldots, m_k)} = S(m_1, \overline{\iota}(m_2, \ldots, m_k))$.
	\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

	In turn since $g$ is $A$-linear and $\overline{\iota}(\prod_{i=2}^{k} M_i)$ spans all of $\bigotimes_{i=2}^{k} M_i$, we can conclude that $g(m_1 \otimes t) = S(m_1, t)$ for all $(m_1, t) \in  M_1 \times (\bigotimes_{i=2}^{k} M_i)$. By the uniqueness of $f_T$, we thus must have that $g = f_T$. And with that, we've proven that $M$ equipped with $\iota$ satisfies the universal property of a tensor product of $k$ many modules.\newpage

	To finish off the proof, we already know our construction of $M_1 \otimes (\bigotimes_{i=2}^{k} M_i)$ in math 200b that that space is spanned by pure tensors of the form $m_1 \otimes t$ where $t \in \bigotimes_{i=2}^{k} M_i$. So, we can write any arbitrary element in $M$ as a sum of pure tensors $\sum_{j=1}^\ell m_1^{(j)} \otimes t^{(j)}$.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		(And via $A$-balance I'm letting $m_1^{(j)}$ absorb any scalars in this sum.)\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	But by induction we can then write $t^{(j)} = \sum_{j^\prime = 1}^{r_j} \overline{\iota}(m_2^{(j, j^\prime)}, \ldots, m_k^{(j, j^\prime)})$ (where again I'm letting the $m_i^{(j, j^\prime)}$ absorb any of the scalars). So:

	{\center\begin{tabular}{l}
		$\sum_{j=1}^\ell m_1^{(j)} \otimes t^{(j)} = \sum_{j=1}^\ell \sum_{j^\prime = 1}^{r_j} m_1^{(j)} \otimes \overline{\iota}(m_2^{(j, j^\prime)}, \ldots, m_k^{(j, j^\prime)})$\\ [4pt]
		$\phantom{\sum_{j=1}^\ell m_1^{(j)} \otimes t^{(j)}} = \sum_{j=1}^\ell \sum_{j^\prime = 1}^{r_j} \iota(m_1^{(j)}, m_2^{(j, j^\prime)}, \ldots, m_k^{(j, j^\prime)})$. $\blacksquare$
	\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

	\begin{myIndent}\myComment
		As a side note: The prior proof can also be interpretted as saying that\\ $M_1 \otimes (M_2 \otimes (\cdots \otimes (M_{k-1} \otimes M_k)\cdots))$ along with the $k$-linear map\\ $\iota(m_1, \ldots, m_k) = m_1 \otimes (m_2 \otimes (\cdots \otimes (m_{k-1} \otimes m_k)\cdots))$ satisfies the\\ universal property of a tensor product of $k$ many $A$-modules.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
\end{myIndent}

\pracOne Note that we can by identical reasoning then prove an analogous proposition as on\\ \inLinkRap{pages}{pages 726-728} if $M_1, \ldots, M_k$ are $A$-algebras (albeit with more cumbersome notation).
\begin{myIndent}\myComment
	In other words, if $M_1, \ldots, M_k$ are $A$-algebras then $\bigotimes_{i=1}^k M_i$ is also an $A$-algebra when equipped with the multiplication operation:
	
	{\centering$(m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_k)(m_1^\prime \otimes \cdots \otimes m_k^\prime) = m_1m_1^\prime \otimes \ldots \otimes m_km_k^\prime$\retTwo\par}
\end{myIndent}

Similarly, given $A$-module homomorphisms $f_i: M_i \to M_i^\prime$ we can show identically as on \inLinkRap{placeholder}{page 700} that there is a unique $A$-module homomorphism $\bigotimes_{i=1}^k M_i \to \bigotimes_{i=1}^k M_i^\prime$ such\\ [1pt] that $f(m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_k) = f(m_1) \otimes \cdots \otimes f(m_k)$.\retTwo

\ul{Lemma B:} Suppose $N, M_1, \ldots, M_k$ are commutative $A$-algebras and $f_i: M_i \to N$ is an\\ $A$-algebra homomorphism for $1 \leq i \leq k$. Then there is a unique $A$-module\\ homomorphism $f: \bigotimes_{i=1}^k M_i \to N$ such that $f(m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_k) = \prod_{i=1}^k f_i(m_i)$.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Proof:\\
	To start off, if we define $T: \prod_{i=1}^k M_i \to N$ by $T(m_1, \ldots, m_k) = \prod_{i=1}^k f_i(m_i)$ then we can easily see that $T$ is $k$-linear. So by the universal property of $\bigotimes_{i=1}^k M_i$, we know there is a unique $A$-module homomorphism $f: \bigotimes_{i=1}^k M_i \to N$ such that:
	
	{\centering$f(m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_k) = \prod_{i=1}^k f_i(m_i)$.\retTwo\par}

	What we need to do now though is show that $f$ also happens to be algebra homomorphism. This is not difficult but involves a lot of tedious symbol pushing which I don't want to type out. $\blacksquare$
	\begin{myIndent}\myComment
		Another observation to make is that if each $f_i: M_i \to N$ is unital then\\ $f$ is also unital.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
\end{myIndent}

\begin{myIndent}\mySepThree\end{myIndent}

{\hTwo \dispDate{7/31/2026}\newpage}

This tangent has actually become significantly longer and deeper than I originally thought it would be. I just don't know enough about algebras. So at this point I'm going to start following the textbook \textit{Multilinear Algebra} by Douglas Northcott. See \inLinkRap{Citation 12}{citation 12} for\\ more information. Also I'm going to switch back to the normal color scheme.\retTwo

\hTwo For the time being, I'll let $R$ denote a fixed commutative unital ring. I'm letting $R$ as\\ opposed to $A$ denote the ring both because the ring I will care about eventually is just\\ $\mathbb{R}$ and also because this frees up $A$ to refer to an $R$-algebra.\retTwo

Let $A$ be an $R$-algebra (which doesn't have to be commutative). We say a family $\{A_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}$ of $R$-submodules of $A$ is a \udefine{grading} on $A$ if $A = \bigoplus_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}A_n$ as an internal direct sum of $R$-modules and $a_r \in A_r$ and $a_s \in A_s$ implies that $a_r a_s \in A_{r + s}$.
\begin{itemize}
	\item An $R$-algebra with a grading $\{A_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}$ is said to be a \udefine{graded $R$-algebra}. If all $A_n = \{0\}$ for $n < 0$ then we say our grading is \udefine{nonnegative}.
	\item Also any elements of $A_n$ are called \udefine{homogeneous of degree $n$}.
	\item By definition, any $a \in A$ can be written uniquely as $\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}a_n$ where each $a_n \in A$ and all but finitely many $a_n$ are zero. We call the $a_n$ in this sum the \udefine{homogeneous coefficients of $a$}.\retTwo
\end{itemize}

\exTwo\ul{Theorem 3.5:} Let $A$ be a unital graded $R$-algebra with the grading $\{A_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$. Then $1_A$ is\\ homogeneous of degree $0$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Let us write $1_A = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} a_n$ as a sum of the homogeneous coefficients of $1_A$. Then for any $m \in \mathbb{Z}$ we consider any $b_m \in A_m$. But now note that:
	
	{\centering$\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} a_n b_m = 1_A b_m = b_m = b_m1_A = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} b_m a_n$\retTwo\par}

	By comparing homogeneous coefficients, we get that $a_0 b_m = b_m = b_m a_0$ (and also that $a_n b_m = 0 = b_m a_n$ if $n \neq 0$). And thus since every $b \in A$ is a sum of $b_m \in A_m$ as $m$ ranges over some finite subset of $\mathbb{Z}$, we can conclude for all $b \in A$ that $a_0 b = b = b a_0$. This shows that $a_0$ is an identity element of $A$. And thus $1_A = 1_A a_0 = a_0$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo Given a unital $R$-algebra $A$, I'll say $B \subseteq A$ is a \udefine{subalgebra} if it is also an $R$-algebra under the algebra operations of $A$ and $1_B = 1_A$.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Corollary:} Let $A$ be a graded unital $R$-algebra with the grading $\{A_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$. Then $A_0$ is a subalgebra of $A$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Why?\\
	$A_0$ is an $R$-module and we know from the definition of a grading that if $a, b \in A_0$ then so is $ab \in A_0$. Finally, $1_A \in A_0$ lets us conclude $A_0$ is a subalgebra. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo Let $A$ be an $R$-algebra. Note that if $\{B_i\}_{i \in I}$ is a collection of subalgebras of $A$ then so is $B \coloneqq \bigcap_{i \in I} B_i$. As a result, given a subset $S$ of $A$ we let the $R$-subalgebra generated by $S$ (denoted $\langle S\rangle$) to be the smallest subalgebra of $A$ containing $S$. We can construct $\langle S\rangle$ as follows:\newpage
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Let $B$ be the collection of all finite linear combinations of finite products of elements of $S$ (where a product of zero-many elements is interpretted as equalling $1_A$). It is easy to justify that $B \subseteq \langle S\rangle$ and that $B$ is itself a subalgebra of $A$ which contains $S$. So, $\langle S\rangle \subseteq B$.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\exTwo\ul{Lemma 3.1:} \hypertarget{Lemma 3.1 page 1071}{Let} $\{A_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}$ be a grading on a unital $R$-algebra $A$, and suppose that $A = \langle A_1\rangle$. Then the grading on $A$ is nonnegative and for all $n \geq 0$ we have that any $a \in A_n$ is a finite linear combinations of products of $n$ many elements of $A_1$. In particular, this means that $A_0$ is generated as an $R$-module by $1_A$. So, $A_0$ is contained in the center of $A$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	$A$ is generated as an $R$-module by all finite products of elements of $A_1$. Therefore, let $B_{0} = R1_A$, let $B_n = \{0\}$ for $n < 0$, and finally for $n > 0$ let $B_n$ be the $R$-module generated by all finite products of $n$ many elements of $A_1$. We know $A = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} B_n$, and we can also easily see that $B_n \subseteq A_n$ for all $n$. The only way both statements can be true is if $A_n = B_n$ for all $n$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo Let $A$ and $B$ be unital graded $R$-algebras with gradings $\{A_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}$ and $\{B_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}$ respectively. We say $f: A \to B$ is a \udefine{homomorphism of graded $R$-algebras} if it is a unital $R$-algebra homomorphism and $f(A_n) \subseteq B_n$ for all $n$.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Lemma:} If $f: A \to B$ is a homomorphism of graded $R$-algebras and a bijection, then\\ $f(A_n) = B_n$ for all $n$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Consider any $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $b_n \in B_n$. Then write $f^{-1}(b_n) = \sum_{m \in \mathbb{Z}} a_m$ where $a_m \in A_m$\\ for each $m$. In turn, $b_n = f(f^{-1}(b_n)) = f(\sum_{m \in \mathbb{Z}} a_m) = \sum_{m \in \mathbb{Z}} f(a_m)$. So if $m \neq 0$\\ then we can compare homogeneous coefficients of $b_n$ to get that $f(a_m) = 0$. Since $f$ is\\ injective, it follows that $a_m = 0$ for all $m \neq 0$. And so, we've shown that $f^{-1}(b_n) \in A_n$.\\ In other words, $f^{-1}(B_n) \subseteq A_n$. And since $f(A_n) \subseteq B_n$, we can now conclude that\\ $f(A_n) = B_n$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo Let $I \subseteq A$ be a two-sided ideal of a graded unital $R$-algebra $A$. We say $I$ is \udefine{homogeneous} if $a \in I$ implies that all the homogeneous components of $A$ are also in $I$.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Lemma 3.2:} \hypertarget{Lemma 3.2 page 1071}{Let} $I \subseteq A$ be a two-sided ideal of a graded unital $R$-algebra $A$ (with a grading $\{A_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}$). Then $I$ is homogeneous if and only if it can be generated by homogeneous elements.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	\begin{myIndent}\myComment
		(Note: to distinguish between the subalgebra generated by a set $S \subseteq A$ and an ideal generated by a set $S \subseteq A$, I'll denote the objects $\langle S\rangle$ and $(S)$ respectively.)\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	$(\Longrightarrow)$\\
	Let $S$ be a generating set for $I$. Then if $I$ is homogeneous, we know the set $S^\prime$ of all the homogeneous components of $S$ is also contained in $I$. Therefore, $I = (S) \subseteq (S^\prime) \subseteq I$.\retTwo

	$(\Longleftarrow)$\\
	Suppose $S$ is a set of homogeneous elements such that $(S) = I$. Then note that any element $y \in I$ is a finite sum of elements of the form $a_jx_jb_j$ where $a_j, b_j \in A$ and $x_j \in S$ for all $j$. By writing each $a_j$ and $b_j$ as finite sums of homogeneous coefficients, we can in turn say without loss generality that any element  $y \in I$ is a (larger) finite sum of\newpage elements $a_jx_jb_j$ where $a_j$ and $b_j$ are homogeneous in $A$ and $x_j \in S$. But now each term $a_j x_j b_j$ is homogeneous and in $I$. So by collecting together homogeneous coefficients, we can say that each the homogeneous coefficients of $y$ are all in $I$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo Now if $A$ is an $R$-algebra and $I \subseteq A$ is a two-sided ideal of $A$, then we know that\\ $B \coloneqq A/I$ is a well-defined ring and $R$-module when equipped with the operations\\ $c(a + I) \coloneqq (ca) + I$, $(a + I) + (b + I) = (a + b) + I$, and $(a + I)(b + I) \coloneqq (ab) + I$\\ for all $c \in R$ and $a, b \in A$. Then proving that $B$ is also an $R$-algebra is easy. And if $A$ is unital then so is $B$.\retTwo

\hypertarget{Page 1072 quotients of graded algebras}{Moreover,} suppose $A$ is graded by $\{A_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}$ and that $I$ is homogeneous. Then there is a standard grading on $B = A/I$.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Put $I_n = I \cap A_n$ for all $n$. Then we can see that $I = \bigoplus_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} I_n$ as an internal direct sum of $R$-modules. Also put $B_n = (A_n + I)/I$. Then the $B_n$ will be $R$-submodules of $B$ such that $B = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}B_n$.\retTwo

	\ul{Claim:} $\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} B_n$ is a direct sum of $R$-modules.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		Why?\\
		Suppose $\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}b_n = 0$ where each $b_n \in B_n$ and all but finitely many $b_n$ are zero. Then for each $n$ we can pick $a_n \in A_n$ such that $b_n = a_n + I$ (and $a_n = 0$ if $b_n = 0$). Yet $0 + I = (\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}a_n) + I$ implies that $\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}a_n \in I$. Since $I$ is homogeneous, we can thus conclude $a_n \in I$ for each $i$. And thus, $b_n = a_n + I = 0 + I$ for all $n$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Since it's obvious that if $b_r \in B_r$ and $b_s \in B_s$ then $b_r b_s \in B_{r + s}$, we can now conclude that $B = A/I$ is graded by the submodules $\{B_n = (A_n + I)/I\}_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}$.\retTwo 

	Furthermore, consider the quotient map $\pi: A \rightarrowdbl A/I$. When $A/I$ is equipped with the grading described above, we have that $\pi$ is a homomorphism of graded algebras. By applying the first isomorphism theorem for modules, we can see that $(A_n + I)/I \cong A_n/I_n$ as $R$-modules. In turn, $A / I \cong \bigoplus_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}A_n /I_n$ as $R$-modules.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo\dispDate{8/1/2026}

First and foremost, today I want to go over some variations on tensor powers.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Observation:} Let $M_1, \ldots, M_k$ be free $R$-modules and in particular suppose\\ $M_i = \bigoplus_{b_i \in B_i} Rb_i$ for each $i$. Then for any $R$-module $N$, any map $\phi: \prod_{i=1}^k B_i \to N$\\ has a unique extension to a $k$-linear map $\widetilde{\phi}: \prod_{i=1}^k M_i \to N$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	This is because the only thing the extension $\widetilde{\phi}$ of $\phi$ can possibly be is:
	
	{\centering$\widetilde{\phi}(m)(\sum_{b_1 \in B_1} c_{b_1}b_1, \ldots, \sum_{b_k \in B_k} c_{b_k}b_k) = \sum_{b_1 \in B_1, \ldots, b_k \in B_k}c_{b_1}\cdots c_{b_k}\phi(b_1, \ldots, b_k)$\retTwo\par}
\end{myIndent}

\exTwo\ul{Theorem 1.3:} \hypertarget{Theorem 1.3 page 1072}{Let} $M_1, \ldots, M_k$ be free $R$-modules and in particular suppose\\ $M_i = \bigoplus_{b_i \in B_i} Rb_i$ for each $i$. Then $\bigotimes_{i=1}^k M_i = \bigoplus_{b_1 \in B_1, \ldots, b_k \in B_k} R(b_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes b_k)$\\ where the latter is an internal direct sum. This also shows that $\bigotimes_{i=1}^k M_i$\\ is a free module (although I already knew this via a less specific result in math 200b).\newpage
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Let $M \coloneqq \bigoplus_{b_1 \in B_1, \ldots, b_k \in B_k} R(b_1, \ldots, b_k)$ be the free $R$-module associated to the set\\ [-3pt] $\prod_{i=1}^k B_i$. Then there is a unique $k$-linear map $\iota: \prod_{i=1}^k M_i \to M$ satisfying that\\ $\iota(b_1, \ldots, b_k) = (b_1, \ldots, b_k) \in M$.\retTwo
	
	Furthermore, suppose $N$ is any other $R$-module and $T: \prod_{i=1}^k M_i \to N$ is a $k$-linear\\ map. If we want the following commuting diagram to hold:
	% https://q.uiver.app/#q=WzAsMyxbMCwxLCJcXHByb2Rfe2k9MX1eayBNX2kiXSxbMSwwLCJNIl0sWzEsMSwiTiJdLFswLDIsIlQiLDJdLFsxLDIsImYiLDAseyJzdHlsZSI6eyJib2R5Ijp7Im5hbWUiOiJkYXNoZWQifX19XSxbMCwxLCJcXGlvdGEiXV0=
	\[\begin{tikzcd}
		& M \\
		{\prod_{i=1}^k M_i} & N
		\arrow["f", dashed, from=1-2, to=2-2]
		\arrow["\iota", from=2-1, to=1-2]
		\arrow["T"', from=2-1, to=2-2]
	\end{tikzcd}\]

	then we need $f(b_1, \ldots, b_n) = T(b_1, \ldots, b_n)$ for all $(b_1, \ldots, b_n) \in \prod_{i=1}^k B_i$. Fortunately, by the universal property of free modules we know a unique such $f: M \to N$ exists. And now since $f \circ \iota$ is a $k$-linear map agreeing with $T$ on the set $\prod_{i=1}^k B_i$, we can conclude by the prior observation that $f \circ \iota = T$.\retTwo

	With that, we've proven that $M$ and $\iota$ satisfy the universal property of a tensor product of $M_1, \ldots, M_k$. And now it is easy to see that $\bigotimes_{i=1}^k M_i$ will be isomorphic to $M$ via an isomorphism sending $b_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes b_k$ to $(b_1, \ldots, b_k) \in M$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo Now given any $R$-module $M$ and $p \in \mathbb{N}$, we let $T_p(M) \coloneqq \bigotimes_{i=1}^p M$. This $R$-module is\\ called the \udefine{$p$th tensor power of $M$}. By the prior theorem, if $M$ is a free module with a\\ linearly independent basis $B \subseteq M$ then $T_p(M)$ is also a free module with a linearly\\ independent basis given by $\{b_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes b_p : b_i \in B \text{ for all } 1 \leq i \leq p\}$.\retTwo

We also want to consider liftings of alternating or symmetric $p$-linear maps on $\prod_{i=1}^p M$. So, we consider the following constructions.\retTwo

If $N$ is an $R$-module and $p > 1$ then we say that a $p$-linear map $T: \prod_{i=1}^p M \to N$ is \udefine{alternating} if $T(m_1, \ldots, m_p) = 0$ if $m_i = m_j$ for any distinct integers $i$ and $j$. Meanwhile, we say all $R$-module homomorphisms (i.e. all $1$-linear maps) are alternating.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Note that the definition of an alternating $k$-linear map given on \inLinkRap{placeholder}{page 104} implies\\ this new definition provided that $1_R + 1_R \neq 0_R$. Conversely, note that:
	
	{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
		$T(m_1, \ldots, m_i, \ldots, m_j, \ldots m_p)$\\ [3pt]
		$\phantom{aaaaaaa} = T(m_1, \ldots, m_i + m_j, \ldots, m_j, \ldots, m_p) - T(m_1, \ldots, m_j, \ldots, m_j, \ldots, m_p)$\\ [3pt]
		$\phantom{aaaaaaa} = T(m_1, \ldots, m_i + m_j, \ldots, m_j, \ldots, m_p) - 0$\\ [3pt]
		$\phantom{aaaaaaa} = T(m_1, \ldots, m_i + m_j, \ldots, m_i + m_j, \ldots, m_p)$\\
		$\phantom{aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa} - T(m_1, \ldots, m_i + m_j, \ldots, m_i, \ldots, m_p)$\\ [3pt]
		$\phantom{aaaaaaa} = 0 - T(m_1, \ldots, m_i + m_j, \ldots, m_i, \ldots, m_p)$\\ [3pt]
		$\phantom{aaaaaaa} = -T(m_1, \ldots, m_j, \ldots, m_i, \ldots, m_p) - T(m_1, \ldots, m_i, \ldots, m_i, \ldots, m_p)$\\ [3pt]
		$\phantom{aaaaaaa} = -T(m_1, \ldots, m_j, \ldots, m_i, \ldots, m_p) - 0$.
	\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

	Therefore, by composing transpositions we can conclude that our new definition always implies the old definition when $M$ is a vector space over any field.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

We say an $R$-module $E_p(M)$ along with an alternating $p$-linear map $\eta: \prod_{i=1}^p M \to E_p(M)$ is the \udefine{$p$th exterior power of $M$} if for any $R$-module $N$ and any alternating $p$-linear map $T: \prod_{i=1}^p M \to N$ there is a unique $R$-module homomorphism $f: E_p(M) \to N$ such that $f \circ \eta = T$.
% https://q.uiver.app/#q=WzAsMyxbMCwxLCJcXHByb2Rfe2k9MX1eayBNIl0sWzEsMCwiRV9wKE0pIl0sWzEsMSwiTiJdLFswLDIsIlQiLDJdLFsxLDIsIlxcZXhpc3RzICFmIiwwLHsic3R5bGUiOnsiYm9keSI6eyJuYW1lIjoiZGFzaGVkIn19fV0sWzAsMSwiXFxldGEiXV0=
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	& {E_p(M)} \\
	{\prod_{i=1}^p M} & N
	\arrow["{\exists !f}", dashed, from=1-2, to=2-2]
	\arrow["\eta", from=2-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow["T"', from=2-1, to=2-2]
\end{tikzcd}\]

\exTwo\phantom{.}\\\ul{Proposition:} Such an $R$-module $E_p(M)$ and alternating $p$-linear map $\eta$ exists, and the elements $m_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge m_p \coloneqq \eta(m_1, \ldots, m_p)$ generate $E_p(M)$ as an $R$-module. Also if $(E_p(M)^{(1)}, \eta^{(1)})$ and $(E_p(M)^{(2)}, \eta^{(2)})$ both satisfy the above universal property then there exists inverse isomorphism $f: E_p(M)^{(1)} \to E_p(M)^{(2)}$ and $g: E_p(M)^{(2)} \to E_p(M)^{(1)}$ such that $f \circ \eta^{(1)} = \eta^{(2)}$ and $f \circ \eta^{(2)} = \eta^{(1)}$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	The uniqueness of $E_p(M)$ upto isomorphism claim can be verified through the same\\ standard arguements that were used on \inLinkRap{placeholder}{page 686}. So, it's only the first sentence of the\\ propositon that needs verifying.\retTwo

	Consider the $p$th tensor power of $M$ and let $J_p(M) \subseteq T_p(M)$ be the submodule\\ generated by all pure tensors $m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p$ where $(m_1, \ldots, m_p)$ contains at least one\\ repeated element.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		Note that $J_1(M)$ is generated by an empty set of elements and so we just take\\ by convention that $J_1(M) = \{0\}$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Next, we let $E_p(M) = T_p(M) / J_p(M)$. And assuming $\pi: T_p(M) \rightarrowdbl E_p(M)$ is the quotient map and $\iota: \prod_{i=1}^p M \to T_p(M)$ is the multilinear map sending $(m_1, \ldots, m_p)$ to $m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p$, we define $\eta \coloneqq \pi \circ \iota$. Thus $\eta$ is a multilinear map as well. And by the definition of $J_p(M)$ we know that $\eta$ is alternating.\retTwo

	I next claim that $E_p(M)$ and $\eta$ satisfy the universal property we want. To prove this,\\ suppose $N$ is any $R$-module and $\phi:\prod_{i=1}^p M \to N$ is an alternating $p$-linear map. By\\ the universal property of $T_p(M)$ we know there is a unique $R$-module homomorphism $f: T_p(M) \to N$ such that $f(m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p) = \phi(m_1, \ldots, m_p)$ for all $(m_1, \ldots, m_p)$\\ in $\prod_{i=1}^p M$. Yet we can also see that each of the generating elements of $J_p(M)$ are in $\ker(f)$. Hence, $J_p(M) \subseteq \ker(f)$ and we can quotient them out to get a well-defined $R$-module homomorphism $\widetilde{f}: E_p(M) \to N$.\retTwo

	To show that $\widetilde{f}$ is unique first we note that since $\pi: T_p(M) \to E_p(M)$ is a surjective map and the pure tensors $m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p$ generate $T_p(M)$ as an $R$-module, we know that the elements of the form $m_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge m_p = \pi(m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p)$ also generate $E_p(M)$ as an $R$-module. Next note that if $g: E_p(M) \to N$ were another $R$-module homomorphism such that $\phi = g \circ \eta$, then we'd have to have that $g = \widetilde{f}$ on all elements of the form $m_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge m_p$. Since those elements generate all of $E_p(M)$, we in turn know that $g = \widetilde{f}$ everywhere on $E_p(M)$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo In general it will be convenient to view the structure of $E_p(M)$ as a blackbox and just rely on its universal property (similarly to how we were already treating $T_p(M)$). And with that mentioned, I now define the \udefine{canonical homomorphism from $T_p(M)$ to $E_p(M)$}:
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Note that the map $\eta(m_1, \ldots, m_p) \coloneqq m_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge m_p$ is a $p$-linear map from $\prod_{i=1}^p M$\\ into $E_p(M)$. As a result, we know by the universal property of $T_p(M)$ that there is a\\ unique $R$-module homomorphism $f: T_p(M) \to E_p(M)$ such that:
	
	{\centering$f(m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p) = m_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge m_p$.\\ [-20pt]\par}
	% https://q.uiver.app/#
	\[\begin{tikzcd}
		&&&& {} \\
		&&& {T_p(M)} \\
		{} && {\prod_{i=1}^p M} & {E_p(M)} \\
		&&&& {}
		\arrow[""{name=0, anchor=center, inner sep=0}, "{m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p}"{description}, color={rgb,255:red,92;green,92;blue,214}, draw=none, from=2-4, to=1-5]
		\arrow["{\exists !f}", dashed, from=2-4, to=3-4]
		\arrow[""{name=1, anchor=center, inner sep=0}, "{(m_1, \ldots, m_p)}"{description}, color={rgb,255:red,92;green,92;blue,214}, draw=none, from=3-1, to=3-3]
		\arrow[from=3-3, to=2-4]
		\arrow[from=3-3, to=3-4]
		\arrow[""{name=2, anchor=center, inner sep=0}, "{m_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge m_p}"{description}, color={rgb,255:red,92;green,92;blue,214}, draw=none, from=3-4, to=4-5]
		\arrow[color={rgb,255:red,92;green,92;blue,214}, between={0.1}{0.9}, maps to, from=0, to=2]
		\arrow[color={rgb,255:red,92;green,92;blue,214}, curve={height=-24pt}, between={0.1}{0.8}, maps to, from=1, to=0]
		\arrow[color={rgb,255:red,92;green,92;blue,214}, curve={height=12pt}, between={0.2}{0.8}, maps to, from=1, to=2]
	\end{tikzcd}\]

	\begin{myIndent}\myComment
		In my explicit construction of a model of $E_p(M)$ on the prior page, $f$ would just be the quotient map $\pi$ and the next theorem would be obvious. However, again I'm trying to treat $E_p(M)$ and $T_p(M)$ as black boxes.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
\end{myIndent}

\exTwo\ul{Theorem 1.5:} Let $f: T_p(M) \to E_p(M)$ be the canonical homomorphism and let\\ $J_p(M)$ be the submodule of $T_p(M)$ defined on the prior page. Then $f$ is surjective and $\ker(f) = J_p(M)$. Moreover, $J_p(M)$ is generated as an $R$-module by all pure tensors $m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p$ where $m_i = m_{i+1}$ for some $i$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	The fact that $f$ is surjective is simply a result of the fact that $f$ maps a generating set for $T_p(M)$ (i.e. the set of pure tensors) to a generating set for $E_p(M)$. As for showing the rest of the theorem's claim, let $J \coloneqq J_p(M)$, let $J^\prime$ be the $R$-submodule of $T_p(M)$ generated by just the pure tensors $m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p$ where $m_i = m_{i+1}$ for some $i$, and finally let $J^\pprime \coloneqq \ker(f)$. It's clear that $J^\prime \subseteq J \subseteq J^\pprime$. And we just need to show all these submodules are equal.\retTwo

	\ul{Lemma 1.2:} Let $\phi: \prod_{i=1}^p M \to N$ be a $p$-linear map. Then $\phi$ is alternating iff\\ $\phi(m_1, \ldots, m_p) = 0$ whenever there exists $i$ such that $m_i = m_{i+1}$.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		Why?\\
		The forwards implication is trivial. Conversely, note by identical reasoning as on two pages, if the latter claim holds then for any $i$ we have that:
		
		{\centering$\phi(m_1, \ldots, m_i, m_{i+1}, \ldots, m_p) = -\phi(m_1, \ldots, m_{i+1}, m_i, \ldots, m_p)$.\retTwo\par}

		But now suppose $m_i = m_j$ for some indices $i < j$. Then:

		{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
			$\phi(m_1, \ldots, m_i, m_{i+1}, m_{i+2}, \ldots, m_j, \ldots m_p)$\\ [4pt]
			$\phantom{aaaaaaaaaaaaaa} = -\phi(m_1, \ldots, m_{i+1}, m_{i}, m_{i+2} \ldots, m_j, \ldots m_p)$\\ [4pt]
			$\phantom{aaaaaaaaaaaaaa} = +\phi(m_1, \ldots, m_{i+1}, m_{i+2}, m_{i} \ldots, m_j, \ldots m_p)$\\ [4pt]
			$\phantom{aaaaaaaaaaaaaa} = \cdots = \pm \phi(m_1, \ldots, m_{j-2}, m_i, m_j, \ldots, m_p) = \pm 0 = 0$.
		\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

		So, $\phi$ is alternating.\newpage
	\end{myIndent}

	Based on the prior lemma, we can now say that if $\pi: T_p(M) \to T_p(M) / J^\prime$ is the quotient map and $\iota: \prod_{i=1}^p M \to T_p(M)$ is the multilinear map $\iota(m_1, \ldots, m_p) = m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p$, then $\pi \circ \iota$ is an alternating multilinear map. It follows by the universal property of $E_p(M)$ that there is a unique $R$-module homomorphism $\lambda: E_p(M) \to T_p(M) / J^\prime$ such that $\lambda(m_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge m_p) = (m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p) + J^\prime$.\retTwo

	Yet also note that $\lambda \circ f = \pi$ After all, by the universal property of $T_p(M)$ we know that $h = \pi$ is the unique $R$-module homomorphism $T_p(M) \to T_p(M) / J^\prime$ with $h \circ \iota = \pi \circ \iota$. And since $\lambda \circ f \circ \iota = \pi \circ \iota$, we must have that $\lambda \circ f = \pi$.\retTwo 

	Consequently, $J^\pprime = \ker(f) \subseteq \ker(\pi) = J^\prime$. And since $J^\prime \subseteq J \subseteq J^\pprime \subseteq J^\prime$, we can conclude that $J^\prime = J = J^\pprime$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo A different type of $p$-linear map is a symmetric multilinear map. Let $G$ denote the\\ $p$th symmetric group. We say a $p$-linear map $T: \prod_{i=1}^p M \to N$ is \udefine{symmetric} if\\ $T(m_1, \ldots, m_p) = T(m_{\sigma^{-1}(1)}, \ldots, m_{\sigma^{-1}(p)})$ for all $\sigma \in G$. Note that trivially all $1$-linear\\ maps are symmetric.\retTwo

We say an $R$-module $S_p(M)$ along with a symmetric $p$-linear map $\theta: \prod_{i=1}^p M \to S_p(M)$ is the \udefine{$p$th symmetric power of $M$} if for any $R$-module $N$ and any symmetric $p$-linear map $T: \prod_{i=1}^p M \to N$ there is a unique $R$-module homomorphism $f: S_p(M) \to N$ such that $f \circ \theta = T$.
% https://q.uiver.app/#q=WzAsMyxbMCwxLCJcXHByb2Rfe2k9MX1eayBNIl0sWzEsMCwiU19wKE0pIl0sWzEsMSwiTiJdLFswLDIsIlQiLDJdLFsxLDIsIlxcZXhpc3RzICFmIiwwLHsic3R5bGUiOnsiYm9keSI6eyJuYW1lIjoiZGFzaGVkIn19fV0sWzAsMSwiXFx0aGV0YSJdXQ==
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	& {S_p(M)} \\
	{\prod_{i=1}^k M} & N
	\arrow["{\exists !f}", dashed, from=1-2, to=2-2]
	\arrow["\theta", from=2-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow["T"', from=2-1, to=2-2]
\end{tikzcd}\]

\phantom{,}\\\exTwo\ul{Proposition:} Such an $R$-module $S_p(M)$ and symmetric $p$-linear map $\theta$ exists, and the\\ elements $m_1 m_2\cdots m_p \coloneqq \theta(m_1, m_2 \ldots, m_p)$ generate $S_p(M)$ as an $R$-module. Also if\\ $(S_p(M)^{(1)}, \theta^{(1)})$ and $(S_p(M)^{(2)}, \theta^{(2)})$ both satisfy the above universal property then there\\ exists inverse isomorphism $f: S_p(M)^{(1)} \to S_p(M)^{(2)}$ and $g: S_p(M)^{(2)} \to S_p(M)^{(1)}$ such\\ that $f \circ \theta^{(1)} = \theta^{(2)}$ and $f \circ \theta^{(2)} = \theta^{(1)}$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	The second sentence of this proposition can be proven through identical arguments as it was for $T_p(M)$ and $E_p(M)$. So like before, we only need to focus on the existence of $S_p(M)$ and $\theta$.\retTwo

	Let $G$ denote the $p$th symmetric group. Then consider the $p$th tensor power of $M$ and let $H_p(M) \subseteq T_p(M)$ be the submodule generated by all differences:
	
	{\centering$(m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p) - (m_{\sigma^{-1}(1)} \otimes \cdots \otimes m_{\sigma^{-1}(p)})$\par}
	
	where $\sigma \in G$ and $(m_1, \ldots, m_p) \in \prod_{i=1}^p M$.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		Note that $H_1(M) = \{0\}$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Let $S_p(M) = T_p(M) / H_p(M)$. Next let $\pi: T_p(M) \to S_p(M)$ be the quotient map and $\iota: \prod_{i=1}^p M \to T_p(M)$ be the $p$-linear map sending $(m_1, \ldots, m_p)$ to $m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p$. Thus $\theta \coloneqq \pi \circ \iota$ is a $p$-linear map which is clearly symmetric.\newpage

	By identical reasoning as in the proof that the $p$th exterior power of $M$ exists, we can\\ conclude that $S_p(M)$ and $\theta$ satisfy the universal property we want. $\blacksquare$
	\begin{myTindent}\myComment
		As a side note, $\theta$ being a symmetric $p$-linear map means that\\ $m_1m_2\cdots m_p = m_{\sigma^{-1}(1)}m_{\sigma^{-1}(2)}\cdots m_{\sigma^{-1}(p)}$ for any $\sigma \in G$ and\\ $m_1, \ldots, m_p \in M$.\retTwo
	\end{myTindent}
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo Like with $E_p(M)$, it will be more convenient to view the structure of $S_p(M)$ as a blackbox and just rely on its universal property. Therefore, like before we shall define the \udefine{canonical homomorphism from $T_p(M)$ to $S_p(M)$} using only universal properties.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	To start off, the map $\theta(m_1, m_2 \ldots, m_p) \coloneqq m_1 m_2\cdots m_p$ is a $p$-linear map from\\ $\prod_{i=1}^p M$ into $S_p(M)$. Thus by the universal property of $T_p(M)$ there is a unique $R$-\\module homomorphism $f: T_p(M) \to S_p(M)$ such that:
	
	{\centering$f(m_1 \otimes m_2 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p) = m_1 m_2\cdots m_p$.\retTwo\par}

	$f: T_p(M) \to S_p(M)$ is called the canonical homomorphism from $T_p(M)$ to $S_p(M)$.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\exTwo\ul{Theorem 1.8:} Let $f: T_p(M) \to S_p(M)$ be the canonical homomorphism and let\\ $H_p(M)$ be the submodule of $T_p(M)$ defined on the prior page. Then $f$ is surjective and\\ $\ker(f) = H_p(M)$. Moreover, $H_p(M)$ is generated as an $R$-module by all differences:

{\centering$(m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_i \otimes m_{i+1} \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p) - (m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_{i+1} \otimes m_i \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p)$\par}

where $1 \leq i < p$ and $m_1, \ldots, m_p \in M$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	$f$ is surjective because $f$ maps a generating set for $T_p(M)$ (i.e. the set of pure tensors) to a generating set for $S_p(M)$. As for showing the rest of the theorem, let $H \coloneqq H_p(M)$, let $H^\prime$ be the $R$-submodule of $T_p(M)$ generated by just the differences described above, and let $H^\pprime \coloneqq \ker(f)$. Clearly $H^\prime \subseteq H \subseteq H^\pprime$.\retTwo

	Like in the proof of theorem 1.5 two pages ago, we shall show that $H^\pprime \subseteq H^\prime$. So let $\pi: T_p(M) \to T_p(M)/H^\prime$ be the quotient map and let $\iota: \prod_{i=1}^p M \to T_p(M)$ be the multilinear map $\iota(m_1, \ldots, m_p) = m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p$. We can see that $\pi \circ \iota$ is a symmetric multilinear map.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		This is because in order to prove a $p$-linear map $\phi$ is symmetric, it suffices to show for any $m_1, \ldots, m_p \in M$ and $1 \leq i < p$ that:

		{\centering $\phi(m_1, \ldots, m_i, m_{i+1}, \ldots, m_p) = \phi(m_1, \ldots, m_{i+1}, m_i, \ldots, m_p)$ \retTwo\par}

		After all, any permutation of indices can be decomposed into a composition of\\ interchanges of adjacent indices.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	By the universal property of $S_p(M)$ we thus know there is a unique $R$-module\\ homomorphism $\lambda: S_p(M) \to T_p(M)/H^\prime$ such that:
	
	{\centering$\lambda(m_1m_2\cdots m_p) = (m_1 \otimes m_2 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p) + H^\prime$.\retTwo\par}

	Yet also by the universal property of $T_p(M)$ we know that $\lambda \circ f = \pi$. In turn,\\ $H^\pprime = \ker(f) \subseteq \ker(\pi) = H^\prime$. And since $H^\prime \subseteq H \subseteq H^\pprime \subseteq H^\prime$, we can conclude\\ that $H^\prime = H = H^\pprime$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo Today's notes took longer than I was hoping. So to finish off I want to restate theorem 1.3 on \inLinkRap{Theorem 1.3 page 1072}{pages 1072-1073} but in a way that applies to $E_p(M)$ and $S_p(M)$.\newpage

Let $M$ be a free $R$-module and in particular let $B \subseteq M$ be a linearly independent basis\\ for $M$. Also let $p \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}$ and let $G$ denote the $p$th symmetric group.
\begin{itemize}
	\item Consider the set of all sequences of $p$ many distinct elements of $B$. We can define an equivalence relation on this set by saying that $(b_1, \ldots, b_p) \sim (b_{\sigma^{-1}(1)}, \ldots, b_{\sigma^{-1}(p)})$ for all $\sigma \in G$. And then we let $I_p(B)$ be a set containing one representative $(b_1, \ldots, b_p)$ from each equivalence class.\retTwo
	
	\exTwo\ul{Theorem 1.6:} $E_p(M)$ is a free $R$-module with a linearly independent basis given by the $b_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge b_p$ as $(b_1, \ldots, b_p)$ ranges over $I_p(B)$.
	\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
		Proof:\\
		Let $N \coloneqq \bigoplus_{(b_1, \ldots, b_p) \in I_p(B)}R(b_1, \ldots, b_p)$ be the free $R$-module associated to $I_p(B)$. We can define a map $\phi: \prod_{i=1}^p B \to N$ given by:
		\begin{itemize}
			\item[$\circ$] $\phi(b_1, \ldots, b_p) \coloneqq 0$ if $(b_1, \ldots, b_p)$ contains any repeated elements of $B$.
			\item[$\circ$] If $b_1, \ldots, b_p$ are all distinct then there exists a unique $\sigma \in G$ such that\\ $(b_{\sigma^{-1}(1)}, \ldots, b_{\sigma^{-1}(p)}) \in I_p(B)$. So, we define $\phi(b_1, \ldots, b_p) \coloneqq \sgn(\sigma) \cdot (b_1, \ldots, b_p)$.\retTwo
		\end{itemize}

		By the observation on \inLinkRap{Theorem 1.3 page 1072}{page 1072}, $\phi$ has a unique extension $\eta: \prod_{i=1}^p M \to N$ such that $\eta$ is a $p$-linear map. Also, I claim that $\eta$ is alternating.
		\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
			Why?\\
