			Consider any $1 \leq i < p$ as well as any elements $b_1, \ldots, b_{i-1}, b_{i+2}, \ldots, b_p \in B$. Then for any $m \in M$ let us pick $b^{(1)}, \ldots, b^{(n)} \in B$ as well as $c^{(1)}, \ldots, c^{(n)} \in R$ such that $m = \sum_{j=1}^n c^{(j)} b^{(j)}$. I claim that:
			
			{\centering$\eta(b_1, \ldots, b_{i-1}, m, m, b_{i+2}, \ldots, b_p) = 0$.\retTwo\par}

			This is because:
			
			{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
				$\eta(b_1, \ldots, b_{i-1}, m, m, b_{i+2}, \ldots, b_p)$\\ [6pt]
				$\phantom{aaaaaa} = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{n} \sum\limits_{j^\prime=1}^{n} c^{(j)} c^{(j^\prime)} \phi(b_1, \ldots, b_{i-1}, b^{(j)}, b^{(j^\prime)}, b_{i+2}, \ldots b_p)$\\ [12pt]
				$\phantom{aaaaaa} = \left(\sum\limits_{j = 1}^n (c^{(j)})^{2} \phi(b_1, \ldots, b_{i-1}, b^{(j)}, b^{(j)}, b_{i+2}, \ldots, b_p)\right)$\\
				$\phantom{aaaaaaaaaaaa} + \left(\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{n-1}\sum\limits_{j^\prime = j + 1}^n c^{(j)}c^{(j^\prime)}\left(\phi(b_1, \ldots, b_{i-1}, b^{(j)}, b^{(j^\prime)}, b_{i+2}, \ldots, b_p)\right.\right.$\\
				$\left.\phantom{\sum\limits_{j^\prime = j + 1}^n aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa}\left. \mathop{+} \phi(b_1, \ldots, b_{i-1}, b^{(j^\prime)}, b^{(j)}, b_{i+2}, \ldots, b_p)\right)\right)$\\ [12pt]
			\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

			Yet now $\phi(b_1, \ldots, b_{i-1}, b^{(j)}, b^{(j)}, b_{i+2}, \ldots, b_p) = 0$ for all $j$. Meanwhile,\\ $\phi(b_1, \ldots, b_{i-1}, b^{(j)}, b^{(j^\prime)}, b_{i+2}, \ldots, b_p) = -\phi(b_1, \ldots, b_{i-1}, b^{(j^\prime)}, b^{(j)}, b_{i+2}, \ldots, b_p)$ for all $j < j^\prime$. So all, the summands in the above manipulation cancel and we are left with the equation $\eta(b_1, \ldots, b_{i-1}, m, m, b_{i_2}, \ldots, b_p) = 0$.\newpage

			In turn, it's now clear that $\eta$ is alternating because for any elements\\ $m_1, \ldots, m_{i-1}, m_{i+2}, \ldots, m_p$ in $M$ we can write:
			
			{\centering$\eta(m_1, \ldots, m_{i-1}, m, m, m_{i+2}, \ldots, m_p)$\par}
			
			as a linear combination of elements $\eta(b_1, \ldots, b_{i-1}, m, m, b_{i+2}, \ldots, b_p)$.\retTwo
		\end{myIndent}

		Now importantly, $N$ and $\eta$ satisfy the universal property of the $p$th exterior power of $M$. After all, suppose $K$ is another $R$-module and $\psi: \prod_{i=1}^p M \to k$ is an alternating $p$-linear map. By the universal property of free modules we know there is a unique $R$-module homomorphism $f: N \to K$ such that $f(b_1, \ldots, b_p) = \psi(b_1, \ldots, b_p)$ for all $(b_1, \ldots, b_p) \in I_p(B)$. Yet then as $f \circ \eta$ is an alternating $p$-linear map, we can conclude that $f \circ \eta = \psi$ on $\prod_{i=1}^p B$. In turn, as any $p$-linear map from $\prod_{i=1}^p M$ is uniquely determined by its restriction to $\prod_{i=1}^p B$, we can conclude that $f \circ \eta = \psi$ on all of $\prod_{i=1}^p M$.\retTwo

		Furthermore, note that if $g: N \to K$ also were to satisfy that $g \circ \eta = \psi$, we'd have to have that $g(b_1, \ldots, b_p) = \psi(b_1, \ldots, b_p)$ for all $(b_1, \ldots, b_p) \in I_p(B)$. This would in turn imply that $f = g$ by the universal property of free $R$-modules. So, we have shown that $N$ along with $\eta$ is a model for the $p$th exterior power of $M$.\retTwo

		With that all proven, we can now conclude that that $E_p(M)$ is isomophic to $M$ via an $R$-module homomorphism sending $b_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge b_p \in E_p(M)$ to $(b_1, \ldots, b_p) \in N$ for all $(b_1, \ldots, b_p) \in I_p(B)$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}\hTwo

	\item Next consider the set of all sequences of $p$ many elements of $B$ (where this time we allow repetitions). We define an equivalence relation on this set by saying that $(b_1, \ldots, b_p) \sim (b_{\sigma^{-1}(1)}, \ldots, b_{\sigma^{-1}(p)})$ for all $\sigma \in G$. And then we let $I_p^*(B)$ be a set containing one representative $(b_1, \ldots, b_p)$ from each equivalence class.\retTwo
	
	\exTwo\ul{Theorem 1.9:} $S_p(M)$ is a free $R$-module with a linearly independent basis given by the  elements $b_1 b_2 \cdots b_p$ as $(b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_p)$ ranges over $I_p^*(B)$.
	\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
		Proof:\\
		Let $N$ be the free $R$-module associated with the set $I_p^*(B)$ and then let\\ $\theta: \prod_{i=1}^p M \to N$ be the unique $p$-linear map satisfying that for all\\ $(b_1,  \ldots, b_p) \in \prod_{i=1}^p B$ we have that $\theta(b_1, \ldots, b_p) = (b_{\sigma^{-1}(1)}, \ldots, b_{\sigma^{-1}}(p))$ where $\sigma \in G$ is the unique permutation with $(b_{\sigma^{-1}(1)}, \ldots, b_{\sigma^{-1}}(p)) \in I^*_p(B)$.\retTwo

		Once we show that $\theta$ is symmetric, the rest of the proof of this theorem follows\\ identically as in the proof of the prior theorem.
		\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
			Fortunately, note for any sequence of $p$ many elements $(b_1, \ldots, b_p)$ in $B$ and any $\sigma \in G$ that $\theta(b_1, \ldots, b_p) = \theta(b_{\sigma^{-1}(1)}, \ldots, B_{\sigma^{-1}(p)})$. Therefore, for any $m_1, \ldots, m_p \in M$ we just need to decompose $\theta(m_{\sigma^{-1}}, \ldots, m_{\sigma^{-1}(p)})$ into a linear combination of $\theta(b_{\sigma^{-1}(1)}, \ldots, B_{\sigma^{-1}(p)})$, apply the prior observation, and then reassemble the linear combination into $\theta(m_1, \ldots, m_p)$. \exThreeP $\blacksquare$\retTwo
		\end{myIndent}
	\end{myIndent}
\end{itemize}

\hTwo\dispDate{8/2/2026}\newpage

Unfortunately, there is still a little more infrastructure that needs to be built up before I can get to constructing interesting $R$-algebras satisfying certain universal properties.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Theorem 2.1:} Let $M_1, \ldots, M_p$ be $R$-modules (where $p > 2$) and suppose $1 \leq q < p$. Then there is an $R$-module isomorphism from $(\bigotimes_{i=1}^q M_i) \otimes (\bigotimes_{i=q + 1}^p M_i)$ to $\bigotimes_{i=1}^p M_i$ such that $(m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_q) \otimes (m_{q +1} \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p) \mapsto m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p$ for all $m_i \in M_i$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	I shall proceed by induction on $p$. For our base case of $p = 3$, recall from \inLinkRap{Page 1067 Lemma A}{pages 1067-1069} that my original construction of $M_1 \otimes M_2 \otimes M_3$ was the set $M_1 \otimes (M_2 \otimes M_3)$ where $m_1 \otimes m_2 \otimes m_3$ is equal to $m_1 \otimes (m_2 \otimes m_3)$. Meanwhile, I showed on \inLinkRap{placeholder}{pages 730-731} that $M_1 \otimes (M_2 \otimes M_3)$ is isomorphic to $(M_1 \otimes M_2) \otimes M_3$ via an isomorphism mapping $m_1 \otimes (m_2 \otimes m_3)$ to $(m_1 \otimes m_2) \otimes m_3$. Hence, our base case is entirely dealt with via prior results.\retTwo

	Next suppose $p > 3$.
	\begin{itemize}
		\item If $q = 1$ then recall that $\bigotimes_{i=2}^p M_i$ is isomorphic to $M_2 \otimes (\cdots \otimes (M_{p-1} \otimes M_p )\cdots)$ via an isomorphism $\phi$ such that:
		
		{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
			$m_2 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_{p-1} \otimes m_p \mapsto m_2 \otimes (\cdots \otimes(m_{p-1} \otimes m_p)\cdots)$.
		\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

		In turn, $\myId_{M_1} \otimes \phi$ is an isomorphism from $M_1 \otimes (\bigotimes_{i=2}^p M_i)$ to\\ $M_1 \otimes (M_2 \otimes (\cdots \otimes (M_{p-1} \otimes M_p )\cdots))$ such that:
		
		{\centering$m_1 \otimes (m_2 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p)\mapsto m_1 \otimes (m_2 \otimes (\cdots \otimes(m_{p-1} \otimes m_p)\cdots))$.\retTwo\par}

		And via the reasoning on \inLinkRap{placeholder}{pages 1067-1069}, we can compose that map with an\\ isomorphism $\psi: M_1 \otimes (M_2 \otimes (\cdots \otimes (M_{p-1} \otimes M_p )\cdots)) \to \bigotimes_{i=1}^p M_i$\\ sending $m_1 \otimes (m_2 \otimes (\cdots \otimes(m_{p-1} \otimes m_p)\cdots))$ to $m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p$.\retTwo 

		\item Meanwhile, if $q > 1$ then we can conclude by our induction hypothesis that $\bigotimes_{i=1}^q M_i$ is isomorphic to $M_1 \otimes \bigotimes_{i=2}^q M_i$ via an isomorphism $\phi$ mapping $m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_q$ to $m_1 \otimes (m_2 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_q)$.\retTwo
		
		In turn, $\phi \otimes \myId_{\bigotimes_{i=q+1}^p M_i}$ is an isomorphism from $(\bigotimes_{i=1}^q M_i) \otimes (\bigotimes_{i=q+1}^p M_i)$ to\\ $(M_1 \otimes (\bigotimes_{i=2}^q M_i)) \otimes (\bigotimes_{i=q+1}^p M_i)$ such that $(m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_q) \otimes (m_{q+1} \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p)$ is mapped to $(m_1 \otimes (m_2 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_q)) \otimes (m_{q+1} \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p)$.\retTwo

		Next, by the exercise on \inLinkRap{placeholder}{pages 730-731} we have an isomorphism from\\ $(M_1 \otimes (\bigotimes_{i=2}^q M_i)) \otimes (\bigotimes_{i=q+1}^p M_i)$ to $M_1 \otimes ((\bigotimes_{i=2}^q M_i) \otimes (\bigotimes_{i=q+1}^p M_i))$\\ sending $(m_1 \otimes (m_2 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_q)) \otimes (m_{q+1} \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p)$ to\\ $m_1 \otimes ((m_2 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_q) \otimes (m_{q+1} \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p))$.\retTwo

		Then by our induction hypothesis, $(\bigotimes_{i=2}^q M_i) \otimes (\bigotimes_{i=q+1}^p M_i)$ is isomorphic to\\ $\bigotimes_{i=2}^p M_i$ via an isomorphism $\psi$ mapping $(m_2 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_q) \otimes (m_{q+1} \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p)$ to\\ $m_2 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p$.\retTwo
		
		In turn, $\myId_{M_1} \otimes \psi$ is an isomorphism from $M_1 \otimes ((\bigotimes_{i=2}^q M_i) \otimes (\bigotimes_{i=q+1}^p M_i))$ to $M_1 \otimes (\bigotimes_{i=2}^p M_i)$ sending $m_1 \otimes ((m_2 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_q) \otimes (m_{q+1} \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p))$ to\\ $m_1 \otimes (m_2 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p)$.\newpage

		Finally, we can now use our reasoning for the case when $q = 1$ to finish up. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
	\end{itemize}
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo Next let $A_1, \ldots, A_p$ be $R$-algebras. I already mentioned how $\bigotimes_{i=1}^p A_i$ can naturally be turned into an $R$-algebra itself. However, here is another interpretation of this natural product operation on $\bigotimes_{i=1}^p A_i$.\\ [-8pt]
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Consider the $2p$-linear map $T: A_1 \times \cdots \times A_p \times A_1 \times \cdots \times A_p \to \bigotimes_{i=1}^p A_i$ given by:
	
	{\centering$T(a_1, \ldots, a_p, a_1^\prime, \ldots, a_p^\prime) \coloneqq (a_1a_1^\prime, \ldots, a_p a_p^\prime)$.\retTwo\par}

	By the universal property of tensor products we thus know there is a unique $R$-module homomorphism $\phi: A_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes A_p \otimes A_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes A_p \to \bigotimes_{i=1}^p A_i$ such that:

	{\centering$\phi(a_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes a_p \otimes a_1^\prime \otimes \cdots \otimes a_p^\prime) \coloneqq (a_1a_1^\prime, \ldots, a_p a_p^\prime)$.\retTwo\par}

	Then by the prior theorem, we can also say that there is a unique $R$-module\\ homomorphism $\widetilde{\phi}: (\bigotimes_{i=1}^p A_i) \otimes (\bigotimes_{i=1}^p A_i) \to \bigotimes_{i=1}^p A_i$ such that:

	{\centering$\widetilde{\phi}((a_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes a_p) \otimes (a_1^\prime \otimes \cdots \otimes a_p^\prime)) \coloneqq (a_1a_1^\prime, \ldots, a_p a_p^\prime)$.\retTwo\par}

	And finally, we can conclude that there is a unique bilinear map\\ $\mu: (\bigotimes_{i=1}^p A_i) \times (\bigotimes_{i=1}^p A_i) \to \bigotimes_{i=1}^p A_i$ such that:
	
	{\centering$\mu((a_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes a_p), (a_1^\prime \otimes \cdots \otimes a_p^\prime)) \coloneqq (a_1a_1^\prime, \ldots, a_p a_p^\prime)$.\retTwo\par}

	\ul{Lemma:} \hypertarget{Lemma middle of page 1081}{Suppose} $M$ is an $R$-module generated by a set $B$, and $\mu: M \times M \to M$ is a bilinear map such that $\mu(\mu(b_1, b_2), b_3) = \mu(b_1, \mu(b_2, b_3))$ for all $b_1, b_2, b_3 \in B$. Then $\mu(\mu(m_1, m_2), m_3) = \mu(m_1, \mu(m_2, m_3))$ for all $m_1, m_2, m_3 \in M$.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		Proof:\\
		Write $m_1 = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i b_i$,\hspace{0.1em} $m_2 = \sum_{j=1}^m c_j^\prime b_j^\prime$,\hspace{0.1em} and $m_3 = \sum_{k=1}^\ell c_k^\pprime b_k^\pprime$. Then:
		\begin{itemize}
			\item $\mu(\mu(m_1, m_2), m_3) = \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^m \sum_{k=1}^\ell c_i c_j^\prime c_k^\pprime \mu(\mu(b_i, b_j^\prime), b_k^\pprime)$,
			\item $\mu(m_1, \mu(m_2, m_3)) = \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^m \sum_{k=1}^\ell c_i c_j^\prime c_k^\pprime \mu(b_i, \mu(b_j^\prime, b_k^\pprime))$.\retTwo
		\end{itemize}

		And now we just invoke that $\mu(\mu(b_i, b_j^\prime), b_k^\pprime) = \mu(b_i, \mu(b_j^\prime, b_k^\pprime))$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Based on that lemma, its now clear that $\mu$ defines an associative operation on $M$. Clearly, $\mu$ is the standard multiplication map on $\bigotimes_{i=1}^p A_i$.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\exTwo\ul{Lemma:} Suppose $A_1, A_2$ are $R$-algebras, $A_1$ is generated as an $R$-module by a subset $B$, $f: A_1 \to A_2$ is an $R$-module homomorphism, and $f(b b^\prime) = f(b)f(b^\prime)$ for all $b, b^\prime \in B$. Then $f$ is an $R$-algebra homomorphism.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	We need to show for any $a, a^\prime \in A_1$ that $f(aa^\prime) = f(a)f(a^\prime)$. Fortunately, we can write $a = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i b_i$ and $a^\prime = \sum_{j=1}^m c_j^\prime b_j^\prime$. Then:

	{\centering \begin{tabular}{l}
		$f(aa^\prime) = f((\sum_{i=1}^n c_i b_i)(\sum_{j=1}^m c_j^\prime b_j^\prime)) = \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^m c_i c_j^\prime f(b_i b_j^\prime)$\\ [4pt]
		$\phantom{f(aa^\prime) = f((\sum_{i=1}^n c_i b_i)(\sum_{j=1}^m c_j^\prime b_j^\prime))} = \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^m c_i c_j^\prime f(b_i)f(b_j^\prime)$\\ [4pt]
		$\phantom{f(aa^\prime) = f((\sum_{i=1}^n c_i b_i)(\sum_{j=1}^m c_j^\prime b_j^\prime))} = \left(\sum_{i=1}^n c_i f(b_i)\vphantom{|_j^j}\right)\left(\sum_{j=1}^m c_j^\prime f(b_j^\prime)\right)$\\ [8pt]
		$\phantom{f(aa^\prime) = f((\sum_{i=1}^n c_i b_i)(\sum_{j=1}^m c_j^\prime b_j^\prime))} = f(\sum_{i=1}^n c_i b_i)f(\sum_{j=1}^m c_j^\prime b_j^\prime) = f(a)f(a^\prime)$. $\blacksquare$
	\end{tabular}\newpage\par}
\end{myIndent}

\exTwo\ul{Theorem 3.2:} Let $A_1, \ldots, A_p$ be $R$-algebras (where $p > 2$) and suppose $1 \leq q < p$. Then the $R$-module isomorphism $f : (\bigotimes_{i=1}^q A_i) \otimes (\bigotimes_{i=q+1}^p A_i) \to \bigotimes_{i=1}^p A_i$ given by theorem 2.1 is also an $R$-algebra homomorphism.

\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Why?\\
	Just apply the prior lemma where:
	
	{\centering$B = \{(a_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes a_q) \otimes (a_{q + 1} \otimes \cdots \otimes a_p) : a_1, \ldots, a_p \in A\}$.\retTwo\par}
\end{myIndent}

\exTwo\ul{Theorem 3.4:} Let $A$ be an $R$-algebra and note that $R$ itself is trivially an $R$-algebra. Thus, we can consider the standard $R$-algebra structure on $R \otimes A$.  I claim that the $R$-module isomorphism $\phi: R \otimes A \to A$ satisfying that $\phi(c \otimes a) = ca$ is also an $R$-algebra\\ homomorphism.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Let $B = \{(c \otimes a) : c \in R \text{ and } a \in A\}$. Then:
	
	{\centering$\phi((c \otimes a) \cdot (c^\prime \otimes a^\prime)) = \phi(cc^\prime \otimes aa^\prime) = cc^\prime aa^\prime = ca c^\prime a^\prime = \phi(c \otimes a) \phi(c^\prime \otimes a^\prime)$.\retTwo\par}

	So, we can apply the lemma at the bottom of the prior page. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo Obviously a similar thing holds if we replace $R \otimes A$ with $A \otimes R$.\retTwo

\dispDate{8/3/2026}

Today I can look forward to constructing another important object which I'll mostly try to treat as a black box satisfying a universal property!!\retTwo

Let $M$ be an $R$-module. Then suppose $A$ is an $R$-algebra and $\phi: M \to A$ is an $R$-\\module homomorphism. If $B$ is a second $R$-algebra and $h: A \to B$ is a unital $R$-algebra\\ homomorphism, we know that $h \circ \phi$ is an $R$-module homomorphism from $M$ to $B$.\\ This brings up the following question:\\ [-6pt]
\begin{myIndent}
	Does there exist a unital $R$-algebra $A$ and an $R$-module homomorphism $\phi: M \to A$\\ such that for any unital $R$-algebra $B$ and any $R$-module homomorphism $f: M \to B$\\ there exists a unique unital $R$-algebra homomorphism $h: A \to B$ with $h \circ \phi = f$?
	% https://q.uiver.app/#q=WzAsMyxbMCwxLCJNIl0sWzEsMSwiQiJdLFsxLDAsIkEiXSxbMCwxLCJmIiwyXSxbMCwyLCJcXHBoaSJdLFsyLDEsIlxcZXhpc3RzICEgaCIsMCx7InN0eWxlIjp7ImJvZHkiOnsibmFtZSI6ImRhc2hlZCJ9fX1dXQ==
	\[\begin{tikzcd}
		& A \\
		M & B
		\arrow["{\exists ! h}", dashed, from=1-2, to=2-2]
		\arrow["\phi", from=2-1, to=1-2]
		\arrow["f"', from=2-1, to=2-2]
	\end{tikzcd}\]

	If such an $R$-algebra $A$ and $R$-module homomorphism $\phi$ exists then we say $A$\\ along with $\phi$ is the \udefine{tensor algebra of $M$}. Furthermore, if $(A_1, \phi_1)$ and $(A_2, \phi_2)$ both satisfy the above universal property then it is easy to see that there exists inverse $R$-algebra isomorphisms $f: A_1 \to A_2$ and $g: A_2 \to A_1$ such that $f \circ \phi_1 = \phi_2$ and $g \circ \phi_2 = \phi_1$. So, assuming a model of the tensor algebra of $M$ exists, it is unique up to isomorphism.\newpage
\end{myIndent}

\exTwo\ul{Theorem 4.1:} Such a unital $R$-algebra $A$ and $R$-module homomorphism $\phi: M \to A$ exists. Furthermore:
\begin{itemize}
	\item[(a)] $\phi: M \to A$ is an injection.
	\item[(b)] $A$ is generated as an $R$-algebra by $\phi(M)$.
	\item[(c)] There is a grading on $\{A_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}$ on $A$ such that $A_1 = \phi(M)$.
	\item[(d)] The grading $\{A_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}$ is nonnegative and $A_0 = R1_A$.
	\item[(e)] For $p \geq 1$, $T_p(M)$ is isomorphic to $A_p$ via the unique $R$-module homomorphism\\ sending $m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p$ to $\phi(m_1)\cdots \phi(m_p)$.
\end{itemize}

\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	I'll first focus on just constructing $A$ and $\phi$. So let $A_p \coloneqq T_p(M)$ for all $p \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}$ and let $A_0 = R$. Then let us set $A \coloneqq \bigoplus_{p=0}^\infty A_p$. Clearly $A$ has an $R$-module structure. But we still need to define a multiplication operation on $A$ such that $A$ becomes an algebra.\retTwo

	Fortunately for any $p, q \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}$ we know by theorem 2.1 that there is a (unique) $R$-\\module homomorphism $\phi_{p,q}: T_p(M) \otimes T_q(M) \to T_{p + q}(M)$ such that:
	
	{\centering$\phi_{p, q}((m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p) \otimes (m_1^\prime \otimes \cdots \otimes m_q^\prime)) = m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p \otimes m_1^\prime \otimes \cdots \otimes m_q^\prime$\retTwo\par}

	In turn, we know there is a (unique) bilinear map $\mu_{p, q} : T_p(M) \times T_q(M) \to T_{p + q}(M)$\\ such that:
	
	{\centering$\mu_{p, q}((m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p), (m_1^\prime \otimes \cdots \otimes m_q^\prime)) = m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p \otimes m_1^\prime \otimes \cdots \otimes m_q^\prime$\retTwo\par}

	Similarly for any $p \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}$ we know there is a (unique) $R$-module homomorphism\\ $\phi_{0, q} : R \otimes T_p(M) \to T_p(M)$ such that:
	
	{\centering$\phi_{0, q}(c \otimes (m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p)) = c(m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p)$.\retTwo\par}

	In turn, we get a (unique) bilinar map $\mu_{0, p}: R \times T_p(M) \to T_p(M)$ such that\\ $\mu(c, m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p) = c(m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p)$. And we can similarly construct (unique)\\ maps $\mu_{0, 0}: R \times R \to R$ and $\mu_{p, 0} : T_p(M) \times R \to T_p(M)$ for all $p \geq 1$.\retTwo

	I now define multiplication on $A$ as follows. Note that any element $x \in A$ can be written uniquely as $\sum_{p=0}^\infty x_p$ where $x_p \in A_p$ for all $p$ and all but finitely many $x_p$ are zero. So, having written $x = \sum_{p = 0}^\infty x_p$ and $y = \sum_{p = 0}^\infty y_p$ then I define:
	
	{\centering$\mu(x, y) \coloneqq \sum_{p = 0}^\infty \sum_{q = 0}^\infty \mu_{p,q}(x_p, y_q)$.\retTwo\par}

	\begin{itemize}
		\item I claim $\mu: A \times A \to A$ is bilinear. After all, let $c_1, c_2 \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $x = \sum_{p = 0}^\infty x_p$, $y = \sum_{p = 0}^\infty y_p$, and $z = \sum_{p = 0}^\infty z_p$ be elements of $A$. Then:
		
		{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
			$\mu(x, c_1y + c_2 z) = \sum\limits_{p,q \geq 0} \mu_{p, q}(x_p, c_1 y_q + c_2 z_q) = \sum\limits_{p,q \geq 0} (c_1\mu_{p, q}(x_p, y_q) + c_2(x_p, z_q))$\\ [12pt]
			$\phantom{\mu(x, c_1y + c_2 z) = \sum\limits_{p,q \geq 0} \mu_{p, q}(x_p, c_1 y_q + c_2 z_q)} = c_1\sum\limits_{p,q \geq 0} \mu_{p, q}(x_p, y_q) + c_2\sum\limits_{p,q \geq 0} \mu_{p, q}(x_p, z_q)$\\ [12pt]
			$\phantom{\mu(x, c_1y + c_2 z) = \sum\limits_{p,q \geq 0} \mu_{p, q}(x_p, c_1 y_q + c_2 z_q)} = c_1\mu(x, y) + c_2\mu(x, z)$
		\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

		And analogous reasoning shows that $\mu(c_1 x + c_2 y, z) = c_1 \mu(x, z) + c_2\mu(y, z)$.\newpage

		\item I also claim $\mu(\mu(x, y), z) = \mu(x, \mu(y, z))$ for all $x, y, z \in A$. After all, let\\ $B = \{1_R\} \cup \left(\bigcup_{p = 1}^\infty\{m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p \in A_p :  m_1, \ldots, m_p \in M\}\right)$. Then $B$\\ generates $A$ as an $R$-module and its easy to see that:
		
		{\centering$\mu(\mu(b_1, b_2), b_3) = \mu(b_1, \mu(b_2, b_3))$ for all $b_1, b_2, b_3 \in B$.\retTwo\par}
		
		So by the lemma on the middle of \inLinkRap{Lemma middle of page 1081}{page 1081}, we know this claim holds.\retTwo

		\item Also note that $1_R \in A_0$ satisfies that $\mu(1_R, x) = x = \mu(x, 1_R)$. Therefore, upon letting $\mu$ be the multiplication operation that $A$ is equipped with, then $A$ is unital with $1_A = 1_R$.\retTwo
	\end{itemize}

	Thus $A$ equipped with $\mu$ becomes a unital $A$-algebra. If we set $A_n = \{0\}$ for all $n < 0$ then it is clear that $A$ is graded by the nonnegative grading $\{A_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}$. Also $A_0 = R1_A$. And since $M = T_1(m)$, if we let $\phi: M \to A = R \oplus \bigoplus_{p = 1}^\infty T_p(M)$ be the embedding map then we have that $\phi$ is injective and $A_1 = \phi(M)$. Plus, it is easy to see that $A$ is generated as an $R$-algebra by $A_1$ and that each $A_p$ is isomorphic to $T_p(M)$ in the way wanted by property (e).\retTwo

	To finish off the main part of the proof, I claim that $A$ and $\phi$ satisfy the universal property of the tensor algebra of $M$.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		After all, let $B$ an $R$-algebra and suppose $f: M \to B$ is an $R$-module\\ homomorphism. Then note for all $p \geq 1$ that $f^{(p)}: M \times \cdots \times M \to B$\\ given by $f(m_1, \ldots, m_p) = f(m_1)f(m_2)\cdots f(m_p)$ is also a $p$-linear map. So,\\ by the universal property of $T_p(M)$ there is a unique $R$-module homomorphism $\psi^{(p)}: T_p(M) \to B$ such that:
		
		{\centering$\psi^{(p)}(m_1 \otimes m_2 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p) = f(m_1)f(m_2)\cdots f(m_p)$.\retTwo\par}

		We also define the $R$-module homomorphism $\psi^{(0)}: R \to B$ by $\psi^{(0)}(c) = c1_B$.\retTwo

		By the universal property of coproducts of $R$-modules, there is a unique $R$-module homomorphism $h$ from $A = \bigoplus_{p = 0}^\infty A_p$ to $B$ such that $h(x_p) = \psi^{(p)}(x_p)$ for all $x_p \in A_p$ (where $p \geq 0$). Also, it's clear that $h(1_A) = \psi^{(0)}(1_R) = 1_B$. And we can further verify $h$ is an $R$-algebra homomorphism via the second lemma on \inLinkRap{Lemma middle of page 1081}{page 1081}. After all if $p, q \geq 1$ then:
		
		{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
			$h((m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p) \cdot ( m_1^\prime \otimes \cdots \otimes m_q^\prime)) = h(m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p \otimes m_1^\prime \otimes \cdots \otimes m_q^\prime)$\\ [6pt]
			$\phantom{h((m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p) \cdot ( m_1^\prime \otimes \cdots \otimes m_q^\prime))} = f(m_1)\cdots f(m_p)f(m_1^\prime)\cdots f(m_q^\prime)$\\ [6pt]
			$\phantom{h((m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p) \cdot ( m_1^\prime \otimes \cdots \otimes m_q^\prime))} = h(m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p) h(m_1^\prime \otimes \cdots \otimes m_q^\prime)$\\ [6pt]
		\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

		Finally, I claim $h$ is the unique unital $R$-algebra homomorphism such that:
		% https://q.uiver.app/#q=WzAsMyxbMCwxLCJNIl0sWzEsMSwiQiJdLFsxLDAsIkEiXSxbMCwxLCJmIiwyXSxbMCwyLCJcXHBoaSJdLFsyLDEsImgiLDAseyJzdHlsZSI6eyJib2R5Ijp7Im5hbWUiOiJkYXNoZWQifX19XV0=
		\[\begin{tikzcd}
			& A \\
			M & B
			\arrow["h", dashed, from=1-2, to=2-2]
			\arrow["\phi", from=2-1, to=1-2]
			\arrow["f"', from=2-1, to=2-2]
		\end{tikzcd}\]
		
		\phantom{.}\newpage

		After all, if $h^\prime: A \to B$ was another unital $R$-algebra homomorphism that worked then we'd have to have that $h = h^\prime$ on $A_1$. Yet since $A_1$ generates $A$ as a unital $R$-algebra, we can conclude $h = h^\prime$ everywhere on $A$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	This finishes showing that there exists a model $(A, \phi)$ of the tensor algebra of $M$.

	\mySepThree

	One more note I want to give is that if $(A^\prime, \phi^\prime)$ is another model of the tensor algebra of $M$, then properties (a) through (e) will still hold for $A^\prime$ and $\phi^\prime$.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		To see why, note that there are unique inverse $R$-algebra isomorphisms $f: A \to A^\prime$ and $g: A^\prime \to A$ satisfying that $f \circ \phi = \phi^\prime$ and $g \circ \phi^\prime = \phi$. And this already guarentees (a) and (b) will hold.\retTwo

		Futhermore, let $A_n^\prime = f(A_n)$ for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}$. Then we can easily see the grading $\{A_n^\prime\}_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}$ on $A^\prime$ will satisfy (c), (d), and (e). \exThreeP$\blacksquare$\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo For hopefully obvious reasons, we denote the tensor algebra of $M$ as $T(M)$. And if\\ $T(M)$ is equipped with the grading $\{A_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}$ described in the last theorem then we\\ identify the $p$th tensor power of $M$, $T_p(M)$ with $A_p$ for all $p \geq 0$ (where $T_0(M)$ is\\ understood to just be $R$). In particular, this means we'll identify $M = T_1(M)$ as a\\ submodule of $T(M)$ and $R = T_0(M)$ as a subring of $T(M)$ sharing the same\\ identity element.\retTwo

Also we'll typically use $\otimes$ as the multiplication sign in $T(M)$.\retTwo

One notable consequence of having a natural way of viewing $M$ as a submodule of $T(M)$ is as follows:
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Suppose $M$ and $N$ are $R$-modules and $f: M \to N$ is an $R$-algebra homomorphism. By viewing $N$ as an $R$-submodule of $T(N)$, we can then say by the universal property of $T(M)$ that there is a unique unital $R$-algebra homomorphism $T(f): T(M) \to T(N)$ such that $T(f)|_M = f$.\retTwo

	Furthermore, note that $x \in T(M)$ is homogeneous of degree $1$ iff $x \in M$. Yet then $(T(f))(x) = f(x) \in N$. So, $(T(f))(x) \in T(N)$ is homogeneous of degree $1$ as well and so we can conclude $(T(f))(T_1(M)) \subseteq T_1(N)$.\retTwo
	
	By lemma 3.1 on \hspace{0.1em}\inLinkRap{Lemma 3.1 page 1071}{page 1071}\hspace{0.2em} it then follows that $T(f)$ maps a generating set for\\ $T_p(M)$ (as an $R$-submodule) into $T_p(N)$ for all $p \geq 2$. Plus, it's obvious that:
	
	{\centering$(T(f))(T_0(M)) = R(T(f))(1_{T(M)}) = R1_{T(N)} = T_0(N)$.\retTwo\par}
	
	So, $T(f): T(M) \to T(N)$ is a graded $R$-algebra homomorphism.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

Another way of describing the prior consequence is as follows. Let $\mcateg{GrAlg}_R$ denote the category whose objects are graded unital $R$-algebras and whose morphisms are (unital) graded algebra homomorphisms.\retTwo

We can define a functor $T: R$-$\mcateg{mod} \to \mcateg{GrAlg}_R$ mapping any $R$-module $M$ to its tensor algebra and mapping any $R$-module homomorphism $f: M \to N$ to the graded $R$-algebra homomorphism $T(f) : T(M) \to T(N)$ described earlier.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Note that $T(\myId_M) = \myId_{T(M)}$ for all $R$-modules $M$. After all, $\myId_{T(M)}: T(M) \to T(M)$\\ is a graded $R$-algebra homomorphism whose restriction to $M$ is just the inclusion map\\ $M \hookrightarrow T(M)$. Yet by the univeral property of tensor algebras there is only one unital $R$-algebra homomorphism $T(\myId_M)$ with that property.\retTwo

	In a similar vein, if $f: M \to N$ and $g: N \to K$ are $R$-module homomorphisms, then $T(g \circ f) = T(g) \circ T(f)$. After all, the restriction of either map to $M$ is just the map $g \circ f$. So, both maps must be the same unique map satisfying that. And this proves that $T: R$-$\mcateg{mod} \to \mcateg{GrAlg}_R$ is a functor.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

One other note is that every element of $T_1(M) = M$ is homogeneous in $T(M)$. Therefore, if $K \subseteq M$ is a submodule then we know from lemma 3.2 on \inLinkRap{Lemma 3.2 page 1071}{page 1071} that the two-sided ideal $I(K) \subseteq T(M)$ generated by $K$ is homogeneous.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Theorem 4.3:} Let $f: M \to N$ be a surjective $R$-module homomorphism and let\\ $K = \ker(f)$. Then $T(f): T(M) \to T(N)$ is surjective and $\ker(T(f)) = I(K)$ where $I(K)$ is the two-sided ideal in $T(M)$ generated by $K$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Firstly, $f$ being surjective means that $T_1(N) \subseteq (T(f))(T(M))$. And since $T_1(N)$ is a\\ generating set for $T(N)$ as an $R$-algebra and we can easily verify that the image of a\\ unital $R$-algebra homomorphism is a subalgebra, we in turn must have that\\ $(T(f))(T(M)) = T(N)$. So, $T(f)$ is surjective.\retTwo

	Next note that it's obvious that $I(K) \subseteq \ker(T(f))$ since $K \subseteq \ker(T(f))$ and we can\\ easily verify that the kernel of an $R$-algebra homomorphism is an ideal and $R$-module.\retTwo
	
	As for the other inclusion, consider the quotient map $\pi: T(M) \to T(M)/I(K)$. We know from \inLinkRap{Page 1072 quotients of graded algebras}{page 1072} that $T(M)/I(K)$ has a natural grading $\{A_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ satisfying that $M/K$ is isomorphic to $A_1$ as an $R$-module via the map $\phi(m + K) \coloneqq m + I(K)$. Also note by the first isomorphism theorem that $f: M \to N$ induces an $R$-module isomorphism $\widetilde{f}: M/K \to N$.\retTwo
	
	So, $g \coloneqq \phi \circ \widetilde{f}^{-1}$ is an $R$-module homorphism from $N$ to $A_1 \subseteq T(M)/I(K)$ satisfying that $g(n) = m + I(K)$ where $m \in M$ is any element satisfying that $f(m) = n$. By the universal property of $T(N)$, we can then extend $g$ to a unique $R$-algebra homomorphism $T(g) : T(N) \to T(M)/I(K)$.\retTwo 

	But now note that $T(g) \circ T(f) = \pi$. After all, we can easily check for pure tensors that $(T(f))(m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p) = f(m_1) \otimes \cdots \otimes f(m_p)$. And then if $n_i = f(m_i)$, we have that:\\ [-8pt]
	
	{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
		$(T(g))(n_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes n_p) = g(n_1)\cdots g(n_p)$\\ [2pt]
		$\phantom{(T(g))(n_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes n_p)} = (m_1 + I(K))\cdots(m_p + I(K)) = (m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p) + I(K)$.
	\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

	So, $T(g) \circ T(f)$ agrees with $\pi$ on a generating set for $T(M)$ as an $R$-module and it follows that $T(g) \circ T(f) = \pi$ everywhere.\newpage

	Consequently, $\ker(T(f)) \subseteq \ker(\pi) = I(K)$ and thus we've shown the other inclusion\\ we wanted. $\blacksquare$
	\begin{myIndent}\myComment
		As a side note, $T(f)$ restricted to $T_p(M)$ is the map $f^{\otimes^p} \coloneqq \underbrace{f \otimes \cdots \otimes f}_{p \text{ times}}$.\\ [-16pt] This is because both maps satisfy that:

		{\centering $m_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes m_p \mapsto f(m_1) \otimes \cdots \otimes f(m_p)$. \retTwo\par}
		
		But also note that we can now conclude that:
		
		{\centering$\ker(f^{\otimes^p}) = I(K) \cap T_p(M) \subseteq T(M)$\\ [4pt]\par}
		
		where $K = \ker(f)$ and $I(K)$ is the two-sided ideal in $T(M)$ generated by $K$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo\dispDate{8/4/2026}

Welp I realized my tangent for the last 5 days might have not been necssary after all. I'd still like to think it was informative though since I don't have much experience right now working with $R$-algebras. I'll start off today though going over two more results about tensor algebras from Northcott's book.\retTwo

To start off, given a set $X$, here's how to construct the free $R$-algebra of $X$.\\ [-8pt]
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Let $M$ be the free $R$-module of $X$ (equipped with the embedding $\iota_m: X \to M$). Next, consider the tensor algebra $T(M)$ of $M$ equipped with the $R$-module homomorphism $\phi: M \to T(M)$. And finally let $\iota : X \to T(M)$ be defined by $\iota \coloneqq \phi \circ \iota_m$. Note that $\iota$ will be injective since both $\phi$ and $\iota_m$ are. Also, $\iota(X)$ will generate $T(M)$ as an $R$-algebra.\retTwo

	\ul{Theorem 4.4:} If $A$ is a unital $R$-algebra and $f: X \to A$ is any function, then there is a unique unital $R$-algebra homomorphism $\widetilde{f}: T(M) \to A$ such that the following diagram holds:
	% https://q.uiver.app/#q=WzAsMyxbMCwxLCJYIl0sWzEsMSwiQSJdLFsxLDAsIlQoTSkiXSxbMCwxLCJmIiwyXSxbMCwyLCJcXGlvdGEiXSxbMiwxLCJcXHdpZGV0aWxkZXtmfSIsMCx7InN0eWxlIjp7ImJvZHkiOnsibmFtZSI6ImRhc2hlZCJ9fX1dXQ==
	\[\begin{tikzcd}
		& {T(M)} \\
		X & A
		\arrow["{\widetilde{f}}", dashed, from=1-2, to=2-2]
		\arrow["\iota", from=2-1, to=1-2]
		\arrow["f"', from=2-1, to=2-2]
	\end{tikzcd}\]
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		Proof:\\
		Firstly such an $\widetilde{f}$ exists. After all, $A$ is also an $R$-module, we can conclude by the universal property of $M$ and $\iota_M$ that there is a unique $R$-module homomorphism $g: M \to A$ such that $g \circ \iota_m = f$. Next, we can use the universal property of $T(M)$ and $\phi$ to say that there is a unique $R$-algebra homomorphism $\widetilde{f}: T(M) \to A$ such that $\widetilde{f} \circ \phi = g$. And thus $\widetilde{f} \circ \iota = (\widetilde{f} \circ \phi) \circ \iota_m = g \circ \iota_m = f$.
		% https://q.uiver.app/#
		\[\begin{tikzcd}
			&& {T(M)} \\
			& M \\
			X && A
			\arrow["{\exists!\widetilde{f}}", dashed, from=1-3, to=3-3]
			\arrow["\phi"', from=2-2, to=1-3]
			\arrow["{\exists!g}"', dashed, from=2-2, to=3-3]
			\arrow["\iota", curve={height=-18pt}, from=3-1, to=1-3]
			\arrow["{\iota_m}"', from=3-1, to=2-2]
			\arrow["f"', from=3-1, to=3-3]
		\end{tikzcd}\]\newpage

		Next suppose $h: T(M) \to A$ is another unital $R$-algebra homomorphism satisfying that $h \circ \iota = f$. Then as $\iota(X)$ generates all of $T(M)$ as an $R$-algebra, we can say that $h$ is uniquely determind by its restriction to $\iota(X)$. Yet the commuting diagram for $\widetilde{f}$ says that $h(\iota(x)) = f(x) = \widetilde{f}(\iota(x))$ for all $x \in X$. So, $h$ must equal $\widetilde{f}$ everywhere on $T(M)$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	As a side note we can also show through standard arguments that if $(A, \iota)$ and $(A^\prime, \iota^\prime)$ both satisfy the universal property of a free $R$-algebra of a set $X$, then there are inverse $R$-algebra isomorphisms $f: A \to A^\prime$ and $g: A^\prime \to A$ such that $f \circ \iota = \iota^\prime$ and $g \circ \iota^\prime = \iota$.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo On a different note, it's easy to see that if $M$ is a free $R$-module with a linearly independent basis $B$ then $T(M)$ is also a free $R$-module with a linearly independent basis consisting of all pure tensors whose components are in $B$.\retTwo

A related result we can prove is that $M$ is a projective $R$-module if and only if the tensor algebra $T(M)$ of $M$ is a projective $R$-module.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Lemma 4.1:} Let $u: N \to M$ and $v: M \to N$ be $R$-module homomorphisms such\\ that $v \circ u = \myId_N$. Then $u$ is an injection, $v$ is a surjection, and $M = u(N) \oplus \ker(v)$ as\\ an internal direct sum.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	That $u$ is an injection and $v$ a surjection is obvious. Also note for any $m \in M$ that\\ $m - u(v(m)) \in \ker(v)$ since:
	
	{\centering$v(m - u(v(m))) = v(m) - v(u(v(m))) = v(m) - v(m) = 0$.\retTwo\par}
	
	Similarly $u(v(m)) \in u(N)$. And since $m = u(v(m)) + (m - u(v(m)))$ we can\\ conclude that $u(N) + \ker(v) = M$. Finally, suppose $m \in u(N) + \ker(v)$. Then\\ there exists $n \in N$ such that $u(n) = m$. Yet also note that:
	
	{\centering$n = \myId_N(n) = v(u(n)) = v(m) = 0$. So $m = u(0) = 0$.\retTwo\par}
	
	And ths proves that $u(N) + \ker(v)$ is actually an internal direct sum. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\ul{Theorem 4.5:} Let $P$ be an $R$-module and let $T(P)$ be the tensor algebra of $P$. Then $P$ is a projective $R$-module if and only if $T(P)$ is a projective $R$-module.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	$(\Longleftarrow)$\\
	Note that $T(P) \cong P \oplus (\bigoplus_{\substack{p \geq 0 \\ p \neq 1}}T_p(P))$ as $R$-modules.\retTwo
	
	But now note that $T(P)$ is projective if and only if there is a free $R$-module $\mathcal{F}$ and some $R$-module $K$ such that $T(P) \oplus K \cong \mathcal{F}$. In turn:
	
	{\centering$\mathcal{F} \cong (P \oplus (\bigoplus_{\substack{p \geq 0 \\ p \neq 1}}T_p(P))) \oplus K \cong P \oplus ((\bigoplus_{\substack{p \geq 0 \\ p \neq 1}}T_p(P)) \oplus K)$\retTwo\par}

	So, $P$ is also a direct summand of a free $R$-module and is thus projective.
	\begin{myIndent}\myComment
		As a side note, analogous reasoning lets us further say that if $T(P)$ is a projective $R$-module then $T_p(P)$ is a projective $R$-module for all $p \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	$(\Longrightarrow)$\\
	Since $P$ is projective we can choose an $R$-module $Q$ such that $P \oplus Q \cong \mathcal{F}$ where $\mathcal{F}$\newpage is a free $R$-module. Then we let $\iota: P \hookrightarrow \mathcal{F}$ be the direct sum embedding and we let\\ $\pi: \mathcal{F} \rightarrowdbl P$ be the direct sum projection. By the universal property of $T(P)$ and $T(\mathcal{F})$, we know that $\iota$ and $\pi$ uniquely extend to $R$-algebra homomorphisms:
	
	{\centering$T(\iota): T(P) \to T(\mathcal{F})$ and $T(\pi) : T(\mathcal{F}) \to T(P)$.\retTwo\par}

	But now as $\pi \circ \iota = \myId_P$, we can conclude that $T(\pi) \circ T(\iota) = T(\myId_P) = \myId_{T(P)}$. So by the prior lemma, we can conclude that $T(\mathcal{F}) \cong T(P) \oplus \ker(T(\pi))$. Yet also note that since $\mathcal{F}$ is a free $R$-module, we know $T(\mathcal{F})$ is also a free $R$-module. So, $T(P)$ is a direct summand of a free $R$-module and is thus projective. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo I'm now going to return to what I was trying and failing to construct on 7/27/2026. Also for the sake of continuity I'll go back to the red and orange text tangent color scheme.\retTwo

\pracOne\begin{myIndent}\mySepThree\end{myIndent}

My endgoal is to show that if $R$ is a unital commutative ring then the category $\mcateg{CAlg}_R$ (whose objects are unital commutative $R$-algebras and whose morphisms are unital $R$-algebra homomorphisms) is cocomplete. There will be three steps to showing this.
\begin{enumerate}
	\item[1.] I need to show $\mcateg{CAlg}_R$ admits \textit{filtered} colimits. In other words, if $(I, \lesssim)$ is a directed set (which we turn into a category $\mcateg{I}$ as described on \inLinkRap{Page 1024 reference}{page 1024}), then any functor $F: \mcateg{I} \to \mcateg{CAlg}_R$ has a colimit.
	\item[2.] Then I need to use the filtered colimit construction to construct coproducts / "tensor products" over arbitrary collections of commutative unital $R$-algebras.
	\item[3.] Finally, I can adapt the construction on \inLinkRap{Colimits of $A$-modules construction page 1023}{pages 1023-1024} for constructing colimits of $R$-modules in order to construct general colimits in the category $\mcateg{CAlg}_R$.\retTwo
\end{enumerate}

Suppose $(I, \lesssim)$ is a directed set, that every $i \in I$ is associated with a commutative\\ unital $R$-algebra $A_i$, and that for all $i, j \in I$ with $i \lesssim j$ there exists a unital $R$-algebra\\ homomorphism $r^{i}_j: A_i \to A_j$ such that:\\ [-18pt]
\begin{itemize}
	\item $i \lesssim j \lesssim k$ in $I$ implies that $r^{i}_k = r^{j}_k \circ r^i_j$,
	\item $r^i_i = \myId_{A_i}$ for all $i \in I$.\retTwo
\end{itemize}

In other words, we have a functor $F: I \to \mcateg{CAlg}_R$. Now here's how to construct $\lim\limits_{\longrightarrow}(F)$.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Let $S \coloneqq \bigcup_{i \in I}(\{i\} \times A_i)$ be the disjoint union of the algebras $A_i$. Then equip $S$ with\\ the equivalence relation where $(i, x) \sim (j, y)$ if there exists $k \in I$ with $i \lesssim k$ and\\ $j \lesssim k$ such that $r^i_k(x) = r^j_k(y)$. Finally, let $A \coloneqq S/_\sim$ and let $\iota_i: A_i \to A$ be the\\ map $x \mapsto [(i, x)]$ for all $i \in I$.\retTwo

	If $\mathcal{G}: \mcateg{CAlg}_R \to \mcateg{Set}$ is the forgetful functor than we know from the construction on\\ \inLinkRap{Page 1024 reference}{pages 1024-1026} that $A$ equipped with all the $\iota_i$ is the colimit $\lim\limits_{\longrightarrow}(\mathcal{G} \circ F)$.\retTwo

	Thus if we can equip $A$ with a unital $R$-algebra structure and then show that $\iota_i: A_i \to A$ is a unital $R$-algebra homomorphism for all $i$, then this will be enough to conclude that $A$ equipped with all the $\iota_i$ is the colimit $\lim\limits_{\longrightarrow}(F)$.\newpage

	Here's how we define are algebra operations on $A$.
	\begin{itemize}
		\item (Scaling): Given any $c \in R$ and $[(i, x)] \in A$, we let $c[(i, x)] \coloneqq [(i, cx)]$.
		\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
			To see that this is well-defined, suppose $[(i, x)] = [(j, y)]$. Then there exists $k \in I$ with $i \lesssim k$, $j \lesssim k$, and $r^{i}_k(x) = r^j_k(y)$. Then as $r^{i}_k$ and $r^j_k$ are $R$-algebra homomorphisms, we have that $r^{i}_k(c \cdot x) = c \cdot r^{i}_k(x) = c \cdot r^j_k(y) = r^j_k(c \cdot y)$. As a result, $[(i, cx)] = [(j, cy)]$.\retTwo
		\end{myIndent}

		\item (Addition): Suppose $[(i, x)], [(j, y)] \in A$. Then given any $k \in I$ with $i \lesssim k$ and $j \lesssim k$ we let $[(i, x)] + [(j, y)] \coloneqq [(k, r^i_k(x) + r^j_k(y))]$.
		\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
			To see that this is well-defined, suppose $[(i_1, x_1)] = [(i_2, x_2)]$ and\\ $[(j_1, y_1)] = [(j_2, y_2)]$, and then consider any $k_1, k_2 \in I$ such that\\ $i_1 \lesssim k_1$, $j_1 \lesssim k_1$, $i_2 \lesssim k_2$, and $j_2 \lesssim k_2$. We need to show that:
			
			{\centering$[(k_1, r^{i_1}_{k_1}(x_1) + r^{j_1}_{k_1}(y_1))] = [(k_2, r^{i_2}_{k_2}(x_2) + r^{j_2}_{k_2}(y_2))]$.\retTwo\par}

			Fortunately, note that as $[(i_1, x_1)] = [(i_2, x_2)]$ there exists $\ell \in I$ such that $r_{\ell}^{i_1}(x_1) = r_\ell^{i_2}(x_2)$. Also without loss of generality we can assume $k_1 \lesssim \ell$ and $k_2 \lesssim \ell$. Similarly, as $[(j_1, y_1)] = [(j_2, y_2)]$ we can find $\ell^\prime \in I$ such that $r_{\ell^\prime}^{j_1}(y_1) = r_{\ell^\prime}^{j_2}(y_2)$. And now I claim without loss of generality that we can just take $\ell = \ell^\prime$ and also assume that $k_1, k_2 \lesssim \ell$.\\ [-8pt]
			\begin{myDindent}
				This is because since $I$ is a directed set, we know there exists\\ $\ell^{\mathrm{new}} \in I$ with $\ell, \ell^\prime, k_1, k_2 \lesssim \ell^{\mathrm{new}}$. And then:

				{\centering $r_{\ell^{\mathrm{new}}}^{i_1}(x_1) = (r_{\ell^{\mathrm{new}}}^{\ell} \circ r_\ell^{i_1})(x_1) =  (r_{\ell^{\mathrm{new}}}^\ell \circ r_\ell^{i_2})(x_2) = r_{\ell^{\mathrm{new}}}^{i_2}(x_2)$ \retTwo\par}

				Similarly, we can show $r_{\ell^{\mathrm{new}}}^{j_1}(y_1) = r_{\ell^{\mathrm{new}}}^{j_2}(y_2)$.\retTwo
			\end{myDindent}

			So, there exists $\ell \in I$ such that $i_1, i_2, j_1, j_2, k_1, k_2 \lesssim \ell$, $r^{i_1}_\ell(x_1) = r^{i_2}_\ell(x_2)$, and $r^{j_1}_\ell(y_1) = r^{j_2}_\ell(y_2)$. And finally, we can now conclude that:

			{\centering \begin{tabular}{l}
				$r_\ell^{k_1}(r^{i_1}_{k_1}(x_1) + r^{j_1}_{k_1}(y_1)) = r_\ell^{i_1}(x_1) + r_\ell^{j_1}(y_1)$\\ [2pt]
				$\phantom{r_\ell^{k_1}(r^{i_1}_{k_1}(x_1) + r^{j_1}_{k_1}(y_1))} = r_\ell^{i_2}(x_2) + r_\ell^{j_2}(y_2) = r_\ell^{k_2}(r^{i_2}_{k_2}(x_2) + r^{j_2}_{k_2}(y_2))$
			\end{tabular} \retTwo\par}
		\end{myIndent}

		\item (Multiplication): Suppose $[(i, x)], [(j, y)] \in A$. Then given any $k \in I$ with $i \lesssim k$ and $j \lesssim k$ we let $[(i, x)][(j, y)] = [(k, r_k^i(x)r_k^j(y))]$.
		\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
			We can use basically identical reasoning to prove multiplication is well-defined as we used to prove addition is well-defined. Just replace all the addition\\ operations with multiplication operations in the prior reasoning.\retTwo
		\end{myIndent}
	\end{itemize}

	Now one major reason why I showed all the algebra operations are well-defined \textit{before} I showed they satisfy the scaling/addition/multiplication axioms for a commutative $R$-algebra is that we can now always insist on working with whichever elements of an equivalence class are most convenient to work with.\retTwo

	As a general observation, it's easy to see that if $i \lesssim j$ then $[(i, x)] = [(j, r^i_j(x))]$. Also, we can see that $[(i, x)] + [(i, y)] = [(i, x + y)]$ and that $[(i, x)][(i, y)] = [(i, xy)]$. Thus, here's how we can "quickly" prove $A$ is a commutative $R$-algebra.\newpage
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		Let $[(i, x)], [(j, y)], [(k, z)] \in A$. By picking a common upper bound to $i$, $j$, and $k$ in $I$ we can assume without loss of generality that $i = j = k$. And then since $A_i$ is a commutative algebra:
		\begin{itemize}
			\item $([(i, x)][(i, y)])[(i, z)] = [(i, xyz)] = [(i, x)]([(i, y)][(i, z)])$,\\ [-10pt]
			\item $[(i, x)]([(i, y)] + [(i, z)]) = [(i, xy + xz)] = [(i, x)][(i, y)] + [(i, x)][(i, z)]$,\\ [-10pt]
			\item $([(i, x)] + [(i, y)])[(i, z)] = [(i, xz + xy)] = [(i, x)][(i, z)] + [(i, y)][(i, z)]$,\\ [-10pt]
			\item $[(i, x)][(i, y)] = [(i, xy)] = [(i, yx)] = [(i, y)][(i, x)]$,\\ [-10pt]
			\item $[(i, x)] + [(i, y)] = [(i, x + y)] = [(i, y + x)] = [(i, y)] + [(i, x)]$.\retTwo
		\end{itemize}

		Additionally suppose $c_1, c_2 \in R$. Then:
		\begin{itemize}
			\item $c_1(c_2[(i, x)]) = [(i, c_1c_2 x)] = c_2c_2 [(i, x)]$\\ [-10pt]
			\item $(c_1 + c_2)[(i, x)] = [(i, (c_1 + c_2)x)] = [(i, c_1x + c_2x)] = c_1[(i, x)] + c_2[(i, x)]$.\retTwo
		\end{itemize}

		Also if $c \in R$ then:
		\begin{itemize}
			\item $(c[(i, x)])[(i, y)] = [(i, (cx)y)] = [(i, x(cy))] = [(i, x)](c[(i, y)])$,\\ [-10pt]
			\item $(c[(i, x)])[(i, y)] = [(i, (cx)y)] = [(i, c(xy))] = c([(i, x)][(i, y)])$,\\ [-10pt]
			\item $c([(i, x)] + [(i, y)]) = [(i, c(x + y))] = [(i, cx + cy)] = c[(i, x)] + c[(i, y)]$.\retTwo
		\end{itemize}

		Finally, we just need to show $A$ has an element $1_A$ and an element $0_A$. So, I define $0_A \coloneqq [(i, 0_{A_i})]$ and $1_A \coloneqq [(i, 1_{A_i})]$ where $i$ is any element of $I$.\\ [-8pt]
		\begin{myIndent}
			To see that this is well-defined, note that $[(i, 0_{A_i})] = [(j, 0_{A_j})]$ and\\ $[(i, 1_{A_i})] = [(j, 1_{A_j})]$ for all $i, j \in I$. This is because if we let $k \in I$ be\\ such that $i\lesssim k$ and $j \lesssim k$ then $r_k^i(0_{A_i}) = 0_{A_k}$, $r_k^i(1_{A_i}) = 1_{A_k}$,\\ $r_k^j(0_{A_j}) = 0_{A_k}$, and $r_k^j(1_{A_j}) = 1_{A_k}$.\retTwo
		\end{myIndent}

		And now we can easily see that $0_A + [(i, x)] = [(i, x)]$ and $1_A [(i, x)] = [(i, x)]$. Also $[(i, x)] + [(i, -x)] = [(i, 0_{A_i})] = 0_A$. So every element of $A$ has an additive inverse.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	It's also now obvious that $\iota_i: A_i \to A$ is a unital $R$-algebra homomorphism for all $i \in I$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

With that I've finished showing how to construct a \textit{filtered} colimit. 
\begin{myIndent}\myComment
	Remark 1: This is actually all we need in order to study stalks and germs on topological spaces. However, I made the claim earlier that $\mcateg{CAlg}_R$ is a cocomplete category. And if I want to actually justify that assertion, I need to do more work.\retTwo

	Remark 2: The prior construction also works for taking filtered colimits of $R$-modules. I mention that because it's much easier to interpret what any element of this construction looks like compared to what any element of the general construction on \inLinkRap{Colimits of $A$-modules construction page 1023}{pages 1023-1024} looks like.\retTwo

	Remark 3: One really important detail I also want to note about this construction is that $A = \bigcup_{i \in I}\iota_i(A_i)$\newpage
\end{myIndent}

{\hTwo\dispDate{8/5/2026}}

I have two more constructions to make before I can conclude that $\mcateg{CAlg}_R$ is cocomplete. Firstly, given an arbitrary collection $\{A_\beta\}_{\beta \in B}$ of unital commutative algebras I need to\\ construct their coproduct.\retTwo

\ul{Lemma A:} Let $A_1, \ldots, A_n$ be unital $R$-algebras and let $1 \leq k \leq n$ be a positive integer. Then there is a unique unital $R$-algebra homomorphism $j: \bigotimes_{i=1}^k A_i \to \bigotimes_{i=1}^n A_i$ satisfying that:

{\centering$j(a_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes a_k) = a_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes a_k \otimes 1_{A_{k+1}} \otimes \cdots \otimes 1_{A_{n}}$.\retTwo\par}

\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Proof:\\
	Note that $\phi: \prod_{i=1}^k A_i \to \bigotimes_{i=1}^n A_i$ given by
	
	{\centering$\phi(a_1, \ldots, a_k) = a_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes a_k \otimes 1_{A_{k+1}} \otimes \cdots \otimes 1_{A_{n}}$.\\ [4pt]\par}

	is a $k$-linear map. Thus by the universal property of tensor products, we know there is a unique $R$-module homomorphism $j: \bigotimes_{i=1}^k A_i \to \bigotimes_{i=1}^n A_i$ such that:

	{\centering$j(a_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes a_k) = a_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes a_k \otimes 1_{A_{k+1}} \otimes \cdots \otimes 1_{A_{n}}$.\retTwo\par}

	Also note that $j(a_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes a_k)j(a_1^\prime \otimes \cdots \otimes a_k^\prime) = j((a_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes a_k)(a_1^\prime \otimes \cdots \otimes a_k^\prime))$ for every pure tensor $a_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes a_k$ and $a_1^\prime \otimes \cdots \otimes a_k^\prime$. Thus by the lemma at the bottom of \inLinkRap{Lemma middle of page 1081}{page 1081}, we can conclude that $j$ is an $R$-algebra homomorphism.\retTwo

	Finally, note that $j(1_{\bigotimes_{i=1}^k A_i}) = j(1_{A_1} \otimes \cdots \otimes 1_{A_k}) = 1_{A_1} \otimes \cdots \otimes 1_{A_n} = 1_{\bigotimes_{i=1}^n A_i}$. So, $j$ is unital. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\ul{Lemma B:} Let $A_1, \ldots, A_n$ be unital $R$-algebras and let $\sigma: \{1, \ldots, n\} \to \{1, \ldots, n\}$\\ be a bijective function (i.e. a permutation). Then there is a unique unital $R$-algebra\\ isomorphism $\phi: \bigotimes_{i=1}^n A_i \to \bigotimes_{i=1}^n A_{\sigma^{-1}(i)}$ such that:

{\centering$\phi(a_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes a_n) = a_{\sigma^{-1}(1)} \otimes \cdots \otimes a_{\sigma^{-1}(n)}$.\retTwo\par}

\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Proof:\\
	Showing that such a unique unital $R$-algebra homomorphism $\phi$ exists uses the same\\ standard argument used in the proof of the last lemma. As for why $\phi$ is an isomorphism, note that we can by identical reasoning conclude that there is a unique unital $R$-algebra homomorphism $\psi: \bigotimes_{i=1}^n A_{\sigma^{-1}(i)} \to \bigotimes_{i=1}^n A_{i} $ such that:

	{\centering$\psi(a_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes a_n) = a_{\sigma(1)} \otimes \cdots \otimes a_{\sigma(n)}$.\retTwo\par}

	But now $\psi \circ \phi = \myId_{\bigotimes_{i=1}^n A_i}$ since both agree on all pure tensors. Similarly,\\ $\phi \circ \psi = \myId_{\bigotimes_{i=1}^n A_{\sigma^{-1}(i)}}$ since both agree on all pure tensors. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

Using the prior lemmas, we're now ready to construct a functor whose (filtered) colimit\\ will be the categorical coproduct of the collection $\{A_\beta\}_{\beta \in B}$ of unital commutative\\ $R$-algebras.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Let $I_f$ be the collection of finite subsets of $B$, and let $I_f$ be directed by increasing inclusion. Then after viewing $I_f$ as a category, we'll define a functor $F: I_f \to \mcateg{CAlg}_R$ as follows:\newpage
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		For each $J \in I_f$ we choose an indexing $J = \{\beta_1^{(J)}, \ldots, \beta_n^{(j)}\}$. Importantly, if\\ $J_1 \subseteq J_2$ then we know there is a unique injection:
		
		{\centering$\sigma_{J_1 \subseteq J_2}: \{1, \ldots, |J_1|\} \to \{1, \ldots, |J_2|\}$\\ [4pt]\par}
		
		such that $\beta_i^{(J_1)} = \beta_{\sigma_{J_1 \subseteq J_2}(i)}^{(J_2)}$ for all $i \in \{1, \ldots, |J_1|\}$. Also, it's easy to verify that if $J_1 \subseteq J_2 \subseteq J_3$ then $\sigma_{J_1 \subseteq J_3} = \sigma_{J_2 \subseteq J_3} \circ \sigma_{J_1 \subseteq J_2}$. And also note that $\sigma_{J \subseteq J} = \myId_{\{1, \ldots, |J|\}}$.\retTwo

		Next, for any $J \in I_f$ let $F(J) \coloneqq \bigotimes_{i=1}^{|J|} A_{\beta_i^{(J)}}$. Note that as multiplication is\\ commutative on pure tensors (since each $A_{\beta_i^{(J)}}$ is commutative), we can further\\ conclude that $F(J)$ is a unital commutative $R$-algebra for all $J$.\retTwo
		
		Also, if $J_1 \subseteq J_2$ then we define $r^{J_1}_{J_2} = F(J_1 \subseteq J_2) : \bigotimes_{i=1}^{|J_1|} A_{\beta_i^{(J_1)}} \to \bigotimes_{i=1}^{|J_2|} A_{\beta_i^{(J_2)}}$ to be the unique unital $R$-algebra homomorphism such that:

		{\centering $r^{J_1}_{J_2}(a_1 \otimes \cdots a_{|J_1|}) = \widetilde{a}_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes \widetilde{a}_{|J_2|}$\\ [4pt]\par}

		where $\widetilde{a}_i = a_j$ if there exists $1 \leq j \leq |J_1|$ with $\sigma_{J_1 \subseteq J_2}(j) = i$ and $\widetilde{a}_i = 1_{A_{\beta_i^{(J_2)}}}$\\ [-2pt] otherwise.\retTwo

		Note that we can show $r^{J_1}_{J_2}$ is unique and well-defined by combining lemmas A\\ and B on the prior page. Also, we can see that $r^J_J = \myId_{F(J)}$ for all pure tensors and similarly that $J_1 \subseteq J_2 \subseteq J_3 \implies \sigma_{J_1 \subseteq J_3} = \sigma_{J_2 \subseteq J_3} \circ \sigma_{J_1 \subseteq J_2} \implies R^{J_1}_{J_3} = r^{J_2}_{J_3} \circ r^{J_1}_{J_2}$ for all pure tensors. So by $R$-linearity we can conclude that:
		
		{\centering$r^J_J = \myId_{F(J)}$ and $R^{J_1}_{J_3} = r^{J_2}_{J_3} \circ r^{J_1}_{J_2}$ for all $J, j_1, J_2, J_3 \in I_f$.\retTwo\par}
	\end{myIndent}

	With that we now have a well-defined functor $F: I_f \to \mcateg{CAlg}_R$. By yesterday's work\\ we know how to construct a unital $R$-algebra $C$ as well a bunch of unital $R$-algebra\\ homomorphisms $\iota_J: \bigotimes_{i=1}^{|J|} A_{\beta_i^{(J)}} \to C$ such that $C$ along with all the $\iota_J$ is a colimit\\ [-1pt] of $F$.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\ul{Lemma C:} Let $A_1, \ldots, A_n$ be unital $R$-algebras and let $A = \bigotimes_{i=1}^n A_i$. Also let $\iota_i: A_i \to A$ be the unital $R$-algebra homomorphism $\iota_i(a) = 1_{A_1} \otimes \cdots \otimes 1_{A_{i-1}} \otimes a \otimes 1_{A_{i+1}} \otimes \cdots \otimes 1_{A_n}$. If $A^\prime$ is another unital $R$-algebra and for each $i$ we have a unital $R$-algebra homomorphism $f_i: A_i \to A^\prime$, then there is a unique unital $R$-algebra homomorphism $f: A \to A^\prime$ such that following diagram holds for all $i$:
% https://q.uiver.app/#q=WzAsMyxbMCwxLCJBX2kiXSxbMSwwLCJBIl0sWzEsMSwiQV5cXHByaW1lIl0sWzAsMiwiZl9pIiwyXSxbMCwxLCJcXGlvdGFfaSJdLFsxLDIsIlxcZXhpc3RzICEgZiIsMCx7InN0eWxlIjp7ImJvZHkiOnsibmFtZSI6ImRhc2hlZCJ9fX1dXQ==
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	& A \\
	{A_i} & {A^\prime}
	\arrow["{\exists ! f}", dashed, from=1-2, to=2-2]
	\arrow["{\iota_i}", from=2-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow["{f_i}"', from=2-1, to=2-2]
\end{tikzcd}\]

\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Proof:\\
	Note that the unique $R$-algebra homomorphism $f: \bigotimes_{i=1}^n A_i \to A^\prime$ such that\\ $f(a_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes a_n) = \prod_{i=1}^n f_i(a_i)$ satisfies the diagram we want. Furthermore, if $g$ were any other $R$-algebra homomorphism also satisfying our diagrams, we'd have to have that $g(a_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes a_n) = g(\prod_{i=1}^n \iota_i(a_i)) = \prod_{i=1}^n g(\iota_i(a_i)) = \prod_{i=1}^n f_i(a_i) = f(a_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes a_n)$. So $g$ and $f$ will agree on all pure tensors and in turn on all of $A = \bigotimes_{i=1}^n A_i$. $\blacksquare$\newpage
\end{myIndent}

As a side note, lemma C also shows us that a tensor product is a categorical coproduct over a finite collection of commutative unital $R$-algebras. This fact will be used when showing that the colimit from earlier is a categorical coproduct over an arbitrary collection of\\ commutative unital $R$-algebras.\retTwo

\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Let's now return to talking about the functor $F: I_f \to \mcateg{CAlg}_R$ defined on the prior\\ two pages, as well as it's colimit $C$ equipped with the unital $R$-algebra homomorphisms\\ $\iota_J: F(J) \to C$. In particular, if $J \in I_f$ is the singleton set $\{\beta\}$ then I'll denote $\iota_J$ as $\iota_{\beta}$.\retTwo

	I claim now that $C$ equipped with the homomorphisms $\iota_{\beta}$ is the coproduct of the collection $\{A_\beta\}_{\beta \in B}$ of commutative unital $R$-algebras.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		Suppose $A^\prime$ is a unital commutative $R$-algebra and $\{f_\beta: A_\beta \to A^\prime\}_{\beta \in B}$ is a\\ collection of unital $R$-algebra homomorphisms.\retTwo

		If $J = \{\beta_1^{(J)}, \ldots, \beta_n^{(J)}\}$ (where $n = |J|$) then we can find a unique unital $R$-algebra homomorphism $f_J: F(J) \to A^\prime$ such that $f_J(a_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes a_n) = \prod_{i=1}^n f_{\beta_i^{(J)}}(a_i)$.\retTwo Yet also note that if $J_1 \subseteq J_2$ then $F_{J_2} \circ r^{J_1}_{J_2}$ agrees with $F_{J_1}$ for all pure tensors (and thus for everything). So by the universal property of the colimit $R$-algebra $C$, there exists a unique unital $R$-algebra homomorphism $f: C \to A^\prime$ such that if $J_1 \subseteq J_2$ then the following commuting diagram holds:
		% https://q.uiver.app/#
		\[\begin{tikzcd}
			{\bigotimes_{i=1}^{|J_1|} A_{\beta_i^{(J_1)}}} && {\bigotimes_{i=1}^{|J_2|} A_{\beta_i^{(J_2)}}} \\
			& C \\
			& {A^\prime}
			\arrow["{r^{J_1}_{J_2}}", from=1-1, to=1-3]
			\arrow["{\iota_{J_1}}"', from=1-1, to=2-2]
			\arrow["{f_{J_1}}"', curve={height=12pt}, from=1-1, to=3-2]
			\arrow["{\iota_{J_2}}", from=1-3, to=2-2]
			\arrow["{f_{J_2}}", curve={height=-12pt}, from=1-3, to=3-2]
			\arrow["{\exists ! f}", dashed, from=2-2, to=3-2]
		\end{tikzcd}\]

		In particular, if we let $J_1 = \{\beta\}$ for any $\beta \in B$ and then focus on just part of the above diagram, we can conclude that:
		% https://q.uiver.app/#q=WzAsMyxbMCwwLCJBX1xcYmV0YSJdLFsxLDEsIkFeXFxwcmltZSJdLFsxLDAsIkMiXSxbMCwyLCJcXGlvdGFfe1xcYmV0YX0iXSxbMCwxLCJmX3tcXGJldGF9IiwyXSxbMiwxLCJmIiwwLHsic3R5bGUiOnsiYm9keSI6eyJuYW1lIjoiZGFzaGVkIn19fV1d
		\[\begin{tikzcd}
			{A_\beta} & C \\
			& {A^\prime}
			\arrow["{\iota_{\beta}}", from=1-1, to=1-2]
			\arrow["{f_{\beta}}"', from=1-1, to=2-2]
			\arrow["f", dashed, from=1-2, to=2-2]
		\end{tikzcd}\]

		Next I claim that if $g: C \to A^\prime$ is any other unital $R$-algebra homomorphism such that $g \circ \iota_\beta = f_\beta$ for all $\beta$, then $g = f$. This is because of the following observation:\retTwo

		\ul{Lemma:} $\bigcup_{\beta \in B}\iota_\beta(A_{\beta})$ generates $C$ as an $R$-algebra.
		\begin{myIndent}\color{red}
			To see why, recall from my remark yesterday that $C = \bigcup_{J \in I_f} \iota_{J}(F(J))$.\retTwo
			
			Then consider any $J = \{\beta_1^{(J)}, \ldots, \beta_n^{(J)}\} \in I_f$ and then pick any pure tensor:
			
			{\centering$a_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes a_n \in \bigotimes_{i=1}^n A_{\beta_i^{(J)}} = F(J)$.\newpage\par}

			Importantly, we can observe from the following commuting diagram of\\ $R$-algebra homomorphisms:\\ [-20pt]
			% https://q.uiver.app/#q=WzAsMyxbMCwwLCJBX3tcXGJldGFfaV57KEopfX0iXSxbMSwxLCJDIl0sWzIsMCwiXFxiaWdvdGltZXNfe2k9MX1ebiBBX3tcXGJldGFfaV57KGopfX0iXSxbMCwxLCJcXGlvdGFfe1xcYmV0YV9pXnsoSil9fSIsMl0sWzIsMSwiXFxpb3RhX0oiXSxbMCwyLCJyXntcXHtcXGJldGFfaV57KEopfVxcfX1fSiJdXQ==
			\[\begin{tikzcd}
				{A_{\beta_i^{(J)}}} && {\bigotimes_{i=1}^n A_{\beta_i^{(j)}}} \\
				& C
				\arrow["{r^{\{\beta_i^{(J)}\}}_J}", from=1-1, to=1-3]
				\arrow["{\iota_{\beta_i^{(J)}}}"', from=1-1, to=2-2]
				\arrow["{\iota_J}", from=1-3, to=2-2]
			\end{tikzcd}\]
			that:
			
			{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
				$\iota_J(a_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes a_n) = \iota_J(\prod_{i=1}^n r^{\{\beta_i^{(J)}\}}_J(a_i))$\\ [4pt]
				$\phantom{\iota_J(a_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes a_n)} = \prod_{i=1}^n (\iota_J \circ r^{\{\beta_i^{(J)}\}}_J)(a_i) = \prod_{i=1}^n \iota_{\{\beta_i^{(J)}\}}(a_i)$
			\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

			But now since $F(J)$ is generated as an $R$-module by the pure tensors\\ $a_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes a_n$, we know that $\iota_J(F(J))$ is also generated as an $R$-module\\ by the elements $\iota_J(a_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes a_n)$ which I just showed are products of\\ elements in $\bigcup_{\beta \in B}\iota_\beta(A_{\beta})$.\retTwo
			
			So, $C$ is a union of $R$-submodules, each of which are generated by elements in the subalgebra of $C$ generated by $\bigcup_{\beta \in B}\iota_\beta(A_{\beta})$. It follows that $\bigcup_{\beta \in B}\iota_\beta(A_{\beta})$ is a generating set for $C$ as a unital $R$-algebra.\retTwo
		\end{myIndent}

		If $g \circ \iota_\beta = f \circ \iota_\beta$ for all $\beta \in B$ then that implies $f = g$ on $\bigcup_{\beta \in B} \iota_\beta(A_\beta)$. As a result of the prior lemma, we in turn must have that $f = g$ on $C$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
\end{myIndent}

\myComment Before continuing on, I'd like to further unpack the prior construction a little bit. Usually, the set $C$ constructed priorly is written as $\bigotimes_{\beta \in B}A_\beta$ and called a "tensor product". In order to justify this nomenclature, we consider the following observations.\retTwo

Let $\prod_{\beta \in B}^\prime A_\beta \coloneqq \{(a_\beta)_{\beta \in B} \in \prod_{\beta \in B} A_\beta : a_\beta = 1_{A_\beta} \text{ for all but finitely many } \beta \in B\}$.\retTwo

Given a commutative unital $R$-algebra $A^\prime$, we can say a function $T: \prod_{\beta \in B}^\prime A_\beta \to A^\prime$ is\\ "multilinear" if it is $R$-linear with respect to each component of $\prod_{\beta \in B}^\prime A_\beta$ individually.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	For example, if we have a collection of unital $R$-algebra homomorphisms\\ $\{f_\beta: A_\beta \to A^\prime\}_{\beta \in B}$ then we can get a well-defined multilinear map\\ $T: \prod_{\beta \in B}^\prime A_\beta \to A^\prime$ given by:

	{\centering $T((a_\beta)_{\beta \in B}) \coloneqq \prod_{\beta \in B} f_\beta(a_\beta)$ \retTwo\par}

	$T$ is well-defined because $f_\beta(a_\beta) = 1_{A^\prime}$ for all but finitely many $\beta \in B$. Ths is because each $f_\beta$ is unital and $a_\beta = 1_{A_\beta}$ for all but finitely many $\beta$. Seeing that $T$ is multilinear is also easy.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

In particular, consider $\bigotimes_{\beta \in B} A_\beta$ equipped with all the $\iota_\beta$. Then set $\iota: \prod_{\beta \in B}^\prime A_\beta \to \bigotimes_{\beta \in B} A_\beta$\\ to be the map $\iota((a_\beta)_{\beta \in B}) \coloneqq \prod_{\beta \in B} \iota_\beta(a_\beta)$. From the prior reasoning we know that $\iota$ is well-\\defined and multilinear.\retTwo

Furthermore, suppose $A^\prime$ is a commutative $R$-algebra and we are given any collection of unital\newpage $R$-algebra homomorphisms $\{f_\beta: A_\beta \to A^\prime\}_{\beta \in B}$, and we let $T((a_\beta)_{\beta \in B}) \coloneqq \prod_{\beta \in B} f_\beta(a_\beta)$.\\ Then there is a unique unital $R$-algebra homomorphism $f: \bigotimes_{\beta \in B} A_\beta \to A^\prime$ such that:
% https://q.uiver.app/#q=WzAsMyxbMCwxLCJcXHByb2ReXFxwcmltZV97XFxiZXRhIFxcaW4gQn0gQV9cXGJldGEiXSxbMSwxLCJBXlxccHJpbWUiXSxbMSwwLCJcXGJpZ290aW1lc197XFxiZXRhIFxcaW4gQn0gQV9cXGJldGEiXSxbMCwxLCJUIiwyXSxbMCwyLCJcXGlvdGEiXSxbMiwxLCJcXGV4aXN0cyAhZiIsMCx7InN0eWxlIjp7ImJvZHkiOnsibmFtZSI6ImRhc2hlZCJ9fX1dXQ==
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	& {\bigotimes_{\beta \in B} A_\beta} \\
	{\prod^\prime_{\beta \in B} A_\beta} & {A^\prime}
	\arrow["{\exists !f}", dashed, from=1-2, to=2-2]
	\arrow["\iota", from=2-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow["T"', from=2-1, to=2-2]
\end{tikzcd}\]

\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	The uniqueness is because $\bigcup_{\beta \in B}\iota_\beta(A_\beta) \subseteq \iota(\prod_{\beta \in B}^\prime A_\beta)$ where the former set generates $\bigotimes_{\beta \in B}A_\beta$ as an $R$-algebra. So any two unital $R$-algebra homomorphisms completing this diagram must equal each other everywhere.\retTwo
	
	As for showing that $f$ exists, just use the fact that $\bigotimes_{\beta \in B} A_\beta$ is a coproduct in order to\\ conclude there is a unique unital $R$-algebra homomorphism $f: \bigotimes_{\beta \in B} A_\beta \to A^\prime$ such\\ that $f \circ \iota_\beta = f_\beta$ for all $\beta$. Then as multiplication passes through $f$, we can conclude:
	
	{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
		$(f \circ \iota)((a_\beta)_{\beta \in B}) = f(\prod_{\beta \in B} \iota_\beta(a_\beta))$\\ [4pt]
		$\phantom{(f \circ \iota)((a_\beta)_{\beta \in B})} = \prod_{\beta \in B} (f \circ \iota_\beta)(a_\beta) = \prod_{\beta \in B} f_\beta(a_\beta) = T((a_\beta)_{\beta \in B})$.
	\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}
\end{myIndent}

Anyways, this connection isn't the most important thing ever.\retTwo

\pracOne To finish off for today, I'll just mention that now that we know how to take coproducts in $\mcateg{CAlg}_R$, the construction on \inLinkRap{Colimits of $A$-modules construction page 1023}{pages 1023-1024} can be easily adapted to construct general colimits of functors $F: \mcateg{I} \to \mcateg{CAlg}_R$.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	We just need to change the direct sum to a tensor product and then we need to make $N$ a two sided ideal instead of a submodule.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

I don't think it is worth my time going further in depth on this. So I'm going to finish my tangent on algebras and colimits and etc now.\retTwo
