\hTwo Suppose $M$ and $N$ are $C^k$ manifolds and $\Phi: M \to N$ is a $C^k$ map. We say a point $p \in M$ is a \udefine{regular point of $\Phi$} if $\df \Phi_p$ is surjective. Otherwise we say $p$ is a \udefine{critical point of $\Phi$}. Also we say a point $c \in N$ is a \udefine{regular value of $\Phi$} if $\Phi^{-1}(\{c\})$ if every $p \in \Phi^{-1}(\{c\})$ is a regular point of $\Phi$. Otherwise, we say $c$ is a \udefine{critical value of $\Phi$}. Finally, a level set $\Phi^{-1}(\{c\})$ is a \udefine{regular level set} if $c$ is a regular value of $\Phi$.
\begin{myIndent}\myComment
	As a side note, the set of regular points in $M$ is always an open subset of $U$. This is\\ because of proposition 4.1 on \inLinkRap{Proposition 4.1 pages 1054-1056}{pages 1054-1056}. So, we can always restrict the domain\\ of $\Phi$ to just an open-submanifold where $\Phi$ is a submersion.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\exTwo\ul{Corollary 5.14 (Regular level set Theorem):} Suppose $M$ and $N$ are $C^k$ manifolds without boundaries and $\Phi: M \to N$ is a $C^k$ map. Every regular level set of $\Phi$ is a properly embedded $C^k$ submanifold without a boundary and with codimension equal to $\dim(N)$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Let $c \in N$ be a regular value of $\Phi$. The set $U \subseteq M$  of regular points of $\Phi$ is open in $M$ and contains $\Phi^{-1}(\{c\})$ since $c$ is a regular value. So, $\Phi|_U$ is a $C^k$ submersion and the prior corollary shows that $\Phi^{-1}(\{c\})$ is a $C^k$ submanifold of $U$ without a boundary and with codimension equal to $\dim(N)$. Since the composition of two $C^k$ embeddings is a $C^k$ embedding, and the inclusion $\Phi^{-1}(\{c\}) \hookrightarrow M$ is the composition of the inclusions\\ $\Phi^{-1}(\{c\}) \hookrightarrow U$ and $U \hookrightarrow M$, we can also conclude $\Phi^{-1}(\{c\})$ is an embedded $C^k$\\ submanifold of $M$.\retTwo
	
	Also once again, $\Phi$ being continuous and $\{c\}$ being a closed subset of $N$ means that\\ $\Phi^{-1}(\{c\})$ is a closed subset of $M$. So, $\Phi^{-1}(\{c\})$ is a properly embedded submanifold. $\blacksquare$\newpage
\end{myIndent}

\exTwo\ul{Proposition 5.16:} \hypertarget{Proposition 5.16 page 1120}{Let} $S$ be a subset of a $C^r$ $m$-dimensional manifold $M$ without a boundary. Then $S$ is a $k$-dimensional embedded submanifold of $M$ without a boundary if and only if every $p \in S$ has an open neighborhood $U \subseteq M$ such that $U \cap S$ is a zero set of a $C^r$ submersion $\Phi: U \to \mathbb{R}^{m - k}$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	$(\Longrightarrow)$\\
	Consider any $p \in S$ and let $(U, \varphi)$ be a slice chart for $S$ in $M$ containing $p$. By translating the codomain of $\varphi$, we can without loss of generality assume that:
	
	{\centering$\varphi(U \cap S) \coloneqq \{(x_1, \ldots, x_m) \in \varphi(U) : x_{k+1} = 0, \ldots, x_m = 0\}$.\retTwo\par}
	
	Now let us write $\varphi(q) = (x_1, \ldots, x_m)$ for all $q \in U$. Next define $\pi: \mathbb{R}^{m} \to \mathbb{R}^{m - k}$ by $(x_1, \ldots, x_m) \mapsto (x_{k+1}, \ldots, x_m)$. And finally, define $\Phi \coloneqq \pi \circ \varphi$. Since both $\pi$ and $\varphi$ are $C^r$ submersions, we can conclude that $\Phi: U \to \mathbb{R}^{m - k}$ is also a $C^r$ submersion. Also, $\Phi^{-1}(\{(0, \ldots, 0)\}) = U \cap S$.\retTwo

	$(\Longleftarrow)$\\
	By the submersion level set theorem, we can conclude that for every $p \in S$ there is an open set $U \subseteq M$ containing $p$ such that $S \cap U$ is a $k$-dimensional $C^r$ embedded submanifold of $M$ without a boundary. And now we just apply the comment on \inLinkRap{Page 1116 comment}{page 1116}. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo\mySepTwo

Up until now, we've worked with submanifolds equipped with the subspace topology. However, this can be limiting. So, we adopt the following terminology.\retTwo

Let $M$ be a $C^r$ manifold. A \udefine{$C^r$ immersed submanifold of $M$} is a subset $S \subseteq M$ endowed with some topology (not necessarily the subspace topology) turning it into a topological manifold, as well a $C^r$ structure such that the inclusion map $\iota: S \hookrightarrow M$ is a $C^r$ immersion.\retTwo

\myComment Remarks:
\begin{itemize}
	\item If $k \leq r$ then we can define immersed $C^k$ submanifolds of $M$ identically as on \inLinkRap{Page 1111 remark}{page 1111}.
	\item Since all embedded submanifolds are also immersed submanifolds, we take the convention that a "$C^r$ submanifold" of $M$ is only understood by default to be immersed. If we want that submanifold to also be embedded then we will add that adjective.
	\item The \udefine{codimension} of a $C^r$ submanifold $S$ of $M$ is still defined as $\dim(M) - \dim(S)$. And $S$ is a \udefine{$C^r$ hypersurface} if $S$ has codimension $1$.\retTwo
\end{itemize}

\exTwo\ul{Proposition 5.18:} Suppose $M$ and $N$ are $C^r$ manifolds, and $F: N \to M$ is an injective $C^r$ immersion. Also let $S \coloneqq F(N)$. Then $S$ has a unique topology and $C^r$ structure making $S$ into a $C^r$ submanifold of $M$ such that $F$ is a $C^r$-diffeomorphism from $N$ to $S$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	To start off, we define a topology on $S$ by saying that $U \subseteq S$ is open if $F^{-1}(U)$ is an open subset of $N$.\newpage
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		Note that this is a well-defined topology. After all, $F^{-1}(S) = N$ and\\ $F^{-1}(\emptyset) = \emptyset$ are both open in $N$ and hence $S$ and $\emptyset$ are open subsets of $S$.\\ Also suppose $\{U_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ is a collection of subsets of $S$ such that $F^{-1}(U_\alpha)$ is open\\ in $N$ for all $\alpha$. Then $F^{-1}(\bigcup_{\alpha \in A} U_\alpha) = \bigcup_{\alpha \in A}F^{-1}(U_\alpha)$ is open in $N$. Similar\\ reasoning shows the topology on $S$ is closed under finite intersections.\retTwo

		Importantly, this topology on $S$ is the \textit{unique} topology $S$ must be equipped with\\ in order for $F$ to be a homeomorphism from $N$ to $S$ (which is necessary if we want $F$ to also be a $C^r$-diffeomorphism).\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Now $N$ being second countable and Hausdorff means that $S$ is as well. Plus we can equip $S$ with an atlas given by the charts $(F(U), \varphi \circ F^{-1})$ where $(U, \varphi)$ is any chart on $N$. By identical reasoning as in the proof of proposition 5.2 on \inLinkRap{proposition 5.2 page 1111}{pages 1111-1112}, this atlas defines a $C^r$ structure on $S$ such that $S$ is a topological manifold and $F: N \to S$ is a $C^r$-diffeomorphism. (In fact this atlas is itself maximal and $F$ being a $C^r$-diffeomorphism from $N$ to $S$ would automatically imply $S$ is equipped with this maximal atlas).\retTwo

	Finally, the inclusion map $S \hookrightarrow M$ is the composition of the diffeomorphism\\ $F^{-1}: S \to N$ and the immersion $F: N \to M$. So, $S \hookrightarrow M$ is an immersion. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\exTwo\ul{Proposition 5.22:} If $M$ is a $C^r$ manifold and $S \subseteq M$ is a $C^r$ (immersed) submanifold\\ without corners, then for every $p \in S$ there is an open set $U \subseteq S$ containing $p$ such that $U$ is a $C^r$ embedded submanifold of $M$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	By the local embedding theorem on \inLinkRap{local embedding theorem page 1105}{pages 1105-1106}, since the inclusion $\iota: S \hookrightarrow M$ is an immersion we know every $p \in S$ has an open neighborhood $U \subseteq S$ such that $\iota|_U$ is an embedding. And then the image of an embedding is always an embedded submanifold. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\myComment As a side note, the prior proposition does \textit{not} say that we can find an open set $U$ in the topology of $M$ containing $p$ such that $U \cap S$ is an embedded submanifold. It only says we can find an open set $U$ in the topology of $S$ containing $p$ such that $U$ is an embedded submanifold.\\ [-6pt]

\hTwo\mySepTwo 

Before talking about parametrizations of submanifolds, I want to skip ahead to some\\ results which I think are more interesting yet still important. Firstly, we will establish two results about restricting the domain or codomain of a $C^r$ map.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Theorem 5.27:} Suppose $M$ and $N$ are $C^r$ manifolds, $F: M \to N$ is a $C^k$ map, and $S \subseteq M$ is an (immersed) $C^r$ submanifold. Then $F|_S : S \to N$ is a $C^k$ map.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	$F|_S = F \circ \iota$ where $\iota: S \hookrightarrow M$ is the $C^r$ inclusion map. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\ul{Theorem 5.29:} Suppose $M$ is a $C^r$ manifold without a boundary, $S \subseteq M$ is an (immersed) $C^r$ submanifold without a boundary, and $N$ is another $C^r$ manifold. Next suppose\\ $F: N \to M$ is a $C^k$ map such that $F(N) \subseteq S$. If $F$ is continuous as a map from $N$\\ to $S$ then $F: N \to S$ is a $C^k$ map.\newpage
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	\hypertarget{idk reference 7}{Let} $p \in N$ be arbitrary and set $q = F(p) \in S$. By proposition 5.22, we know there\\ is an open neighborhood $V \subseteq S$ of $q$ such that the inclusion map $\iota|_V: V \hookrightarrow M$ is\\ a $C^r$ embedding. But now $V$ (equipped with the open submanifold structure relative\\ to $S$) is an embedded $C^r$ submanifold of $M$ without a boundary. So, we let\\ $\pi: \mathbb{R}^{\dim(M)} \to \mathbb{R}^{\dim(S)}$ be the projection map onto the first $\dim(S)$ many\\ coordinates. Then by the comment on \inLinkRap{idk reference 7 back}{page 1115} we can find a smooth chart\\ $(W, \psi)$ on $M$ containing $q$ such that $(W \cap V, \pi \circ \psi|_V)$ is a smooth chart on $V$\\ containing $q$. Since every smooth chart on an open submanifold is also a smooth\\ chart on the original manifold, we can further conclude $(W \cap V, \pi \circ \psi|_V)$\\ is a smooth chart on $S$ containing $q$.\retTwo

	Now since $F: N \to S$ is continuous, we know that $U \coloneqq F^{-1}(W \cap V)$ is an open\\ subset of $N$ containing $p$. So, we let $(U_0, \varphi)$ be any smooth chart on $N$ such that\\ $p \in U_0 \subseteq U$. And now $(\pi \circ \psi|_V) \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1} = \pi \circ (\psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1})$ will be a $C^k$ map\\ since $F: N \to M$ is a $C^k$ map.\retTwo

	This finishes proving that $F: N \to S$ is a $C^k$ map. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\ul{Corollary 5.30 (The Embedded Case):} Suppose $M$ is a $C^r$ manifold without a boundary, $S \subseteq M$ is an embedded $C^r$ submanifold, and $N$ is another $C^r$ manifold. If $F: N \to M$ is a $C^k$ map with $F(N) \subseteq S$ then $F: N \to S$ is also a $C^k$ map.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Since $S$ is equipped with the subspace topology, we automatically have that $F: N \to M$ being continuous means that $F: N \to S$ is continuous. So, we can apply the prior theorem. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo Suppose $M$ is a $C^r$ manifold and $S \subseteq M$ is an immersed $C^r$ submanifold of $M$. We say $S$ is \udefine{weakly embedded in $M$} and also an \udefine{initial submanifold of $M$} if every $C^k$ map $F: N \to M$ (where $k \leq r$) whose image lies in $S$ is also a $C^k$ map from $N$ into $S$. The prior corollary says that every embedded $C^r$ submanifold is also a weakly embedded $C^r$ submanifold.\retTwo

A particularly important consequence of the prior corollary can be stated as follows:\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Theorem 5.31:} Suppose $M$ is a $C^r$ manifold without a boundary and $S \subseteq M$ is a\\ weakly embedded $C^r$ submanifold without a boundary. Then there is no other topology and $C^r$ structure that $S$ can be equipped with such that $S$ is an immersed $C^r$ submanifold of $M$ without a boundary.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Suppose $\widetilde{S}$ is the set $S$ equipped with some other topology and $C^r$ structure such that $\widetilde{S}$ is an immersed $C^r$ submanifold of $M$ without a boundary. Also let $\iota$ denote the inclusion map $S \hookrightarrow M$ and $\widetilde{\iota}$ denote inclusion map $\widetilde{S} \hookrightarrow M$.\retTwo

	Because $\widetilde{\iota}(S)$ is contained in $S$ which is weakly embedded, we know $\widetilde{\iota}$ is a $C^r$ map from $\widetilde{S}$\\ into $S$. Yet then note for any $p \in S$ that $\df \widetilde{\iota}_p : T_p \widetilde{S} \to T_p M$ is both injective and the\\ [2pt] composition of the maps:\\ [-14pt]
	% https://q.uiver.app/#q=WzAsMyxbMCwwLCJUX3AgXFx3aWRldGlsZGV7U30iXSxbMSwwLCJUX3AgUyJdLFsyLDAsIlRfcCBNIl0sWzAsMSwiXFxkZiBcXHdpZGV0aWxkZXtcXGlvdGF9X3AiXSxbMSwyLCJcXGRmIFxcaW90YV9wIl1d
	\[\begin{tikzcd}
		{T_p \widetilde{S}} & {T_p S} & {T_p M}
		\arrow["{\df \widetilde{\iota}_p}", from=1-1, to=1-2]
		\arrow["{\df \iota_p}", from=1-2, to=1-3]
	\end{tikzcd}\]\newpage

	Thus we must have that $\widetilde{\iota}$ is a $C^r$ immersion from $\widetilde{S}$ into $S$. In other words, $\widetilde{\iota}$ has constant rank. And since $\widetilde{\iota}$ is a bijection between $S$ and $\widetilde{S}$, we can then conclude by the corollary on \inLinkRap{page 1066 corollary}{page 1066} that $\widetilde{\iota}: \widetilde{S} \to S$ is a $C^r$-diffeomorphism. This implies that the topology and $C^r$ structure on $S$ and $\widetilde{S}$ are the same. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo In particular, the prior theorem tells us that there is only one $C^r$ structure that an\\ embedded submanifold $S$ of $M$ (without a boundary) can be equipped with. So, the\\ $C^r$ structure constructed in theorem 5.8 based on the local $k$-slice condition (see \inLinkRap{Theorem 5.8 page 1114}{pages\\ 1114-1116}) is the unique structure on $S$.\retTwo

For a general immersed submanifold of $M$ though, we have the following weaker\\ uniqueness result.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Theorem 5.32:} Suppose $M$ is a $C^r$ manifold without a boundary and $S \subseteq M$ is an\\ immersed $C^r$ submanifold without a boundary. Then with the given topology on $S$\\ there is no other $C^r$ structure that $S$ can be equipped with such that $S$ is an immersed\\ $C^r$ submanifold of $M$ without a boundary.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Let $\widetilde{S}$ be the set $S$ equipped with the same topology but just a different $C^r$ structure. Then the proof of theorem 5.31 works entirely the same, except that instead of using corollary 5.30, we instead note that $\widetilde{\iota}$ is a continuous function from $\widetilde{S}$ into $S$ and so theorem 5.29 applies. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo\mySepTwo

\dispDate{8/31/2026}

I could allow for more types of corner charts and then try to prove an immersion rank theorem for those manifolds but ehhh I don't think it would likely be the end of the world to just limit myself to having a rank theorem for boundary charts (non-corner charts) in the domain.\retTwo

Let $M$ be an $n$-dimensional $C^r$ manifold without a boundary (where $n \geq 1$) and let $(U, \varphi)$ be a smooth chart on $M$. Given an integer $k \in \{0, 1, \ldots, n\}$, we say a \udefine{$k$-dimensional half slice of $U$} is a set $V \subseteq U$ such that:

{\centering $\varphi(V) = \{(x_1, \ldots, x_n) \in \varphi(U) : x_{k+1} = c_{k+1}, \ldots, x_n = c_n, \text{ and } x_k \geq 0\}$,\\ [4pt]\par}

where $c_{k+1}, \ldots, c_n \in \mathbb{R}$.\retTwo

We say a subset $S \subseteq M$ satisfies the \udefine{local $k$-slice condition for a manifold with a boundary} (what a mouthful) if every $p \in S$ is contained in a smooth chart $(U, \varphi)$ such that $S \cap U$ is either a $k$-slice or a $k$-half slice of $U$. In the former case, $(U, \varphi)$ is called an \udefine{interior slice chart} for $S$ in $M$. Meanwhile, in the latter case $(U, \varphi)$ is called a \udefine{boundary slice chart} for $S$ in $M$.\retTwo

By using the local immersion theorem for manifolds with boundaries (see \inLinkRap{Local Immersion Theorem boundary page 1101}{pages 1101-1102}) in place of the rank theorem, we can prove an analogous result to theorem 5.8 on \inLinkRap{Theorem 5.8 page 1114}{pages 1114-1116}. Then in turn, we can also prove an analogous result to theorem 5.29. I shall write those results right belows. There's no new ideas in proving them though.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Theorem 5.51:} Let $M$ be a $C^r$ $n$-dimensional manifold without a boundary and let $S \subseteq M$ be a $C^r$ embedded $k$-dimensional submanifold without corners. Then $S$ satisfies the local $k$-slice condition for a manifold with a boundary.
\begin{myIndent}\color{red}
	In particular, let $\pi: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^k$ be the projection map onto the first $k$-coordinates. Then for any $p \in S$ we can find a boundary or interior slice chart $(U, \varphi)$ on $M$ such that $(S \cap U, \pi \circ \varphi|_S)$ is a smooth chart on $S$ containing $p$ and:
	
	{\centering\fontsize{12}{13}\selectfont$S \cap U = \varphi^{-1}(\{(x_1, \ldots, x_n) : x_{k+1} = \cdots = x_n = 0 \text{ }(\text{and } x_k \geq 0 \text{ if } p \in \partial S)\})$.\retTwo\par}
\end{myIndent}

Conversely, if $S \subseteq M$ satisfies the local $k$-slice condition for a manifold with a boundary, then $S$ equipped with the subspace topology is a topological manifold. Furthermore, it has a $C^r$ structure making it into an embedded $C^r$ submanifold in $M$ without corners.
\begin{myIndent}\color{red}
	Specifically, we equip $S$ with the structure generated by the charts $(U \cap S, \pi \circ \varphi|_S)$ where $(U, \varphi)$ is any boundary or interior slice chart for $S$ and $\pi: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^k$ is the projection map onto the first $k$-coordinates.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\ul{Theorem 5.53(b):} Suppose $M$ and $N$ are $C^r$ manifolds such that $M$ has no boundary,\\ and also suppose $S \subseteq M$ is an (immersed) $C^r$ submanifold without corners. Now let\\ $F: N \to M$ be a $C^k$ map such that $F(N) \subseteq S$. If $F$ is continuous as a function from $N$\\ to $S$ then $F: N \to S$ is a $C^k$ map.\retTwo

\hTwo As a side note, theorem 5.51 is enough to tell us that there is at most one $C^r$ structure on a set $S \subseteq M$ equipped with the subspace topology turning it into an embedded $C^r$ submanifold of $M$ without corners.\\ [-8pt]
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	To see why, suppose $S \subseteq M$ is any subset equipped with a $C^r$ structure such that it\\ becomes a $C^r$ embedded submanifold of $M$. Next let $\widetilde{S}$ be the subset $S$ equipped\\ with the $k$-slice $C^r$ structure constructed on the converse direction of theorem 5.51.\\ [1pt] By the red text, we can see that the $C^r$ structures of $S$ and $\widetilde{S}$ both contain a common\\ atlas of smooth charts. So, both structures must be identical. And since the $C^r$ structure\\ [1pt] of $\widetilde{S}$ is defined entirely independently from the $C^r$ structure on $S$, we can conclude that\\ the $C^r$ structure on $\widetilde{S}$ is the unique $C^r$ structure turning $S$ into an embedded $C^r$\\ submanifold of $M$.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo\mySepTwo

Now the connection between abstract manifolds and the definition of manifolds given on \inLinkRap{placeholder}{pages 77-99} is that Munkres works with embedded submanifolds of $\mathbb{R}^n$ (equipped with the standard structure).\retTwo

To see one direction of this equivalence, consider the following:
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo 
	Note that Munkres' definition of a coordinate patch on a $C^r$ manifold $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is equivalent to that of a $C^r$ embedding $\alpha: U \to \mathbb{R}^n$ where $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^k$ (or $H^k$) is an open set and $\alpha(U) = V$ is an open subset of $S$ (equipped with the subspace topoloy). Since every point is in the image of a coordinate patch, we can conclude there is a covering for $S$ consisting of open sets $\{W_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ in $M$ such that $W_\alpha \cap S$ is an embedded submanifold (without corners because none of the coordinate patches are from $\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^k$) for all $\alpha$. It follows that $S$ satisfies the local $k$-slice condition for a manifold with a boundary. So, $S$ is an embedded $C^r$ submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^n$.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

Going the other way, I want to introduce parametrizations more generally.\retTwo

Suppose $M$ is a $C^r$ manifold and $S \subseteq M$ is an immersed $k$-dimensional $C^r$\\ submanifold of $M$. Then \udefine{a local parametrization of $S$} is a continuous map $X: U \to M$ (where $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^k$, $H^k$, or $\mathbb{R}^k_{\geq 0}$ is an open set) whose image is an open subset of $S$ and which is a homeomorphism when considered as a function from $U$ to $X(U) \subseteq S$. If $X$ is also a $C^r$ diffeomorphism from $U$ to $X(U) \subseteq S$, it is called a $C^r$ parametrization. Meanwhile, if $X(U) = S$ then we say $X$ is a \udefine{global parametrization}.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Proposition 5.23:} \hypertarget{Proposition 5.23 page 1125}{Suppose} $M$ is a $C^r$ manifold, $S \subseteq M$ is an immersed $k$-dimensional $C^r$ submanifold of $M$, $\iota: S \hookrightarrow M$ is the inclusion map, and $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^k$ (or $H^k$ or $\mathbb{R}^k_{\geq 0}$) is an open set. A map $X: U \to M$ is a $C^r$ parametrization if and only if there is a smooth coordinate chart $(V, \varphi)$ on $S$ such that $U = \varphi(V)$ and $X = \iota \circ \varphi^{-1}$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	$(\Longleftarrow)$\\
	Let $(V, \varphi)$ be a smooth chart on $S$ such that $U = \varphi(V)$ and $X = \iota \circ \varphi^{-1}$. Then $X$ is a continuous map with a continuous inverse $\varphi$ from $X(U) = V \subseteq S$ to $U$. Also $X$ is a $C^r$ diffeomorphism from $U$ to $V$.\retTwo

	$(\Longrightarrow)$\\
	Let $X: U \to M$ be a $C^r$ paremtrization. Then let $V = X(U)$ and $\varphi = X^{-1}$ (considered as a $C^r$ map from $V \subseteq S$ to $U$). Clearly $X = \iota \circ \varphi^{-1}$ and $U = \varphi(V)$. Also I claim that $(V, \varphi)$ is a smooth chart on $M$. After all, let $(W, \psi)$ be any other smooth chart on $M$.\retTwo

	Since $\varphi^{-1}$ is a $C^r$ map by assumption, we know that $\myId_{U} \circ \varphi \circ \psi^{-1} = \varphi \circ \psi^{-1}$ is a $C^r$ map. Similarly, as $X$ is a $C^r$ map from $U$ into $V$, we know $ \psi \circ X \circ \myId_U = \psi \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is a $C^r$ map. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo In particular, this proposition shows that every point in an immersed submanifold is\\ contained in some parametrization.

\pracOne\mySepTwo

{\hTwo\dispDate{9/5/2026}}

Augh never mind I want to broaden the corner charts I'm allowed to use.\retTwo

Suppose $M$ is an $n$-dimensional $C^r$ manifold with corners and $p \in M$ is a corner point. Then given any chart $(U, \varphi)$ on $M$ containing $p$ we must have that $\varphi(U)$ is open in $\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^n$ and that $\varphi(p) \coloneqq (x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ where two of the coordinates of $\varphi(p)$ are zero. In particular, suppose exactly $k$ coordinates of $\varphi(p)$ are zero. By permuting those coordinates, we can\newpage assume without loss of generality it is the first $k$ coordinates of $\varphi(p)$ are zero. And then by translating the codomain of $\varphi$ by the vector $(0, \ldots, 0, x_{k+1}, \ldots, x_n)$, we get a "chart" $(U, \varphi^\prime)$ where $\varphi^\prime(U)$ is an open subset of $[0, \infty)^k \times \mathbb{R}^{n - k}$ with $\varphi^\prime(p) = 0$. And this "chart" will be $C^r$ compatible with the $C^r$ structure on $M$.\retTwo

\ul{Lemma:} Suppose $k_1, k_2 < n$ with $k_1 \neq k_2$ and that $U \subseteq [0, \infty)^{k_1} \times \mathbb{R}^{n - k_1}$ and\\ $V \subseteq [0, \infty)^{k_2} \times \mathbb{R}^{n - k_2}$ are open subsets of the respective subspace topologies which\\ both contain $0$. Then there is no $C^1$ diffeomorphism $\varphi: U \to V$ such that $\varphi(0) = 0$.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Proof:\\
	We basically proceed by identical reasoning as on \inLinkRap{Page 1041 Theorem}{page 1041}. Without loss of generality we can assume $k_1 < k_2$. Then suppose for the sake of contradiction that such a map $\varphi: U \to V$ did exist.\retTwo

	Let $S \coloneqq \{y = (y_1, \ldots, y_n) \in \mathbb{R}^n : y_1 = 0, \ldots, y_{k_1} = 0\}$. Thus $S$ is an $(n - k_1)$-dimensional vector subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n$. Next note that $\Df \varphi(0)$ must be an invertible linear map (with the inverse map $\Df \varphi^{-1}(0)$). Therefore, we can conclude that $T \coloneqq (\Df \varphi(0))(S)$ is also an $(n - k_1)$-dimensional vector subspace.\retTwo
	
	Yet then there must exist $v = (v_1, \ldots, v_n) \in T$ such that one of the $v_1, \ldots, v_{k_2}$ equals zero. Otherwise, $T$ would be contained in an $(n - k_2)$-dimensional vector space. And since $k_1 < k_2$, this would contradict that $(n - k_1)$-dimensional vector subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n$.\retTwo

	By negating $v$ if necessary we can assume $v_i < 0$ for some $1 \leq i \leq k_2$. Finally, let\\ $\gamma: (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \to U \cap S$ be a $C^1$ curve such that $\gamma(0) = 0$ and
	
	{\centering$(\varphi \circ \gamma)^\prime(0) = (\Df \varphi(0))\gamma^\prime(0) = v$.\\ [4pt]\par}
	
	Then for small enough $t \in (0, \varepsilon)$ we must have that $(\alpha \circ \gamma)(t) \cdot e_i < 0$. But this contradicts that $\varphi(U \cap S) \subseteq [0, \infty)^{k_2} \times \mathbb{R}^{n - k_2}$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

Given a smooth chart $(W, \psi)$ about a corner point $p$ in a $C^r$ manifold $M$ such that $\psi(W)$ is an open subset of $\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^n$, we say $p$ has \udefine{depth} $k$ if exactly $k$ of the components of $\psi(p)$ are zero. The prior lemma lets us conclude that the depth of $p$ is defined independently of which chart we choose.\retTwo

That said, because I want to allow smooth charts $(W, \psi)$ about a corner point $p \in M$ to be "centered" (i.e. satisfy that $\psi(p) = 0$), I'm going to start letting corner charts map to $[0, \infty)^k \times \mathbb{R}^{n - k}$ instead of just $[0, \infty)^{n}$.\retTwo

Importantly, once we allow these new charts then we can by identical reasoning prove\\ that the local immersion theorem for manifolds with boundaries on \inLinkRap{Local Immersion Theorem boundary page 1101}{pages 1101-1102}\\ holds for a $C^r$ manifold $M$ with corner points. Then in turn, the local embedding theorem\\ on \inLinkRap{local embedding theorem page 1105}{pages 1105-1106} also holds if the $C^r$ manifold $M$ has corners.

\mySepTwo 

\hTwo\dispDate{9/6/2026}

\hTwo If $M$ is a $C^r$ manifold, we say $D \subseteq M$ is a \udefine{regular domain in $M$} if it is a properly embedded codimension $0$ submanifold of $M$.\newpage

\exTwo\ul{Proposition 5.46:} Suppose $M$ is a $C^r$ manifold without a boundary and $D \subseteq M$ is a regular domain. Then the topological interior and boundary of $D$ is equivalent to the manifold interior and boundary of $D$ respectively.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	For the sake of notation, I will let $\partial D$ refer to the manifold boundary of $D$ and $\Int(D)$ refer to the manifold interior of $D$.\retTwo

	Suppose $p \in \partial D$ with depth $k \geq 1$. Then by the local immersion theorem for manifolds with boundaries, there exists a smooth chart $(U, \varphi)$ centered at $p$ in $D$ and a smooth chart $(V, \psi)$ centered at $p$ in $M$ such that $\varphi(p) = 0$ and $\psi \circ \varphi(x_1, \ldots, x_n) = (x_1, \ldots, x_n)$. (Here $n = \dim(M) = \dim(D)$).\retTwo

	But now since $D$ has the subspace topology, we know  there is an open set $W \subseteq M$ \\such that $U = W \cap D$. In turn, $V_0 \coloneqq V \cap W$ is an open set in $M$ such that\\ $V_0 \cap D = \psi^{-1}([0, \infty)^k \times \mathbb{R}^{n - k})$. And since $\psi(p) = (0, \ldots, 0)$ and $\psi(V_0)$ is an\\ open subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ containing $\psi(p)$, we can conclude that any open subset of $p$ will\\ contain points inside and outside $D$. So, $p$ is in the topological boundary of $D$.\retTwo

	Meanwhile, suppose $p$ is in the manifold interior of $D$. Importantly, the manifold interior is an open submanifold of $M$ (see \inLinkRap{Proposition 5.1 page 1111}{page 1111}). So, $p$ is contained in an open subset of $M$ which is contained in $D$. Thus $p$ is in the topological interior of $D$.\retTwo

	Since the topological interior of $D$ is contained in $D$ we can now conclude that the topological interior of $D$ is precisely $\Int(D)$. Meanwhile, because $D$ is a closed subset of $M$ (since it is properly embedded), we know that the topological boundary of $D$ is also contained in $D$. So, it must be precisely $\partial D$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\exTwo\ul{Proposition 5.47:} \hypertarget{Proposition 5.47 page 1127}{Suppose} $M$ is a $C^r$ manifold without a boundary and $f \in C^r(M, \mathbb{R})$.
\begin{enumerate}
	\item[(a)] \hypertarget{Proposition 5.47 page 1127}{For} each regular value $b \in \mathbb{R}$ we have that $f^{-1}((-\infty, b])$ is a regular domain in $M$ without corners.
	\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
		Proof:\\
		To start off, $f$ being continuous implies that $D \coloneqq f^{-1}((-\infty, b])$ will be a closed subset of $M$. Thus, once we show $D$ is an embedded $C^r$ submanifold of $M$, it will be obvious that $D$ is properly embedded.\retTwo

		We proceed by showing that if $p \in D$ then there is an open set $U \subseteq M$ containing\\ $p$ such that $D \cap U$ is an embedded submanifold of codimension $0$. Fortunately, by the continuity of $f$, if $f(p) \neq b$ then $f^{-1}((-\infty, b))$ is an open subset of $M$ and of $D$ containing $p$. Since open subsets of $M$ are submanifolds of codimension $0$ without boundaries, we are done in that case.
		\begin{myIndent}\myComment
			(In fact this would show that $f^{-1}((-\infty, b)) \subseteq \Int(D)$.)\retTwo
		\end{myIndent}

		Meanwhile suppose $f(p) = b$. Since $b$ is a regular value of $f$, we know that $\df f_p$ is surjective. In turn, by proposition 4.1 on \inLinkRap{Proposition 4.1 pages 1054-1056}{page 1054} we can find an open set $U \subseteq M$ containing $p$ such that $\df f_q$ is surjective for all $q \in U$.\newpage

		By the rank theorem, there's a smooth chart $(V, \varphi)$ on $U$ and a smooth chart $(W, \psi)$ on $\mathbb{R}$ such that $\varphi(p) = 0$ and $\psi \circ f \circ \varphi^{-1}$ equals the projection map $\pi: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$\\ onto the first coordinate. (Here $n = \dim(M)$.) Yet since $\psi(b) = 0$ and $\psi$ must map connected components of $W - \{b\}$ to $\psi(W) - \{0\}$, we can conclude that $W \cap (-\infty, b]$ is precisely given by either $\psi^{-1}((-\infty, 0])$ or $\psi^{-1}([0, \infty))$. By negating components of $\varphi$ and $\psi$ if necessary, we can without loss of generality assume\\ $W \cap (-\infty, b] = \psi^{-1}([0, \infty))$.\retTwo

		Now $q \in V \cap D$ iff $q \in V$ and $f(q) \leq b$. Yet $f(q) \leq b$ iff:
		
		{\centering$\psi(f(q)) = (\psi \circ f \circ \varphi^{-1})(\varphi(q)) \geq 0$.\\ [4pt]\par}
		
		So $V \cap D = \varphi^{-1}([0, \infty) \times \mathbb{R}^{n-1})$. In other words, $V \cap D$ is an $n$-half slice of the smooth chart $(V, \varphi)$ on $M$ containing $p$. It follows that $D \cap V$ is an embedded submanifold of $M$ of codimension $0$.
		\begin{myIndent}\myComment
			(And in particular $p$ is a boundary point. Thus $f^{-1}(\{b\}) = \partial D$).\retTwo
		\end{myIndent}
	\end{myIndent}

	\item[(b)] Given any two regular values $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$, we have that $f^{-1}([a, b])$ is a regular domain in $M$ without corners. 
	\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
		Proof:\\
		The proof of part (a) translates basically verbatim. The only additional step is that you need to shrink the open set $U$ containing $p \in f^{-1}(\{b\})$ by intersecting it with $f^{-1}(b -\varepsilon, b + \varepsilon)$ for some small enough $\varepsilon > 0$. And you'd do an analogous thing when showing the case for some $p \in f^{-1}(\{a\})$. $\blacksquare$

		\begin{myIndent}\myComment
			(In particular, if $D \coloneqq f^{-1}([a, b])$ then $f^{-1}((a, b)) = \Int(D)$ and\\ $f^{-1}(\{a, b\}) = \partial D$).\retTwo
		\end{myIndent}
	\end{myIndent}
\end{enumerate}

\dispDate{9/10/2026}

\exTwo\ul{Lemma 5.34:} Suppose $M$ is a $C^r$ manifold without a boundary, $S \subseteq M$ is an (immersed) $C^r$ submanifold, and $f \in C^r(S, \mathbb{R})$ (meaning $f$ is a $C^r$ map according to the differentiable structure on $S$).
\begin{itemize}
	\item[(a)] If $S$ is embedded and without a boundary, then there exists an open set $U \subseteq M$\\ containing $S$ and a function $\widetilde{f} \in C^r(U, \mathbb{R})$ such that $f = \widetilde{f}|_S$.
	\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
		Proof:\\
		First I shall show that for every $p \in S$ there is an open set $U_p \subseteq M$ and a function $f_p \in C^r(U_p, \mathbb{R})$ such that $f = f_p$ on $U \cap S_p$.
		\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
			Let $k = \dim(S)$, $n = \dim(M)$, and $\pi: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^k$ be the projection onto\\ the first $k$ coordinates. Then we can find a slice chart $(U_p, \varphi)$ for $S$ in $M$\\ containing $p$. In particular, $(S \cap U_p, \pi \circ \varphi)$ is a smooth chart on $S$ with\\ $S \cap U_p = \varphi^{-1}(\{(x_1, \ldots, x_n) : x_{k+1} = c_{k+1}, \ldots, x_n = c_n\})$. Next, let\\ $\iota: \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be the function $(x_1, \ldots, x_k) \mapsto (x_1, \ldots, x_k, c_{k+1}, \ldots, c_n)$.\newpage

			Given the local coordinates defined by $(V, \varphi)$ we want\\ $f_p(x_1, \ldots, x_n) = f(x_1, \ldots, x_k)$. So, let:

			{\centering $f_p = f \circ \varphi^{-1} \circ \iota \circ \pi \circ \varphi$\retTwo\par}

			Then $f_p \in C^r(U_p, \mathbb{R})$. Also for all $(x_1, \ldots, x_k, c_{k+1}, \ldots, c_n) \in S \cap U_p$ we know that:
			
			{\centering$f_p \circ \varphi^{-1}(x_1, \ldots, x_k, c_{k+1}, \ldots, c_n) = f \circ \varphi^{-1}(x_1, \ldots, x_k, c_{k+1}, \ldots, c_n)$\\ [4pt]\par}

			So, $f = f_p$ on $S \cap U_p$.\retTwo
		\end{myIndent}

		Now for every $p \in S$ let $U_p \subseteq M$ be an open set containing $p$ and $f_p \in C^r(U_p, \mathbb{R})$ be a function with $f = f_p$ on $U \cap S_p$. Next, let $\{\psi_{p}\}_{p \in S}$ be a $C^r$  partition of unity on\\ the open submanifold $U \coloneqq \bigcup_{p \in S}U_p$ of $M$ subordinate to the sets $U_p$. (In other words $\supp(\psi_p) \subseteq U_p$ for every $p$ and $\sum_{p \in S}\psi_p \equiv 1$.)\retTwo
		
		Then set $\widetilde{f} = \sum_{p \in S}f_p \psi_p$. This will be a $C^r$ map from the open set $U$ containing $S$. After all, every $q \in U$ has a neighborhood in $U$ where only finitely many $\psi_p$ are nonzero. And then $\widetilde{f}$ is automatically a $C^r$ function on that neighborhood. Plus, since $f_p = f$ on $S \cap \supp(\psi_p)$ for all $p \in S$, we have that $\widetilde{f} = f \cdot 1 = f$ on $S$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	\item[(b)] If $S$ is properly embedded then we can take $U$ to be all of $M$. 
	\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
		Proof:\\
		Let $\{(U_p, \varphi_p)\}_{p \in S}$ be the open covering of $S$ consisting of slice charts from part (a). Then also let $U = M - S$. Since $S$ is closed, we know that $U$ is an open set. And now, we let $\{\psi_p\}_{p \in S} \cup \{\psi\}$ be a partition of unity on $M$ subordinate to those slice charts as well as $U$. In other words, $\supp(\psi_p) \subseteq U_p$ for all $p \in S$, $\supp(\psi) \subseteq U$, and $\psi + \sum_{p \in S}\psi_p \equiv 1$ on $M$.\retTwo

		Now set $\widetilde{f} = \sum_{p \in S}f_p \psi_p$. Then $\widetilde{f}$ will be a $C^r$ map from $M$ into $\mathbb{R}$ After all, every $q \in M$ has a neighborhood where only finitely many of the $\psi_p$ and $\psi$ are nonzero. Furthermore, since $\psi \equiv 0$ on $S$, we know that $\sum_{p \in S}\psi_p \equiv 1$ on $S$. So, $\widetilde{f} = f \cdot 1 = f$ on $S$. $\blacksquare$
	\end{myIndent}
\end{itemize}
% ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

\hTwo\mySepTwo

\hypertarget{Page 1129 reference}{I'd} like to take a break from John Lee chapter 5 and introduce a different important topic in the theory of manifolds.\retTwo

Let $M$ be a topological space. A \udefine{(real) vector bundle of rank $k$ over $M$} is a topological space $E$ with a surjective continuous map $\pi: E \to M$ satisfying that:
\begin{enumerate}
	\item[(a)] For each $p \in M$ the fiber $E_p \coloneqq \pi^{-1}(\{p\})$ over $p$ is endowed with a structure turning it into a $k$-dimensional real vector space.
	\item[(b)] For each $p \in M$ there is an open neighborhood $U$ of $p$ in $M$ and a homeomorphism $\Phi: \pi^{-1}(U) \to U \times \mathbb{R}^k$ (called a \udefine{local trivialization of $E$ over $U$}) satisfying that:\newpage
	\begin{itemize}
		\item $\pi_U \circ \Phi = \pi$ (where $\pi_U: U \times \mathbb{R}^k \to U$ is the projection);
		\item For each $q \in U$ the restriction of $\Phi$ to $E_q$ is a vector space isomorphism from $E_q$ to $\{q\} \times \mathbb{R}^k \cong \mathbb{R}^k$.
	\end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

If $E$ and $M$ are $C^r$ manifolds, $\pi: E \to M$ is a $C^r$ map, and the local trivializations can be chosen to be $C^r$ diffeomorphisms, then $E$ is said to be a \udefine{$C^r$ vector bundle over $M$}. Also, any local trivialization that is a $C^r$ diffeomorphism is called a "smooth" local trivialization.\retTwo

We call $E$ the \udefine{total space of the bundle}, $M$ the \udefine{base space of the bundle}, and $\pi: E \to M$ the \udefine{projection of the bundle}.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Exercise 10.1:} Suppose $\pi: E \to M$ is a $C^r$ vector bundle (of rank $k$). Then the projection\\ map $\pi$ is a $C^r$ submersion.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Let $q \in E$ be any point, and then set $p = \pi(q)$. We can find an open set $U \subseteq M$ containing $p$ and a $C^r$ diffeomorphism $\Phi: \pi^{-1}(U) \to U \times \mathbb{R}^k$ that is a local trivialization. Because $\Phi$ is continuous, we know $V \coloneqq \pi^{-1}(U)$ is an open subset of $E$ containing $q$.\retTwo

	But now note that $\pi|_V = \pi_U \circ \Phi$ where $\pi_U: U \times \mathbb{R}^k \to U$ is the projection map. Therefore, $\df \pi_q = \df (\pi_U)_{\Phi(q)} \circ \df \Phi_q$. Yet we can also see that $\pi_U$ is a submersion. After all, for any $x \in U \times \mathbb{R}^k$ we have that:
	
	{\centering$T_x (U \times \mathbb{R}^k) \cong T_{\pi_U(x)} U \oplus T_{\pi_{\mathbb{R}^k}(x)}\mathbb{R}^k$ via the map sending $v$ to $(\df (\pi_U)_{x}v, \hspace{0.2em}\df (\pi_{\mathbb{R}^k})_x v)$.\retTwo\par}

	Thus, $\df (\pi_U)_x$ must be a surjection onto $T_{\pi_U(q)}U$. And since $x$ was arbitrary, we can\\ conclude $\pi_U$ is a submersion.
	\begin{myIndent}\myComment
		More generally, if $M_1, \ldots, M_k$ are any manifolds, $1 \leq i \leq k$, and\\ $\pi: M_1 \times \cdots \times M_k \to M_i$ is the projection map, then this reasoning\\ shows that $\pi$ is a submersion.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Also $\df \Phi_q$ must be an invertible map since $\Phi$ is a diffeomorphism. So, $\df \pi_q$ is the composition of two surjective linear maps, and in turn must be a surjective linear map itself. Since $q$ was arbitrary, this proves that $\pi: E \to M$ is a submersion. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\pracOne\mySepTwo 

\ul{Lemma 1.35:} \hypertarget{Lemma 1.35 page 1130}{Let} $M$ be a set, $r \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} \cup \{\infty\}$ and suppose we are given a collection\\ $\{U_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ of subsets of $M$ together with maps $\varphi_\alpha: U_\alpha \to \mathbb{R}^n$ such that:
\begin{itemize}
	\item[(i)] For each $\alpha \in A$, $\varphi_\alpha$ is a bijection between $U_\alpha$ and an open subset $\varphi_\alpha(U_\alpha)$ of\\ $[0, \infty)^k \times \mathbb{R}^{n - k}$ (where $0 \leq k \leq n$);
	\item[(ii)] For every $\alpha, \beta \in A$ we have that $\varphi_\alpha(U_\alpha \cap U_\beta)$ is an open subset of $\varphi_\alpha(U_\alpha)$; 
	\item[(iii)] Whenever $U_\alpha \cap U_\beta \neq \emptyset$ then the map $\varphi_\beta \circ \varphi_\alpha^{-1}: \varphi_\alpha(U_\alpha \cap U_\beta) \to \varphi_\beta(U_\alpha \cap U_\beta)$ is a $C^r$ map;
	\item[(iv)] Countably many of the $U_\alpha$ cover $M$;\newpage
	\item[(v)] For any $p, q \in M$ either there exists $U_\alpha$ with both $p, q \in U_\alpha$ or there exists disjoint $U_\alpha$ and $U_\beta$ with $p \in U_\alpha$ and $q \in U_\beta$. 
\end{itemize}

Then $M$ has a unique topology such that each $(U_\alpha, \varphi_\alpha)$ is a chart. And if $r \geq 1$ then $M$ has a unique $C^r$ structure such that each $(U_\alpha, \varphi_\alpha)$ is a smooth chart.

\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	To start off, we equip $M$ with the topology generated by the collection:
	
	{\centering$\{\varphi_\alpha^{-1}(V) : \alpha \in A \text{ and } V \text{ is an open subset of } \varphi_\alpha(U_\alpha)\}$.\retTwo\par}
	
	To prove that the latter set is a basis, first note by (iv) that every $x \in M$ is contained in\\ some $U_\alpha$. Also suppose that $x \in \varphi_\alpha^{-1}(V) \cap \varphi_\beta^{-1}(W)$. Then (iii) implies that:
	
	{\centering$(\varphi_\beta \circ \varphi_\alpha^{-1})^{-1}(W)$ is an open subset of $\varphi_\alpha(U_\alpha \cap U_\beta)$.\retTwo\par} 
	
	By (ii), we also know $\varphi_\alpha(U_\alpha \cap U_\beta)$ is an open subset of $\varphi_\alpha(U_\alpha)$. Thus, $(\varphi_\beta \circ \varphi_\alpha^{-1})^{-1}(W)$ is also an open subset of $\varphi_\alpha(U_\alpha)$. And now, we can say that:
	
	{\centering$\varphi_\alpha^{-1}(V \cap (\varphi_\beta \circ \varphi_\alpha^{-1})^{-1}(W)) = \varphi_\alpha^{-1}(V) \cap \varphi_\beta^{-1}(W)$\\ [4pt]\par}
	
	is also a basis set. Equality here is due to (i) saying $\varphi_\alpha$ and $\varphi_\beta$ are bijections.\retTwo
	
	Having equipped $M$ with this topology, it's now clear that each $\varphi_\alpha$ is a homeomorphism between $U_\alpha$ and $\varphi_\alpha(U_\alpha)$.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		To see why, first note by the definition of the topology that each $\varphi_\alpha$ is\\ continuous. I also claim each $\varphi_\alpha$ is an open map. After all, suppose $V \subseteq U_\alpha$\\ is any open set and $x \in V$ is any point. Then we know there exists some open\\ set $B \coloneqq \varphi_\beta^{-1}(W)$ where $W$ is an open subset of $\varphi_\beta(U_\beta)$ and $x \in \varphi_\beta^{-1}(W) \subseteq V$. Yet also note that as $B \subseteq V \subseteq U_\alpha$, we can further say that $W$ is an open subset of $\varphi_\beta(U_\beta \cap U_\alpha)$. In turn, by (ii) and (iii) we know that $(\varphi_\beta \circ \varphi^{-1}_\alpha)^{-1}(W) = \varphi_\alpha(B)$ is\\ an open subset of $\varphi_\alpha(U_\alpha)$. And since $\varphi_\alpha(B) \subseteq \varphi_\alpha(V)$, we've proven that $\varphi_\alpha(x)$ is in the topological interior of $\varphi_\alpha(V)$. Yet $x$ was arbitrary. So, $\varphi_\alpha(V)$ is an open subset of $\varphi_\alpha(U_\alpha)$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	It follows that $M$ is locally Euclidean. Furthermore, (iv) guarentees that $M$ is second\\ countable. Also, (v) guarentees that $M$ is Hausdorff. So, we've equipped $M$ with a\\ topology turning it into a topological $n$-dimensional manifold.
	\begin{myIndent}\myComment
		As a side note, this topology is the coarsest topology such that every $\varphi_\alpha$ is\\ continuous. Also suppose $\mathcal{T}^\prime$ is another topology on $M$ turning it into a\\ topological manifold with each $(U_\alpha, \varphi_\alpha)$ as a chart. Then suppose $V \in \mathcal{T}^\prime$. Since each $\varphi_\alpha$ is a homeomorphism, we must have that $\varphi_\alpha(V \cap U_\alpha)$ is an open subset of $\varphi_\alpha(U_\alpha)$ for all $\alpha$. Yet in turn $V \cap U_\alpha$ must be in our original topology. And since $V = V \cap M = V \cap \bigcup_{\alpha \in A}U_\alpha = \bigcup_{\alpha \in A} (V \cap U_\alpha)$, we can conclude that $V$ is open in our original topology. So, our original topology is also the finest topology that works. And this proves the topology we equipped $M$ with is unique.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Finally, if $r \geq 1$ then (iii) also tells us the $(U_\alpha, \varphi_\alpha)$ are $C^r$ compatible. And since they cover all of $M$, we know that they define a unique $C^r$ structure on $M$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

The prior lemma is useful for constructing $C^r$ manifolds. Here's one other observation that's necessary for what I'm about to do.\newpage

Suppose $M$ is a $C^r$ manifold (where $r \geq 1$) and $(U, \varphi)$ and $(V, \psi)$ are smooth charts such that $U \cap V = \emptyset$. We'll write $\varphi(p) = (x_1(p), \ldots, x_n(p))$ and $\psi(p) = (\widetilde{x_1}(p), \ldots, \widetilde{x_n}(p))$ Then for any $p \in U \cap V$ we can write $v \in T_p M$ as either $\sum_{i=1}^n c_i \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\right|_p$ or as $\sum_{i=1}^n \widetilde{c_i} \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial \widetilde{x}_i}\right|_p$\\ [-2pt] (where each representation is unique). Importantly though, by taking coordinate\\ representations of the identity map $\myId_M$, we can see that:

{\centering$| \widetilde{c}_1, \ldots, \widetilde{c}_n {\rangle} = (\Df (\psi \circ \varphi^{-1})(\varphi(p)))| c_1, \ldots, c_n{\rangle}$.\retTwo\par}
\mySepTwo

\hTwo \hypertarget{Definition of the tangent bundle}{The} most important vector bundle is the \udefine{tangent bundle} $TM$ of a $C^r$ manifold $M$.\retTwo
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	We'll define $TM \coloneqq \coprod_{p \in M} T_p M = \{(p, v) : p \in M \text{ and } v \in T_p M\}$. Then we'll also define $\pi: TM \to M$ by $\pi(p, v) = p$.\retTwo

	\exTwo\ul{Lemma 3.18:} Suppose $r \geq 1$. For any $C^r$ $n$-dimensional manifold $M$, $TM$ has a natural topology (and $C^{r-1}$ structure if $r \geq 2$) turning $TM$ into a $2n$-dimensional $C^{r-1}$ manifold. Also, $\pi: TM \to M$ is a $C^{r-1}$ map.
	\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
		Proof:\\
		Let $(U, \varphi)$ be any smooth chart and let $\varphi(p) = (x_1(p), \ldots, x_n(p))$ be the local coordinates on that chart. Then we define a map $\widetilde{\varphi}: \pi^{-1}(U) \to \varphi(U) \times \mathbb{R}^n$ by:
		
		{\centering$\widetilde{\varphi}(p, \sum\limits_{i=1}^n c_i \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\right|_p) = (x_1(p), \ldots, x_n(p), c_1, \ldots, c_n)$.\retTwo\par}

		This is a bijection to the open set $\varphi(U) \times \mathbb{R}^n$. So, we let $(\pi^{-1}(U), \widetilde{\varphi})$ be a chart. By constructing such charts for all smooth charts on $M$, we get a collection of smooth charts for which condition (i) in the prior lemma is satisfied.\retTwo

		Next suppose $(U, \varphi)$ and $(V, \psi)$ are smooth charts on $M$. Then we can easily see that
		\begin{itemize}
			\item $\widetilde{\varphi}(\pi^{-1}(U) \cap \pi^{-1}(V)) = \varphi(U \cap V) \times \mathbb{R}^n$;
			\item $\widetilde{\psi}(\pi^{-1}(U) \cap \pi^{-1}(V)) = \psi(U \cap V) \times \mathbb{R}^n$.
		\end{itemize}

		The latter sets are all open so condition (ii) is satisfied.\retTwo

		Furthermore, $\widetilde{\psi} \circ \widetilde{\varphi}^{-1} : \widetilde{\varphi}(\pi^{-1}(U) \cap \pi^{-1}(V)) \to \widetilde{\psi}(\pi^{-1}(U) \cap \pi^{-1}(V))$ is\\ given by the map:
		
		{\centering\fontsize{12}{13}\begin{tabular}{l}$((x_1, \ldots, x_n),\hspace{0.2em} (c_1, \ldots, c_n)) \mapsto (\psi \circ \varphi^{-1}(x_1, \ldots, x_n),\hspace{0.2em} (\Df (\psi \circ \varphi^{-1})(\varphi(p)))| c_1, \ldots, c_n{\rangle})$\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

		Since $\psi \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is a $C^r$ map, $\widetilde{\psi} \circ \widetilde{\varphi}^{-1}$ is thus a $C^{r-1}$ map. And this fulfills condition (iii).\retTwo

		To show condition (iv), note that a countable collection $\{(U_n, \varphi_n)\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of smooth charts covers $M$. In turn, we can see that $\{(\pi^{-1}(U_n), \widetilde{\varphi_n})\}$ is a countable collection of charts covering $TM$.\newpage

		Finally, to show condition (v) just note that if $p, q \in TM$ are in the same fiber of $\pi$ then there is a single chart $(\pi^{-1}(U), \widetilde{\varphi})$ containing $p$ and $q$. Meanwhile, if $\pi(p) \neq \pi(q)$ then we can find disjoint charts $(U, \varphi)$ and $(V, \psi)$ on $M$ such that $\pi(p) \in U$ and $\pi(q) \in V$. And then $\pi^{-1}(U)$ and $\pi^{-1}(V)$ are disjoint sets containing $p$ and $q$ respectively.\retTwo

		And now we just apply lemma 1.35 to get our topology and $C^{r-1}$ structure on $TM$ turning it into a  $2n$-dimensional $C^{r-1}$ manifold.\retTwo

		To see that $\pi: TM \to M$ is a $C^{r-1}$ map, just note for any smooth chart $(U, \varphi)$ on $M$ that $\pi(\pi^{-1}(U)) = U$ (since $\pi$ is surjective) and $\varphi \circ \pi \circ \widetilde{\varphi}^{-1} = \pi_U$ where $\pi_U$ is the projection map $U \times \mathbb{R}^n \to U$. It follows that every $q \in TM$ has a neighborhood on which $\pi$ is a $C^{r-1}$ map. So, $\pi$ is a $C^{r-1}$ map.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
\end{myIndent}

Now I claim that $\pi: TM \to M$ (where $TM$ is equipped with the topology described priorly) is a vector bundle of rank $n \coloneqq \dim(M)$ over $M$.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Proof:\\
	For every $p \in M$ we have that $\pi^{-1}(\{p\}) \cong T_p M$. Thus every fiber is an $n$-dimensional real vector space.\retTwo

	Also for any $p \in M$ we can pick a smooth chart $(U, \varphi)$ on $M$ containing $p$. And then after writing $\varphi(q) = (x_1(q), \ldots, x_n(q))$, we define $\Phi: \pi^{-1}(U) \to U \times \mathbb{R}^n$ by:
	
	{\centering$\Phi(q, \sum_{i=1}^n c_i \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\right|_p) = (q, (c_1, \ldots, c_n))$.\retTwo\par}

	To see that $\Phi$ is a local trivialization, first note that $\pi_U \circ \Phi = \pi$ (where $\pi_U : U \times \mathbb{R}^n \to U$ is the projection map). Also note for each $q \in U$ that $\Phi|_{T_q M}$ is a linear map from $T_q M$ to $\mathbb{R}^n$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

Furthermore, if $M$ is a $C^{r}$ manifold where $r \geq 2$, then $TM$ is a $C^{r-1}$ vector bundle over $M$.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Proof:\\
	It suffices to show that $\Phi$ from before is a $C^{r-1}$ diffeomorphism. Fortunately, note\\ that $\varphi^{-1} \times \myId_{\mathbb{R}^n} : \varphi(U) \times \mathbb{R}^n \to U \times \mathbb{R}^n$ is a $C^r$ diffeomorphism. Also, recall that $\widetilde{\varphi}: \pi^{-1}(U) \to \varphi(U) \times \mathbb{R}^n$ given by $\widetilde{\varphi}(p, \sum_{i=1}^n \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\right|_p) = (\varphi(p), (c_1, \ldots, c_n))$ is a smooth chart on $TM$ (and thus a $C^{r-1}$ diffeomorphism). And since $\Phi = (\varphi^{-1} \times \myId_{\mathbb{R}^n}) \circ \widetilde{\varphi}$, we know that $\Phi$ is a $C^{r-1}$ diffeomorphism. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\mySepTwo

Given a $C^k$ map $F: M \to N$ between $C^r$ manifolds, we define a map $\df F: TM \to TN$ (called the \udefine{global differential}) by $\df F(p, v) \coloneqq (F(p), \df F_p(v))$.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Proposition 3.21:} Suppose $k \geq 1$. Then $\df F$ is a $C^{k-1}$ map.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	We'll let $\pi_1 : TM \to M$ and $\pi_2: TN \to N$ denote the projection maps of our vector bundles. Now suppose $(p, v) \in TM$. Then we know there exists smooth charts $(U, \varphi)$ on\newpage $M$ containing $p$ and $(V, \psi)$ on $N$ containing $F(U)$. In turn, we consider the smooth charts $(\pi^{-1}(U), \widetilde{\varphi})$ on $TM$ and $(\pi^{-1}(V), \widetilde{\psi})$ on $TN$ (where $\widetilde{\varphi}$, $\widetilde{\psi}$ were constructed in lemma 3.18). These charts will satisfy that $(p, v) \in \pi^{-1}(U)$ and $\df F(\pi^{-1}(U)) \subseteq \pi^{-1}(V)$.\retTwo

	But now let us write $\varphi(q) = (x_1(q), \ldots, x_m(q))$ and $\psi(q) = (y_1(q), \ldots, y_n(q))$. Also let us set $\widehat{F} \coloneqq \psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1}$. Then:

	{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
		$\widetilde{\psi} \circ \df F \circ \widetilde{\varphi}^{-1}((x_1, \ldots, x_m), (c_1, \ldots, c_m))$\\ [4pt]
		$\phantom{aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa} = (\widehat{F}(x_1, \ldots, x_m),\hspace{0.2em} (\Df \widehat{F}(x_1, \ldots, x_m))|c_1, \ldots, c_m{\rangle})$
	\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

	This proves that $\df F : TM \to TN$ is a $C^{k-1}$ map. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo As a side note, if $r \geq 2$ we can now define a functor $\mcateg{Diff}^r_c \to \mcateg{Diff}^{r-1}_c$ sending any manifold $M$ to $TM$ and any $C^r$ map $F: M \to N$ to $\df F$. Meanwhile, if $r = 1$ then we can similarly define a functor $\mcateg{Diff}^1_c \to \mcateg{Man}_b$. After all, because $\df (G \circ F)_p = \df G_{F(p)} \circ \df F_p$, we can easily conclude that $\df (G \circ F) = \df G \circ \df F$. Similarly, we can conclude $\df (\myId_M) = \myId_{TM}$. So, these functors are well-defined.\retTwo

Typically, given the map $\pi: TM \to M$ we'll just identify $T_p M$ with $\pi^{-1}(\{p\})$ for every $p \in M$. That way, we can formally write $\df F$ instead of $\df F_p$ if the point $p$ is obvious from context.\retTwo

\mySepTwo

Let $J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be some interval and suppose $M$ is a $C^r$ manifold. Given a $C^1$ map $\gamma: J \to M$ and any $t_0 \in J$ we define the \udefine{velocity of $\gamma$ at $t_0$} to be $\gamma^\prime(t_0) \coloneqq \df \gamma(\left.\frac{\df}{\df t}\right|_{t_0})$. Some other common notations for $\gamma^\prime(t_0)$ are $\dot{\gamma}(t_0)$ and $\frac{\df \gamma}{\df t}(t_0)$.\retTwo

Note that if $f \in C^1(U, \mathbb{R})$ where $U$ is an open set containing $\gamma(t_0)$ then:

{\centering$\gamma^\prime(t_0)f = \df \gamma\left(\left.\frac{\df}{\df t}\right|_{t_0}\right)f = \left.\frac{\df}{\df t}\right|_{t_0}(f \circ \gamma) = (f \circ \gamma)^\prime(t_0)$\retTwo\par}

Next let $(U, \varphi)$ be a smooth chart on $M$ containing $\gamma(t_0)$. Then by restricting to a\\ small enough neighborhood of $t_0$ we can assume $\gamma(J) \subseteq U$. Thus, we can write\\ $\varphi \circ \gamma(t) = (\gamma_1(t), \ldots, \gamma_n(t))$. And now in coordinates, we have that:

{\centering $\gamma^\prime(t_0) = \sum\limits_{i=1}^n \frac{\df \gamma_i}{\df t}(t_0) \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\right|_p$\retTwo\par}

\exTwo\ul{Proposition 3.23:} Suppose $M$ is a $C^r$ manifold without corners and $p \in M$. Then every $v \in T_p M$ is the velocity of some $C^r$ curve $\gamma$ at $0$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Hopefully this is obvious from \inLinkRap{Page 1046 tangent}{pages 1046-1051} and \inLinkRap{page 1057 tangent}{page 1057-1058}.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo\mySepTwo

Now back to chapter 5.\newpage

Given an immersed $C^r$ submanifold $S$ of a $C^r$ manifold $M$, we can view its tangent space $T_p S$ at a point $p \in S$ as a subspace of the tangent space $T_p M$ of $M$ at $p$. To see how, recall by definition that the inclusion map $\iota: S \hookrightarrow M$ is an immersion. Thus at every $p \in S$ we have that $\df \iota_p : T_p S \to T_p M$ is an injection.\retTwo

In particular, suppose $v \in T_p S$ and $\widetilde{v} = \df \iota_p v \in T_p M$. Then:

{\centering$\widetilde{v}([f]) = \widetilde{v}([f, U]) = v([f \circ \iota, U \cap S]) = v([f|_{S}])$.\retTwo\par}

Now we shall view the injection $\df \iota_p$ as an identification of $T_p S$ as a subspace of $T_p M$.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Proposition 5.35:} Suppose $M$ is a $C^r$ manifold, $S \subseteq M$ is an immersed $C^r$ submanifold without corners, and $p \in S$. A vector $v \in T_p M$ is in $T_p S$ if and only if there is a $C^r$ curve $\gamma: J \to M$ such that:\\ [-20pt]
\begin{itemize}
	\item $J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact interval containing $0$,
	\item $\gamma(J) \subseteq S$,
	\item $\gamma(0) = p$, 
	\item $\gamma^\prime(0) = v$, 
	\item $\gamma$ is a $C^r$ curve when viewed as a function from $J$ into $S$.
\end{itemize}

\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	$(\Longrightarrow)$\\
	Suppose there exists $\widetilde{v} \in T_p S$ such that $v = \df \iota_p \widetilde{v}$. Then we know there is a $C^r$ curve $\gamma: J \to S$ such that $J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact interval containing $0$, $\gamma(0) = p$, and $\gamma^\prime(0) = \widetilde{v}$. But now $\iota \circ \gamma: J \to M$ is also a $C^r$ curve (since it is a composition of two $C^r$ functions). Also $(\iota \circ \gamma)^\prime(0) = \df \iota_p \circ \df \gamma_0(\left.\frac{\df}{\df t}\right|_0) = \df \iota_p(\gamma^\prime(0)) = \df \iota_p (\widetilde{v}) = v$\retTwo
	
	$(\Longleftarrow)$\\
	If we let $\widetilde{\gamma}$ be the curve $\gamma$ with it's codomain restricted to $S$ and then set $\widetilde{v} = \gamma^\prime(0)$, we have that:
	
	{\centering$\df \iota_p(\widetilde{v}) = \df \iota_p \circ \df \widetilde{\gamma}_0(\left.\frac{\df}{\df t}\right|_0) = \df (\iota \circ \widetilde{\gamma})_0(\left.\frac{\df}{\df t}\right|_0) = (\iota \circ \widetilde{\gamma})^\prime(0) = \gamma^\prime(0) = v$.\retTwo\par}

	So, $v \in T_p M$ is also in $T_p S$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\ul{Proposition 5.37:} Suppose $M$ is a $C^r$ manifold without a boundary, $S \subseteq M$ is an embedded $C^r$ submanifold (without corners), and $p \in S$. As a subspace of $T_p M$, we have that:

{\centering $T_p S = \{v \in T_p M : v(f) = 0 \text{ if } f \in C^r(M, \mathbb{R}) \text{ with } f \equiv 0 \text{ on } S\}$. \retTwo\par}

\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	First suppose $v \in T_p S \subseteq T_p M$. In other words, if $\iota: S \hookrightarrow M$ is the inclusion map\\ then we know there exists $w \in T_p S$ such that $\df \iota_p (w) = v$. But now if $f \in C^r(M, \mathbb{R})$\\ is a function vanishing on $S$, we know that $f \circ \iota \equiv 0$. So:
	
	{\centering$v(f) = \df \iota_p(w)f = w(f \circ \iota) = w(0) = 0$.\retTwo\par}

	Conversely, suppose $v \in T_p M$ satisfies that $v(f) = 0$ for all $f \in C^r(M, \mathbb{R})$ with $f \equiv 0$ on $S$. Now we want to show that there is some $w \in T_p S$ with $v = \df \iota_p(w)$. Fortunately, we can pick some slice (or half slice) chart $(U, \varphi)$ on $M$ containing $p$ such that:
	
	{\centering $U \cap S = \{\varphi^{-1}(x_1, \ldots, x_n) : (x_1, \ldots, x_n) \in \varphi(U) \text{ and } x_{k+1} = 0, \ldots, x_n = 0\}$ \newpage\par}

	If we let $\pi: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^k$ be the projection onto the first $k$ coordinates, we have that\\ $(U \cap S, \pi \circ \varphi)$ is a smooth chart on $S$. But now with respect to this coordinate chart and the chart $(U, \varphi)$ on $M$, we have that the coordinate representation of $\iota: S \hookrightarrow M$ is $\iota(x_1, \ldots, x_k) = (x_1, \ldots, x_k, 0, \ldots, 0)$. It then follows that if $\varphi(q) = (x_1(q), \ldots, x_n(q))$ then $T_p S$ is the subspace of $T_p M$ spanned by $\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_1}\right|_p, \ldots, \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_k}\right|_p$.\retTwo
	
	Now write $v = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\right|_p \in T_p M$. We just need to show that $c_j = 0$ for all $j \geq k + 1$ in order to prove that $v \in T_p S$.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		Fortunately, we can define a $C^r$ function $f: M \to [0, 1]$ such that $\supp(f) \subseteq U$ and $f \equiv 1$ on a neighborhood of $p$ in $M$. Next given any given any $j \geq k + 1$ we can define a $C^r$ map $g: M \to \mathbb{R}$ by $g(q) = f(q) \cdot x_j(q)$. Then:
		
		{\centering$v(g) = v(q \mapsto x_j(q)) = c_j$.\retTwo\par}
		
		Yet we also know that $g \equiv 0$ on $U^\comp$ and $g \equiv 0$ on $U \cap S$. So, $g \equiv 0$ on $S$ and in turn $v(g) = 0$ by assumption. So, $c_j = 0$ for all $j \geq k + 1$. \exThreeP $\blacksquare$\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo If $S \subseteq M$ is an embedded $C^r$ submanifold of a manifold $M$, we say a $C^r$ map $\Phi: M \to N$ such that $S$ is a regular level set of $\Phi$ is a \udefine{defining map for $S$}. If $N = \mathbb{R}^{\dim(M) - \dim(S)}$, we also call $\Phi$ a \udefine{defining function}.\retTwo

Also suppose $U \subseteq M$ is an open subset and $\Phi: U \to N$ is a $C^r$ map such that $S \cap U$ is a regular level set of $\Phi$. Then $\Phi$ is called a \udefine{local defining map / function for $S$}. Note that proposition 5.16 on \inLinkRap{Proposition 5.16 page 1120}{page 1120} guarentees that all embedded submanifolds without boundaries admit local defining functions on neighborhoods around all their points.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Proposition 5.38:} Suppose $M$ is a $C^r$ manifold without a boundary and $S \subseteq M$ is an embedded submanifold without a boundary. If $\Phi: U \to N$ is a local defining map for $S$ then $T_p S = \ker(\df \Phi_p)$ for all $p \in S \cap U$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Let $\iota: S \cap U \hookrightarrow M$ be the inclusion map and recall that $T_p S$ is identified with the\\ subspace $\myIm(\df \iota_p)$ of $T_p M$. But also note $\Phi \circ \iota$ is a constant map. Therefore, $\df \Phi_p \circ \df \iota_p$\\ will be the zero map. And this proves that $\myIm(\df \iota_p) \subseteq \ker(\df \Phi_p)$.\retTwo

	On the other hand, since $\df \Phi_p$ is surjective, the rank-nullity theorem tells us that\\ $\dim(\ker(\df \Phi_p)) = \dim(T_p M) - \dim(T_{\Phi(p)}N) = \dim(T_p S) = \dim(\myIm(\df \iota_p))$. So, we\\ can actually conclude that $\myIm(\df \iota_p) = \ker(\df \Phi_p)$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}
