I need to cram some other topics quickly. So I'm going to make a hard departure from John Lee for now. I'll come back to the topic of embedding manifolds into $\mathbb{R}^{2n + 1}$ on \inLinkRap{idk reference 9}{page 1239}.\retTwo

I need to learn about singular homology. So I'm going to read Haynes Miller's lectures on it. See \inLinkRap{Citation 14}{citation 14} for more info.\retTwo

If $0 \leq n \leq m$ and $p_0, p_1, \ldots, p_n \in \mathbb{R}^m$ then we define $[p_0, p_1, \ldots, p_n]$ to be the convex\\ hull $\conv(\{p_0, p_1, \ldots, p_n\}) = \{\sum_{i=0}^{n} c_i p_i : \sum_{i=0}^{n} c_i = 1\}$.\retTwo

If $e_0, e_1, \ldots, e_n$ denote the standard basis on $\mathbb{R}^{n + 1}$, then we'll define:

{\centering$\Delta^n \coloneqq [e_0, e_1, \ldots, e_n]$.\retTwo\par}

Note that if $u_0, u_1, \ldots, u_{n-1}$ is the standard basis on $\mathbb{R}^n$, then for each $0 \leq i \leq n$ we can define a continuous map $d^{(i)}: \Delta^{n - 1} \to \Delta^n$ by:

{\centering $d^{(i)}(\sum_{j=0}^{n-1} c_j u_j) = \left(\sum_{j=0}^{i - 1} c_j e_j\right) + \left(\sum_{j = i}^{n} c_j e_{j + 1}\right)$.\retTwo\par}

\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Importantly the image of $d^{(i)}$ is the face of $\Delta^n$ not containing the point $e_i$ as a corner. In other words, $d^{(i)}([u_0, u_1, \ldots, u_{n-1}]) = [e_0, e_1, \ldots, \widehat{e_i}, \ldots, e_n]$.
	\begin{myIndent}\myComment
		(Here we add a circumflex above the vector in the list to denote that we removed it.)\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Also note for any $0 \leq j \leq n - 1$ that $d^{(i)}(u_j) = e_k$ for some $k$. And importantly if $j < j^\prime$ and $d^{(i)}(u_{j^\prime}) = e_{k^\prime}$ then $k < k^\prime$.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

Let $X$ be any topological space. A \udefine{singular $n$-simplex} in $X$ is a continuous map\\ $\sigma: \Delta^n \to X$. We'll denote by $\Sin_n(X)$ the set of all singular $n$-simplices on $X$. Next,\\ we'll let $S_n(X)$ denote the free abelian group (i.e. $\mathbb{Z}$-module) generated by $\Sin_n(X)$. An element of $S_n(X)$ (called a \udefine{singular $n$-chain}) will be a formal sum of singular $n$-simplices on $X$.\retTwo

If $n < 0$, then we take $\Sin_n(X) = \emptyset$ and $\Sin_n(X) = \{0\}$.\retTwo

And now for every $n \geq 1$ we can define a boundary operator / group homomorphism $\partial: S_n(X) \to S_{n - 1}(X)$ by setting:

{\centering $\partial(\sigma) \coloneqq \sum_{i=0}^n (-1)^i (\sigma \circ d^{(i)})$ \\ [4pt]\par}

for all $\sigma \in \Sin_n(X)$.
\begin{myIndent}\myComment
	Remark 1: By the universal property of free modules there exists a unique group\\ homomorphism from $S_n(X)$ whose restriction to $\Sin_n(X)$ is as defined here.\retTwo

	Remark 2: I will be making a consistent abuse of notation where $\partial$ can denote the map $S_n(X) \to S_{n-1}(X)$ or $S_{n-1}(X) \to S_{n-2}(X)$ or etc. It will always be clear from context what map $\partial$ is.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

We'll also define $\partial$ to just be the zero map if $n \leq 0$. And now I shall show that

% https://q.uiver.app/#q=WzAsNyxbMSwwLCJTXzMiXSxbMiwwLCJTXzIiXSxbMywwLCJTXzEiXSxbNCwwLCJTXzAiXSxbNSwwLCJTX3stMX0iXSxbNiwwLCJcXGNkb3RzIl0sWzAsMCwiXFxjZG90cyJdLFswLDEsIlxccGFydGlhbCJdLFsxLDIsIlxccGFydGlhbCJdLFsyLDMsIlxccGFydGlhbCJdLFszLDQsIlxccGFydGlhbCJdLFs0LDVdLFs2LDBdXQ==
{\centering$\begin{tikzcd}
	\cdots & {S_3} & {S_2} & {S_1} & {S_0} & {S_{-1}} & \cdots
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow["\partial", from=1-2, to=1-3]
	\arrow["\partial", from=1-3, to=1-4]
	\arrow["\partial", from=1-4, to=1-5]
	\arrow["\partial", from=1-5, to=1-6]
	\arrow[from=1-6, to=1-7]
\end{tikzcd}$\\ [4pt]\par}

is a complex (see \inLinkRap{placeholder}{page 614} for a definition).\newpage

\exTwo\ul{Lemma:} Suppose $0 \leq i \leq j \leq n - 1$. Then $d^{(i)} \circ d^{(j)} = d^{(j + 1)} \circ d^{(i)}$ as maps from $\Delta^{n-2}$\\ to $\Delta^n$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Note that both maps send $e_k$ to $e_k$ if $0 \leq k < i$, $e_k$ to $e_{k + 1}$ if $i \leq k < j$, and $e_k$ to $e_{k + 2}$ if $j \leq k \leq n - 2$. In other words, both maps send the corners of $\Delta^{n-2}$ to the same points in $\Delta^n$. Furthermore, as both maps are compositions of affine maps, we know that both are affine maps themselves. In other words, they preserve convex linear combinations. And this is enough to now guarentee that both maps agree everywhere on $\Delta^{n-2}$.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\exTwo\ul{Proposition:} $\partial^2: S_{n} \to S_{n - 2}$ is the zero map.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Since $\Sin_n(X)$ generates the group $S_n$, it suffices to show that $\partial^2(\Sin_n(X)) = \{0\}$. When $n \leq 1$, this is obvious. So, we can assume that $n \geq 2$.\retTwo

	Let $\sigma: \Delta^n \to X$ be a singular $n$-simplex. Then note that:
	
	{\centering\exThreeP\fontsize{11}{13}\selectfont\begin{tabular}{l}
		$\partial^2(\sigma) = \sum\limits_{i=0}^n (-1)^{i}\partial(\sigma \circ d^{(i)}) = \sum\limits_{i=0}^n \sum\limits_{j=0}^{n-1}(-1)^{i + j} \cdot (\sigma \circ d^{(i)} \circ d^{(j)})$\\ [12pt]
		$\phantom{\partial^2(\sigma) = \sum\limits_{i=0}^n (-1)^{i}\partial(\sigma \circ d^{(i)})} = \sum\limits_{j = 0}^{n - 1} \sum\limits_{i = 0}^j(-1)^{i + j} (\sigma \circ d^{(i)} \circ d^{(j)}) + \sum\limits_{j = 0}^{n - 1} \sum\limits_{i = j + 1}^n  (-1)^{i + j} (\sigma \circ d^{(i)} \circ d^{(j)})$.
	\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

	But now by the prior lemma, we know that:

	{\centering\fontsize{11}{13}\selectfont\begin{tabular}{l}
		$\sum\limits_{j = 0}^{n - 1} \sum\limits_{i = 0}^j (-1)^{i + j}(\sigma \circ d^{(i)} \circ d^{(j)}) = \sum\limits_{j = 0}^{n - 1} \sum\limits_{i = 0}^j (-1)^{i + j}(\sigma \circ d^{(j + 1)} \circ d^{(i)})$ {\color{red}(using lemma)}\\ [12pt]
		$\phantom{\sum\limits_{j = 0}^{n - 1} \sum\limits_{i = 0}^j (-1)^{i + j}(\sigma \circ d^{(i)} \circ d^{(j)})} = \sum\limits_{i=0}^{n - 1} \sum\limits_{j = i}^{n - 1}(-1)^{i + j}(\sigma \circ d^{(j+1)} \circ d^{(i)})$ {\color{red}(changing order of indexing)}\\ [12pt]
		$\phantom{\sum\limits_{j = 0}^{n - 1} \sum\limits_{i = 0}^j (-1)^{i + j}(\sigma \circ d^{(i)} \circ d^{(j)})} = \sum\limits_{j=0}^{n - 1} \sum\limits_{i = j}^{n - 1}(-1)^{i + j}(\sigma \circ d^{(i+1)} \circ d^{(j)})$ {\color{red}(relabeling indices)}\\ [12pt]
		$\phantom{\sum\limits_{j = 0}^{n - 1} \sum\limits_{i = 0}^j (-1)^{i + j}(\sigma \circ d^{(i)} \circ d^{(j)})} = \sum\limits_{j=0}^{n - 1} \sum\limits_{i = j + 1}^{n}(-1)^{i + j - 1}(\sigma \circ d^{(i)} \circ d^{(j)})$
	\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}
	
	Therefore:

	{\centering\exThreeP\fontsize{11}{13}\selectfont\begin{tabular}{l}
		$\sum\limits_{j = 0}^{n - 1} \sum\limits_{i = 0}^j(-1)^{i + j} (\sigma \circ d^{(i)} \circ d^{(j)}) + \sum\limits_{j = 0}^{n - 1} \sum\limits_{i = j + 1}^n  (-1)^{i + j} (\sigma \circ d^{(i)} \circ d^{(j)})$\\ [4pt]
		$\phantom{aaaaaa} = \sum\limits_{j=0}^{n - 1} \sum\limits_{i = j + 1}^{n}(-1)^{i + j - 1}(\sigma \circ d^{(i)} \circ d^{(j)}) + \sum\limits_{j = 0}^{n - 1} \sum\limits_{i = j + 1}^n  (-1)^{i + j} (\sigma \circ d^{(i)} \circ d^{(j)}) = 0$. $\blacksquare$
	\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo We say an \udefine{$n$-cycle} in $X$ is an element of $\ker(\partial : S_n(X) \to S_{n-1}(X))$. The set of $n$-cycles is denoted $Z_n(X)$.\retTwo

Meanwhile, we say an \udefine{$n$-boundary} in $X$ is an element of $\myIm(\partial: S_{n+1}(X) \to S_n(X))$. The set of $n$-boundaries is denoted $B_n(X)$, and by the prior proposition we know that $B_n(X) \subseteq Z_n(X)$.\retTwo

And now we define the \udefine{$n$th singular holomology group of $X$} to be $H_n(X) \coloneqq \frac{Z_n(X)}{B_n(X)}$.
\begin{myIndent}\myComment
	As a side note, this definition of $n$-cycles, $n$-boundaries, and $n$-homologies works for any complex of modules over commutative rings.\newpage
\end{myIndent}

Let $f: X \to Y$ be a continuous map. It induces a map $f_\sharp: \Sin_n(X) \to \Sin_n(Y)$ by $f_\sharp(\sigma) = f \circ \sigma$. And then by the universal property of free groups, this extends to a unique group homomorphism $f_\sharp: S_n(X) \to S_n(Y)$. Also, we can easily see that the following commuting diagram holds for all $n$.
% https://q.uiver.app/#q=WzAsNCxbMCwwLCJTX24oWCkiXSxbMSwwLCJTX3tuLTF9KFgpIl0sWzAsMSwiU19uKFkpIl0sWzEsMSwiU197bi0xfShZKSJdLFswLDEsIlxccGFydGlhbCJdLFsyLDMsIlxccGFydGlhbCJdLFsxLDMsImZfKiJdLFswLDIsImZfKiIsMl1d
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	{S_n(X)} & {S_{n-1}(X)} \\
	{S_n(Y)} & {S_{n-1}(Y)}
	\arrow["\partial", from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow["{f_\sharp}"', from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow["{f_\sharp}", from=1-2, to=2-2]
	\arrow["\partial", from=2-1, to=2-2]
\end{tikzcd}\]

More importantly though, we want to show that $f_\sharp$ quotients out to a homomorphism $f_* : H_n(X) \to H_n(Y)$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	To start off, we shall prove that $f_\sharp(Z_n(X)) \subseteq Z_n(Y)$.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		Suppose $c \in Z_n(X)$. Then we know that $\partial(c) = 0$. In turn:
		
		{\centering$\partial(f_\sharp(c)) = f_\sharp(\partial(c)) = f_\sharp(0) = 0$.\retTwo\par}
		
		This proves that $f_\sharp(c) \in Z_n(Y)$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Next, we shall prove that $f_\sharp(B_n(X)) \subseteq B_n(Y)$.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		Suppose $b \in B_n(X)$. Then we know there exists $c \in S_{n + 1}(X)$ such that\\ $\partial(c) = b$. Yet now $f_\sharp(b) = f_\sharp(\partial(c)) = \partial(f_\sharp(c))$. This proves $f_\sharp(b) \in B_n(Y)$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	It now follows that $f_*(c + B_n(X)) \coloneqq f_\sharp(c) + B_n(Y)$ is a well-defined group\\ homomorphism from $H_n(X)$ to $H_n(Y)$.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\pracOne\mySepTwo
\hypertarget{Chain homomorphism tangent page 1160}{As} a side note, we can also use similar reasoning in more general cases. Suppose we have the following chains of $R$-modules (where $R$ is a commutative ring):
% https://q.uiver.app/#
\[\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=tiny]
	\cdots & {A_3} & {A_2} & {A_1} & {A_0} & {A_{-1}} & \cdots \\
	\cdots & {B_3} & {B_2} & {B_1} & {B_0} & {B_{-1}} & \cdots
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow[from=1-2, to=1-3]
	\arrow[from=1-3, to=1-4]
	\arrow[from=1-4, to=1-5]
	\arrow[from=1-5, to=1-6]
	\arrow[from=1-6, to=1-7]
	\arrow[from=2-1, to=2-2]
	\arrow[from=2-2, to=2-3]
	\arrow[from=2-3, to=2-4]
	\arrow[from=2-4, to=2-5]
	\arrow[from=2-5, to=2-6]
	\arrow[from=2-6, to=2-7]
\end{tikzcd}\]

A \udefine{chain homomorphism} between those complexes would be a sequence of $R$-module\\ homomorphisms $\{f_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that the following diagram commutes for all $n$.
% https://q.uiver.app/#q=WzAsNCxbMCwwLCJBX24iXSxbMSwwLCJBX3tuLTF9Il0sWzAsMSwiQl9uIl0sWzEsMSwiQl97bi0xfSJdLFswLDFdLFsyLDNdLFsxLDMsImZfe24tMX0iXSxbMCwyLCJmX24iLDJdXQ==
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	{A_n} & {A_{n-1}} \\
	{B_n} & {B_{n-1}}
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow["{f_n}"', from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow["{f_{n-1}}", from=1-2, to=2-2]
	\arrow[from=2-1, to=2-2]
\end{tikzcd}\]

The same reasoning from before shows that any chain homomorphism quotients out to\\ a homomorphism between the $n$th homology modules of this chain.

\mySepTwo\newpage

\Hstatement\blab{Exercise 3.7:} Let $\pi_0(X)$ denote the set of path components of a topological space $X$. Then\\ construct an isomorphism from the free abelian group $\mathbb{Z}\pi_0(X)$ to $H_0(X)$.
\begin{myIndent}\HexOne
	To start off, a $0$-simplex on $X$ is just a map from a singleton set to a point in $X$. Therefore, we can identify $S_0(X)$ with $\mathbb{Z} X$ where the latter denotes the free abelian group on $X$. Next, we trivially have that every singular $0$-chain is a $0$-cycle (because $S_{-1}(X) = \{0\}$). Therefore, $Z_0(X) = S_0(X)$.\retTwo
	
	Now we can define a map $f: X \to \pi_0(X)$ mapping each $p \in X$ to the path component of $X$ containing $p$. By the universal property of free groups, this then extends to a unique group homomorphism $f: Z_0(X) \to \mathbb{Z}\pi_0(X)$. Also, we trivially have that this group homomorphism is surjective because every generator of $\mathbb{Z} \pi_0(X)$ is in the image.\retTwo

	To finish off, it suffices to prove that $\ker(f) = B_0(X)$. 
	\begin{myIndent}\HexTwoP
		To start off, suppose $b \in B_0(X)$. In turn, we know there is a singular $1$-chain\\ $\sum_{i=1}^m n_i \gamma_i$ such that $\partial(\sum_{i=1}^m n_i \gamma_i) = b$. Yet we can then solve that:

		{\centering $b = \sum_{i=1}^m n_i[\gamma_i(1, 0) - \gamma_i(0, 1)]$ \retTwo\par}

		In turn, $f(b) = \sum_{i=1}^m n_i [f(\gamma_i(1, 0)) - f(\gamma_i(0, 1))]$. Yet also note that a $1$-simplex\\ can be reparametrized into being a path. Therefore, $f(\gamma_i(1, 0))$ and $f(\gamma_i(0, 1))$ will\\ be in the same path component of $X$. So, $f(b) = \sum_{i=1}^m n_i 0 = 0$ and this proves that\\ $B_0(X) \subseteq \ker(f)$.\retTwo

		Conversely, suppose $c = \sum_{i=1}^m n_i p_i \in \ker(f)$. For ease of notation, by allowing the $p_i$ to repeat themselves I can assume without loss of generality that:
		
		{\centering$c = \sum_{i=1}^{m_1} p_i - \sum_{j=1}^{m_2} q_j$.\retTwo\par}

		But now I claim that $m_1 = m_2$.
		\begin{myIndent}\HexPPP
			To see why, let $h: \mathbb{Z} \pi_0(X) \to \mathbb{Z}$ be defined by sending $\sum n_i E_i$ to $\sum n_i$. This a group homomorphism which importantly satisfies that $h(f(p)) = +1$ for all $p \in X$. Therefore, $h(f(c)) = m_1 - m_2$. At the same time though, we also have that $h(0) = 0$. So, we can conclude that $m_1 - m_2 = 0$.\retTwo
		\end{myIndent}

		So, we've shown that there is an integer $m \geq 0$ such that $c = \sum_{i=1}^m p_i - \sum_{i=1}^m q_i$. Next I shall prove that all these elements must cancel $\mathrm{mod}\text{ } B_0(X)$.
		\begin{myIndent}\HexPPP
			I shall proceed by induction on $m$. For our base case, note that if $m = 0$ then $c$\\ is obviously in $B_0(X)$. Meanwhile, suppose $m \geq 1$.\retTwo

			Let $E$ be the path component containing $p_1$. Then we can define $h_i: \mathbb{Z} \pi_0(X) \to \mathbb{Z}$\\ to be the group homomorphism projecting $\mathbb{Z} \pi_0(X)$ onto the $E$th coordinate. Again we importantly have that $h_i(f(p)) = +1$ if $p \in E$ and $h_i(f(p)) = 0$ if $p \notin E$. Yet also note that $h_i(0) = 0$. Therefore:
			
			{\centering$0 = h_i(0) = h_i(f(c)) = (\# \text{ of } p_i \text{ in E}) - (\# \text{ of } q_i \text{ in E})$\retTwo\par}

			Since $(\# \text{ of } p_i \text{ in E}) \geq 1$ since $p_1 \in E$, we can conclude that there must exist some $q_{i^\prime} \in E$ as well. But then we also can find a path (which via a reparametrization is a $1$-simplex) from $p_1$ to $q_{i^\prime}$. So, $p_1 + B_0(X) = q_{i^\prime} + B_0(X)$. And after canceling out those terms, we get that:
			
			{\centering$c + B_0(X) = \sum\limits_{i=2}^m p_i - \sum\limits_{\substack{i = 1 \\ i \neq i^\prime}}^m  q_i$.\retTwo\par}

			By induction, we can conclude that $c + B_0(X) = 0 + B_0(X)$. So, $\ker(f) \subseteq B_0(X)$.\retTwo
		\end{myIndent}
	\end{myIndent}

	With that we can now just apply the first isomorphism theorem to get our result. $\blacksquare$\newpage
\end{myIndent}

\exTwo\ul{Lemma 1.4:} Let $M$ be a paracompact Hausdorff space and $\{U_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ \textit{any} open cover. Then there exists a locally finite open cover $\{V_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ such that $\overline{V_\alpha} \subseteq U_\alpha$ for all $\alpha$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Our first step is showing that paracompact and Hausdorff implies regular (i.e. $T_3$).
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		Let $A \subseteq M$ be a closed set and suppose $p \notin A$. Then since $M$ is Hausdorff, for all $q \in A$ we can pick an open set $V_q \subseteq M$ such that $p \notin \overline{V_q}$. Next, note that $\{M - A\} \cup \{V_q\}_{q \in A}$ is an open cover of $M$. So by paracompactness, we can take a locally finite refinement $\{W_\beta\}_{\beta \in B}$ covering $M$.\retTwo

		Let $B^\prime$ be the collection of $\beta \in B$ such that $W_\beta \cap A \neq \emptyset$. Since we know that\\ $M = \bigcup_{\beta \in B} W_\beta$, we can thus conclude that $A \subseteq \bigcup_{\beta \in B^\prime} W_\beta$. At the same time though, because $\{W_\beta\}_{\beta \in B^\prime}$ is locally finite, we can say that:
		
		{\centering$\overline{\bigcup_{\beta \in B^\prime}W_\beta} = \bigcup_{\beta \in B^\prime} \overline{W_\beta} \subseteq \bigcup_{q \in A} \overline{V_q}$ where the latter set doesn't contain $p$.\retTwo\par}

		So, the open sets $U \coloneqq \bigcup_{\beta \in B^\prime} W_\beta$ and $V \coloneqq M - \overline{U}$ separate $p$ and the closed set $A$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Next, let $\mathcalli{A}$ be the collection of open subsets of $M$ whose closures are contained in a set $U_\alpha$. Because $M$ is regular, we know that $\mathcalli{A}$ covers all of $M$. So by paracompactness, we can take a locally finite refinement $\{W_\beta\}_{\beta \in B}$ of $\mathcalli{A}$ covering $M$.\retTwo

	Define a function $f : B \to A$ such that $\overline{W_\beta} \subseteq U_{f(\beta)}$ for all $\beta$. Then for every $\alpha$ define $V_\alpha \coloneqq \bigcup_{\beta \in f^{-1}(\{\alpha\})} W_\beta$. Clearly $\bigcup_{\alpha \in A} V_\alpha = \bigcup_{\beta \in B} W_\beta = M$. Also note that because the $W_\beta$ are locally finite:

	{\centering $\overline{V_\alpha} = \overline{\bigcup_{\beta \in f^{-1}(\{\alpha\})} W_\beta} = \bigcup_{\beta \in f^{-1}(\{\alpha\})} \overline{W_\beta} \subseteq U_\alpha$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo\par}
\end{myIndent}

\ul{Theorem 2.23:} Let $M$ be a paracompact Hausdorff space and let $\mathcalli{U} = \{U_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ be\\ \textit{any} open cover. Then there is a continuous partition of unity $\{f_\alpha: M \to [0, 1]\}_{\alpha \in A}$\\ subordinate to $\mathcalli{U}$ such that $\supp(f_\alpha) \subseteq U_\alpha$ for all $\alpha \in A$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	We know from before that paracompact and Hausorff implies regular. As it turns out, we can also use an identical argument (except that we replace $p$ with a disjoint closed set $B$ from $A$) in order to prove that paracompact and regular implies normal (i.e. $T_4$). This is useful because we can apply Urysohn's lemma to any normal space.\retTwo

	By lemma 1.4, we can find two locally finite open covers $\{V_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ and $\{W_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ such that $\overline{W_\alpha} \subseteq V_\alpha \subseteq \overline{V_\alpha} \subseteq U_\alpha$ for all $\alpha$. And then by Urysohn's lemma we can for every $\alpha \in A$ find a function $g \in C(M, [0, 1])$ such that $g \equiv 1$ on $\overline{W_\alpha}$ and $g \equiv 0$ on $M - V_\alpha$.\retTwo

	But now note that as $\supp(g_\alpha) \subseteq \overline{V_\alpha}$ and $\{\overline{V_\alpha}\}_{\alpha \in A}$ is locally finite, we know that every $p \in M$ has a neighborhood on which only finitely many $g_\alpha$ are nonzero. So, we can define a continuous function $h = \sum_{\alpha \in A} g_\alpha$. And then we define $f_\alpha = g_\alpha / h$ for all $\alpha$. This satisfies what we want. $\blacksquare$\newpage
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo\dispDate{9/29/2026}

The following terminology is taken from my math 290a class. Recall from \inLinkRap{placeholder}{page 117} what a homotopy and path homotopy is. We can give the following slight generalization of what a path homotopy is.
\begin{myIndent}\hThree
	Suppose $f_0, f_1 : X \to Y$ are continuous maps that agree on a subset $A \subseteq X$. Then a \udefine{homotopy $\mathrm{rel}\text{ } A$} from $f_0$ to $f_1$ is a continuous map $F: X \times [0, 1] \to Y$ such that $F(x, 0) = f_0(x)$, $F(x, 1) = f_1(x)$, and $F(a, t) = f_0(a, t) = f_1(a, t)$ for all $a \in A$.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\myComment\ul{Remarks:}\\ [-16pt]
\begin{enumerate}
	\item A path homotopy is a just a homotopy between two maps $f_0, f_1 : [0, 1] \to Y$ rel $\{0, 1\}$.
	\item If $f_0, f_1: X \to Y$ satisfy that there is a homotopy rel $A \subseteq X$ between $f_0$ and $f_1$, we write $f_0 \simeq_A f_1$ and say $f_0$ is homotopic to $f_1$ $\mathrm{rel}\text{ }A$. Also we still write $\simeq_p$ for path homotopies. And if $A = \emptyset$ we just write $\simeq$.
	\item $\simeq_A$ is an equivalence relation via identical reasoning as in the proof of lemma 51.1 on \inLinkRap{placeholder}{page 117}.\retTwo
\end{enumerate}

\hTwo Here is some more terminology (given two topological spaces $X$ and $Y$):\\ [-16pt]
\begin{itemize}
	\item We let $[X, Y]$ denote the set of homotopy classes of continuous maps from $X$ to $Y$.
	\item We say $X$ and $Y$ are \udefine{homotopy equivalent} if there exists maps $f: X \to Y$ and $g: Y \to X$ such that $f \circ g \simeq \myId_Y$ and $g \circ f \simeq \myId_X$. In this case we say $f$ and $g$ are homotopy equivalences.
	\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
		Note that while being homeomorphic trivially implies being homotopy equivalent, it is also possible to be homotopy equivalent and \textit{not} homeomorphic.\retTwo

		\ul{Lemma:} Given any topological space $X$ and any convex subspace $K$ of a topological vector space, we have that any two functions $f_0: X \to K$ and $f_1: X \to K$ are homotopic.
		\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
			Why?\\
			We can just use the linear homotopy $F(x, t) = (1 - t)f_0(x) + t f_1(x)$.\retTwo
		\end{myIndent}

		Based on this lemma, we can now for example see that $\mathbb{R}^n$ is homotopy equivalent to a singleton set $\{*\}$ for all $n \geq 1$. 
		\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
			Why?\\
			We can pick any point $x_0 \in \mathbb{R}^n$. Then we let $f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \{*\}$ be the unique function that exists going from $\mathbb{R}^n$ to $\{*\}$, and we let $g: \{*\} \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be the map sending $*$ to $x_0$.\retTwo

			$f \circ g = \myId_{\{*\}}$ so we have no issues there. Meanwhile both $g \circ f$ and $\myId_{\mathbb{R}^n}$ are functions from $\mathbb{R}^n$ to $\mathbb{R}^n$. So by the prior lemma we know that they are homotopic. And this finishes proving that $\mathbb{R}^n$ is homotopy equivalent to $\{*\}$.
		\end{myIndent}
	\end{myIndent}
	\item A space $X$ that is homotopy equivalent to a singleton set is called \udefine{contractible}. We can easily see that $X$ is contractible iff there is a homotopy sending $\myId_X$ to a constant map.\newpage
\end{itemize}

One more concept is that if $X$ is a topological space, $A \subseteq X$, and $r: X \to A$ is a retraction (i.e. a continuous map such that $r|_A = \myId_A$), then we say $r$ is a \udefine{deformation retraction} if $\iota \circ r \simeq \myId_X$ $\mathrm{rel}\text{ } A$. (Here $\iota: A \hookrightarrow X$ is the inclusion map.)\retTwo

\mySepTwo 

There's a category theory lense that I can give to all of the homology theory established so far.\retTwo

We say a \udefine{graded abelian group} (or $R$-module where $R$ is a commutative ring) is a sequence $\{A_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}$ of abelian groups (or $R$-modules). Typically, we just denote the graded abelian group by $A_*$.\retTwo

A \udefine{(chain) complex} is then just a graded abelian group (or graded $R$-module) equipped with a sequence of homomorphisms $\{d: A_n \to A_{n-1}\}_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}$ such that $d^2: A_n \to A_{n-2}$ is the zero map.\retTwo

Also recall from \inLinkRap{Chain homomorphism tangent page 1160}{page 1160} what a homomorphism $\{f_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}$ between chains is. Typically,\\ we just denote this homomorphism by $f_\sharp$. Also its clear that a composition of chain\\ homomorphisms (given by $\{g_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \circ \{f_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} = \{g_n \circ f_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}$) is another chain\\ homomorphism. Plus, $\myId_{B_*} \circ f_\sharp = f_\sharp = f_\sharp \circ \myId_{A^*}$ for all chain homomorphisms\\ $f_\sharp : A_* \to B_*$.\retTwo

We let $\mathrm{ch}\mcateg{Ab}$ denote the category whose objects are all chain complexes of abelian groups and whose morphisms are all chain homomorphisms.

\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Under this lens, we have a functor $S_*$ from $\mcateg{Top}$ (the category of topological spaces and continuous maps) to $\mathrm{ch}\mcateg{Ab}$. After all, for any topological space we let:

	{\centering $S_*(X) = \{S_n(X)\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ \\ [4pt]\par}

	where the latter is a graded abelian group that becomes a chain complex when equipped with the boundary operator $\partial$.\retTwo

	Also, we also, we already noted for any continuous map $f: X \to Y$ that $S_*(f) \coloneqq f_\sharp$\\ is a chain homomorphism from $S_*(X)$ to $S_*(Y)$.\retTwo
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		Technically we still need to show that if $f: X \to Y$ and $g: Y \to Z$ are continuous maps then $(g \circ f)_\sharp = g_\sharp \circ f_\sharp$. This is easy though. If $\sigma: \Delta^n \to X$ is any singular $n$-simplex then:
		
		{\centering$(g \circ f)_\sharp(\sigma) = g \circ f \circ \sigma = g \circ (f \circ \sigma) = g_\sharp(f_\sharp(\sigma))$.\retTwo\par}

		Similarly, we can easily show that $\myId_X$ induces the identity chain homomorphism.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
\end{myIndent}

Next, we can define a homology functor $H_n : \mathrm{ch}\mcateg{Ab}$ to $\mcateg{Ab}$ as follows.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Suppose $A_*$ is a chain complex equiped with the maps $d: A_m \to A_{m-1}$ for all $m$ such that $d^2 = 0$. Then we define a functor $H_n$ sending $A_*$ to $\frac{\ker(d: A_n \to A_{n-1})}{\myIm(d: A_{n+1} \to A_n)}$.\newpage

	Also by the note on \inLinkRap{Chain homomorphism tangent page 1160}{page 1160}, we know that any chain homomorphism $f_\sharp: A_* \to B_*$ can be restricted and quotiented to a well defined map $f_*: H_n(A_*) \to H_m(B_*)$. So, we define the $n$th homology functor to send $f_\sharp$ to the map $a + d(A_{n + 1}) \mapsto f_\sharp(a) + d(B_{n + 1})$. This similarly behaves well with composition of homomorphisms and identity homomorphisms.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

For time being I'll let the \udefine{$n$th singular homology functor} $H_n : \mcateg{Top} \to \mcateg{Ab}$ be the functor defined by composing the prior two functors I've defined.
\begin{myIndent}\myComment
	I'm sorry if its confusing that the same letters and names keep getting reused for different slightly adjacent functors / functions.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

One more category I want to define is $\mcateg{HoTop}$.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	The objects of $\mcateg{HoTop}$ are the same as the objects of $\mcateg{Top}$. Meanwhile, we let the\\ morphisms of $\mcateg{HoTop}$ between any topological spaces $X$ and $Y$ be the homotopy\\ equivalence classes in $[X, Y]$.\retTwo

	\ul{Lemma:} Suppose $X, Y, Z$ are topological spaces, $f_0, f_1 \in C(X, Y)$ with $f_0 \simeq f_1$,\\ and $g_0, g_1 \in C(Y, Z)$ with $g_0 \simeq g_1$. Then $g_0 \circ f_0 \simeq g_1 \circ f_1$.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		Proof:\\
		Let $F : X \times [0, 1] \to Y$ be a homotopy from $f_0$ to $f_1$ and $G: Y \times [0, 1] \to Z$ be a homotopy from $g_0$ to $g_1$. Then $H: X \times [0, 1] \to Z$ defined by:
		
		{\centering$H(x, t) \coloneqq G(F(x, t), t)$\\ [4pt]\par}
		
		is a homotopy from $g_0 \circ f_0$ to $g_1 \circ f_1$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Also note that trivially $\myId_X \circ f \simeq f$. So, $\mcateg{HTop}$ is a well-defined category.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

We can also see that there is a well-defined functor $\mathrm{Ho}: \mcateg{Top} \to \mcateg{HoTop}$ sending any topological space $X$ to $X$ and any continuous map $f: X \to Y$ to its equivalence class $[f]_\simeq$.\retTwo
