I'm going to take a break from studying singular homology so that I can instead briefly come up with a basic formulation of divergence theorem. I'm doing this because I will need it tomorrow in my PDE class.\retTwo

Firstly, here's some terminology from John Lee:\retTwo

Suppose $M$ is a $C^r$ manifold without corners. If $p \in \partial M$ then $v \in T_p M - T_p (\partial M)$ is said to be \udefine{inward pointing} if for some $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a $C^1$ curve $\gamma : [0, \varepsilon) \to M$ such that $\gamma(0) = p$ and $\gamma^\prime(0) = v$. Similarly, $v \in T_p M - T_p(\partial M)$ is said to be \udefine{outward pointing} if for some $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a $C^1$ curve $\gamma : (-\varepsilon, 0] \to M$ such that $\gamma(0) = p$ and $\gamma^\prime(0) = v$.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Proposition 5.41:} Suppose $M$ is a $C^r$ manifold, $p \in \partial M$, and $(U, \varphi)$ is a smooth boundary chart on $M$. (In other words $\widehat{U} = \varphi(U)$ is an open subset of $H^n \coloneqq \mathbb{R}^{n-1} \times [0, \infty)$.) We'll\newpage let $\varphi(p) = (x_1(p), \ldots, x_n(p))$. Then any $v \in T_p M$ can be written uniquely as $\sum_{i=1}^n c_i \frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}$.\\ $v$ is inward pointing iff $c_n > 0$. $v$ is outward pointing iff $c_n < 0$. And finally, $v \in T_p(\partial M)$ iff $c_n = 0$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	If $v \in T_p (\partial M)$ then we know we can find a $C^1$ path $\gamma: J \to M$ such that $\gamma(J) \subseteq \partial M$, $\gamma(0) = p$, and $\gamma^\prime(0) = v$. But then if we look at the local coordinates on $(U, \varphi)$, we have that $\varphi(\partial M \cap U) = \{(x_1, \ldots, x_n) \in \widehat{U} : x_n = 0\}$. So, $(\varphi \circ \gamma)(t) \cdot e_n = 0$ for all $t$. And this proves that if $v = \gamma^\prime(0) = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i \frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}$ then $c_n = 0$.\retTwo

	Conversely, if $v = \sum_{i=1}^{n - 1} c_i \frac{\partial}{\partial x_i} \in T_p M$ then the straight line path $\gamma: J \to M$ in the direction of $v$ (according to the local coordinates) satisfies that $\gamma(0) = p$, $\gamma^\prime(0) = v$, and that the $n$th coordinate of $\gamma(t)$ is always $0$. Yet this equivalently means that $\gamma(J) \subseteq \partial M$. And since $\partial M$ has the subspace topology, we can conclude that $\gamma$ is a $C^1$ path into $\partial M$. So, $v \in T_{p}(\partial M)$.\retTwo

	Next, suppose $v$ is inward pointing and let $\gamma: [0, \varepsilon) \to M$ be such that $\gamma(0) = p$ and $\gamma^\prime(0) = v$. By shrinking $\varepsilon$ we can include that $\gamma([0, \varepsilon)) \subseteq  U$. But now note that the $n$th component of $(\varphi \circ \gamma)^\prime(0)$ must be positive. This is because the $n$th coordinate of $\gamma(t)$ is always nonnegative with it equaling zero at $t = 0$. So, if $(\varphi \circ \gamma)^\prime(0) \cdot e_n < 0$ we'd have a contradiction. At the same time, since $v \notin T_p( \partial M)$ we know from before that $(\varphi \circ \gamma)^\prime(0) \cdot e_n \neq 0$. So, upon writing $v = \gamma^\prime(0) = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i \frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}$ we have that $c_n > 0$.\retTwo

	Conversely, if $v = \sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i \frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}$ then the straight line path (according to the local coordinates) will give an example path proving that $v$ is inward pointing.\retTwo

	Finally, we can use analogous reasoning when $v$ is outward pointing. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\ul{Corollary:} Suppose $M$ is a $C^r$ manifold and $p \in \partial M$. Then $v \in T_p M$ is outward pointing iff $-v$ is inward pointing.\retTwo

\hTwo\begin{myIndent}\mySepThree\end{myIndent}

Now the next reasoning will be hyper-specific to any $C^1$ regular domain $D$ without corners in $\mathbb{R}^N$ (equipped with the standard smooth structure). To start off, note that $\partial D$ will be a $C^1$ $(N - 1)$-dimensional embedded submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^N$ without a boundary.\retTwo

One consequence of this is that from \inLinkRap{placeholder}{pages 95-99} of my journal we have a standard way of defining a surface measure $S$ on $\partial D$.
\begin{myIndent}\color{red}
	Namely, we let $S$ be the unique measure on $\partial D$ satisfying that if $(U, \varphi)$ is a\\ coordinate chart on $\partial D$ and $E \subseteq U$ then:

	{\centering  $S(E) = \int_{\varphi(E)} \sqrt{\det\left((\Df \varphi^{-1})^T(\Df \varphi^{-1})\right)} \df x$ \retTwo\par}
\end{myIndent}

Also, because $T_p \mathbb{R}^N$ can be identified with $\mathbb{R}^N$ for all $p \in \mathbb{R}^N$ via a standard\\ identification (see \inLinkRap{Proposition 3.13 page 1043}{proposition 3.13 on pages 1043-1044}), we can identify $T_p(\partial D)$ with a geometric hyperplane for all $p \in \partial D$. And in turn, it makes sense to think of the orthogonal complement to that tangent plane.\newpage

Thus, for all $p \in \partial D$ I'll let $v(p) \in \mathbb{R}^N$ be the unique outward pointing unit vector in the orthogonal complement of $T_p (\partial D)$. My next goal will be to show that it is always possible locally to find a nice parametrization of the boundary of $\partial D$ that also makes it easy to calculate the surface measure and normal vector $\gamma$.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Theorem 5.48:} If $M$ is a $C^r$ manifold without boundary and $D \subseteq M$ is a regular domain without corners, then there exists a $C^r$ function $f: M \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $\partial D = f^{-1}(\{0\})$, $D = f^{-1}((-\infty, 0])$, and $0$ is a regular value of $f$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Let $D^\circ$ be equipped with the constant function $-1$. Meanwhile, let $D^\comp$ be equipped with the constant function $+1$. And finally, for every $p \in \partial D$ let $(U_p, \varphi_p)$ be a half-slice chart on $M$ containing $p$. Thus $\varphi_p(U_p \cap D) = \{(x_1, \ldots, x_n) \in \varphi(U_p) : x_n \geq 0\}$. We can define a function $g_p : U_p \to \mathbb{R}$ by just setting $g_p(p) = -x_n(p)$. And this will be a $C^r$ map such that $g_p < 0$ on $D^\circ \cap U_p$, $g_p = 0$ on $\partial D \cap U_p$,and $g_p > 0$ on $U_p - D^\circ$.\retTwo

	Now take a $C^r$ partition of unity $\{\phi_{D^\circ}, \phi_{D^\comp}\} \cup \{\psi_p\}_{p \in \partial D}$ subordinate to the open sets $D^\circ$, $D^\comp$, and all the $U_p$. Next, define:

	{\centering $f = \psi_{D^\comp} - \psi_{D^\circ} + \sum_{p \in \partial D} \psi_p g_p$ \retTwo\par}

	If $q \notin D$ then $\psi_{D^\circ}(q) = 0$ and all the other summands of $f$ are positive or zero (and some will be positive). So, $D^\comp \subseteq f^{-1}((0, \infty))$. On the other hand, if $q \in D$ then we know that $\psi_{D^\comp}(q) = 0$ and the other terms are all nonpositive. So $D \subseteq f^{-1}((-\infty, 0])$. Putting these observations together, we have that $D = f^{-1}((-\infty, 0])$.\retTwo

	Next I claim that $0$ is a regular value of $f$. To see why, first note that $f^{-1}(\{0\}) = \partial D$.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		Hopefully this is obvious to see.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	So, it suffices to show for all $p \in \partial D$ that $\df f_p$ is not the zero map. Fortunately, given any fixed $p \in \partial D$ we can find a neighborhood $V$ containing $p$ that intercepts the support of only finitely many $\psi_{p^\prime}$. Furthermore, as $p \notin D^\circ$ and $p \notin D^\comp$, we can shrink $V$ to assume that $\psi_{D^\circ} = 0$ and $\psi_{D^\comp} = 0$ on $V$. So, there are $p_1, \ldots, p_M$ such that
	
	{\centering$f(q) = \sum_{i=1}^M \psi_{p_i}(q) g_{p_i}(q)$ for all $q \in V$.\retTwo\par}

	By shrinking $V$ more, we can assume that $p \in \supp(\psi_{p_i})$ for each $i$. This is important because it also now lets us conclude that $p \in \bigcap_{i=1}^M U_{p_i}$. So by shrinking $V$ one more time we can assume without loss of generality that $V \subseteq \bigcap_{i=1}^M U_{p_i}$.\retTwo

	One last note I'll make is that by reordering the $p_i$, I can assume without loss of generality that $\psi_{p_1}(p) > 0$.\retTwo

	Now to show that $\df f_p$ does not vanish it suffices to show that gradient of $f$ at $p$ with respect to the smooth coordinate chart $(U_{p_1}, \varphi_{p_1})$ does not vanish. So, let $\pi: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ be the projection onto the $n$th coordinate. Then for all $x \in \varphi_{p_1}(U_{p_1})$ we have that:

	{\centering\fontsize{12}{13}\selectfont\begin{tabular}{l}
		$\nabla(f \circ \varphi^{-1}_{p_1})(x)$\\ [4pt]
		$\phantom{aaa} = -\sum\limits_{i=1}^m \left[(\psi_{p_i} \circ \varphi^{-1}_{p_1})(x) \nabla(\pi \circ (\varphi_{p_i} \circ \varphi^{-1}_{p_1}))(x) + (\pi \circ (\varphi_{p_i} \circ \varphi^{-1}_{p_1}))(x) \nabla(\psi_{p_i} \circ \varphi^{-1}_{p_1})(x) \right]$
	\end{tabular}\newpage\par}

	In the special case that $x \in \varphi_p(\partial D)$ though, we know that $(\pi \circ (\varphi_{p_i} \circ \varphi^{-1}_{p_1}))(x) = 0$ for all $i$. Therefore, our expression simplies to:

	{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
		$\nabla(f \circ \varphi^{-1}_{p_1})(\varphi_{p_1}(p)) = -\sum\limits_{i=1}^m (\psi_{p_i} \circ \varphi^{-1}_p)(\varphi_{p_1}(p)) \nabla(\pi \circ (\varphi_{p_i} \circ \varphi^{-1}_{p_1}))(\varphi_{p_1}(p))$\\ [12pt]
		$\phantom{\nabla(f \circ \varphi^{-1}_{p_1})(\varphi_{p_1}(p))} = -\sum\limits_{i=1}^m \psi_{p_i}(p) \nabla(\pi \circ (\varphi_{p_i} \circ \varphi^{-1}_{p_1}))(\varphi_{p_1}(p))$.\\ [12pt]
		$\phantom{\nabla(f \circ \varphi^{-1}_{p_1})(\varphi_{p_1}(p))} = -\psi_{p_1}(p)(0, \ldots, 0, 1) - \sum\limits_{i=2}^m \psi_{p_i}(p) \nabla(\pi \circ (\varphi_{p_i} \circ \varphi^{-1}_{p_1}))(\varphi_{p_1}(p))$.
	\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

	To finish off, write $x = (x_1, \ldots, x_n)$. We know that $\pi \circ (\varphi_{p_i} \circ \varphi^{-1}_{p_1})(x) > 0$ if $x_n > 0$ and that $\pi \circ (\varphi_{p_i} \circ \varphi^{-1}_{p_1})(x) < 0$ if $x_n < 0$. (This is just because the transition map $\varphi_{p_i} \circ \varphi^{-1}_{p_1}$ has to send the upper half space to the upper half space and the lower half space to the lower half space). But now in turn, we must have that the $n$th partial derivative of $\pi \circ (\varphi_{p_i} \circ \varphi^{-1}_{p_1})$ is nonnegative when $x_n = 0$.\retTwo

	Putting everything together, we have that the $n$th component of $\nabla(f \circ \varphi^{-1}_{p_1})(\varphi_{p_1}(p))$ is equal to something strictly negative minus a bunch of nonnegative terms. So, the $n$th\\ component of $\nabla(f \circ \varphi^{-1}_{p_1})(\varphi_{p_1}(p))$ doesn't vanish. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo We can use the prior result to show that if $D$ is a regular domain without corners of a $C^r$ manifold $M$ without a boundary, then $\partial(D^\circ) = \partial D$. In other words, $D$ is a regular closed set (see \inLinkRap{Regular open and regular closed page 927}{page 927} for what that means). 
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Proof:\\
	Suppose $p \in \partial(D^\circ)$. Therefore, we know that $p \notin \partial(D^\circ)$ and yet we can find a\\ sequence $\{p_k\}_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ in $D^\circ$ converging to $p$. Next, let $f: M \to \mathbb{R}$ be a $C^r$ function such that $D = f^{-1}((-\infty, 0])$ and $0$ is a regular value of $f$. Because $f$ is continuous, we know that $f(p_k) \to f(p)$ as $k \to \infty$. Yet $f(p_k) \leq 0$ for all $k$. So, we can also guarentee that $f(p) \leq 0$. So, $p \in D$. And since $p \notin \partial(D^\circ)$, we can guarentee that $p \in \partial D$.\retTwo

	With that we've shown that $\partial(D^\circ) \subseteq \partial D$. To get the other inclusion, suppose $p \in \partial D$. Then we know that $p \notin D^\circ$. That said, we can take a chart $(U, \varphi)$ about the point $p$. And then using that chart we can easily get a sequence of interior points $\{p_k\}_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ of $D$ converging to $p$. Since the manifold interior of $D$ corresponds to the topological interior, this proves that $p \in \partial (D^\circ)$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

Equivalently, this means that $D^\circ$ is a regular open set because the interior of any regular closed is a regular open set.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Proof:\\
	\ul{Lemma:} If $X$ is a toplogical space, a closed set $F \subseteq X$ is regular iff $F = \overline{F^\circ}$.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		$(\Longrightarrow)$\\
		If $F$ is regular we know that $\partial F = \partial (F^\circ)$. But now:
		
		{\centering$\overline{F^\circ} = F^\circ \cup \partial(F^\circ) = F^\circ \cup \partial F =  F^\circ \cup (F - F^\circ) = F$.\retTwo\par}

		$(\Longleftarrow)$\\
		Suppose $F = \overline{F^\circ}$. Then $\partial F = F - F^\circ = \overline{F^\circ} - F^\circ = \partial(F^\circ)$.\newpage
	\end{myIndent}

	Based on the prior lemma, we can now conclude that:
	
	{\centering$\partial (\overline{D^\circ}) = \overline{D^\circ} - (\overline{D^\circ})^\circ = D - D^\circ = \partial D$.\retTwo\par}
	
	And since $D$ is regular, we know that $\partial D = \partial (D^\circ)$. So, $\partial (\overline{D^\circ})  = \partial (D^\circ)$. And this proves that $D^\circ$ is a regular open set. $\blacksquare$
	\begin{myIndent}\myComment
		More generally, this shows that the interior of a regular closed set is a regular open set.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
\end{myIndent}

This is important because this would let us apply the lemma on \inLinkRap{Page 928 lemma}{page 928}. Although, I'm also now realizing that we can also show the following lemma way more directly. Oops.\retTwo

\begin{myIndent}
	\exTwo\ul{Lemma:} Suppose $M$ is a $C^r$ manifold without boundary and $D \subseteq M$ is a regular domain without corners. Suppose $p \in \partial D$ and $U \subseteq M$ is an open set containing $p$. Then we can find an open set $V \subseteq U$ containing $p$ such that $V - \partial D$ has two nonempty connected components: $V \cap D^\circ$ and $V \cap D^\comp$. Furthermore, we can find a $C^r$ map $f: V \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $0$ is a regular value of $f$,
	
	{\centering$V \cap D^\circ = f^{-1}{(-\infty, 0)}$, $V \cap \partial D = f^{-1}(\{0\})$, and $V \cap D^\comp = f^{-1}((0, \infty))$\retTwo\par}

	\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
		Proof:\\
		We can find a half-slice chart $(W, \varphi)$ on $M$ containing $p$ such that:
		\begin{itemize}
			\item $\varphi(U \cap D) = \{(x_1, \ldots, x_n) \in \varphi(U) : x_n \geq 0\}$
			\item $\varphi(U \cap \partial D) = \{(x_1, \ldots, x_n) \in \varphi(U) : x_n = 0\}$.\retTwo
		\end{itemize}

		By shrinking $U$, we can without loss of generality assume $U \subseteq W$. And now since $\varphi(U)$ is an open subset of $\varphi(W)$ which is an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$, there exists $r > 0$ such that $B_r(\varphi(p)) \subseteq \varphi(U)$. So, let $V \coloneqq \varphi^{-1}(B_r(\varphi(p)))$. Then we know $V \subseteq U$.\retTwo
		
		Now, $\varphi(V - \partial D) = B_r(\varphi(p)) - (\mathbb{R}^{n-1} \times \{0\})$ has two connected (even convex) disjoint components, which are the subset where $x_n < 0$ and the subset where $x_n > 0$. Yet note that the subset where $x_n < 0$ is precisely $\varphi(V \cap D^\comp)$ and the subset where $x_n > 0$ is precisely $\varphi(V \cap D^\circ)$. Since homeomorphisms map connected components to connected components, we can conclude that $V \cap D^\comp$ and $V \cap D^\circ$ are the conected components of $V - \partial D$.\retTwo

		As for getting our function $f$, just apply theorem 5.48 from two pages ago and then restrict the function you get to the set $V$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
\end{myIndent}

\pracOne\mySepTwo
I realize at this rate I'm just letting myself distracted but I thought this was a cool thought of mine so I wanted to write it down.\retTwo

\ul{Proposition:} Suppose $M$ is a $C^r$ manifold without a boundary and $D \subseteq M$ is a regular domain without corners. Then $\overline{D^\comp} = D^\comp \cup \partial(D^\comp) = D^\comp \cup \partial D$ is also a regular domain without corners and its boundary is $\partial D$.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Proof:\newpage
	By theorem 5.48 we can find a function $f: M \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $0$ is a regular value of $f$, $D = f^{-1}((-\infty, 0])$ and $\partial D = f^{-1}(\{0\})$. But now consider the function $g = -f$. Then we have that $0$ is a regular value of $g$, $\overline{D^\comp} = g^{-1}((-\infty, 0])$, and $\partial D = g^{-1}(\{0\})$. So by proposition 5.47 on \inLinkRap{Proposition 5.47 page 1127}{page 1127}, we know ghat $\overline{D^\comp}$ is a regular domain with boundary $\partial D$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\mySepTwo

\hTwo Now I get to the important result that I will need to get my basic formulation of divergence theorem. In particular, from here on out I will assume $M = \mathbb{R}^N$ and $D \subseteq M$ is a $C^1$ regular domain without corners.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Theorem:} \hypertarget{Theorem page 1170}{Suppose} $D$ is a $C^r$ regular domain without corners of $\mathbb{R}^N$ and $p \in \partial D$.\\ Then for some $1 \leq i \leq N$ there exists open sets $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$ and $V \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{N-1}$, as well as a\\ $C^r$ function $g: V \to \mathbb{R}$ such that the following holds:
\begin{enumerate}
	\item[(a)] if $\widehat{\pi_{i}}: \mathbb{R}^N \to \mathbb{R}^{N-1}$ is the projection onto all but the $i$th component, we have that $\widehat{\pi_{i}}(U) = V$. In other words, $(x_1, \ldots, x_n) \in U$ implies that $(x_1, \ldots, \widehat{x_i}, \ldots, x_N) \in V$.
	\item[(b)] $U \cap \partial D = \{(x_1, \ldots, x_N) \in U : x_i = g(x_1, \ldots, \widehat{x_i}, \ldots, x_N)\}$.
	\item[(c)] Also, we can guarentee that one of the two things holds.\\ [-16pt]
	\begin{itemize}
		\item $U \cap D = \{(x_1, \ldots, x_N) \in U : x_i \leq g(x_1, \ldots, \widehat{x_i}, \ldots, x_N)\}$
		\item $U \cap D = \{(x_1, \ldots, x_N) \in U : x_i \geq g(x_1, \ldots, \widehat{x_i}, \ldots, x_N)\}$.
		
		\begin{myDindent}\myComment
			As a side note, the vector $(x_1, \ldots, \widehat{x_i}, \ldots, x_N) \in \mathbb{R}^N$ just denotes the result of removing the $i$th component from a vector $(x_1, \ldots, x_N) \in \mathbb{R}^N$.
		\end{myDindent}
	\end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Let $f: \mathbb{R}^N \to \mathbb{R}$ be a $C^r$ map such that $D = f^{-1}((-\infty, 0])$, $\partial D = f^{-1}(\{0\})$, and $0$ is a regular value of $f$. Then suppose $p = (p_1, \ldots, p_N) \in \partial D$. By the implicit function theorem, we know for some $1 \leq i \leq N$ that there is an open set $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$, an open set $V \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{N - 1}$ and a $C^r$ function $g: V \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying that:
	\begin{itemize}
		\item $p \in U$ and $\widehat{p} = (p_1, \ldots, \widehat{p}_i, \ldots, p_N) \in V$,
		\item For all $\widehat{q} = (q_1, \ldots, \widehat{q_i}, \ldots, q_N) \in V$ we have that $q_i = g(\widehat{q}) \in \mathbb{R}$ is the unique real number such that $q = (q_1, \ldots, q_N) \in U$ with $f(q) = 0$.
		\begin{myIndent}\myComment
			Technically, in my math 140c notes I only proved $g$ is $C^1$. But the same proof can show it is $C^r$.\retTwo
		\end{myIndent}
	\end{itemize}

	Next, let $G: V \to U$ be the graph function given by:

	{\centering $G(x_1, \ldots, \widehat{x_i}, \ldots, x_n) = (x_1, \ldots, x_{i-1}, g(x_1, \ldots, \widehat{x_i}, \ldots, x_n), x_{i+1}, \ldots, x_N)$ \retTwo\par}

	We know that $G$ is a $C^r$ map. Furthermore, if we let $\widehat{\pi_{i}}: \mathbb{R}^N \to \mathbb{R}^{N-1}$ be the projection onto all but the $i$th component, then we have that $G(V) = U \cap (\widehat{\pi_{i}})^{-1}(V) \cap \partial D$. So, I'll firstly replace $U$ with the open set $U^\prime = U \cap (\widehat{\pi_{i}})^{-1}(V)$. This is useful because it guarentees for every $\mVecAst{y} \in U^\prime$ that $\widehat{\pi_{i}}(\mVecAst{y}) \in V$. Also, now $G(V) = U^\prime \cap \partial D$.
	\begin{myIndent}\myComment
		In other words, we've shown that $U^\prime$, $V^\prime$, and $g|_{V^\prime}$ satisfy properties (a) and (b) that we wanted.\newpage
	\end{myIndent}

	Next let us define $H: U^\prime \to \mathbb{R}$ by:
	
	{\centering$H(x_1, \ldots, x_N) = x_i - g(x_1, \ldots, \widehat{x_i}, \ldots, x_N)$.\\ [4pt]\par}

	A key observation is that $H$ is $C^r$ and that $H^{-1}(\{0\}) = U^\prime \cap \partial D$.\retTwo

	Now by the prior lemma we know there is an open set $U^\pprime \subseteq U^\prime$ containing $p$ such that $U^\pprime - \partial D$ has two nonempty connected components: $U^\pprime \cap D^\circ$ and $U^\pprime - D$. Now granted, by restricting to $U^\pprime$, we might have lost properties (a) and (b). That said, connectedness is useful here because $H$ must map $U^\pprime \cap D^\circ$ and $U^\pprime - D$ each to connected subsets (i.e. intervals) of $\mathbb{R}$. Yet we also know that $0$ cannot be contained in the image of either set (since $H^{-1}(\{0\}) = U^\prime \cap \partial D$). So, we know that either:

	{\centering $H(U^\pprime \cap D^\circ) \subseteq (-\infty, 0)$ or $H(U^\pprime \cap D^\circ) \subseteq (0, \infty)$.\\ [4pt]\par}

	And similarly we know that either:

	{\centering $H(U^\pprime - D) \subseteq (-\infty, 0)$ or $H(U^\pprime - D) \subseteq (0, \infty)$.\\ [4pt]\par}

	Yet because $U^\pprime$ is an open subset containing $p$, we also know that there must be some $\varepsilon > 0$ such that $p + te_i \in U^\pprime$ for all $|t| < \varepsilon$. (Here $e_i$ is the $i$th standard basis vector.) So, we can guarentee that $H(U^\pprime)$ contains both positive and negative values. Hence, we can conclude that either:
	
	{\centering$U^\pprime \cap D^\circ = H|_{U^\pprime}^{-1}((-\infty, 0))$ and $U^\pprime - D = H|_{U^\pprime}^{-1}((0, \infty))$\\ [4pt]\par}

	or:

	{\centering$U^\pprime \cap D^\circ = H|_{U^\pprime}^{-1}((0, \infty))$ and $U^\pprime - D = H|_{U^\pprime}^{-1}((-\infty, 0))$\retTwo\par}

	\begin{myIndent}\myComment
		This is equivalent to property (c) that we wanted.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	To finish off, we just need to regain properties (a) and (b). So let $V^{\prime\prime\prime} \coloneqq G^{-1}(U^\pprime)$ and let $U^{\prime\prime\prime} \coloneqq U^\pprime \cap (\widehat{\pi_{i}})^{-1}(V^{\prime\prime\prime})$. Then $U^{\prime\prime\prime}$, $V^{\prime\prime\prime}$, and $g|_{V^{\prime\prime\prime}}$ satisfies our theorem. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
	\begin{myIndent}\myComment
		As a side note, I might have destroyed the connectedness of $U^{\prime\prime\prime} - \partial D$. That said, I don't care about it anymore.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo In particular, the prior theorem show that the boundary of any $C^1$ regular domain $D$ can be locally parametrized as the graph of a $C^1$  function $g: V \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{N - 1} \to \mathbb{R}$.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	To see why, let $V$, $U$, and $g$ be from the original theorem. Then define $G: V \to \mathbb{R}^N$ by:
	
	{\centering$G(x_1, \ldots, \widehat{x_i}, \ldots, x_n) = (x_1, \ldots, x_{i-1}, g(x_1, \ldots, \widehat{x_i}, \ldots, x_n), x_{i+1}, \ldots, x_N)$\retTwo\par}

	Then $G$ is an injective $C^1$ map of rank $N - 1 = \dim(\partial D)$ whose image is contained in $\partial D$. Since $\partial D$ is an embedded submanifold, we thus know that $G$ is a $C^1$ map from $V$ to $\partial D$. Also, $G$ must still have rank $N - 1$ as a map from $V$ to $\partial D$. By the inverse function theorem, we can conclude that $G$ is a local $C^1$ diffeomorphism from $V$ to $\partial D$. And since $G$ is injective, we can conclude that $G$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism from $V$ to an open set $G(V) \subseteq \partial D$.\retTwo
	
	It follows that $(G(V), G^{-1}) = (U \cap \partial D, G^{-1})$ is a smooth chart on $\partial D$ by proposition 5.23 on \inLinkRap{Proposition 5.23 page 1125}{page 1125}.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

Furthermore, this parametrization will satisfy that $D \cap U$ is the volume below or above the graph $G$ (intercepted with $U$).\newpage

This is useful for us because the surface measure of a graph is incredibly easy to calculate.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Suppose $V \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{N - 1}$, $g: V \to \mathbb{R}$ is a $C^1$ map, and $G: V \to \mathbb{R}^N$ is the map:
	
	{\centering$G(x_1, \ldots, x_{N-1}) = (x_1, \ldots, x_{N-1}, g(x_1, \ldots, x_{N - 1}))$.\retTwo\par}

	We know $\Df G = \begin{bmatrix}1 & & \\ & \ddots & \\ & & 1 \\ \partial_{x_1}g & \cdots & \partial_{x_{N-1}}g\end{bmatrix}$.\retTwo

	Therefore, if we write the gradient of $g$ as a column vector, we can calculate that:
	
	{\centering$(\Df G)^T (\Df G) = \mathbf{I}_{N - 1} + (\nabla g)(\nabla g)^T$.\retTwo\par}

	Then we have the following result.\retTwo

	\ul{Lemma:} Suppose $v = (v_1, \ldots, v_{n}) \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is interpretted as a column vector. Then:
	
	{\centering$\det(\mathbf{I}_{n} + vv^T) = 1 + |v|^2$.\\ [4pt]\par}

	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		Proof:\\
		Note that $(\mathbf{I}_n + vv^T)v = v + vv^Tv = (1 + |v|^2)v$. Therefore, we can see that $(1 + |v|^2)$ is an eigenvalue of $\mathbf{I}_n + vv^T$ with a corresponding eigenvector $v$.\retTwo

		Next let $u_2, \ldots, u_n$ be some more vectors such that $v, u_2, \ldots, u_n$ is an orthogonal basis for $\mathbb{R}^n$. Then for each $i$ we have that $(\mathbf{I}_n + vv^T)u_i = u_i + 0v = u_i$. So, we have that $1$ is repeated $n - 1$ times as an eigenvalue of $\mathbf{I}_n + vv^T$, and its corresponding eigenspace is the span of $u_2, \ldots, u_n$.\retTwo

		Since the determinant of a matrix is equal to the product of its eigenvalues, we can thus conclude that $\det(\mathbf{I}_n + vv^T) = 1 + |v|^2$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	It follows that $\sqrt{\det\left((\Df G)^T(\Df G)\right)} = \sqrt{1 + |\nabla g|^2}$.\retTwo
	\begin{myIndent}\myComment
		As a side note, if $S: \mathbb{R}^N \to \mathbb{R}^N$ is an orthogonal map (which any permutation of coordinates in the codomain would be), then:

		{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
			$(\Df (S \circ G))^T(\Df (S \circ G)) = (S  (\Df G))^T (S(\Df G)) = (\Df G)^T S^T S (\Df G)$\\
			$\phantom{(\Df (S \circ G))^T(\Df (S \circ G)) = (S  (\Df G))^T (S(\Df G))} = (\Df G)^T(\Df G)$
		\end{tabular} \retTwo\par}

		So, we can also now conclude that the prior reasoning also holds for any graph where the dependent variable is $x_i$ even when $i \neq N$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
\end{myIndent}

Calculating a normal vector to a graph is also really easy.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Proof:\\
	Let $V \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{N - 1}$, $g: V \to \mathbb{R}$, and $G: V \to \mathbb{R}^N$ be the function defined by:

	{\centering $G(x_1, \ldots, \widehat{x_i}, \ldots, x_N) = (x_1, \ldots, x_{i-1}, g(x_1, \ldots, \widehat{x_i}, \ldots, x_N), x_{i+1}, \ldots, x_N)$.\retTwo\par}

	We need our normal vector $v$ to be orthogonal to each column of $\Df G$ (which I've written on the next page). As it turns out, a vector that works is:
	
	{\centering$(-\partial_{x_1} g, \ldots, -\partial_{x_{i-1}}g, 1, -\partial_{x_{i}}g, \ldots, -\partial_{x_{N - 1}}g)$.\newpage\par}

	Also the norm of this vector is $\sqrt{1 + |\nabla g|^2}$. So we can divide by this to normalize our normal vector. Also, depending on whether the regular domain $D$ is below or above the graph $G$, we can negate or not negate our vector in order to make sure it points outwards away from $D$.\retTwo
	
	\begin{myIndent}\myComment
		\begin{myClosureOne}{5}
			Note: the derivative matrix of $G$ is:

			{\center$\Df G = \begin{bmatrix}1 & & & & & \\ & \ddots & & & & \\ & & 1 & & & \\ \partial_{x_1}g & \cdots & \partial_{x_{i-1}}g & \partial_{x_i}g & \cdots & \partial_{x_{N - 1}}g \\ & & & 1 & & \\ & & & & \ddots &\\ & & & & & 1\end{bmatrix}$.\retTwo\par}
		\end{myClosureOne}\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
\end{myIndent}

As a side note, the prior theorem plus the prior calculation would let us prove that for a regular domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$, the map $p \mapsto v(p)$ (sending $p \in \partial D$ to the unit outward pointing normal vector to $T_p (\partial D)$) is continuous on a neighborhood about any point in $\partial D$. As a result, the map $p \mapsto v(p)$ is globally continuous from $\partial D$ to $\mathbb{R}^N$. Hence, it is also measurable.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Theorem:} \hypertarget{Theorem Page 1173}{Let} $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$ be a bounded $C^1$ regular domain without corners (where $N \geq 2$). Then suppose there exists an open set $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$ containing $D$ such that $f \in C^1(\Omega, \mathbb{R})$. For every $i \in \{1, \ldots, N\}$ we have that $\int_D \partial_{x_i}f(x)\df x = \int_{\partial D} f(p)v_i(p)\df S(p)$.
\begin{myDindent}\myComment
	Here we write $v(p) = (v_1(p), \ldots, v_N(p))$ for all $p \in \partial D$.
\end{myDindent}
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	To start off, without loss of generality we can assume $f$ is compactly supported. After all, as $D$ is compact we can find precompact open sets $E_1$ and $E_2$ such that $D \subseteq E_1 \subseteq \overline{E_1} \subseteq E_2 \subseteq \overline{E_2} \subseteq \Omega$, as well as a $C^\infty$ function $\phi: \mathbb{R}^N \to [0, 1]$ such that $\phi \equiv 1$ on $\overline{E_1}$ and $\supp(\phi) \subseteq \overline{E_2} \subseteq \Omega$.\retTwo

	But now $\partial_{x_i}\phi \equiv 0$ on $D$ and $\phi \equiv 1$ on $D$. Hence, we can calculate that:
	\begin{itemize}
		\item $\int_D \partial_{x_i}(f\phi)(x)\df x = \int_D \phi(x)\partial_{x_i}f(x) + 0\df x = \int_D \partial_{x_i}f(x)\df x$;
		\item $\int_{\partial D}(f\phi)(p)v_i(p)\df S(p) = \int_{\partial D}f(p)v_i(p)\df S(p)$.\retTwo
	\end{itemize}

	Thus, we might as well replace $f$ with $f \phi$.\retTwo

	Next, for every $p \in \partial D$ we can pick open sets $U_p \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$, $V \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{N - 1}$, and a $C^1$ function $g_p: V \to \mathbb{R}$ with the properties described in the theorem on \inLinkRap{Theorem page 1170}{pages 1170-1171}. But now because $\partial D$ is compact, we know that it is covered by finitely many of the $U_p$. Hence, we can pick finitely many $p_1, \ldots, p_n$ such that $D \subseteq D^\circ \cup U_{p_1} \cup \cdots \cup U_{p_n}$. Then, we can pick a $C^\infty$ partition of unity $\phi, \phi^{(1)}, \ldots, \phi^{(n)}$ subordinate to the sets $D^\circ, U_{p_1}, \ldots, U_{p_n}$ respectively such that $\phi + \sum_{j=1}^n \phi^{(j)} \equiv 1$ on $D$.\newpage

	But now let $u = \phi f$ and $u^{(j)} = \phi^{(j)}f$. Then:
	
	{\centering$f = u + \sum_{j=1}^n u^{(j)}$ and $\partial_{x_i} f = \partial_{x_i}u + \sum_{j=1}^n \partial_{x_i}u^{(j)}$.\\ [4pt]\par}
	
	Also, $\supp(u) \subseteq D^\circ$ and $\supp(u^{(j)}) \subseteq U_{p_j}$ for each $j$. In turn, we have that:
	\begin{itemize}
		\item $\int_D \partial_{x_i} f(x) \df x = \int u(x) \df x + \sum\limits_{j=1}^n \int_{D \cap U_{p_j}} \partial_{x_i} u^{(j)}(x) \df x$.
		\item $\int_{\partial D} f(q) v_i(q) \df S(q) =  \sum\limits_{j=1}^n \int_{\partial D \cap U_{p_i}} u^{(j)}(q) v_i(q) \df S(q)$.\retTwo
	\end{itemize}

	\ul{Calculation 1:} $\int_{D^\circ} \partial_{x_i} u(x) \df x = 0$
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		Why?\\
		By Fubini's theorem and the fundamental theorem of calculus, we get that:
		
		{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
			$\int \partial_{x_i} u(x) \df x = \int_{\mathbb{R}^{N - 1}} (\int_{-\infty}^\infty \partial_{x_i} u(x) \df x_i) \df (x_1, \ldots, \widehat{x_i}, \ldots, x_N)$\\ [8pt]
			$\phantom{\int \partial_{x_i} u(x) \df x} = \int_{\mathbb{R}^{N - 1}} 0 \df (x_1, \ldots, \widehat{x_i}, \ldots, x_N) = 0$.
		\end{tabular} \retTwo\par}
	\end{myIndent}

	\ul{Calculation 2:} For each $j$ we have that $\int_{D \cap U_{p_j}} \partial_{x_i} u^{(j)}(x) \df x = \int_{\partial D \cap U_{p_i}} u^{(j)}(q) v_i(q) \df S(q)$.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		Why?\\
		Recall that for some $k \in \{1, \ldots, N\}$ we have that $U^{p_j} \cap \partial D$ is parametrized by the function:
		
		{\centering$G(x_1, \ldots, \widehat{x_k}, \ldots, x_N) = (x_1, \ldots, x_{k-1}, g(x_1, \ldots, \widehat{x_k}, \ldots, x_N), x_{k+1}, \ldots, x_N)$\retTwo\par}

		Furthermore, we can guarentee that one of the two following things is true:
		\begin{itemize}
			\item $U_{p_j} \cap D = \{(x_1, \ldots, x_N) \in U_{p_j} : x_k \leq g_{p_j}(x_1, \ldots, \widehat{x_k}, \ldots, x_N)\}$
			\item $U_{p_j} \cap D = \{(x_1, \ldots, x_N) \in U_{p_j} : x_k \geq g_{p_j}(x_1, \ldots, \widehat{x_k}, \ldots, x_N)\}$.\retTwo
		\end{itemize}

		\ul{Easy case:} Suppose $i = k$. Then the first of two possibilities is that:
		
		{\centering$v_i(G(y)) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + |\nabla g(y)|^2}}$,\\ [4pt]\par}
		
		and by fundamental theorem of calculus plus the fact that $u^{(j)}$ is compactly supported in $U_{p_j}$, we can conclude that:

		{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
			$\int_{D \cap U_{p_j}} \partial_{x_i} u^{(j)}(x)\df x = \int_V \int_{-\infty}^{g(x_1, \ldots, \widehat{x_i}, \ldots, x_n)} \partial_{x_i} u^{(j)}(x_1, \ldots, x_n) \df x_i \df (x_1, \ldots, \widehat{x_i}, \ldots, x_n)$\\ [8pt]
			$\phantom{\int_{D \cap U_{p_j}} \partial_{x_i} u^{(j)}(x)\df x} = \int_V u^{(j)}(G(y)) - 0 \df y$\\ [8pt]
			$\phantom{\int_{D \cap U_{p_j}} \partial_{x_i} u^{(j)}(x)\df x} = \int_V u^{(j)}(G(y))v_i(G(y))\sqrt{1 + |\nabla g(y)|^2}\df y$\\ [8pt]
			$\phantom{\int_{D \cap U_{p_j}} \partial_{x_i} u^{(j)}(x)\df x} = \int_{\partial D \cap U_{p_j}} u^{(j)}(q) v_i(q) \df S(q)$\\ [8pt]
		\end{tabular} \retTwo\par}

		The other possibility is that $v_i(G(y)) = \frac{-1}{\sqrt{1 + |\nabla g(y)|^2}}$ and:

		{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
			$\int_{D \cap U_{p_j}} \partial_{x_i} u^{(j)}(x)\df x = \int_V \int_{g(x_1, \ldots, \widehat{x_i}, \ldots, x_n)}^\infty \partial_{x_i} u^{(j)}(x_1, \ldots, x_n) \df x_i \df (x_1, \ldots, \widehat{x_i}, \ldots, x_n)$
		\end{tabular} \retTwo\par}

		But then our calculation just introduces two minus signs which cancel each other out.\retTwo

		\ul{Hard case 1:} Suppose $i < k$. Then we have that $v_i(G(y)) = \mp \frac{\partial_{y_i}g(y)}{\sqrt{1 + |\nabla g(y)|^2}}$. 
		\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo\fontsize{11}{13}
			(Specifically, the sign is $-$ if $D$ lies below the graph $G$ and the sign is $+$ if $D$ lies above the graph $G$.)\newpage
		\end{myIndent}

		In order to keep notation cleaner, let $\theta: V \times \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^N$ be defined by:
		
		{\centering$\theta(y_1, \ldots, y_{N-1}, s) = (y_1, \ldots, y_{k-1}, s, y_{k+1}, \ldots, y_N)$.\retTwo\par}

		Then for all $y \in V$ and $s \in \mathbb{R}$ define $\eta(\theta(y, s)) \coloneqq u^{(j)}(\theta(y, g(y) + s))$. In other words, we have that:

		{\centering\begin{tabular}{l} 
			$\eta(x_1, \ldots, x_{k-1}, s, x_{k+1}, \ldots, x_N) = $\\ [4pt]
			$\phantom{aaaaaaaaaa} u^{(j)}(x_1, \ldots, x_{k-1}, g(x_1, \ldots, \widehat{x_k}, \ldots, x_N) + s, x_{k+1}, \ldots, x_N)$.
		\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}
		
		Importantly, $\eta$ is continuously differentiable. Also, $\eta$ is the composition of $u^{(j)}$ and the inverse map of a homeomorphism. So, $u^{(j)}$ being compactly supported implies that $\eta$ is as well. By chain rule, we can calculate that:
		
		{\centering $(\partial_{x_i}\eta)(\theta(y, s)) = (\partial_{x_i}u^{(j)})(\theta(y, g(y) + s)) + (\partial_{x_k}u^{(j)})(\theta(y, g(y) + s)) \cdot \partial_{y_i}g(y)$ \retTwo\par}

		In turn, in the case that $D$ lies below the graph $G$ we have that:

		{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
			$\int_{D \cap U_{p_j}} \partial_{x_i} u^{(j)}(x)\df x = \int_V \int_{-\infty}^{g(y)} (\partial_{x_i} u^{(j)})(\theta(y, x_k)) \df x_k \df y$\\ [8pt]
			$\phantom{\int_{D \cap U_{p_j}} \partial_{x_i} u^{(j)}(x)\df x} = \int_V \int_{-\infty}^{0} (\partial_{x_i} u^{(j)})(\theta(y, g(y) + s)) \df s \df y$\\ [8pt]
			$\phantom{\int_{D \cap U_{p_j}} \partial_{x_i} u^{(j)}(x)\df x} = \int_V \int_{-\infty}^{0} (\partial_{x_i} \eta)(\theta(y, s)) \df s \df y$\\ [4pt]
			$\phantom{\int_{D \cap U_{p_j}} \partial_{x_i} u^{(j)}(x)\df x aaaaaa+} - \int_V \int_{-\infty}^0 (\partial_{x_k}u^{(j)})(\theta(y, g(y) + s)) \cdot \partial_{y_i}g(y) \df s \df y$.
		\end{tabular}\\ [-4pt]\par}

		\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
			\lparen As for the case that $D$ lies above the graph $G$, we instead have that:

			{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
				$\int_{D \cap U_{p_j}} \partial_{x_i} u^{(j)}(x)\df x = \int_V \int_0^\infty (\partial_{x_i} \eta)(\theta(y, s)) \df s \df y$\\ [4pt]
				$\phantom{\int_{D \cap U_{p_j}} \partial_{x_i} u^{(j)}(x)\df x aaaaaa+} - \int_V \int_0^\infty (\partial_{x_k}u^{(j)})(\theta(y, g(y) + s)) \cdot \partial_{y_i}g(y) \df s \df y$.\rparen
			\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}
		\end{myIndent}

		But now I claim that $\int_V \int_{-\infty}^{0} (\partial_{x_i} \eta)(\theta(y, s)) \df s \df y = 0$. To see why, for all\\ $(y_1, \ldots, \widehat{y_i}, \ldots, y_N) \in \mathbb{R}$ let $V_{(y_1, \ldots, \widehat{y_i}, \ldots, y_{N - 1})} \coloneqq \{y_i \in \mathbb{R} :  (y_1, \ldots, y_{N - 1}) \in V\}$. Then by fubini's theorem, we have that:\\ [-8pt]

		\hspace{-4em}\begin{tabular}{l}
			$\int_V \int_{-\infty}^{0} (\partial_{x_i} \eta)(\theta(y, s)) \df s \df y$\\ [6pt]
			$\phantom{aaa} = \int_{\mathbb{R}^{N - 2}}\int_{V_{(y_1, \ldots, \widehat{y_i}, \ldots, y_{N - 1})}} \int_{-\infty}^0 (\partial_{x_i} \eta)(\theta((y_1, \ldots, y_{N-1}), s)) \df s \df y_i \df (y_1, \ldots, \widehat{y_i}, \ldots, y_{N-1})$\\ [8pt]
			$\phantom{aaa} = \int_{\mathbb{R}^{N - 2}} \int_{-\infty}^0 \int_{V_{(y_1, \ldots, \widehat{y_i}, \ldots, y_{N - 1})}} (\partial_{x_i} \eta)(\theta((y_1, \ldots, y_{N-1}), s)) \df y_i \df s\df (y_1, \ldots, \widehat{y_i}, \ldots, y_{N-1})$\\ [8pt]
		\end{tabular}\retTwo

		But now $V_{(y_1, \ldots, \widehat{y_i}, \ldots, y_{N - 1})}$ is an open subset of $\mathbb{R}$. So, there exists countably many intervals $\{I_\ell\}_{\ell \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that:

		{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
			$\int_{V_{(y_1, \ldots, \widehat{y_i}, \ldots, y_{N - 1})}} (\partial_{x_i} \eta)(\theta((y_1, \ldots, y_{N-1}), s)) \df y_i$\\ [6pt]
			$\phantom{aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa} = \sum\limits_{\ell \in \mathbb{N}}\int_{I_\ell} (\partial_{y_i} \eta)(\theta((y_1, \ldots, y_{N-1}), s)) \df y_i$\\ [8pt]
		\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

		Then since $* \mapsto \eta(\theta(y_1, \ldots, y_{i-1}, *, y_{i+1}, \ldots, y_{N - 1}, s))$ is compactly supported in\\ $\bigcup_{\ell \in \mathbb{N}} I_\ell$, we know by the fundamental theorem of calculus that:

		{\centering $\sum\limits_{\ell \in \mathbb{N}}\int_{I_\ell} (\partial_{y_i} \eta)(\theta((y_1, \ldots, y_{N-1}), s)) \df y_i = 0$ \retTwo\par}

		So, $\int_V \int_{-\infty}^{0} (\partial_{x_i} \eta)(\theta(y, s)) \df s \df y = \int_{\mathbb{R}^{N - 2}} \int_{-\infty}^0 0 \df s\df (y_1, \ldots, \widehat{y_i}, \ldots, y_{N-1}) = 0$.\retTwo

		\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
			\lparen Or in the case that $D$ lies above the graph $G$, we instead have that:

			{\centering$\int_V \int_0^\infty (\partial_{x_i} \eta)(\theta(y, s)) \df s \df y = \int_{\mathbb{R}^{N - 2}} \int_0^\infty 0 \df s\df (y_1, \ldots, \widehat{y_i}, \ldots, y_{N-1}) = 0$.\rparen\newpage\par}
		\end{myIndent}

		And now in the case that $D$ lies below the graph $G$, we have that:
		
		{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
			$\int_{D \cap U_{p_j}} \partial_{x_i} u^{(j)}(x)\df x = \int_V \left(\int_{-\infty}^0 (\partial_{x_k}u^{(j)})(\theta(y, g(y) + s)) \df s\right) \cdot -\partial_{y_i}g(y) \df y$\\ [8pt]
			$\phantom{\int_{D \cap U_{p_j}} \partial_{x_i} u^{(j)}(x)\df x} = \int_V \left( \int_{-\infty}^{g(y)} (\partial_{x_k}u^{(j)})(\theta(y, x_k)) \df x_k\right) \cdot -\partial_{y_i}g(y) \df y$\\ [8pt]
			$\phantom{\int_{D \cap U_{p_j}} \partial_{x_i} u^{(j)}(x)\df x} = \int_V (u^{(j)}(G(y)) - 0) \cdot -\partial_{y_i}g(y) \df y = \int_{U_{p_j} \cap \partial D} u^{(j)}(q)v_i(q) \df S(q)$
		\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

		\color{orange} \lparen Alternatively, if $D$ lies below the graph $G$ then:

		{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
			$\int_{D \cap U_{p_j}} \partial_{x_i} u^{(j)}(x)\df x = \int_V \left(\int_0^\infty (\partial_{x_k}u^{(j)})(\theta(y, g(y) + s)) \df s\right) \cdot -\partial_{y_i}g(y) \df y$\\ [8pt]
			$\phantom{\int_{D \cap U_{p_j}} \partial_{x_i} u^{(j)}(x)\df x} = \int_V \left( \int_{g(y)}^\infty (\partial_{x_k}u^{(j)})(\theta(y, x_k)) \df x_k\right) \cdot -\partial_{y_i}g(y) \df y$\\ [8pt]
			$\phantom{\int_{D \cap U_{p_j}} \partial_{x_i} u^{(j)}(x)\df x} = \int_V (u^{(j)}(0 - G(y))) \cdot -\partial_{y_i}g(y) \df y = \int_{U_{p_j} \cap \partial D} u^{(j)}(q)v_i(q) \df S(q)$.\rparen
		\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

		\exPPP\ul{Hard Case 2:} Suppose $k < i$. The only difference between this case and the prior case is that now the indexing is slightly fucked up. After all, we have that:
		
		{\centering$v_i(G(y)) = \mp \frac{\partial_{y_{i - 1}}g(y)}{\sqrt{1 + |\nabla g(y)|^2}}$.\\ [-4pt]\par}
		\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo\fontsize{11}{13}
			(Specifically, the sign is $-$ if $D$ lies below the graph $G$ and the sign is $+$ if $D$ lies above the graph $G$.)\retTwo
		\end{myIndent}

		But also when we define $\eta$ and $\theta$ as before, we now get that:

		{\centering $(\partial_{x_i}\eta)(\theta(y, s)) = (\partial_{x_i}u^{(j)})(\theta(y, g(y) + s)) + (\partial_{x_k}u^{(j)})(\theta(y, g(y) + s)) \cdot \partial_{y_{i-1}}g(y)$ \retTwo\par}

		And now the entire rest of the proof goes identically as in the prior case.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Putting the prior two calculations together, we can now conclude the desired theorem. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo\mySepTwo

\dispDate{10/3/2026}

A weak version of the divergence theorem is a direct consequence of the prior theorem. Recall from \inLinkRap{Derivative operators page 829}{pages 829-830} some notations for derivative operators.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Corollary (Divergence Theorem):} Let $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$ (where $N \geq 2$) be a bounded $C^1$ regular domain without corners. Then suppose there exists an open set $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$ containing $D$ and a map $f \in C^1(\Omega, \mathbb{R}^N)$. If $v(p)$ denotes the outward pointing normal vector to $\partial D$ at a point $p \in \partial D$, we have that:

{\centering $\int_D \nabla \cdot F \df x = \int_{\partial D} F \cdot v  \df S$\retTwo\par}

\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Write $F = (F_1, \ldots F_N)$. Then by the prior theorem:

	{\centering $\int_D \nabla \cdot F \df x = \sum_{i=1}^N \int_D \partial_{x_i} F_i \df x = \sum_{i=1}^N \int_\partial D F_i v_i \df S = \int_\partial D F \cdot v \df S$. $\blacksquare$\newpage\par}

	\begin{myIndent}\myComment
		As a side note, if $N = 1$, $[a, b] \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, we let $v(b) \coloneqq 1$ and $v(a) \coloneqq -1$, and\\ we equip $\partial([a, b]) = \{a, b\}$ with the counting measure, then the divergence\\ theorem becomes just the fundamental theorem of calculus. We'll use these\\ conventions when dealing with regular domains of $\mathbb{R}$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo Since we have a formulation of divergence theorem, we can also prove \color{OliveGreen} Green's identities:\retTwo

\ul{Theorem:} Let $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$ be a $C^1$ regular domain without corners.
\begin{itemize}
	\item[(a)] (Green's 1st Identity): Let $f \in C^1(D)$ and $g \in C^2(D)$ be scalar-valued functions. Then $\int_{\partial D} f\frac{\partial g}{\partial v} \df S = \int_D \nabla f \cdot \nabla g \df x + \int_D f\triangle g \df x$.
	\begin{myTindent}\myComment
		(Here, a function $h$ being in $C^k(D)$ is used to mean that there exists an open set $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$ containing $D$ such that $f \in C^k(\Omega)$).
	\end{myTindent}
	\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP\color{LimeGreen}
		Proof:\\
		Note that $\nabla \cdot (f \nabla g) = \sum_{i=1}^N (f_{x_i} g_{x_i} + fg_{x_i,x_i}) = (\nabla f \cdot \nabla g) + f\triangle g$. In turn, we can just integrate and apply divergence theorem.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	\item[(b)] (Green's 2nd Identity): Let $f, g \in C^2(D)$ be scalar-valued fnctions. Then:
	
	{\centering$\int_{\partial D} f\frac{\partial g}{\partial v} - g\frac{\partial f}{\partial v} \df S = \int_D(f\triangle g - g\triangle f)\df x$\\ [4pt]\par}

	\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP\color{LimeGreen}
		Proof:\\
		Apply the first identity to $\int_{\partial D} f \frac{\partial g}{\partial v}\df S$ and $\int_{\partial D} g \frac{\partial f}{\partial v}\df S$ separately and then take their difference. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
\end{itemize}

\hTwo For the sake of being able to do calculations, I do need to actually know how to compute the manifold surface measure of at least a sphere. Fortunately, I can show as follows that I already know how to do that.\retTwo

In math 240a we showed there's a unique Borel measure $\sigma$ on $S^{N -1} \coloneqq \partial B_1(0) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$ with $\int_E \df x = \int_0^\infty\int_{S^{N - 1}} \chi_{E}(rx^\prime)\df \sigma(x^\prime)r^{N - 1}\df r$ for any measurable set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N - \{0\}$.
\begin{myTindent}\myComment
	Here $\chi_E$ denotes the characteristic function of the set $E$.\retTwo
\end{myTindent}

\exTwo\ul{Lemma:} The manifold surface measure $S$ on $S^{N-1}$ (where $N \geq 2$) is precisely equal to $\sigma$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	To start off, I'll denote by $S_\varepsilon$ the manifold surface measure of $\partial B_{\varepsilon}(0)$. My first claim is that $S_\varepsilon(\partial B_\varepsilon(0)) = \varepsilon^{N-1}\sigma(S^{N-1})$.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		Why?\\
		First note that if $x \in \partial B_\varepsilon(0)$ then $|x| = \varepsilon$ and the outward pointing unit normal vector is $\frac{x}{|x|} = \varepsilon^{-1}x$. Also note that $x \mapsto x$ is a $C^\infty$ map from $\mathbb{R}^N$ to $\mathbb{R}^N$. Therefore, by the divergence theorem we have that:\\ [-10pt]

		{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
			$\varepsilon S_\varepsilon(\partial B_\varepsilon(0)) = \int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(0)} \varepsilon \df S_\varepsilon(x)$\\ [6pt]
			$\phantom{S_\varepsilon(\partial B_\varepsilon(0))} = \int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(0)} x \cdot \frac{x}{|x|}\df S_\varepsilon(x) = \int_{B_\varepsilon(0)}  \nabla \cdot x \df x$\\ [6pt]
			$\phantom{S_\varepsilon(\partial B_\varepsilon(0)) = \int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(0)} x \cdot \frac{x}{|x|}\df S_\varepsilon(x)} = N \int_{B_\varepsilon(0)}\df x = N\sigma(S^{N-1})\int_0^\varepsilon r^{N-1}\df r$\\ [6pt]
			$\phantom{S_\varepsilon(\partial B_\varepsilon(0)) = \int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(0)} x \cdot \frac{x}{|x|}\df S_\varepsilon(x) = N \int_{B_\varepsilon(0)}\df x} = \varepsilon^N \sigma(S^{N-1})$.
		\end{tabular}\newpage\par}

		We can divide both sides by $\varepsilon$ to get that $S_\varepsilon(\partial B_\varepsilon(0)) = \varepsilon^{N - 1}\sigma(S^{N - 1})$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	The prior result is useful because it now lets us show for any $f \in C^1(S^{N-1}, \mathbb{R})$ that:
	
	{\centering$\int_{S^{N - 1}} f(x^\prime) \df S(x^\prime) = \int_{S^{N-1}} f \df \sigma(x^\prime)$.\retTwo\par}
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		Why?\\
		To start off, note that given such an $f$, we can define a function $g \in C^1(\mathbb{R}^{N} - \{0\}, \mathbb{R})$ by $g(x) = f(\frac{x}{|x|})$. This map is $C^1$ because it is a composition of $C^1$ maps. Also importantly, we know it stays constant as one travels radially outwards or inwards. And when $x \in S^{N-1}$ we know $f(x) = g(x)$.\retTwo

		But now for all $x \in S^{N-1}$ we have that $|x| = 1$ and the outward pointing normal vector from $x$ is $x$. Thus by the divergence theorem, we have for any $\varepsilon > 0$ that:

		{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
			$\int_{S^{N-1}} f(x^\prime) \df S(x^\prime) = \int_{S^{N-1}} g(x^\prime)x^\prime \cdot x^\prime \df S(x^\prime)$\\ [6pt]
			$\phantom{\int_{S^{N-1}} f(x^\prime) \df S(x^\prime)} = \int_{\varepsilon \leq |x| \leq 1}  \nabla \cdot (g(x)x)\df x + \int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(0)} (g(x^\prime)x^\prime) \cdot (\varepsilon^{-1}x^\prime)\df S_\varepsilon(x^\prime)$
		\end{tabular} \retTwo\par}

		\begin{myIndent}\myComment
			Beware that because $g$ is not continuously extendable to $0$, we can only apply the divergence theorem to a solid shell and not the entire unit ball.\retTwo
		\end{myIndent}

		But now note that $\nabla \cdot (g(x)x) = Ng(x) + x \cdot \nabla g(x)$. Since $g(x)$ is constant as one travels radially, we know that $x \cdot \nabla g(x)= 0$. Therefore, we can now calculate via polar coordinates that:

		{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
			$\int_{\varepsilon \leq |x| \leq 1}  \nabla \cdot (g(x)x)\df x = N\int_{\varepsilon \leq |x| \leq 1} g(x)\df x$\\ [6pt]
			$\phantom{\int_{\varepsilon \leq |x| \leq 1}  \nabla \cdot (g(x)x)\df x} = N\int_\varepsilon^1 \int_{S^{N-1}} g(rx^\prime)\df \sigma(x^\prime) r^{N-1}\df r$\\ [6pt]
			$\phantom{\int_{\varepsilon \leq |x| \leq 1}  \nabla \cdot (g(x)x)\df x} = N\int_\varepsilon^1 \int_{S^{N-1}} f(x^\prime)\df \sigma(x^\prime) r^{N-1}\df r$\\ [6pt]
			$\phantom{\int_{\varepsilon \leq |x| \leq 1}  \nabla \cdot (g(x)x)\df x} = N\int_\varepsilon^1 r^{N-1} \df r \int_{S^{N-1}} f(x^\prime)\df \sigma(x^\prime)$\\ [6pt]
			$\phantom{\int_{\varepsilon \leq |x| \leq 1}  \nabla \cdot (g(x)x)\df x} = (1 - \varepsilon^N)\int_{S^{N-1}} f(x^\prime)\df \sigma(x^\prime)$
		\end{tabular} \retTwo\par}

		Meanwhile, note that since $S^{N-1}$ is compact, we know that $|f|$ (and in turn $|g|$) is bounded from above by some constant $M \geq 0$. So,
		
		{\centering\begin{myIndent}
			$\left|\int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(0)} (g(x)x) \cdot (\varepsilon^{-1}x)\df S_\varepsilon(x)\right| \leq \int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(0)} \varepsilon|g(x)| \df S_\varepsilon(x)$\\ [4pt]
			$\phantom{\left|\int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(0)} (g(x)x) \cdot (\varepsilon^{-1}x)\df S_\varepsilon(x)\right|} \leq \varepsilon M S_\varepsilon(\partial B_\varepsilon(0)) = \varepsilon^N M \sigma(S^{N-1})$
		\end{myIndent}\retTwo\par}

		And now we can just take $\varepsilon \to 0$ in order to prove that:
		
		{\centering$\int_{S^{N-1}} f(x^\prime) \df S(x^\prime) = \int_{S^{N-1}} f(x^\prime) \df \omega(x^\prime)$.\retTwo\par}
	\end{myIndent}

	Having proven the prior result, we are now basically done. After all, given any open set $U \subseteq S^{N - 1}$ we can let $\{K_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of compact sets whose union is $U$. And then we can inductively pick $C^1$ maps $f_n \in C^1(S^{N-1}, [0, 1])$ such that $\supp(f_n) \subseteq U$ and $f_n \equiv 1$ on $(\bigcup_{m=1}^n K_m) \cup (\bigcup_{m=1}^{n-1}\supp(f_m))$. But now by the monotone convergence theorem, we have that:
	
	{\centering$S(U) = \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} \int_{S^{N-1}} f_n(x^\prime)\df S(x^\prime) = \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} \int_{S^{N-1}} f_n(x^\prime)\df \sigma(x^\prime) = \sigma(U)$.\newpage\par}

	Next since both $S$ and $\sigma$ are Radon measures (they are both finite on a second countable LCH space), them equaling on open sets implies they equal on all Borel sets. $\blacksquare$
	\begin{myIndent}\myComment
		As a side note, if we consider the surface measure on the $0$-dimensional manifold $S^{0} = \{-1, 1\}$ to be the counting measure, then this result also trivially holds. So, we shall make that a convention.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo I also want to be able to apply affine transformations to my manifolds before integrating. So, I'll also prove the following results.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Lemma:} Suppose $M$ is a $k$-dimensional $C^r$ embedded submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^N$ without corners and $\Phi: \mathbb{R}^N \to \mathbb{R}^N$ is a $C^r$ diffeomorphism. Then $M^\prime \coloneqq \phi(M)$ is also a $k$-dimensional $C^r$ embedded submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^N$.\retTwo
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP 
	Proof:\\
	The fact that $M^\prime$ is an embedded submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^N$ is just a result of proposition 5.2 on \inLinkRap{proposition 5.2 page 1111}{pages 1111-1112}. In particular, given a smooth chart $(U, \varphi)$ on $M$ containing a point $p$ we have that $(\Phi(U), \varphi \circ \Phi^{-1})$ is a smooth chart on $M^\prime$ containing the point $p^\prime$. Or in other words, if $X: V \subseteq \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}^N$ is a $C^r$ parametrization for $M$, then we have that $(X^{-1} \circ \Phi^{-1})^{-1} = \Phi \circ X: V \to \mathbb{R}^N$ is also a $C^r$ parametrization of $M^\prime$ by proposition 5.23 on \inLinkRap{Proposition 5.23 page 1125}{page 1125}. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo Next suppose $\Phi(x) \coloneqq Ax + a$ where $A$ is an orthogonal matrix and $a \in \mathbb{R}^N$. This is a $C^\infty$ diffeomorphism and I claim the following result\dots\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Lemma 2:} Let $M$ and $M^\prime$ be defined as in the prior lemma. Also let $S_M$ be the surface measure on $M$ and let $S_{M^\prime}$ be the surface measure on $M^\prime$. Then for any borel set $E \subseteq M$ we have that $S_{M^\prime}(\Phi(E)) = S_M(E)$ (or equivalently $S_{M^\prime}(E) = S_M(\Phi^{-1}(E))$ for all $E \in \mathcalli{B}_{M^\prime}$).
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	By a result I showed on \inLinkRap{placeholder}{pages 98-99}, it suffices to prove this lemma for any Borel set $E$ contained in the image of some $C^r$ parametrization $X: V \to \mathbb{R}^N$. But now note that:

	{\centering $S_M(E) = \int_{X^{-1}(E)} \sqrt{\det(\Df X^T \Df X)} \df x$ \retTwo\par}

	Meanwhile:
	
	{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
		$S_{M^\prime}(\Phi(E)) = \int_{(\Phi \circ X)^{-1}(\Phi(E))} \sqrt{\det((\Df (\Phi \circ X))^T \Df (\Phi \circ X))} \df x $\\ [8pt]
		$\phantom{S_{M^\prime}(\Phi(E))}= \int_{X^{-1}(E)}\sqrt{(\Df X)^T A^T A \Df X}$.
	\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}
	
	And because $A$ is orthogonal, $A^T A$ cancels and we are also left with:
	
	{\centering$S_{M^\prime}(\Phi(E)) = \int_{X^{-1}(E)} \sqrt{\det(\Df X^T \Df X)} \df x = S_M(E)$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo\par}
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo Similarly, we can also consider the map $\Phi(x) \coloneqq cx$ where $c \in \mathbb{R}$. This is also a $C^\infty$ diffeomorphism.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Lemma 3:} Let $M$ and $M^\prime$ be $k$-dimensional defined as in two lemmas ago. Also let $S_M$ be the surface measure on $M$ and let $S_{M^\prime}$ be the surface measure on $M^\prime$. Then for any borel set $E \subseteq M$ we have that $S_{M^\prime}(\Phi(E)) = |c|^k S_M(E)$ (or equivalently $S_{M^\prime}(E) = \frac{1}{|c|^k}S_M(\Phi^{-1}(E))$ for all $E \in \mathcalli{B}_{M^\prime}$).
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	The idea of this proof is identical to that in lemma 2. $\blacksquare$\newpage
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo Just for convenience sake, I also want to list a few results here from Folland that I proved in math 240a. Here, $m$ will denote the Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}^N$ and $\sigma$ will denote the surface measure of $S^{N - 1}$.
\begin{itemize}
	\item $\sigma(S^{N - 1}) = \frac{2\pi^{N/2}}{\Gamma(N/2)}$.
	\item $m(B_1(0)) = \frac{\pi^{N/2}}{\Gamma(1 + \frac{N}{2})} = \frac{1}{N}\sigma(S^{N - 1})$. {\color{red} (My 231 professor refers to this number as $\alpha(N)$.)}
	\item If $N \geq 0$ then $\Gamma(N) = (N - 1)!$.
	\item If $N \geq 0$ then $\Gamma(N + \frac{1}{2}) = (N - \frac{1}{2})(N - \frac{3}{2})\cdots (\frac{1}{2})\sqrt{\pi}$.\retTwo
\end{itemize}

\blect{Math 231A Lecture Notes:}\\
Like in the undergrad PDE class, in this class gradients, laplacians, divergences, and etc. will all be assumed to only be with respect to the spacial variables.\retTwo

We first address the Laplace equation on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Namely we want to find a function\\ $u \in C^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$ such that $- \triangle u \equiv 0$. To find such a $u$, we first consider that the Laplacian\\ is invariant under rotations and reflections.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Proof:\\
	Suppose $T$ is a linear isometry. (Hence $|\det(T)| = 1$ and $T^{-1} = T^*$. {\color{red} Also here I'm using a "$*$" to denote taking a matrix transpose.}) Then letting $\widehat{f}$ or $f^\wedge$ denote the Fourier transform of a function (which I am taking to be $\widehat{f}(\xi) \coloneqq \int f(x)e^{-2\pi i \xi \cdot x}$), recall from \inLinkRap{Page 919 reference}{page 919} that for any Schwartz function $u: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ that:

	{\center\begin{tabular}{l}
		$(\triangle(u \circ T))^\wedge(\xi) = -4\pi^2|\xi|^2(u \circ T)^\wedge(\xi) = -4\pi^2|T(\xi)|^2\widehat{u}(T(\xi)) = (\triangle u)^\wedge \circ T(\xi)$. 
	\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

	But now by applying the inverse Fourier transform, we get that:

	{\centering $\triangle(u \circ T)(x) = ((\triangle u)^\wedge \circ T)^\vee(x) = ((\triangle u)^\wedge)^\vee \circ T(x) = (\triangle u) \circ T(x)$ \retTwo\par}

	Thus in the special case of a Schwartz function $u$, we are done. The next logical step is to show that $\triangle (F \circ T) = (\triangle F) \circ T$ for any distribution $F \in \mathcal{D}^\prime(\mathbb{R}^n)$.\retTwo

	Let $\phi \in C_c^\infty$ be a test function. Then recalling \inLinkRap{Page 959 reference}{pages 959-974} for a reminder on how we work with distributions, we know that:

	{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
		$(\triangle(F \circ T), \phi) = (F \circ T, \triangle \phi) = |\det(T)|^{-1}(F, (\triangle \phi) \circ T^{-1})$.
	\end{tabular} \retTwo\par}

	Yet because $\phi$ is Schwartz, we then know that:

	{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
		$|\det(T)|^{-1}(F, (\triangle \phi) \circ T^{-1}) = |\det(T)|^{-1}(F, \triangle(\phi \circ T^{-1})) = |\det(T)|^{-1}(\triangle F, \phi \circ T^{-1})$\\ [4pt]
		$\phantom{|\det(T)|^{-1}(F, (\triangle \phi) \circ T^{-1}) = |\det(T)|^{-1}(F, \triangle(\phi \circ T^{-1}))} = ((\triangle F) \circ T, \phi)$
	\end{tabular} \retTwo\par}

	This also proves that classically $\triangle$ is rotation / reflection invariant for every $C^2$ function $u$. After all, since $\triangle (u \circ T)$ and $(\triangle u) \circ T$ defining the same distributions means that they equal a.e. And since they are continuous, that means they are equal everywhere. $\blacksquare$\newpage
\end{myIndent}

Based on the prior result, it would seem a good idea to look for radial solutions. In other words, we shall try to find a solution $u(x) = v(r)$ where $v: [0, \infty) \to \mathbb{R}$ is a function and $r = |x|$.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Fortunately though, note that $\frac{\partial r}{\partial x_i} = \frac{x_i}{r}$. In turn, $\partial_{x_i}u(x) = v^\prime(r)\frac{x_i}{r}$. And then\\ differentiating again we get that:

	{\centering $\partial_{x_i}^2 y(x) = v^\pprime(r)\frac{x_i^2}{r^2} + v^\prime(r)\left(\frac{1}{r} - \frac{x_i^2}{r^3}\right)$ \retTwo\par}

	So, $0 = \triangle u = v^\pprime(r) + (\frac{n - 1}{r})v^\prime(r)$. Or in other words:

	{\centering $(\ln|v^\prime|)^\prime(r) = \frac{v^\pprime(r)}{v^\prime(r)} = \frac{1 - n}{r}$ \retTwo\par}

	By taking antiderivatives we get that:

	{\centering $\ln|v^\prime| = (1 - n)\ln(r) + C = \ln(r^{1 - n}) + C$.\retTwo\par}

	So, $|v^\prime| = Cr^{1- n}$. By allowing $C$ to be negative we can just say $v^\prime = Cr^{1 - n}$. Finally, we can take one more antiderivative to get that:

	{\centering $v(r) = \begin{cases} C_1\ln(r) + C_2 & \text{ if } n = 2 \\ \frac{C_1}{r^{n - 2}} + C_2 & \text{ if } n \geq 3\text{.} \end{cases}$ \retTwo\par}
\end{myIndent}

Based on the prior reasoning, we define a function $\Phi: \mathbb{R}^n - \{0\} \to \mathbb{R}$ by:

{\centering $\Phi(x) = \begin{cases} \frac{-1}{2\pi}\ln|x| & \text{ if } n = 2 \\ \frac{1}{n(n - 2)\alpha(n)} \cdot \frac{1}{|x|^{n - 2}} & \text{ if } n \geq 3\text{.} \end{cases}$ \retTwo\par}

\hypertarget{Fundamental Solution of $-\triangle$}{This} is called the \udefine{fundamental solution of $-\triangle$}. 
\begin{myIndent}\myComment
	The reason this is called the fundamental solution will become obvious when I pick up this subject again on \inLinkRap{idk reference 10}{page 1184}. However, until then I will just note that $\Phi$ is locally integrable on $\mathbb{R}^n$.
\end{myIndent}

\blect{Math 290A Lecture Notes:}\\
Everything in this class will be building off notes I already took while studying Munkres' Topology on \inLinkRap{placeholder}{pages 117-130}. That said, the class uses slightly different notation. I'll list that notation here:
\begin{itemize}
	\item Given a topological space $X$ and a point $a \in X$, $\pi_1(X, a)$ shall denote the first fundamental group of $X$ based at $a$.
	\item Given any path $\gamma: [0, 1] \to X$ (where $X$ is a topological space), I'll denote by $[\gamma]$ the path homotopy equivalence class of $\gamma : [0, 1] \to X$. The composition of paths $\gamma$ (going from $a$ to $b$) and $\sigma$ (going from $b$ to $c$) will be denoted $\gamma \cdot \sigma$. Also, the reversed parametrization of a path $\gamma$ will be denoted $\overline{\gamma}$.
	\item If $\gamma(0) = a$ and $\gamma(1) = b$ then we define the map $\gamma_{\sharp}: \pi_1(X, a) \to \pi_1(X, b)$ by $[f] \mapsto [\overline{\gamma} \cdot f \cdot \gamma]$.\newpage
\end{itemize}

To start off, when I was introducing singular homology before getting distracted by vector calculus, I made a point of trying to give a category theoretic perspective to homology groups. I'd also like to give a category theoretic perspective to the 1st fundamental group.\retTwo

We let $\mcateg{Top}_*$ be the category consisting of pairs $(X, a)$ where $X$ is a topological space and $a \in X$ is some element. Also, we say a morphism from $(X, a)$ to $(Y, b)$ is a continuous function $f:X \to Y$ such that $f(a) = b$. Checking that this is a category is easy.

Next note that we can define a functor $\pi_1: \mcateg{Top}_* \to \mcateg{Grp}$ as follows:
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Map any pair $(X, a)$ to the 1st fundamental group $\pi_1(X, a)$. Also, associate to any\\ morphism $f: (X, a) \to (Y, b)$ the map $f_*: \pi_1(X, a) \to \pi_2(Y, b)$ given by\\ $f_*([\gamma]) \coloneqq [f \circ \gamma]$. Theorem 52.4 on \inLinkRap{placeholder}{page 120} shows that this is a well-defined\\ functor.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

It's obvious that for any homeomorphism $f: X \to Y$ we'll have that\\ $f_* : \pi_1(X, a) \to \pi_1(Y, f(a))$ is a group isomorphism. I'd like to prove that this\\ also holds if we weaken $f$ to only being a homotopy equivalence.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Theorem:} Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are topological spaces and $f, g: X \to Y$ are continuous maps that are homotopic by a continuous map $H: X \times [0, 1] \to Y$. Fix $a \in X$, and let $\gamma: [0, 1] \to Y$ be the function defined by $\gamma(t) = H(a, t)$. Then we have the following commuting diagram:
% https://q.uiver.app/#q=WzAsMyxbMCwxLCJcXHBpXzEoWCwgYSkiXSxbMSwwLCJcXHBpXzEoWSwgZihhKSkiXSxbMSwxLCJcXHBpXzEoWSwgZyhhKSkiXSxbMCwyLCJnXyoiLDJdLFswLDEsImZfKiJdLFsxLDIsIlxcZ2FtbWFfXFxzaGFycCJdLFsxLDIsIlxcc2ltIiwzLHsib2Zmc2V0IjoyLCJzdHlsZSI6eyJib2R5Ijp7Im5hbWUiOiJub25lIn0sImhlYWQiOnsibmFtZSI6Im5vbmUifX19XV0=
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	& {\pi_1(Y, f(a))} \\
	{\pi_1(X, a)} & {\pi_1(Y, g(a))}
	\arrow["{\gamma_\sharp}", from=1-2, to=2-2]
	\arrow["\sim"{marking, allow upside down}, shift right=2, draw=none, from=1-2, to=2-2]
	\arrow["{f_*}", from=2-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow["{g_*}"', from=2-1, to=2-2]
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Suppose $[\alpha] \in \pi_1(X, a)$. Then we have that $(\gamma_\sharp \circ f_*)([\alpha]) = \gamma_\sharp([f \circ \alpha]) = [\overline{\gamma} \cdot (f \circ \alpha) \cdot \gamma]$. So to prove the theorem we need to show that $[\overline{\gamma} \cdot (f \circ \alpha) \cdot \gamma] = [g \circ \alpha]$.

	Equivalently, it suffices to show that:

	{\centering$[f \circ \alpha] = [\gamma \cdot (g \circ \alpha) \cdot \overline{\gamma}]$\retTwo\par}

	Fortunately, we can define a continuous map $H_0: [0, 1] \times [0, 1] \to Y$ by:
	
	{\centering$H_0(s, t) \coloneqq H(\alpha(s), t)$.\retTwo\par}

	This will be a homotopy (but not a path homotopy necessarily) from $f \circ \alpha$ to $g \circ \alpha$\\ because we have that:

	{\centering$H_0(s, 0) = (f \circ \alpha)(s)$, $H_0(s, 1) = (g \circ \alpha)(s)$, and $H_0(0, t) = H_0(1, t) = \gamma(t)$.\retTwo\par}

	And now we can reparametrize the homotopy $H_0$ as shown below to get a path homotopy from $f \circ \alpha$ to $\gamma \cdot (g \circ \alpha) \cdot \overline{\gamma}$.

	{\centering\includegraphics[scale=0.35]{Math 290a homotopy reparametrization.png}\newpage\par}

	One way of doing this is to define a reparametrization $k : [0, 1]^2 \to [0, 1]^2$ by:

	{\centering $k(s, t) \coloneqq \begin{cases}(s - st, 3st) & \text{ if } 0 \leq s\leq \frac{1}{3} \\ (s + 2st - t, t) & \text{ if } \frac{1}{3} \leq s \leq \frac{2}{3} \\ (s + t - st, (3 - 3s)t) & \text{ if } \frac{2}{3} \leq s \leq 1\end{cases}$ \retTwo\par}

	By pasting lemma we can see that $k$ is a continuous map. Also, $\widetilde{H_0}(s, t) \coloneqq H_0(k(s, t))$ is a path homotopy from $f \circ \alpha$ to $\gamma \cdot (g \circ \alpha) \cdot \overline{\gamma}$. $\blacksquare$
	\begin{myIndent}\myComment
		Technically $\gamma \cdot (g \circ \alpha) \cdot \overline{\gamma}$ was formally defined as having a different parametrization from what $s \mapsto \widetilde{H_0}(s, 1)$ would give. That said, reparametrizing a curve does not\\ [1pt] change its path homotopy equivalence class.\retTwo

		More specifically, given any path $\alpha: [0, 1] \to X$ and any continuous map\\ $k: [0, 1] \to [0, 1]$ such that $k(0) = 0$ and $k(1) = 1$, we have that $\alpha \simeq_p \alpha \circ k$\\ via the homotopy $H(s, t) \coloneqq \alpha((1 - t)s + tk(s))$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
\end{myIndent}

\ul{Theorem:} If $f: X \to Y$ and $g:Y \to X$ are inverse  homotopy equivalences and $x_0 \in X$, then $f_* : \pi_1(X, x_0) \to \pi_1(Y, f(x_0))$ is an isomorphism.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Let $y_1 = f(x_0)$, let $x_2 = g(y_1)$, and let $y_3 = f(x_2)$. Then by the prior theorem we know there are group isomorphisms $\phi$ and $\psi$ such that the following commuting diagrams holds:
	% https://q.uiver.app/#
	\[\begin{tikzcd}
		&&& {\pi_1(Y, y_1)} \\
		& {\pi_1(Y, y_1)} & {\pi_1(X, x_2)} & {\pi_1(Y, y_3)} \\
		{\pi_1(X, x_0)} & {\pi_1(Y, y_1)} & {\pi_1(X, x_2)} \\
		&& {\pi_1(X, x_0)}
		\arrow["\sim"{marking, allow upside down}, shift left=2, draw=none, from=1-4, to=2-4]
		\arrow["{(\mathrm{Id}_Y)_* = \mathrm{Id}_{\pi_1(Y, y_1)}}"{description}, from=2-2, to=1-4]
		\arrow["{g_*}"', from=2-2, to=2-3]
		\arrow["{f_*}"', from=2-3, to=2-4]
		\arrow["\psi", from=2-4, to=1-4]
		\arrow["{f_*}", from=3-1, to=3-2]
		\arrow["{(\mathrm{Id}_X)_* = \mathrm{Id}_{\pi_1(X, x_0)}}"{description}, from=3-1, to=4-3]
		\arrow["{g_*}", from=3-2, to=3-3]
		\arrow["\phi", tail reversed, no head, from=4-3, to=3-3]
		\arrow["\sim"{marking, allow upside down}, shift right=2, draw=none, from=4-3, to=3-3]
	\end{tikzcd}\]

	Yet note that top and bottom commuting diagrams show that $g_*: \pi_1(Y, y_1) \to \pi_1(X, x_2)$ must be injective and surjective respectively. Hence it is a bijection (and thus a group\\ isomorphism). Then using that information, I claim that $(f_*)^{-1} = \phi \circ g_*$. After all, it\\ was already clear that $(\phi \circ g_*) \circ f_* = \myId_{\pi_1(X, x_0)}$. In turn, we have that:
	
	{\centering$f_*([\alpha]) = (\phi \circ g_*)^{-1}([\alpha])$ for all $[\alpha] \in \pi_1(X, x_0)$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo\par}
\end{myIndent}
