\blect{Math 231A Lecture Notes:}\newpage

\hypertarget{idk reference 10}{I'm} going to now return to discussing the fundamental solution of $-\triangle$. Scroll back three pages for a reminder on its definition.\retTwo

The reason $\Phi$ is called the fundamental solution of $-\triangle$ is that we can calculate that in\\ the weak sense, $-\triangle \Phi = \delta_0$ where $\delta_x$ denotes the dirac delta function at $x$.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	\ul{Case when $n = 2$:}\\
	Recalling that $\Phi(x) = \frac{-1}{2\pi}\ln|x|$ define for any $\varepsilon \geq 0$ the function:
	
	{\centering$\Phi_\varepsilon(x) = \frac{-1}{4\pi}\ln(|x|^2 + \varepsilon^2)$\\ [4pt]\par}
	
	Note that $\Phi_\varepsilon$ and $\Phi$ are both locally integrable. Also $\Phi_\varepsilon \to \Phi$ on $\mathbb{R}^2 - \{0\}$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$\\ (where specifically $|\Phi_\varepsilon|$ is increasing on $B_1(0)$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$ and decreasing on $B_1(0)^\comp$\\ as $\varepsilon \to 0$). So, we can show by exerciese 9.1(b) on \inLinkRap{Exercise 9.1 page 963}{pages 963-964} that $\Phi_\varepsilon \to \Phi$ in $\mathcal{D}^\prime$. And since partial derivatives are continuous on $\mathcal{D}^\prime$, we can conclude that $-\triangle \Phi_\varepsilon \to - \triangle \Phi$.\retTwo
	
	Yet also after some manipulations, we can compute for all $\varepsilon > 0$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}^2 - \{0\}$ that:
	
	{\centering$-\triangle \Phi_\varepsilon(x) = \frac{1}{\pi}(\frac{\varepsilon}{|x|^2 + \varepsilon^2})^2 = \frac{1}{\pi}(\frac{\varepsilon}{\varepsilon^2|\varepsilon^{-1}x|^2 + \varepsilon^2})^2 = \frac{1}{\pi}(\frac{1}{\varepsilon|\varepsilon^{-1}x|^2 + \varepsilon})^2 = \frac{1}{\varepsilon^2} \cdot \frac{1}{\pi}(\frac{1}{|\varepsilon^{-1}x|^2 + 1})^2$.\retTwo\par}

	In other words, we can let $g(x) = \frac{1}{\pi}(\frac{1}{|x|^2 + 1})^2$. And then we have that:
	
	{\centering$-\triangle \Phi_\varepsilon(x) = \frac{1}{\varepsilon^2}g(\varepsilon^{-1}x)$.\retTwo\par}

	Also note that $\int_{\mathbb{R}^2} \frac{1}{\pi}(\frac{1}{|x|^2 + 1})^2 \df x = \int_0^\infty (\frac{1}{r^2 + 1})^2 2r\df r = \int_1^\infty \frac{1}{u^2}\df u = 1$. Therefore, we can say by proposition 9.1 on \inLinkRap{Folland Proposition 9.1}{page 960} that $-\triangle \Phi_\varepsilon \to \delta_0$ in $\mathcal{D}^\prime$.\retTwo

	\ul{Case when $n > 2$}:\\
	We can adapt the prior reasoning but with different functions $\Phi_\varepsilon$ and $g$. Or alternatively, I can show this through more a direct path (which we could have also taken in the $n = 2$ case by the way).\retTwo

	Let $\psi \in C_c^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$. We have to be careful because $\Phi$ is not differentiable at the origin.\\ That said, since $\psi$ is compactly supported, we can choose some $R > 0$ such that\\ $\supp(\psi) \subseteq B_{R/2}(0)$. And now for any $0 < \varepsilon < 1$ we have that:

	{\centering $\int_{\mathbb{R}^2} \Phi \cdot (-\triangle \psi) \df x = \int_{B_\varepsilon(0)}\Phi \cdot (-\triangle \psi)\df x + \int_{\{\varepsilon \leq |x| \leq R\}}\Phi \cdot (-\triangle \psi)\df x$ \retTwo\par}

	Now as $\triangle \psi \in C_c(\mathbb{R}^n)$, there is a constant $M \geq 0$ such that $|-\triangle \psi| \leq M$. And now we have that:

	{\centering $\left|\int_{B_\varepsilon(0)}\Phi \cdot (-\triangle \psi)\df x\right| \leq M \int_{B_\varepsilon(0)}|\Phi|\df x = M\int_0^\varepsilon \frac{1}{(n - 2)} \cdot \frac{r^{n-1}}{r^{n-2}} \df r = \frac{M\varepsilon^2}{2(n - 2)}$ \\ [4pt]\par}

	So as $\varepsilon \to 0$ we have that $\int_{B_\varepsilon(0)}\Phi \cdot (-\triangle \psi)\df x \to 0$.\retTwo

	Meanwhile, by {\color{OliveGreen}Green's first identity} we have that:

	{\centering\fontsize{11}{12}\selectfont\begin{tabular}{l}
		$\int_{\{\varepsilon \leq |x| \leq R\}}\Phi \cdot (-\triangle \psi)\df x = -\int_{\partial B_R(0)} \Phi(x^\prime) \nabla \psi(x^\prime) \cdot \frac{x^\prime}{|x^\prime|} \df S(x^\prime) + \int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(0)} \Phi(x^\prime) \nabla \psi(x^\prime) \cdot \frac{x^\prime}{|x^\prime|} \df S(x^\prime)$\\ [6pt]
		$\phantom{\int_{\{\varepsilon \leq |x| \leq R\}}\Phi\cdot (-\triangle \psi)\df x = -\int_{\partial B_R(0)} \Phi(x^\prime) \nabla \psi(x^\prime) \cdot \frac{x^\prime}{|x^\prime|} \df S(x^\prime)} + \int_{\{\varepsilon \leq |x| \leq R\}} \nabla \Phi \cdot \nabla \psi \df x$
	\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

	Based on how we chose $R$, we know that $-\int_{\partial B_R(0)} \Phi(x^\prime) \nabla \psi(x^\prime) \cdot \frac{x^\prime}{|x^\prime|} \df S(x^\prime) = 0$. So, our expression simplifies to:

	{\centering\fontsize{11}{12}\selectfont\begin{tabular}{l}
		$\int_{\{\varepsilon \leq |x| \leq R\}}\Phi \cdot (-\triangle \psi)\df x = \int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(0)} \Phi(x^\prime) \nabla \psi(x^\prime) \cdot \frac{x^\prime}{|x^\prime|} \df S(x^\prime) + \int_{\{\varepsilon \leq |x| \leq R\}} \nabla \Phi \cdot \nabla \psi \df x$.
	\end{tabular}\newpage\par}

	But now because $\nabla \psi(x^\prime)$ is continuous and nonzero only on a compact set, we can find some constant $M^\prime \geq 0$ such that $|\nabla \psi| \leq M^\prime$. And now we have that:

	{\centering $\left|\int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(0)} \Phi(x^\prime) \nabla \psi(x^\prime) \cdot \frac{x^\prime}{|x^\prime|} \df S(x^\prime)\right| \leq \frac{M^\prime}{n(n-2)\alpha(n)\varepsilon^{n - 2}} \cdot \varepsilon^{n-1}n\alpha(n) = \frac{M^\prime \varepsilon}{n-2}$ \retTwo\par}

	The latter goes to $0$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$. Hence to recap, we have that:

	{\centering $\int_{\mathbb{R}^2} \Phi \cdot (-\triangle \psi) \df x = \lim\limits_{\varepsilon \to 0} \int_{\{\varepsilon \leq x \leq R\}} \nabla \Phi \cdot \nabla \psi \df x$\retTwo\par}

	By another application of {\color{OliveGreen}Green's first identity}, we have that:

	{\centering\fontsize{11}{12}\selectfont\begin{tabular}{l}
		$\int_{\{\varepsilon \leq |x| \leq R\}} \nabla \Phi \cdot \nabla \psi \df x = \int_{\partial B_R(0)} \psi(x^\prime) \nabla \Phi(x^\prime) \cdot \frac{x^\prime}{|x^\prime|}\df S(x^\prime) - \int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(0)}\psi(x^\prime) \nabla \Phi(x^\prime) \cdot \frac{x^\prime}{|x^\prime|}\df S(x^\prime)$\\ [6pt]
		$\phantom{\int_{\{\varepsilon \leq |x| \leq R\}} \nabla \Phi \cdot \nabla \psi \df x = \int_{\partial B_R(0)} \psi(x^\prime) \nabla \Phi(x^\prime) \cdot \frac{x^\prime}{|x^\prime|}\df S(x^\prime)} - \int_{\varepsilon \leq |x| \leq R}\psi(x^\prime) \psi \triangle \Phi \df x$.
	\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

	$\int_{\partial B_R(0)} \psi(x^\prime) \nabla \Phi(x^\prime) \cdot \frac{x^\prime}{|x^\prime|}\df S(x^\prime)$ cancels though because $\psi \equiv 0$ on $\partial B_R(0)$. Similarly, $\int_{\varepsilon \leq |x| \leq R}\psi(x^\prime) \psi \triangle \Phi \df x$ cancels because we can compute through a straightforward\\ computation that $\triangle \Phi \equiv 0$ on $\mathbb{R}^n - \{0\}$. Hence, we are left with:

	{\centering $\int_{\mathbb{R}^2} \Phi \cdot (-\triangle \psi) \df x = -\lim\limits_{\varepsilon \to 0} \int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(0)}\psi(x^\prime) \nabla \Phi(x^\prime) \cdot \frac{x^\prime}{|x^\prime|}\df S(x^\prime)$\retTwo\par}

	We can compute that $\nabla \Phi(x^\prime) = \frac{-1}{n\alpha(n)} \cdot \frac{x^\prime}{|x^\prime|^n}$. In turn, we get that:

	{\centering $-\int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(0)}\psi(x^\prime) \nabla \Phi(x^\prime) \cdot \frac{x^\prime}{|x^\prime|}\df S(x^\prime) = \frac{1}{n \alpha(n) \varepsilon^{n-1}}\int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(0)}\psi(x^\prime)\df x^\prime$ \retTwo\par}

	But now as $\psi$ is continuous, we can say that:

	{\centering $\frac{1}{n \alpha(n) \varepsilon^{n-1}}\int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(0)}\psi(x^\prime)\df x^\prime \to \psi(0)$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$\retTwo\par}

	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		Why?\\
		We can write $\psi(x) = \psi(0) + u(x)$ where $u(x) \to 0$ as $x \to 0$. And then\\ as $S(\partial B_\varepsilon(0)) = n\alpha(n)\varepsilon^{n-1}$, we have that:

		{\centering $\frac{1}{n \alpha(n) \varepsilon^{n-1}}\int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(0)}\psi(x^\prime)\df x^\prime = \psi(0) + \frac{1}{n \alpha(n) \varepsilon^{n-1}}\int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(0)} u(x^\prime)\df x^\prime$\retTwo\par}

		Meanwhile, $\left|\frac{1}{n \alpha(n) \varepsilon^{n-1}}\int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(0)} u(x^\prime)\df x^\prime\right| \leq \max\limits_{x \in B_\varepsilon(0)}|u(x)| \to 0$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	So, we've finished showing that $\int_{\mathbb{R}^2} \Phi \cdot (-\triangle \psi) \df x = \psi(0)$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo As mentioned already, I could have done both of the prior approaches in the opposite cases I actually did them in. The approach I took in the $n > 2$ case has the advantage that I only had to assume $\psi$ is twice differentiable instead of infinitely differentiable. Although, I think it's computationally less neat.\retTwo

Anyways, this then leads us to the following theorem:\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Theorem:} \hypertarget{Existence of Solution page 1185}{Assume} $f \in C_c^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$ (where $n \geq 2$). Then the function $u = \Phi * f$ satisfies that\\ $u \in C^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$ and $-\triangle u = f$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	To see that $u \in C^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$, we just need to note that $\Phi$ is locally integrable and $f$ is compactly supported and in $C^2$. So by Folland exercise 8.7 (which I did for homework in math 240c), we know $u \in C^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$.\newpage

	Also by the prior reasoning, plus some Leibniz rule spam, we can conclude that:
	
	{\centering $-\triangle u = \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \Phi(y) \cdot -\triangle f(x - y)\df x = f(x - 0) = f(x)$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo\par}
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo\mySepTwo

Some properties of harmonic functions: (Also for all these results assume $n \geq 2$)\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Mean Value Formula:} Suppose $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is an open set and $u \in C^2(U)$ satisfies that\\ $\triangle u  = 0$. Then for any $x \in U$ and $r > 0$ such that $\overline{B_r(x)} \subseteq U$ we have that:

{\centering $u(x) = \frac{1}{nr^{n-1}\alpha(n)}\int_{\partial B_r(x)} u(y)\df S(y) = \frac{1}{r^n\alpha(n)}\int_{B_r(x)}u(y)\df y$ \retTwo\par}

\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	To start off, note for any $r$ small enough so that $\overline{B_r(x)} \subseteq U$ as well as any measurable function $u: U \to \mathbb{R}$ we have that:
	
	{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
		$\frac{1}{nr^{n-1}\alpha(n)}\int_{\partial B_r(x)}u(y) \df S(y) = \frac{1}{nr^{n-1}\alpha(n)}\int_{\partial B_r(0)}u(y + x) \df S(y)$\\ [6pt]
		$\phantom{\frac{1}{nr^{n-1}\alpha(n)}\int_{\partial B_r(x)}u(y) \df S(y)} = \frac{1}{n\alpha(n)}\int_{\partial B_1(0)}u(ry + x)\df S(y)$.
	\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}
	
	All of the prior equalities can be checked first for simple functions, then nonnegative\\ functions, and then general complex or extended-real valued functions. 	Hence, we can now define:
	
	{\centering$\phi(r) \coloneqq \frac{1}{nr^{n-1}\alpha(n)}\int_{\partial B_r(x)}u(y) \df S(y)$.\retTwo\par}

	By Leibniz's rules, we will get that:

	{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
		$\phi^\prime(r) = \frac{1}{n\alpha(n)}\int_{\partial B_1(0)}\nabla u(ry + x) \cdot y \df S(y)$\\ [6pt]
		$\phantom{\phi^\prime(r)} = \frac{1}{n\alpha(n)r^{n-1}}\int_{\partial B_r(x)}\nabla u(y) \cdot \frac{y - x}{r}\df S(y)$\\ [6pt]
		$\phantom{\phi^\prime(r)} = \frac{1}{n\alpha(n)r^{n-1}}\int_{B_r(x)}\triangle u(y) \df y = 0$ {\color{red} (by divergence theorem)}\\ [6pt]
	\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

	Therefore $\phi$ is constant. And since $\phi(r) \to u(x)$ as $r \to 0$ because $u$ is continuous, we can conclude that $\phi(r) = u(x)$ for all $r$.\retTwo
	
	With that we can also now conclude the other desired formula because:
	
	{\centering \begin{tabular}{l}
		$\frac{1}{r^n \alpha(n)}\int_{B_r(x)}u(y) \df y = \frac{1}{r^n\alpha(n)}\int_0^r \rho^{n-1} \int_{\partial B_1(0)} u(\rho y^\prime + x)\df S(y^\prime)\df \rho$\\ [6pt]
		$\phantom{\frac{1}{r^n \alpha(n)}\int_{B_r(x)}u(y) \df y} = \frac{1}{r^n\alpha(n)}\int_0^r \int_{\partial B_\rho(x)} u(y^\prime)\df S(y^\prime)\df \rho$\\ [6pt]
		$\phantom{\frac{1}{r^n \alpha(n)}\int_{B_r(x)}u(y) \df y} = \frac{1}{r^n\alpha(n)}\int_0^r  n\rho^{n-1}\alpha(n) u(x)\df \rho = u(x)$. $\blacksquare$
	\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo A function $u: U \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying the formula $u(x) = \frac{1}{nr^{n-1}\alpha(n)}\int_{\partial B_r(x)} u(y)\df S(y)$\\ [-2pt] whenever $\overline{B_r(x)} \subseteq U$ is said to have the \udefine{mean value property}. Note that the\\ [2pt] reasoning above generalizes the theorem on \inLinkRap{harmonic functions have MVP}{page 804}.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Theorem:} If $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is an open set and $u \in C^2(U, \mathbb{R})$ satisfies the mean value property then $\triangle u = 0$ on $U$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Assume to the contrary that there exists $x_0 \in U$ such that $\triangle u(x_0) \neq 0$. Then define $\phi(r) \coloneqq \frac{1}{nr^{n-1}\alpha(n)}\int_{\partial B_r(x_0)}u(y)\df S(y)$ like in the proof of the prior result. Trivially, we now\newpage have that $\phi^\prime(r) = 0$ (since $\phi \equiv u(x_0)$ is a constant function). Yet we can also calculate identically to before that $\phi^\prime(r) = \frac{1}{n\alpha(n)r^{n-1}}\int_{B_r(x_0)}\triangle u(y) \df y$. Since $\triangle u$ is a continuous function, we can shrink $r$ so that eventually $u(y) \neq 0$ for any $y \in B_r(x_0)$ and $u(y)$ and $u(x_0)$ share a sign for all $y \in B_r(x_0)$. And now we have a contradiction. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\ul{(Regularity of Harmonic Functions):} Suppose $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is an open set and $u \in C(U, \mathbb{R})$ satisfies the mean value property. Then $u \in C^\infty(U, \mathbb{R})$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Let $\{V_j\}_{j \in \mathbb{N}}$ be an increasing sequence of precompact open sets in $U$ whose union is all of $U$. If we can show that $u$ restricted to each $V_j$ is smooth, then we will be done.\retTwo

	Fortunately, for any fixed $j$ we can find some constant $R > 0$ such that $|x - y| > R$ for all $x \in \overline{V_j}$ and $y \in U^\comp$. And now we let $\eta \in C^\infty_c(B_R(0))$ be a radial nonnegative bump function with $\int \eta = 1$. In other words, there exists some smooth compactly supported function $\widetilde{\eta}: [0, R) \to [0, \infty)$ such that $\eta(x) = \widetilde{\eta}(|x|)$ and $\int_0^R r^{n-1}\widetilde{\eta}(r)\df r = 1$.\retTwo
	
	We can convolve $u$ and $\eta$ to get a well-defined smooth function $f: V_j \to \mathbb{R}$ defined by $f(x) = \int u(x - y)\eta(y)\df y$. Yet now note by an easy change of variables that:

	{\centering \begin{tabular}{l}
		$f(x) = \int_{B_R(0)} u(x + y)\eta(-y)\df y = \int_0^R \int_{\partial B_1(0)} u(x + rz)\widetilde{\eta}(r) r^{n-1} \df S(z)\df r$\\ [4pt]
		$\phantom{f(x) = \int_{B_R(x)} u(x + y)\eta(-y)\df y} = \int_0^R \widetilde{\eta}(r) r^{n-1} \cdot \int_{\partial B_r(x)}u(z)\df S(z) \df r$\\ [4pt]
		$\phantom{f(x) = \int_{B_R(x)} u(x + y)\eta(-y)\df y} = u(x)\int_0^R \widetilde{\eta}(r) r^{n-1} \df r = u(x) \cdot 1$\\ [4pt]
	\end{tabular} \retTwo\par}

	Thus, $u = f$ on $V_j$ and we've actually shown that $u$ is a smooth function on $V_j$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\myComment As a side note, because smoothness of harmonicity are local properties, the combination of the prior three results also shows that if the mean value property holds locally for a continuous\\ function, then the function is smooth and harmonic globally. So we have the following theorem.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Theorem:} Given an open set $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ and a continuous function $f: U \to \mathbb{R}$, the following are equivalent:
\begin{itemize}
	\item $f$ is $C^2$ and harmonic.
	\item $f$ is $C^\infty$ and harmonic.
	\item $f$ locally has the mean value property.\retTwo
\end{itemize}

\hTwo By basically identical reasoning as on \inLinkRap{harmonic functions have MVP}{page 804}, we can show that if $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a connected open set and $u: U \to \mathbb{R}$ is a continuous function satisfying the mean value property, then $u$ satisfies the \udefine{maximal principle}. In other words, if there exists $a \in U$ with $u(a) \geq u(z)$ for all $z \in G$ then $u$ is a constant function.\retTwo

In a similar vein, we can then prove analogous results to three results starting at the \inLinkRap{Math 220c Max modulus principle +}{bottom of page 805} (using identical reasoning). I don't feel like proving these things since there are no new ideas.\newpage

Since we know harmonic functions are smooth, the next leap I want to make is that\\ harmonic functions are (real) analytic.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Theorem:} \hypertarget{Math 231a Theorem page 1188}{Assume} $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is an open set and $u: U \to \mathbb{R}$ is harmonic. Then for all $x_0 \in U$,\\ $r > 0$ such that $\overline{B_r(x_0)} \subseteq U$, and all multi-indices $\alpha$ with $|\alpha| = k$, we have that:

{\centering $|\partial^\alpha u(x_0)| \leq \frac{C_k}{r^{n + k}}\|u\|_{L^1(B_r(x_0))}$ \\ [4pt]\par}

where $C_0 = \frac{1}{\alpha(n)}$ and $C_k = \frac{(2^{n+1}nk)^k}{\alpha(n)}$ for all $k \geq 1$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	We proceed by induction. Firstly, when $k = 0$ then $u(x_0) = \frac{1}{r^n \alpha(n)}\int_{B_r(x_0)}u$ by the mean value theorem. Therefore:
	
	{\centering $|u(x_0)| \leq \frac{1}{r^n\alpha(n)}\|u\|_{L^1(B_r(x_0))} = \frac{C_0}{r^{n + k}}\|u\|_{L^1(B_r(x_0))}$.\retTwo\par}

	Next, since $u$ is smooth in addition to being harmonic, partial derivative operators\\ commute. Therefore, for any $1 \leq i \leq n$ we have that $\partial_{x_i}u$ is harmonic on $U$ since:

	{\centering$0 = \partial_{x_i}(0) = \partial_{x_i} \triangle u = \triangle\partial_{x_i} u$\retTwo\par}

	And now upon writing $y = (y_1,\ldots, y_n)$ for any $y \in \mathbb{R}^n$, we can apply the mean value theorem in order to get that:

	{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
		$|\partial_{x_i} u(x_0)| = \left|\frac{2^n}{r^n\alpha(n)}\int_{B_{\frac{r}{2}}(x_0)} \partial_{x_i} u(y)\df y\right|$\\ [12pt]
		$\phantom{|\partial_{x_i}u(x_0)|} = \frac{2^n}{r^n \alpha(n)}\left|\int_{\partial B_{\frac{r}{2}(x_0)}}  u(y) \frac{2y_i}{r} \df S(y)\right|$ {\color{red}(See the theorem on \inLinkRap{Theorem Page 1173}{pages 1173-1176})}\\ [12pt]
		$\phantom{|\partial_{x_i} u(x_0)|} \leq \frac{2^{n}}{r^{n} \alpha(n)}\int_{\partial B_{\frac{r}{2}(x_0)}} \left| u(y)\right| \df S(y)$\\ [12pt]
		$\phantom{|\partial_{x_i} u(x_0)|} \leq \frac{2^{n}}{r^{n}\alpha(n)} \cdot \frac{nr^{n-1}\alpha(n)}{k^{n-1}} \cdot\| u\|_{L^\infty(B_{\frac{r}{2}}(x_0))} = \frac{2n}{r}\| u\|_{L^\infty(B_{\frac{r}{2}}(x_0))}$\\ [12pt]
	\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

	But now by induction plus the fact that $\overline{B_{\frac{r}{2}}(y)} \subseteq U$ for all $y \in \overline{B_{\frac{r}{2}}(x_0)}$, we can\\ conclude that:

	{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
		$\frac{2n}{r}\| u\|_{L^\infty(B_{\frac{r}{2}}(x_0))} \leq \frac{2n}{r} \cdot \frac{2^n}{\alpha(n)r^n} \sup\limits_{y \in B_{{\frac{r}{2}}}(x_0)}\|u\|_{L^1(B_{\frac{r}{2}}(y))} \leq \frac{2^{n+1}n}{\alpha(n)} \cdot \frac{1}{r^{n+1}}\|u\|_{L^1(B_r(x_0))}$\\ [8pt]
		$\phantom{\frac{2n}{r}\| u\|_{L^\infty(B_{\frac{r}{2}}(x_0))} \leq \frac{2n}{r} \cdot \frac{2^n}{\alpha(n)r^n} \sup\limits_{y \in B_{{\frac{r}{2}}}(x_0)}\|u\|_{L^1(B_{\frac{r}{2}}(y))}} \leq \frac{C_1}{r^{n+1}}\|u\|_{L^1(B_r(x_0))}$
	\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

	Finally, we get to the induction step. Suppose $\alpha$ is a multi-index of order $k - 1$ (where $k \geq 2$) and then let $1 \leq i \leq n$. By identical reasoning as before, we can conclude that $\partial_{x_i}\partial^\alpha u$ is harmonic. So, we can apply the mean value theorem identically to before in order to show that $|\partial_{x_i}\partial^\alpha u(x_0)| \leq \frac{nk}{r}\|\partial^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(B_{\frac{r}{k}}(x_0))}$.\retTwo

	But now by induction plus the fact that $\overline{B_{\frac{r(k-1)}{k}}(y)} \subseteq U$ for all $y \in \partial {B_{\frac{r}{k}}(x_0)}$, we can\\ conclude that:

	{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
		$\|\partial^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(B_{\frac{r}{2}}(x_0))} \leq C_{k-1}\left(\frac{k}{r(k - 1)}\right)^{n + k - 1}\sup\limits_{y \in B_{{\frac{r}{k}}}(x_0)}\|u\|_{L^1(B_{\frac{r(k-1)}{k}}(y))}$
		\end{tabular}\newpage\begin{tabular}{l}
		$\phantom{\|\partial^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(B_{\frac{r}{2}}(x_0))}} \leq  \frac{(2^{n+1}n(k-1))^{k-1}}{\alpha(n)} \cdot \frac{k^{n + k - 1}}{r^{n + k - 1}(k-1)^{n + k - 1}}\|u\|_{L^1(B_r(x_0))}$\\ [8pt]
		$\phantom{\|\partial^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(B_{\frac{r}{2}}(x_0))}} = \frac{(2^{n+1}nk)^{k-1}}{\alpha(n)} \cdot \frac{1}{r^{n + k - 1}}\left(\frac{k}{k-1}\right)^n\|u\|_{L^1(B_r(x_0))}$
	\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

	So, we get that: 
	
	{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
		$|\partial_{x_i}\partial^\alpha u(x_0)| \leq \frac{nk}{r} \cdot \frac{(2^{n+1}nk)^{k-1}}{\alpha(n)} \cdot \frac{1}{r^{n + k - 1}}\left(\frac{k}{k-1}\right)^n\|u\|_{L^1(B_r(x_0))}$\\ [6pt]
		$\phantom{|\partial_{x_i}\partial^\alpha u(x_0)|} \ \frac{(2^{n+1}nk)^k}{\alpha(n)} \cdot \frac{1}{r^{n + k}} \cdot \|u\|_{L^1(B_r(x_0))} = \frac{C_k}{r^{n + k}}\|u\|_{L^1(B_r(x_0))}$. $\blacksquare$
	\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}
\end{myIndent}

\ul{Corollary (Liouville's Theorem):} Suppose $u: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is harmonic and bounded on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Then $u$ is constant.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	We shall show for every $1 \leq i \leq n$ that $\partial_{x_i} u \equiv 0$. So, let $C > 0$ be a constant such that $|u(x)| \leq C$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$. Then by the prior theorem, for any $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $r > 0$ we have that:

	{\centering $|\partial_{x_i} u(x)| \leq \frac{2^{n+1}n}{\alpha(n) r^{n+1}}\|u\|_{L^1(B_r(x))} \leq \frac{2^{n+1}n}{\alpha(n) r^{n+1}} \cdot Cr^n \alpha(n) = \frac{2^{n+1}nC}{r}$ \retTwo\par}

	And now we just take $r \to 0$ to get that $|\partial_{x_i} u(x)| = 0$. Since all the partial derivatives\\ of $u$ are identically zero on $\mathbb{R}^n$, this proves that $u$ is constant. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\ul{Corollary 2:} Let $f \in C_c^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$ (where $n \geq 3$). Then any bounded solution of $-\triangle u = f$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ has the form $u = (\Phi * f) + C$ (where $\Phi$ is the fundamental solution of $-\triangle$ and $C$ is a real constant).
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	To start off, we can easily see that $v \coloneqq \Phi * f$ is a bounded function. Plus, by the theorem on \inLinkRap{Existence of Solution page 1185}{page 1185} we know that it does solve $-\triangle v = f$.\retTwo

	Now supposing $u$ is another bounded solution, we then know that $w = u - v$ is bounded and solves that $-\triangle w = 0$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. So by the prior corollary, we know $w \equiv C$ for some constant. And then $u = v + C$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo I'm about finally ready to prove that harmonic functions are analytic. But first there are two things I need to go over.\retTwo

Firstly, what do I mean when I say a function $f: U \to \mathbb{R}$ is analytic?
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Suppose $f: U \to \mathbb{R}$ is a smooth function and $c \in U$. For any $k \geq 0$ we define the $k$th Taylor polynomial of $f$ centered at $c$ by the expression:

	{\centering $P_k(x) = \sum\limits_{|\alpha| \leq k} \frac{\partial^\alpha f(c)}{\alpha!}(x - c)^\alpha$ \retTwo\par}

	Notably, $P_k$ will have all the same derivatives as $f$ at $c$ up to order $k$.\retTwo

	We shall say that $f \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathbb{R})$ is \udefine{analytic at $c$} if there exists some $r > 0$ such that $P_k(x) \to f(x)$ for all $x \in B_r(c)$. Equivalently, this means that the remainder formula $R_k(x) \coloneqq f(x) - P_{k-1}(x)$ must go to $0$ on $B_r(c)$ as $k \to \infty$. If $f$ is analytic at every $c \in U$ we say $f$ is \udefine{analytic}. I will hopefully deal with more of the loose ends of this definition in the future as I learn about functions of multiple complex variables.\newpage
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo Secondly, I need to prove an approximation which will undoubtedly come up many more times in my life. I'm going to follow the steps layed out by an exercise in Folland Real Analysis. This is a proof from probability theory so I will be using probability notation.\retTwo

\Hstatement\blab{Exercise 10.21:} Let $\{X_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of independent random variables, each having the Poisson distribution with mean $1$.
\begin{myIndent}\color{BrickRed}
	In other words, the probability distribution on $\mathbb{R}$ induced by each $X_i$ is the measure:
	
	{\centering$\lambda_1 \coloneqq \frac{1}{e}\sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{1}{k!}\delta_k$.\par}
\end{myIndent}
Define $S_n \coloneqq \sum\limits_{i=1}^n X_i$ and $Y_n \coloneqq \max\left(\frac{n - S_n}{\sqrt{n}}, 0\right)$.
\begin{enumerate}
	\item[(a)] $E(Y_n) = e^{-n}\sum\limits_{k=0}^{n-1} \left(\frac{n - k}{\sqrt{n}} \cdot \frac{n^k}{k!}\right) = \frac{n^{n + \frac{1}{2}}e^{-n}}{n!}$.
	
	\begin{myIndent}\HexOne
		Proof:\\
		To start off, note that the probability distribution of $S_n$ is the Poisson distribution\\ $\lambda_n \coloneqq \frac{1}{e^n}\sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{n^k}{k!}\delta_k$.
		\begin{myIndent}\myComment
			In fact more generally, if $X_1, \ldots, X_n$ are independent and have Poisson\\ distributions with means $a_1, \ldots, a_n$ respectively then $X_1 + \ldots + X_n$ has a Poisson distribution with mean $a_1 + \ldots + a_n$. For a proof of this see my math 180a notes.\retTwo
		\end{myIndent}

		And now we can calculate that $E(Y_n) = \sum\limits_{k=0}^{n-1} \frac{n - k}{\sqrt{n}}P(S_n = k) = e^{-n}\sum\limits_{k=0}^{n-1} \left(\frac{n - k}{\sqrt{n}} \cdot \frac{n^k}{k!}\right)$.\retTwo

		To prove the other equation, it suffices to show that:

		{\centering $\sum\limits_{k=0}^{n-1} \left(\frac{n - k}{\sqrt{n}} \cdot \frac{n^k}{k!}\right) = \frac{n^{n + \frac{1}{2}}}{n!}$ \retTwo\par}

		Fortunately, obeserve that:

		{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
			$\sum\limits_{k=0}^{n-1} \left(\frac{n - k}{\sqrt{n}} \cdot \frac{n^k}{k!}\right) = \sum\limits_{k=0}^{n} \left(\frac{n - k}{\sqrt{n}} \cdot \frac{n^k}{k!}\right) = \sum\limits_{k=0}^n \frac{n^{k + \sfrac{1}{2}}}{k!} - \sum\limits_{k=0}^n \frac{kn^{k - \sfrac{1}{2}}}{k!}$\\ [12pt]

			$\phantom{\sum\limits_{k=0}^{n-1} \left(\frac{n - k}{\sqrt{n}} \cdot \frac{n^k}{k!}\right) = \sum\limits_{k=0}^{n} \left(\frac{n - k}{\sqrt{n}} \cdot \frac{n^k}{k!}\right)} = \sum\limits_{k=0}^n \frac{n^{k + \sfrac{1}{2}}}{k!} - \sum\limits_{k=1}^n \frac{n^{k - \sfrac{1}{2}}}{(k-1)!}$\\ [12pt]

			$\phantom{\sum\limits_{k=0}^{n-1} \left(\frac{n - k}{\sqrt{n}} \cdot \frac{n^k}{k!}\right) = \sum\limits_{k=0}^{n} \left(\frac{n - k}{\sqrt{n}} \cdot \frac{n^k}{k!}\right)} = \sum\limits_{k=0}^n \frac{n^{k + \sfrac{1}{2}}}{k!} - \sum\limits_{k=0}^{n-1} \frac{n^{k + \sfrac{1}{2}}}{k!} = \frac{n^{n + \sfrac{1}{2}}}{n!}$.
		\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}
	\end{myIndent}

	\item[(b)] $P_{Y_n} \to \frac{1}{2}\delta_0 + \chi_{[0, \infty)}\nu_0^1$ vaguely (where $\nu_0^1$ is the standard normal distribution $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{\frac{-t^2}{2}}\df t$).
	\begin{myIndent}\HexOne
		\begin{myIndent}\color{BrickRed}
			Note that it makes sense to multiply $\chi_{[0, \infty)}$ and $\nu_0^1$ since the measure $\nu_0^1$ can be identified with a function in $L^1(\mathbb{R})$ (considered as a subspace of the set of complex measurs on $\mathbb{R}$).
		\end{myIndent}

		Proof:\\
		Let $F_n(x) \coloneqq P_{Y_n}((-\infty, x])$ be the CDF function of $Y_n$ for each $n$. Similarly,\\ let $F(x) \coloneqq (\frac{1}{2}\delta_0 + \chi_{[0, \infty)}\nu_0^1)((-\infty, x])$ be the CDF function of the probability\\ distribution we claim the $P_{Y_n}$ vaguely approach. Since all the measures we are dealing\newpage with trivially have total measure $1$, it suffices by \inLinkRap{placeholder}{proposition 7.19 on pages 170-172}\\ to show that $F_n(x) \to F(x)$ pointwise (Lebesgue)-a.e.\retTwo

		We can calculate that $F(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{ if } x < 0 \\ \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_0^x e^{\frac{-t^2}{2}}\df t & \text{ if } x \geq 0\text{.} \end{cases}$\retTwo

		Meanwhile, note for each $n$ that:

		{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}$P_{Y_n} = \left(1 - e^{-n}\sum\limits_{k=0}^{n-1} \frac{n^k}{k!}\right)\delta_0 + \sum\limits_{k=0}^{n-1}(e^{-n}\frac{n^k}{k!})\delta_{\frac{n-k}{\sqrt{n}}} = \left(e^{-n}\sum\limits_{k=n}^\infty \frac{n^k}{k!}\right)\delta_0 + \sum\limits_{k=0}^{n-1}(e^{-n}\frac{n^k}{k!})\delta_{\frac{n-k}{\sqrt{n}}}$\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

		Its immediate that $F_n(x) = 0$ for all $x < 0$ and so trivially $F_n(x) \to F(x)$ if $x < 0$. Meanwhile observe that $\frac{n - k}{\sqrt{n}} \leq x$ iff $n - x\sqrt{n} \leq k$. Therefore, for any \textit{fixed}\\ $x \geq 0$ we have that:
		
		{\centering$F_n(x) = \left(e^{-n}\sum\limits_{k=n}^\infty \frac{n^k}{k!}\right) + \hspace{-0.8em}\sum\limits_{k= \lceil n - x\sqrt{n}\rceil}^{n-1}\hspace{-0.5em} e^{-n}\frac{n^k}{k!} = \left(e^{-n}\sum\limits_{k=n+1}^\infty \frac{n^k}{k!}\right) + \hspace{-0.8em}\sum\limits_{k= \lceil n - x\sqrt{n}\rceil}^{n}\hspace{-0.5em} e^{-n}\frac{n^k}{k!}$.\retTwo\par}

		To evaluate the limit of the expression as $n \to \infty$, we employ the following trick:
		
		\begin{myIndent}\HexTwoP
			Note that $\frac{S_n - n}{\sqrt{n}} = \sum\limits_{k=0}^\infty \left(e^{-n}\frac{n^k}{k!}\right)\delta_{\frac{k - n}{\sqrt{n}}} \to \nu_0^1$ vaguely by the central limit\\ [-6pt] theorem.\retTwo

			Also note for any $a \in \mathbb{R}$ that $\frac{k - n}{\sqrt{n}} \leq a$ iff $k \leq n + a\sqrt{n}$. This has the\\ consequence that:

			\begin{itemize}
				\item If $a = 0$ then $e^{-n}\sum\limits_{k=0}^{n} \frac{n^k}{k!} = P(\frac{S_n - n}{\sqrt{n}} \leq 0) \to \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^0 e^{\frac{-t^2}{2}}\df t = \frac{1}{2}$.
				\item If $a = -x$ then $e^{-n}\hspace{-0.8em}\sum\limits_{k=0}^{\lfloor n - x\sqrt{n}\rfloor} \frac{n^k}{k!} = P(\frac{S_n - n}{\sqrt{n}} \leq -x) \to \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{-x} e^{\frac{-t^2}{2}}\df t$.
			\end{itemize}

			In turn, as $e^{-n}\sum\limits_{k=n+1}^\infty \frac{n^k}{k!} = 1 - e^{-n}\sum\limits_{k=0}^{n} \frac{n^k}{k!}$ we can also conclude that:

			{\centering $e^{-n}\sum\limits_{k=n+1}^\infty \frac{n^k}{k!} \to \frac{1}{2}$ as $n \to \infty$\retTwo\par}

			Similarly, we can conclude that:
			
			{\centering$\sum\limits_{\lfloor n - x\sqrt{n}\rfloor + 1}^n e^{-n}\frac{n^k}{k!} \to \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-x}^0 e^{\frac{-t^2}{2}}\df t = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_0^x e^{\frac{-t^2}{2}}\df t$ as $n \to \infty$ \retTwo\par}

			To finish off, note that $\lfloor n - x\sqrt{n}\rfloor + 1 = \lceil n - x\sqrt{n} \rceil$ iff $n - x\sqrt{n} \notin \mathbb{Z}$, and that happens iff $x\sqrt{n} \notin \mathbb{Z}$. Thus, so long as $x \notin \bigcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\mathbb{Z}$ (where the latter is a countable and thus null subset of $\mathbb{R}$), we have finished proving that $F_n(x) \to F(x)$ as $n \to \infty$.\retTwo
		\end{myIndent}
	\end{myIndent}

	\item[(c)] $\int t^2 \df P_{Y_n}(t) = E(Y_n^2) \leq 1$ for all $n$.
	\begin{myIndent}\HexOne
		Proof:\\
		To start off, note that $0 \leq Y_n^2 \leq (\frac{n - S_n}{\sqrt{n}})^2 = \frac{(S_n - n)^2}{n}$. As a result, we can say that\newpage $E(Y_n^2) \leq \frac{1}{n}E((S_n - n)^2)$. Yet now note that since $S_n$ has a Poisson distribution with mean $n$, we have that $E((S_n - n)^2)$ is equal to the variance of $S_n$ (which will also equal $n$). So, $\frac{(S_n - n)^2}{n} = \frac{n}{n} = 1$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	\item[(d)] Conclude \udefine{Stirling's approximation} that $\lim\limits_{n \to \infty} \frac{n^n\sqrt{2\pi n}}{n!e^n} \to 1$.
	\begin{myIndent}\HexOne
		Proof:\\
		Recall the moment convergence theorem on \inLinkRap{placeholder}{pages 198-199}. By parts (b) and (c) of this problem in addition to that theorem, we are able to conclude that:

		{\centering $E(Y_n) \to E(\frac{1}{2}\delta_0 + \chi_{[0, \infty)}\nu_0^1)$ as $n \to \infty$.\retTwo\par}

		But now by part (a) we know that $E(Y_n) = \frac{n^n \sqrt{n}}{n! e^n}$. Meanwhile:

		{\centering $E(\frac{1}{2}\delta_0 + \chi_{[0, \infty)}\nu_0^1) = \int_0^\infty \frac{t}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{\frac{-t^2}{2}}\df t = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_0^\infty e^{-u}\df u = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}$ \retTwo\par}

		So, $\frac{n^n \sqrt{n}}{n! e^n} \to \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}$ as $n \to \infty$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
\end{enumerate}

\hTwo Finally, I'm ready for the big result I wanted to show.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Theorem:} Suppose $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is an open set and $u: U \to \mathbb{R}$ is a harmonic function. Then $u$ is analytic on $U$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	If $x_0 \in U$ then set $r = \frac{1}{4}\inf\limits_{y \in U^\comp}|x_0 - y|$.\retTwo
	
	Importantly for all $x \in B_r(x_0)$ we have that $B_{r}(x) \subseteq B_{2r}(x_0)$ and also that the closure of $B_{2r}(x_0)$ is contained in $U$. Now let $M > 0$ be such that $|u(x)| \leq M$ for all $x \in \overline{B_{2r}(x_0)}$. By the theorem on \inLinkRap{Math 231a Theorem page 1188}{pages 1188-1189}, we know for any multi-index $\alpha$ that:
	
	{\centering$\|\partial^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(B_r(x_0))} \leq \frac{(2^{n+1}n)^{|\alpha|}|\alpha|^{|\alpha|}}{\alpha(n)r^{n + |\alpha|}}\sup\limits_{x \in B_r(x_0)}\|u\|_{L^1(B_r(x))} \leq M\frac{(2^{n+1}n)^{|\alpha|}|\alpha|^{|\alpha|}}{r^{|\alpha|}}$\\ [6pt]\par}

	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		(Here when $|\alpha| = 0$ I'm interpretting $0^0 = 1$.)\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Next, by Stirling's approximation we know there is a constant $C > 0$ such that\\ $|\alpha|^{|\alpha|} \leq Ce^{|\alpha|}|\alpha|!$ for all multi-indices $\alpha$.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		(Actually fuck I'm realizing the professor is massively over complicating this. By\\ looking at a series representation of $e^{|\alpha|}$ we can always see that $\frac{|\alpha|^{|\alpha|}}{|\alpha|!} \leq e^{|\alpha|}$. So, literally the constant $C = 1$ works.)\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	So, we have that $\|\partial^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(B_r(x_0))} \leq M\left(\frac{2^{n+1} n e}{r}\right)^{|\alpha|}|\alpha|!$\retTwo

	For one more bound, note that $n^k = \sum\limits_{|\alpha| = k} \frac{|\alpha|!}{\alpha!}$. So, we can conclude $|\alpha|! \leq \alpha! n^{|\alpha|}$ and in\\ [-6pt] turn that:
	
	{\centering$\|\partial^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(B_r(x_0))} \leq M\left(\frac{2^{n+1} n^2 e}{r}\right)^{|\alpha|}\alpha!$.\newpage\par}

	Based on that, I shall now only consider $x$ such that $|x - x_0| < \frac{r}{2^{n+2} n^3 e}$.\retTwo

	Consider the $N$th remainder formula $R_N(x) = u(x) - \sum\limits_{|\alpha| \leq N - 1} \frac{\partial^\alpha u(x_0)}{\alpha!}(x - x_0)^\alpha$.\retTwo

	By using Taylor's theorem from math 140b, we can show for any fixed $x \in B_r(x_0)$ that there exists some $t \in (0, 1)$ such that:

	{\centering $R_N(x) = \sum\limits_{|\alpha| = N}\frac{\partial^{\alpha} u(x_0 + t(x - x_0))}{\alpha!}(x - x_0)^\alpha$\retTwo\par}

	In turn, if $|x - x_0| < \frac{r}{2^{n+2} n^3 e}$ then:

	{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
		$|R_N(x)| \leq M\sum\limits_{|\alpha| = N} \left(\frac{2^{n+1}n^2e}{r}\right)^N \left(\frac{r}{2^{n + 2}n^3 e}\right)^N$\\ [12pt]
		$\phantom{|R_N(x)|} = \frac{M}{(2n)^N}\sum\limits_{|\alpha| = N}1 = \frac{M}{2^N} \to 0$ as $N \to \infty$. $\blacksquare$
	\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}
\end{myIndent}

\myComment One last comment I'd like to make is that in the $n = 1$ case every harmonic function has the form $u(x) = ax + b$. So harmonic functions on the real number line aren't that interesting and that's why I've been avoiding talking about them.\retTwo

\hTwo\mySepTwo

\blect{Math 250A Homework:}\\

\Hstatement\blab{Set 1 Problem 3:} Firstly some notes on notation. Oprea denotes a "presheaf of sets" on a\\ topological space $X$ (i.e. a functor $\mathcal{F}: \mcateg{Op}(X)^\mathrm{op} \to \mcateg{Set}$) by "$\mathcal{F} \to X$". Also Oprea denotes the restriction homomorphism $\mathcal{F}(U) \to \mathcal{F}(V)$ by $r_{UV}$.
\begin{itemize}
	\item[(ii)] Suppose $M$ is a smooth manifold with at least $2$ points, $\mathcal{F} \to M$ is the presheaf given by the assignment $\mathcal{F}(U) = \{\text{ constant functions on }U\}$ for all open sets $U$, and the restriction maps are given by domain restrictions. This $\mathcal{F}$ is called the \udefine{presheaf of constant functions}. Show that $\mathcal{F}$ is \textit{not} a sheaf.
	\begin{myIndent}\HexOne
		Since $M$ is Hausdorff with two distinct points, we can find disjoint open sets $U_1$ and $U_2$. And now we let $U \coloneqq U_1 \cup U_2$. Now if $c_1$ and $c_2$ are distinct constants and $f: U_1 \to \{c_1\}$ and $f_2: U_2 \to \{c_2\}$ are functions, automatically we have that $f_1|_{U_1 \cap U_2} = f_2|_{U_1 \cap U_2}$ since $U_1 \cap U_2 = \emptyset$. Yet there is no constant function $f$ on $U$ such that $f|_{U_1} = f_1$ and $f|_{U_2} = f_2$ simultaneously.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	\item[(iii)] Suppose $X$ is a topological space and  $\mathcal{F} \to X$ and $\mathcal{G} \to X$ are sheaves. A morphism $f: \mathcal{F} \to \mathcal{G}$ between sheaves is just a natural transformation between $\mathcal{F}$ and $\mathcal{G}$.\retTwo
	
	Prove that for any $p \in X$, the morphism $f: \mathcal{F} \to \mathcal{G}$ induces a morphism $f_p: \mathcal{F}_p \to \mathcal{G}_p$ between stalks.
	\begin{myIndent}\HexOne
		Given any germ (Oprea denotes as $(s, U)$) in $\mathcal{F}_p$ I define $f_p((s, U)) = (f_U(s), U)$.I claim this is a well-defined function. After all, suppose $(s, U) = (t, V)$ as germs. Thus, there exists an open set $W \subseteq U \cap V$ such that $r_{UW}(s) = r_{VW}(t)$. And now we have that:
		
		{\centering$r_{UW}(f_U(s)) = f_W(r_{UW}(s)) = f_W(r_{VW}(t)) = r_{VW}(f_V(t))$.\newpage\par}

		So, $(f_U(s), U) = (f_V(t), V)$.
		
		\begin{myIndent}\myComment
			Note: If $\mathcal{F}$ and $\mathcal{G}$ are abelian group valued or $R$-module valued or $R$-algebra valued, clearly $f_p$ will preserve the group/ring/module structure of $\mathcal{F}_p$ and $\mathcal{G}_p$.\retTwo
		\end{myIndent}
	\end{myIndent}

	\item[(iv)] Now we say a \udefine{sheaf of continuous functions} on a topological space $X$ is a sheaf $\mathcal{F} \to X$ such that $\mathcal{F}(U)$ is a subset of $C(U, \mathbb{R})$ for every open set $U$ and $r_{UV}(f: U \to \mathbb{R})$ is given by restricting the domain of $f$ to $V$.\retTwo
	
	A topological space $X$ together with a sheaf of continuous functions is called a \udefine{ringed space}. A \udefine{morphism of ringed spaces} $f: (X, \mathcal{F}) \to (Y, \mathcal{G})$ is a continuous map $f: X \to Y$ such that if $V \subseteq Y$ is open and $\phi \in \mathcal{G}(V)$ is a section, then the $\phi \circ f \in \mathcal{F}(f^{-1}(V))$.\retTwo
	
	How would you define an isomorphism of ringed spaces?
	\begin{myIndent}\HexOne
		This took me four hours to think about and understand the definitions, and I'm\\ probably not going to finish my homework because of this :\lparen. Oh well.\retTwo

		We can easily see that the identity map on $X$ is always a morphism of ringed spaces.\\ (In fact it is the identity morphism). Thus, the obvious starting point is that\\ $f: (X, \mathcal{F}) \to (Y, \mathcal{G})$ will be an isomorphism iff there exists a morphism of ringed\\ spaces $g: (Y, \mathcal{G}) \to (X, \mathcal{F})$ such that $f \circ g = \myId_Y$ and $g \circ f = \myId_X$. I'd like to get a better (actually testable) statement of a definition though.\retTwo

		Clearly $f$ and $g$ are inverse homeomorphisms. Also, I claim that if $\phi \in C(V)$\\ where $V \subseteq Y$ is open, then $\phi \in \mathcal{G}(V)$ iff $\phi \circ f \in \mathcal{F}(f^{-1}(V))$.
		\begin{myIndent}\HexTwoP
			Why?\\
			We know by the definition of a morphism of ringed spaces that if\\ $\phi \in \mathcal{G}(V)$ then $\phi \circ f \in \mathcal{F}(f^{-1}(V))$. As for the other implication, note\\ that if $\phi \circ f \in \mathcal{F}(f^{-1}(V))$ then we know by definition of a morphism of\\ ringed spaces that $\phi = \phi \circ f \circ g$ is in $\mathcal{G}(V)$.\retTwo
		\end{myIndent}

		Based on the prior reasoning, we now have a necessary condition for $f$ to be an\\ isomorphism of ringed spaces. I'd also like to show this condition is sufficient.
		\begin{myIndent}\HexTwoP
			Suppose $(X, \mathcal{F})$ and $(Y, \mathcal{G})$ are ringed spaces and $f: X \to Y$ is a\\ homeomorphism such that for any open set $V \subseteq Y$, $\phi \in \mathcal{G}(V)$ iff\\ $\phi \circ f \in \mathcal{F}(f^{-1}(V))$. nmWe can see that if $U \subseteq X$ is open and $\phi \in \mathcal{F}(U)$, then $\phi \circ f^{-1} \in \mathcal{G}(f(U))$ because we know $(\phi \circ f^{-1}) \circ f \in \mathcal{F}(f^{-1}(f(U))) = \mathcal{F}(U)$. So, $f^{-1}$ is a morphism of ringed spaces.\retTwo
		\end{myIndent}

		So all in all, we say an \udefine{isomorphism of ringed spaces} $f: (X, \mathcal{F}) \to (Y, \mathcal{G})$ is a\\ homeomorphism $f: X \to Y$ such that for any open set $V \subseteq Y$, $\phi \in \mathcal{G}(V)$ iff $\phi \circ f \in \mathcal{F}(f^{-1}(V))$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Note that if $(X, \mathcal{F})$ is a ringed space then $U$ is also a ringed space when equipped with the restriction of sheaf $\mathcal{F}$ to just the open sets $V \subseteq U$. 
	\begin{myIndent}\HexOne
		(Hopefully this is obvious\dots)\newpage
	\end{myIndent}
	
	Also note the inclusion map $\iota: U \hookrightarrow M$ is a morphism of ringed spaces.
	\begin{myIndent}\HexOne
		Why?\\ 
		If $V \subseteq X$ is an open set then $\iota^{-1}(V) = V \cap U$. But also note that if $\phi \in \mathcal{F}(V)$ then we know that $\phi \circ \iota|_{V \cap U} = \phi|_{V \cap U} \in \mathcal{F}(V \cap U)$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
\end{itemize}

Now observe that any $C^r$ manifold $M$ is a ringed space when the sheaf of $C^r$ functions (denoted $\mathscr{C}^r_M$.)\retTwo

\ul{Theorem:} If $M$ is an $n$-dimensional $C^r$ manifold then the ringed space $(M, \mathscr{C}_M^r)$ is locally\\ isomorphic to an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ or $[0, \infty)^k \times \mathbb{R}^{n - k}$ (where $k < n$) equipped\\ with the sheaf of $C^r$ functions. 
\begin{myDindent}\color{BrickRed} 
	In other words, for every $p \in M$ there is an open set $U \subseteq M$ containing $p$ and an open set $V \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ or $[0, \infty)^k \times \mathbb{R}^{n - k}$ (where $k < n$) such that $(U, \mathscr{C}_U^r)$ and $(V, \mathscr{C}_V^r)$ are isomorphic as ringed spaces.\retTwo
\end{myDindent}
\begin{myIndent}\HexOne 
	Proof:\\
	Given any $p \in M$ we can pick a smooth chart $(U, \varphi)$ on $M$ containing $p$. Also we let $V = \varphi(U)$. I claim that $\varphi$ is a ringed space isomorphism between $(U, \mathscr{C}_U^r)$ and $(V, \mathscr{C}_V^r)$. After all, clearly $\varphi: U \to V$ is a homeomorphism. Also suppose $W \subseteq V$ is an open set and $f \in C(W, \mathbb{R})$
	\begin{myIndent}\HexTwoP 
		If $f \in C^r(W, \mathbb{R})$ then $f \circ \varphi \in C^r(\varphi^{-1}(W), \mathbb{R})$ since $(f \circ \varphi) \circ \varphi^{-1} = f$ is a $C^r$ map from $W = \varphi(\varphi^{-1}(W))$ to $\mathbb{R}$.\retTwo

		Conversely, suppose $f \circ \varphi \in C^r(\varphi^{-1}(W), \mathbb{R})$. Then by definition we know that $f = (f \circ \varphi) \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is a $C^r$ map from $W = \varphi(\varphi^{-1}(W))$ to $\mathbb{R}$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
\end{myIndent}

Conversely, given any ringed space $(M, \mathcalli{S})$ that is Hausdorff, second countable, and locally\\ isomorphic to an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ or $[0, \infty)^k \times \mathbb{R}^{n - k}$ (where $k \leq n)$ equipped with the\\ sheaf of $C^r$ functions, we have that there is a unique $C^r$ structure $\mathcal{A}$ on $M$ turning $M$\\ into a $C^r$ manifold with $\mathcalli{S} = \mathscr{C}_M^r$ when $M$ is equipped with $\mathcal{A}$.
\begin{myIndent}\HexOne 
	Proof:\\
	Hopefully it is obvious that $M$ is a topological $n$-dimensional manifold. Also given any\\ $p \in M$ let $(U_p, \varphi_p)$ be a coordinate chart containing $p$ with $\varphi_p: (U_p, \mathcalli{S}) \to (V_p, \mathscr{C}^r_{V_p})$ a ringed space isomorphism.\retTwo

	Firstly I claim the collection $\mathcal{U} \coloneqq \{(U_p, \varphi_p)\}_{p \in M}$ are all $C^r$ compatible with each other.
	\begin{myIndent}\HexTwoP
		To see why, let $p, q \in M$ be distinct points such that $U_p \cap U_q \neq \emptyset$. We'll write $\varphi_p(m) = (x_1(m), \ldots, x_n(m))$ for all $m \in U_p$. And now in order to prove that $\varphi_p \circ \varphi_q^{-1}|_{\varphi_q(U_p \cap U_q)}$ is a $C^r$ map it suffices to show to show that each component function $x_i \circ \varphi_q^{-1}|_{\varphi_q(U_p \cap U_q)}$ is a $C^r$ map.\retTwo
		
		Note that $\myId_{V_p} \in C^r(V_p, \mathbb{R}^n)$ implies that $\mathrm{Proj}_i \circ \varphi_p = x_i \in \mathcalli{S}(\varphi_p^{-1}(V_p)) = \mathcalli{S}(U_p)$. And then by applying a restriction map, we get that $x_i|_{U_p \cap U_q} \in \mathcalli{S}(U_p \cap U_q)$. Next, because $\varphi_q^{-1}$ is a ringed isomorphism from $(V_q, \mathscr{C}_{V_q}^r)$ to $(U_q, \mathcalli{S})$, we must have that:
		
		{\centering$x_i|_{U_p \cap U_q} \circ \varphi_q^{-1}|_{\varphi_q(U_p \cap U_q)} = x_i \circ \varphi_q^{-1}|_{\varphi_q(U_p \cap U_q)}$ is a $C^r$ map.\retTwo\par}
	\end{myIndent}

	Secondly, I claim that if $M$ is equipped with any $C^r$ structure $\mathcal{A}$ turning $M$ into a $C^r$\\ manifold with $\mathcalli{S} = \mathscr{C}_M^r$ then we must have that $\mathcal{U} \subseteq \mathcal{A}$. (This will prove uniqueness since there is only one maximal atlas containing $\mathcal{U}$.)\newpage
	\begin{myIndent}\HexTwoP
		To see why, let $(W, \psi)$ be any chart in $\mathcal{A}$ and then consider any chart $(U_p, \varphi_p)$ in $\mathcal{U}$. We need to show that these two charts are $C^r$ compatible. After all, since $(W, \psi)$ is arbitrary this will tell us that $(U_p, \varphi_p) \in \mathcal{A}$.\retTwo

		Fortunately, by the reasoning in the proof of the first part of this theorem\\ (see the prior page), we know that $\psi$ is a ringed space isomorphism between\\ $(W, \mathscr{C}_W^r = \mathcalli{S})$ and $(\psi(W), \mathscr{C}_{\psi(W)}^r)$. Hence, we can now apply similar reasoning as in the proof that $\mathcal{U}$ is a $C^r$ atlas to prove that $(W, \psi)$ and $(U_p, \varphi_p)$ are $C^r$ compatible.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Thirdly, I claim that if $M$ is equipped with the $C^r$ structure generated by $\mathcal{U}$ then $\mathcalli{S} = \mathscr{C}_M^r$.
	\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
		To see why, let $W \subseteq M$ be any open set and first suppose $f \in \mathcalli{S}(W)$.\\ For any $p \in W$ there is a smooth chart $(U_p, \varphi_p) \in \mathcal{U}$ containing $p$. In turn,\\ $(W \cap U_p, \varphi_p|_{W \cap U_p})$ is also a smooth chart. But also note $f|_{W \cap U_p} \in \mathcalli{S}(W \cap U_p)$.\\ In turn, as $\varphi_p$ is a ringed space isomorphism we know that:
		
		{\centering$f \circ \varphi_p^{-1}|_{\varphi_p(W \cap U_p)} \in C^r(\varphi_p(W \cap U_p), \mathbb{R})$.\retTwo\par}
		
		Since every $p \in W$ has a smooth chart $(U^\prime, \varphi^\prime)$ satisfying that $p \in U^\prime \subseteq W$\\ and $f \circ (\varphi^\prime)^{-1}$ is a $C^r$ map, we can thus conclude that $f \in \mathscr{C}_M^r(W)$.\retTwo

		Conversely, suppose $f \in \mathscr{C}_M^r(W)$. Then as $(W \cap U_p, \varphi_p|_{W \cap U_p})$ is a smooth chart\\ for every $p$, we know that $f \circ \varphi_p^{-1} \in C^r(\varphi(W \cap U_p), \mathbb{R})$ for every $p \in W$. Then in turn, as $\varphi$ is a ringed space isomorphism we can conclude that $f|_{W \cap U_p} \in \mathcalli{S}(W \cap U_p)$ for every $p \in W$. Finally, as $\mathcalli{S}$ is a sheaf and $\bigcup_{p \in W}(W \cap U_p) = W$, we can conclude that $f \in \mathcalli{S}(W)$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
\end{myIndent}

The T.L.D.R. to the prior theorem is that we can equivalently consider a $C^r$ manifold to be a ringed space. This approach has advantages because it generalizes to weirder spaces. (In fact Wells in \textit{Differential Analysis on Complex Manifolds} [see \inLinkRap{Ninth Citation}{citation 9}] actually defines the $C^r$ structure of a manifold to be a sheaf of a ringed space as opposed to a maximal atlas.)\retTwo

\ul{Theorem:} Suppose $M$ and $N$ are both $C^r$ manifolds equipped with the sheafs $\mathscr{C}_M^r$ and $\mathscr{C}_N^r$\\ respectively. Then $F: M \to N$ is a ringed space isomorphism from $(M, \mathscr{C}_M^r)$ to $(N, \mathscr{C}_N^r)$ if\\ and only if $f$ is a $C^r$ map.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	$(\Longrightarrow)$\\
	Let $p \in M$ be any point and let $(V, \psi)$ be a chart on $N$ containing $F(p)$. We'll write $\psi(q) = (y_1(q), \ldots, y_n(q))$ for all $q \in V$. Next, because $F$ is continuous, we know that $F^{-1}(V)$ is an open set containing $p$. So, we can find a smooth chart $(U, \varphi)$ on $M$ such that $p \in U \subseteq F^{-1}(V)$. and now as $F$ and $\varphi^{-1}$ are both ringed homomorphisms, we know that $y_i \in C^r(V, \mathbb{R})$ implies that $y_i \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1} \in C^r(\varphi(U), \mathbb{R})$ for each $i$. In turn, $\psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is a $C^r$ map.\retTwo

	$(\Longleftarrow)$\\
	Suppose $V \subseteq N$ is any open set and $f \in C^r(V, \mathbb{R})$. Then $f \circ F \in C^r(F^{-1}(V), \mathbb{R})$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\begin{myIndent}\mySepThree\end{myIndent}

\hTwo Before doing more homework, I want to take some notes. These will be a mix of lecture notes (by Oprea) and notes from John Lee \textit{Smooth Manifolds}.\newpage

Firstly, I want to study more about vector bundles. For a reminder on them, look at \inLinkRap{Page 1129 reference}{pages 1129-1133}.\retTwo

Note that $\GL_k(\mathbb{R})$ is an open submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^{k^2}$ and hence it makes sense to talk about $C^r$ maps from a $C^r$ manifold $M$ to $\GL_k(\mathbb{R})$.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Proposition 10.5:} Let $\pi: E \to M$ be a $C^r$ vector bundle of rank $k$ over $M$ (where $r \geq 0$). Suppose $\Phi: \pi^{-1}(U) \to U \times \mathbb{R}^k$ and $\Psi: \pi^{-1}(V) \to V \times \mathbb{R}^k$ are two $C^r$ local trivializations of $E$ with $U \cap V \neq \emptyset$. Then there exists a $C^r$ map $\tau: U \cap V \to \GL_k(\mathbb{R})$ such that the composition $\Phi \circ \Psi^{-1}: (U \cap V) \times \mathbb{R}^k \to (U \cap V) \times \mathbb{R}^k$ has the form:

{\centering$\Phi \circ \Psi^{-1}(p, v) = (p, \tau(p)v)$.\retTwo\par}

\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Let $\pi_1: (U \cap V) \times \mathbb{R}^k \to (U \cap V)$ be the projection map. Then we have the following commuting diagram:
	% https://q.uiver.app/#
	\[\begin{tikzcd}
		{(U \cap V)\times \mathbb{R}^k} & {\pi^{-1}(U \cap V)} & {(U \cap V) \times \mathbb{R}^k} \\
		& {U\cap V}
		\arrow["{\pi_1}"', from=1-1, to=2-2]
		\arrow["\sim"{description}, shift left=2, draw=none, from=1-2, to=1-1]
		\arrow["\Psi"', from=1-2, to=1-1]
		\arrow["\Phi", from=1-2, to=1-3]
		\arrow["\sim"{description}, shift right=2, draw=none, from=1-2, to=1-3]
		\arrow["\pi"', from=1-2, to=2-2]
		\arrow["{\pi_1}", from=1-3, to=2-2]
	\end{tikzcd}\]

	In other words, we can see that $\pi_1 \circ (\Phi \circ \Psi^{-1}) = \pi_1$. And this is enough to guarentee that $(\Phi \circ \Psi^{-1})(p, v) = (p, \sigma(v))$ for some $C^r$ function $\sigma: (U \cap V) \times \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}^k$.\retTwo

	Next because $\Phi, \Psi$ are vector space isomorphisms from $\pi^{-1}(\{p\})$ to $\{p\} \times \mathbb{R}^k$ for every $p \in U \cap V$, we know for every $p \in U \cap V$ that there is a matrix $\tau(p) \in \GL_k(\mathbb{R})$ such that $\sigma(p, v) = \tau(p)v$.\retTwo

	Finally, to prove that the map $\tau: U \cap V \to \GL_k(\mathbb{R})$ is a $C^r$ map, let $e_1, \ldots, e_k$ be the standard basis for $\mathbb{R}^k$. Also let us write $\tau(p) = |c_1(p), \ldots, c_k(p){\rangle}$ where each $c_i(p)$ is the $i$th column of the matrix $\tau(p)$. To show that $\tau$ is a $C^r$ map we equivalently need to show that each $c_i: U \cap V \to \mathbb{R}^k$ is a $C^r$ map. Fortunately, this is as easy as noting that $c_i(p) = \sigma(p, e_i)$ is a $C^r$ map. $\blacksquare$\retTwo

	\begin{myIndent}\myComment
		Remark: The function $\tau: U \cap V \to \GL_k(\mathbb{R})$ is called a \udefine{transition function}\\ between local trivializations $\Phi$ and $\Psi$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
\end{myIndent}

\Hstatement\blab{Problem 10-5:} Let $\pi: E \to M$ be a $C^r$ vector bundle of rank $k$ over $M$ (where $r \geq 0)$. Also suppose $\Phi_\alpha: \pi^{-1}(U_\alpha) \to U_\alpha \times \mathbb{R}^k$, $\Phi_\beta: \pi^{-1}(U_\beta) \to U_\beta \times \mathbb{R}^k$, and $\Phi_\gamma: \pi^{-1}(U_\gamma) \to U_\gamma \times \mathbb{R}^k$ are three $C^r$ local trivializations of $E$ with $U_\alpha \cap U_\beta \cap U_\gamma \neq \emptyset$. Let $\tau_{\alpha, \beta}$, $\tau_{\beta, \gamma}$ and $\tau_{\alpha, \gamma}$ be transition functions from the former trivialization in the subscript to the latter. Then $\tau_{\beta, \gamma} \circ \tau_{\alpha, \beta} = \tau_{\alpha, \gamma}$.
\begin{myIndent}\HexOne
	Proof:\\
	Let $W \coloneqq U_\alpha \cap U_\beta \cap U_\gamma$. Then we have the following commuting diagram:\\ [-24pt]
	% https://q.uiver.app/#
	\[\begin{tikzcd}
		{} && {} && {} \\
		{W \times \mathbb{R}^k} && {W \times \mathbb{R}^k} && {W \times \mathbb{R}^k} \\
		\\
		{} &&&& {}
		\arrow[""{name=0, anchor=center, inner sep=0}, "{(p, v)}"{description}, color={rgb,255:red,92;green,92;blue,214}, draw=none, from=2-1, to=1-1]
		\arrow["{\Phi_\beta \circ \Phi_\alpha^{-1}}", from=2-1, to=2-3]
		\arrow["{\Phi_\gamma \circ \Phi_\alpha^{-1}}"', curve={height=12pt}, from=2-1, to=2-5]
		\arrow[""{name=1, anchor=center, inner sep=0}, "{(p, v)}"{description}, color={rgb,255:red,92;green,92;blue,214}, draw=none, from=2-1, to=4-1]
		\arrow[""{name=2, anchor=center, inner sep=0}, "{(p, \tau_{\alpha,\beta}(p)v)}"{description}, color={rgb,255:red,92;green,92;blue,214}, draw=none, from=2-3, to=1-3]
		\arrow["{\Phi_\gamma \circ \Phi_{\beta}^{-1}}", from=2-3, to=2-5]
		\arrow[""{name=3, anchor=center, inner sep=0}, "{(p, \tau_{\beta, \gamma}(p)\tau_{\alpha, \beta}(p)v) }"{description}, color={rgb,255:red,92;green,92;blue,214}, draw=none, from=2-5, to=1-5]
		\arrow[""{name=4, anchor=center, inner sep=0}, "{(p, \tau_{\alpha, \gamma}(p)v)}"{description}, color={rgb,255:red,92;green,92;blue,214}, draw=none, from=2-5, to=4-5]
		\arrow[color={rgb,255:red,92;green,92;blue,214}, between={0.2}{0.7}, maps to, from=0, to=2]
		\arrow[color={rgb,255:red,92;green,92;blue,214}, between={0.1}{0.8}, maps to, from=1, to=4]
		\arrow[color={rgb,255:red,92;green,92;blue,214}, between={0.3}{0.6}, maps to, from=2, to=3]
	\end{tikzcd}\]\newpage

	Thus for all $p \in W$ and $v \in \mathbb{R}^k$, we have that $\tau_{\beta, \gamma}(p) \tau_{\alpha, \beta}(p)v = \tau_{\alpha, \gamma}(p)v$. Since\\ matrices are uniquely determined by where they send all $v \in \mathbb{R}^k$, we can conclude\\ that $\tau_{\beta, \gamma} \circ \tau_{\alpha, \beta}(p) = \tau_{\alpha, \gamma}(p)$ for all $p \in W$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo Now it would be particularly helpful to have a general theorem for being to able construct vector bundles, especially as there are vector bundles other than the tangent bundle of a manifold that we care about.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Lemma 10.6:} \hypertarget{Lemma 10.6 page 1198}{Let} $M$ be a $C^r$ manifold and suppose for each $p \in M$ we are given a real $k$-dimensional vector space $E_p$. Let $E = \coprod_{p \in M} E_p$ and let $\pi: E \to M$ be the map that takes each element of $E_p$ to the point $p$. Furthermore, suppose that we given:
\begin{enumerate}
	\item[(i)] an open cover $\{U_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ of $M$;
	\item[(ii)] for each $\alpha \in A$ a bijective map $\Phi_{\alpha} : \pi^{-1}(U_\alpha) \to U_\alpha \times \mathbb{R}^k$ whose restriction to each $E_p$ is a vector space isomorphism from $E_p$ to $\{p\} \times \mathbb{R}^k \cong \mathbb{R}^k$;
	\item[(iii)] For every $\alpha, \beta \in A$ with $U_\alpha \cap U_\beta \neq \emptyset$ a $C^r$ map $\tau_{\alpha,\beta} : U_\alpha \cap U_\beta \to \GL_k(\mathbb{R})$ such that the map $\Phi_\beta \circ \Phi_\alpha^{-1}$ from $(U_\alpha \cap U_\beta) \times \mathbb{R}^k$ to itself has the form:
	
	{\centering $\Phi_\beta \circ \Phi_\alpha^{-1}(p, v) = (p, \tau_{\alpha, \beta}(p)v)$. \retTwo\par}
\end{enumerate}

Then $E$ has a unique topology and $C^r$ structure making it into a $C^r$ manifold and a $C^r$ rank $k$ vector bundle over $M$ with $\pi$ as it's projection and $\{(U_\alpha, \Phi_\alpha)\}_{\alpha \in A}$ all as $C^r$ local trivializations.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Let $\{(V_\beta, \varphi_\beta)\}_{\beta \in B}$ be the collection of smooth charts on $M$ such that $V_\beta$ is contained\\ in some open set $U_\alpha$. Let $\widehat{V_\beta} = \varphi_\beta(V_\beta)$. Then for each $\beta$ we can define a map\\ $\widetilde{\varphi_\beta}: \pi^{-1}(V_\beta) \to \widehat{V_\beta} \times \mathbb{R}^k$ by $\widetilde{\varphi_\beta} = (\varphi_\beta \times \myId_{\mathbb{R}^k}) \circ \Phi_\alpha$ (where $\alpha$ is some fixed element\\ such that $V_\beta \subseteq U_\alpha$).\retTwo

	We shall show that the charts $\{(\pi^{-1}(V_\beta), \widetilde{\varphi_\beta})\}_{\beta \in B}$ satisfy the conditions of lemma 1.35 on \inLinkRap{Lemma 1.35 page 1130}{pages 1130-1132}. Hence, $E$ has a unique topology and $C^r$ structure such that $E$ is a $C^r$ manifold and all those charts are smooth charts on $E$.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		Requirement (i) holds since each $\widetilde{\varphi_\beta}$ is a composition of two bijections and whose image $\widehat{V_\beta} \times \mathbb{R}^k$ is an open subset of $[0, \infty)^\ell \times \mathbb{R}^{n - \ell + k}$ for some $0 \leq \ell \leq n$.\retTwo

		Similarly, to see requirement (ii) note for every $\beta_1, \beta_2 \in B$ that:
		
		{\centering$\widetilde{\varphi_{\beta_1}}(\pi^{-1}(V_{\beta_1}) \cap \pi^{-1}(V_{\beta_2})) = \varphi_p(V_{\beta_1} \cap V_{\beta_2}) \times \mathbb{R}^k$ is an open subset of $\widehat{V_{\beta_1}} \times \mathbb{R}^k$.\retTwo\par}
		
		To see requirement (iii), note for any $\beta_1, \beta_2 \in B$ with $V_{\beta_1} \cap V_{\beta_2} \neq \emptyset$ that there exists $\alpha_1, \alpha_2 \in A$ with:
		
		{\centering$\widetilde{\varphi_{\beta_2}} \circ \widetilde{\varphi_{\beta_1}}^{-1} = (\varphi_{\beta_2} \times \myId_{\mathbb{R}^k}) \circ (\Phi_{\alpha_2} \circ \Phi_{\alpha_1}^{-1}) \circ (\varphi_{\beta_1}^{-1} \times \myId_{\mathbb{R}^k})$\retTwo\par}

		The functions being composed on the right side though are $C^r$ diffeomorphisms. So,\\ $\widetilde{\varphi_{\beta_2}} \circ \widetilde{\varphi_{\beta_1}}^{-1}: \varphi_{\beta_1}(V_{\beta_1} \cap V_{\beta_2}) \times \mathbb{R}^k \to \varphi_{\beta_2}(V_{\beta_1} \cap V_{\beta_2}) \times \mathbb{R}^k$ is a $C^r$ diffeomorphism.\retTwo

		Requirement (iv) follows from the fact that we can cover $M$ with countably many of the sets $V_\beta$ (since $M$ is second countable).\retTwo

		Finally, to see requirement (v) first note that if $\xi, \zeta \in E$ both lie in some common $E_p$ then they are obviously contained in a single common chart. Meanwhile if\\ $\xi \in E_p$ and $\zeta \in E_q$ where $p, q$ are distinct, then we can find disjoint smooth charts $(V_{\beta_p}, \varphi_{\beta_p})$ and $(V_{\beta_q}, \varphi_{\beta_q})$ containing $p$ and $q$ respectively.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	\hypertarget{Page 1199 reference}{Next,} I claim that $E$ is now equipped with the unique topology and $C^r$ structure such\\ that each of the $\Phi_\alpha: \pi^{-1}(U_\alpha) \to U_\alpha \times \mathbb{R}^k$ are $C^r$ diffeomorphisms.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		Firstly, note that when $E$ is equipped with this topology then $\pi^{-1}(U_\alpha)$ is an open subset of $E$ for every $\alpha$. This because if $(V, \varphi)$ is a smooth chart on $M$ such that $V \subseteq U_\alpha$ then we know by definition that $\pi^{-1}(V)$ is open in $E$. And since $\pi^{-1}(U_\alpha)$ is a union of such subsets, we know $\pi^{-1}(U_\alpha)$ is open in $E$.\retTwo

		If $E$ is equipped with the topology and $C^r$ structure we gave it, then for any $p \in U_\alpha$ we can find a smooth chart $(V, \varphi)$ on $M$ with $p \in V \subseteq U_\alpha$. With respect to the\\ smooth chart $(\pi^{-1}(V), \widetilde{\varphi} \coloneqq (\varphi \times \myId_{\mathbb{R}^k}) \circ \Phi_\alpha)$ on $E$ and $(V \times \mathbb{R}^k, \varphi \times \myId_{\mathbb{R}^k})$ on\\ $U \times \mathbb{R}^k$ we have that:

		{\centering$(\varphi \times \myId_{\mathbb{R}^k}) \circ \Phi_\alpha \circ \widetilde{\varphi}^{-1} = \myId_{\varphi(V) \times \mathbb{R}^k}$.\retTwo\par}

		This proves that each $\Phi_\alpha$ is a diffeomorphism when $E$ is equipped with the topology and smooth structure we gave it.\retTwo

		Conversely, suppose $E$ is equipped with another topology $\mathcal{T}$ and $C^r$ structure $\mathcal{A}$ still satisfying that $\Phi_\alpha$ is a $C^r$ diffeomorphism from an open set $\pi^{-1}(U_\alpha) \subseteq E$ to the set $U_\alpha \times \mathbb{R}^k$. Then $\myId_{U_\alpha} = \Phi_{\alpha}^{-1} \circ \Phi_\alpha$ will be a $C^r$ diffeomorphism from one topology and $C^r$ structure on $\pi^{-1}(U_\alpha)$ to the other. It follows that the topology and $C^r$ structure on $E$ restricted to any $\pi^{-1}(U_\alpha)$ is unique.\retTwo

		But now as the $\pi^{-1}(U_\alpha)$ cover $E$, any set $U \in \mathcal{T}$ can be written as a union of sets $U \cap U_\alpha$ which are all open in our original topology. Hence, $\mathcal{T}$ must be our original topology. Secondly, since smooth charts in each of the open submanifolds $\pi^{-1}(U_\alpha)$ which are in $\mathcal{A}$ and our original structure cover all of $M$, we know they determine a unique maximal $C^r$ atlas on $E$. Hence, $\mathcal{A}$ is our original atlas.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Thirdly, I claim $\pi: E \to M$ is a $C^r$ map.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		This is as simple as noting for any smooth chart $(V, \varphi)$ on $M$ and smooth chart $(\pi^{-1}(V), (\varphi \times \myId_{\mathbb{R}^k}) \circ \Phi_\alpha)$ on $E$ we have that the representation of $\pi$ with respect to those local coordinates is just the projection map $(x, v) \mapsto x$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Finally, the fact that $\pi: E \to M$ is a vector bundle is just a result of the latter assumptions given in (ii). $\blacksquare$
	\begin{myIndent}\myComment
		Note that if $r = 0$ then this proposition still gives a unique topology. Just no smooth structure.\newpage
	\end{myIndent}
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo It will also be helpful to establish some terminology about frames and sections of vector bundles. Firstly, if $M$ is a topological space, and $\pi: E \to M$ is a vector bundle, we say $\sigma: M \to E$ is a \udefine{section / local section of $E$} if it is a section / local section for the map $\pi$.
\begin{myIndent}\hThree
	(See \inLinkRap{Local Section Theorem page 1106}{page 1106} for a reminder on the definition of a section or local section.)\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

If we want to drop the continuity requirement of $\sigma$, then we'll say the section is \udefine{rough}.\retTwo

Also if $\pi: E \to M$ is a $C^r$ vector bundle then we shall say $\sigma$ is a "$C^r$" section if it is a $C^r$ map.\retTwo

Next, suppose $\pi: E \to M$ is a vector bundle. If $U \subseteq M$ is an open set, a $(\sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_k)$ is a $k$-tuple of local sections of $E$ over $U$ is said to be \udefine{linearly independent} if for every $p \in U$ we have that $(\sigma_1(p), \ldots, \sigma_k(p))$ forms a linearly independent $k$-tuple of vectors in $E_p$. Also $(\sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_k)$ is said to \udefine{span $E$} if $\sigma_1(p), \ldots, \sigma_k(p)$ span $E_p$ for all $p \in U$.\retTwo

A \udefine{local frame for $E$ over $U$} is an ordered $k$-tuple of local sections $(\sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_k)$ of linearly independent sections over $U$ that span $E$. It is called a \udefine{global frame} if $U = M$. Also, if every $\sigma_i$ is a $C^r$ map we say that it is a \udefine{$C^r$ frame}.\retTwo

Often, we denote a local frame by $(\sigma_i)_{1 \leq i \leq k}$.\retTwo

A key result is that there is a one-to-one correspondance between $C^r$ local frames and $C^r$ local trivializations.\\ [-8pt]
\begin{myIndent}
	\exTwo\ul{Example 10.18:} Suppose $\pi: E \to M$ is a $C^r$ vector bundle of rank $k$.\\ We let $e_1, \ldots, e_k$ denote the standard basis on $\mathbb{R}^k$. If $\Phi: \pi^{-1}(U) \to U \times \mathbb{R}^k$\\ is a $C^r$ local trivialization of $E$ then we can define maps $\sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_k: U \to E$\\ by $\sigma_i(p) = \Phi^{-1}(p, e_i) = \Phi^{-1} \circ \widetilde{e_i}(p)$ (where $\widetilde{e_i}: U \to U \times \mathbb{R}^k$ is the $C^r$ map\\ sending $p$ to $(p, e_i)$). I claim $(\sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_k)$ is a $C^r$ local frame for $E$ over $U$.
	\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
		Why?\\
		Each $\sigma_i$ is a $C^r$ map since it is a composition of $C^r$ maps. Also, note that if\\ $\pi_1 : U \times \mathbb{R}^k \to U$ is the projection map, then:
		
		{\centering$\pi \circ \sigma_i(p) = \pi \circ \Phi^{-1}(p, e_i) = \pi_1(p, e_i) = p$.\\ [4pt]\par}
		
		So, $\sigma_i$ is a local section of $E$.\retTwo

		To finish off, to show that $(\sigma_i)_{1 \leq i \leq k}$ is linearly independent and spans $E$, we can note that $\Phi$ restricts to a vector space isomorphism from $E_p$ to $\{p\} \times \mathbb{R}^k$ for all $p \in U$. Also, $\Phi(\sigma_i(p)) = (p, e_i)$. So, $\Phi$ takes the vectors $\sigma_1(p), \ldots, \sigma_k(p)$ to the standard basis on $\mathbb{R}^k$.\retTwo

		\myComment Remark: The local frame for $E$ over $U$ constructed in this example is called the \udefine{local frame associated with $\Phi$}.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	\exTwo\ul{Proposition 10.19:} Let $\pi: E \to M$ be a $C^r$ vector bundle. Every $C^r$ local frame $(\sigma_i)_{1 \leq i \leq k}$ for $E$ over an open set $U \subseteq M$ is associated with a $C^r$ local trivialization $\Phi: \pi^{-1}(U) \to U \times \mathbb{R}^k$.\newpage
	\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
		Proof:\\
		Define a map $\Psi: U \times \mathbb{R}^k \to \pi^{-1}(U)$ by $\Psi(p, (v_1, \ldots, v_k)) = \sum_{i=1}^k v_i \sigma_i(p)$.\\ (Here the right side is an element of the vector space $E_p$.)\retTwo

		Trivially, for every $p \in U$ the map $\Psi$ restricts to a linear map between $\{p\} \times \mathbb{R}^k$ and $E_p$. Also, the $\sigma_i(p)$ forming a basis for $E_p$ at every $p \in U$ guarentees that the linear map that $\Psi$ restricts to is a vector space isomorphism for all $p$. Thirdly, if $e_1, \ldots, e_k$ is the standard basis for $\mathbb{R}^k$, and if for each $i$ we define $\widetilde{e_i}: U \to U \times \mathbb{R}^k$ by $\widetilde{e_i}(p) = (p, e_i)$, then we can see that $\sigma_i = \Psi \circ \widetilde{e_i}$ for each $i$. Hence once we show that $\Psi$ is a $C^r$ diffeomorphism from $U \times \mathbb{R}^k$ to $\pi^{-1}(U)$ then we will be able to conclude that $\Psi^{-1}: \pi^{-1}(U) \to U \times \mathbb{R}^k$ is a local trivialization whose associated local frame is our original frame $(\sigma_i)_{1 \leq i \leq k}$.\retTwo

		Fortunately, because $\Psi$ is a bijection, to prove that $\Psi$ is a $C^r$ diffeomorphism it\\ suffices to prove that $\Psi$ is a local $C^r$ diffeomorphism. In particular, we know to show that there is an open cover $\{V_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ of $U$ such that $\Psi|_{V_\alpha \times \mathbb{R}^k}$ is a $C^r$ diffeomorphism for every $\alpha \in A$.
		\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
			Consider any $q \in U$. There exists an open set $V \subseteq M$ containing $q$ over which there is a $C^r$ local trivialization $\Phi: \pi^{-1}(V) \to V \times \mathbb{R}^k$. By shrinking $V$, we can without loss of generality assume $V \subseteq U$. And now if $\pi_1: V \times \mathbb{R}^k \to V$ is the projection map, we have the following commuting diagram:

			% https://q.uiver.app/#
			\[\begin{tikzcd}
				{V\times \mathbb{R}^k} && {\pi^{-1}(V)} && {V \times \mathbb{R}^k} \\
				&& V
				\arrow["{\Psi|_{V \times \mathbb{R}^k}}", from=1-1, to=1-3]
				\arrow["{\pi_1}"', from=1-1, to=2-3]
				\arrow["\Phi", from=1-3, to=1-5]
				\arrow["\sim"{description}, shift right=2, draw=none, from=1-3, to=1-5]
				\arrow["\pi", from=1-3, to=2-3]
				\arrow["{\pi_1}", from=1-5, to=2-3]
			\end{tikzcd}\]

			Note that $\Phi \circ \Psi|_{V \times \mathbb{R}^k}$ is a bijection from $V \times \mathbb{R}^k$ to itself. Since $\Phi$ is a $C^r$\\ diffeomorphism, in order to prove that $\Psi|_{V \times \mathbb{R}^k}$ is a $C^r$ diffeomorphism it\\ suffices to prove that $\Phi \circ \Psi|_{V \times \mathbb{R}^k}$ is a $C^r$ diffeomorphism.\retTwo

			To do this, note that $\Phi \circ \sigma_i|_V : V \to V \times \mathbb{R}^k$ is a $C^r$ map for each $i$. In turn, we know for every $1 \leq i, j \leq k$ that there is a $C^r$ map $\sigma_i^{(j)}: V \to \mathbb{R}$ such that:

			{\centering $\Phi \circ \sigma_i|_V(p) = \left(p, (\sigma_i^{(1)}(p), \ldots, \sigma_i^{(k)}(p))\right)$. \retTwo\par}

			But now as $\Phi: E_p \to \{p\} \times \mathbb{R}^k$ is a vector space isomorphism, we know for\\ all $p \in V$ and $(v_1, \ldots, v_k) \in \mathbb{R}^k$ that:

			{\centering $\Phi \circ \Psi(p, (v_1, \ldots, v_k)) = \Phi(\sum_{i=1}^k v_i \sigma_i(p)) = \sum_{i=1}^k v_i \Phi \circ \sigma_i(p)$ \retTwo\par}

			We can define $\tau: V \to \GL_k(\mathbb{R})$ by $\tau(p) \coloneqq \begin{bmatrix} \sigma_1^{(1)} & \cdots & \sigma_k^{(1)} \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \sigma_1^{(k)} & \cdots & \sigma_k^{(k)} \end{bmatrix}$.\newpage

			Note that $\tau$ is a $C^r$ map into the space of $k$x$k$ matrices because each\\ component function is a $C^r$ map. Furthermore, by the prior reasoning we\\ know that $\Phi \circ \Psi(p, v) = (p, \tau(p)v)$. And finally since $\Phi \circ \Psi|_{\{p\} \times \mathbb{R}^k}$ is the\\ composition of two vector space isomorphisms, we know $\tau(p) \in \GL_k(\mathbb{R})$\\ for all $p \in V$.\retTwo

			Since matrix inversion is a $C^\infty$ diffeomorphism on $\GL_k(\mathbb{R})$, we can conclude that $\Phi \circ \Psi|_{V \times \mathbb{R}^k}$ is a $C^r$ map with the $C^r$ inverse:
			
			{\centering$(\phi \circ \Psi)^{-1}(p, v) = (p, (\tau(p))^{-1}v)$. \exThreeP$\blacksquare$\retTwo\par}
		\end{myIndent}

		\myComment Remark: We call $\Psi^{-1}: \pi^{-1}(U) \to U \times \mathbb{R}^k$ the local trivialization associated with\\ $(\sigma_i)_{1 \leq i \leq k}$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
\end{myIndent}

\exTwo\ul{Corollary 10.21:} \hypertarget{Corollary 10.21 page 1202}{Let} $\pi: E \to M$ be a $C^r$ vector bundle of rank $k$, let $(V, \varphi = (x_1, \ldots, x_n))$ be a smooth chart on $M$, and suppose there exists a $C^r$ local frame $(\sigma_i)_{1 \leq i \leq k}$ for $E$ over $V$. Define $\widetilde{\varphi}: \pi^{-1}(V) \to \varphi(V) \times \mathbb{R}^k$ by:

{\centering $\widetilde{\varphi}(\sum_{i=1}^k v_i \sigma_i(p)) = ((x_1(p), \ldots, x_n(p)), (v_1, \ldots, v_k))$. \\ [4pt]\par}

Then $(\pi^{-1}(V), \widetilde{\varphi})$ is a smooth chart on $E$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Note that $\widetilde{\varphi} = (\varphi \times \myId_{\mathbb{R}^k}) \circ \Phi$ where $\varphi \times \myId_{\mathbb{R}^k}$ is a $C^r$ diffeomorphim and $\Phi$ (which\\ is the local trivialization associated with $(\sigma_i)_{1 \leq i \leq k}$) is also a $C^r$ diffeomorphism. So,\\ $\widetilde{\varphi}$ is a $C^r$ diffeomorphism. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo Using the prior results, we can also now give a neat criteria for showing if a rough section of a vector bundle $\pi: E \to M$ is continuous and $C^r$.\retTwo

Let $\pi: E \to M$ be a $C^r$ vector bundle of rank $k$. Also suppose $(\sigma_i)_{1 \leq i \leq k}$ is a $C^r$ local frame for $E$ over some open subset $U \subseteq M$. Given any rough local section $\tau: V \to E$ we can for every $p \in V \cap U$ write $\tau(p) = \sum_{i=1}^k \tau_i(p) \sigma_i(p)$ for some uniquely determined numbers $\tau_1(p), \ldots, \tau_k(p)$. This gives us functions $\tau_1, \ldots, \tau_k$ from $V \cap U$ to $\mathbb{R}$ which we call the \udefine{component functions} of $\tau$ with respect to the frame $(\sigma_i)_{1 \leq i \leq k}$.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Theorem 10.22:} Let $\pi: E \to M$ be a $C^r$ vector bundle, let $\tau: V \to E$ be a rough section, and let $(\sigma_i)_{1 \leq i \leq k}$ be a $C^r$ local frame for $E$ over some open subset $U \subseteq M$. Then $\tau|_{U \cap V}$ is a $C^r$ section iff its components functions with respect to the frame $(\sigma_i)_{1 \leq i \leq k}$ are $C^r$ maps.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Let $\Phi: \pi^{-1}(U) \to U \times \mathbb{R}^k$ be the local trivialization associated to the frame $(\sigma_i)_{1 \leq i \leq k}$. Because $\Phi|_{\pi^{-1}(V \cap U)}$ is a $C^r$ diffeomorphism to $(V \cap U) \times \mathbb{R}^k$, we have that $\tau$ is a $C^r$ map iff $\Phi \circ \tau|_{V \cap U}$ is a $C^r$ map. Yet we can calculate that $\Phi \circ \tau(p) = (p, (\tau_1(p), \ldots, \tau_k(p)))$. So, $\Phi \circ \tau|_{V \cap U}$ is a $C^r$ map iff $\tau_1|_{U \cap V}, \ldots, \tau_k|_{U \cap V}$ are all $C^r$ maps. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\myComment As a side note, the prior four results and proofs all still hold when $r = 0$, provided that we\\ substitute in "homeomorphism" for "$C^0$ diffeomorphism".\retTwo

\hTwo\begin{myIndent}\mySepThree\newpage\end{myIndent}

As I mentioned when first defining vector bundles, the most important vector bundle is the tangent bundle $TM$ of a $C^r$ manifold $M$ (where $r \geq 1$).\retTwo

In the special case of the tangent bundle $\pi: TM \to M$, we call a section of $TM$ a \udefine{vector field}. We can also add the adjectives "rough", "$C^r$", and "local" as we did for sections of more general vector bundles.

\pracOne\mySepTwo 

For an alternate lens, suppose $U \subseteq M$ is an open subset of a $C^r$ manifold $M$ and\\ $X: U \to TM$ is a rough local vector field. Given any open set $W \subseteq U$ we can define:
	
{\centering$\widetilde{X}_W: C^r(W, \mathbb{R}) \to \mathbb{R}^W$ by $(\widetilde{X}_W(f))(p) \coloneqq (X(p))(f)$\\ [4pt]\par}

for all $p \in U$ and $f \in C^r(W, \mathbb{R})$. This is clearly a linear map. Also, for convenience we\\ denote $\widetilde{X}_U$ as just $\widetilde{X}$.\retTwo

\ul{Propositon 8.14:} Let $0 \leq k \leq r - 1$. Then the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
	\item[(a)] $X$ is a $C^k$ local vector field over $U$,
	\item[(b)] the codomain of $\widetilde{X}$ is contained in $C^k(U, \mathbb{R})$,
	\item[(c)] for any open set $W \subseteq U$ the codomain of $\widetilde{X}_W$ is contained in $C^k(W, \mathbb{R})$.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	$(a \Longrightarrow b)$\\
	Let $f \in C^r(U, \mathbb{R})$. Then for any $p \in U$ let $(V, \varphi)$ be a smooth chart on $M$ such that $p \in V \subseteq U$. Also denote the local coordinate functions of $\varphi$ by $x_1, \ldots, x_n$. Then, we can define a $C^{r-1}$ local trivialization $(\pi^{-1}(V), \Phi)$ on $TM$ by:
		
	{\centering$\Phi(p, \sum_{i=1}^n c_i \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\right|_p) = (p, (c_1, \ldots, c_n))$.\retTwo\par}

	Yet now for each $1 \leq i \leq n$ let $\sigma_i: V \to TM$ be the $C^{r-1}$ vector field (i.e. section) defined by $\sigma_i(p) = \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\right|_p$. Then $(\sigma_i)_{1 \leq i \leq n}$ is the frame associated with $\Phi$.\retTwo
	
	From theorem 10.22 on the prior page applied to the $C^k$ vector field $X$ we thus\\ know there are $C^k$ component functions $X_1, \ldots, X_n: V \to \mathbb{R}$ such that:
	
	{\centering$X(p) = (p, \sum_{i=1}^n X_i(p) \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\right|_p)$.\retTwo\par}

	In turn, we can calculate for every $p \in V$ that:
	
	{\centering$\left(\widetilde{X}(f)\right)(p) = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i(p) \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\right|_p f$\retTwo\par}

	Switching to local coordinates and setting $\widehat{p} = \varphi(p)$ for all $p \in V$, we then get:

	{\centering$\widetilde{X}(f) \circ \varphi^{-1}(\widehat{p}) = \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i \circ \varphi^{-1})(\widehat{p}) \frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}(f \circ \varphi^{-1})(\widehat{p})$.\retTwo\par}

	Every summand on the right hand side is a $C^k$ map. So, we are done.\retTwo

	$(b \Longrightarrow c)$\\
	Suppose $f \in C^r(W, \mathbb{R})$. It suffices to show locally in $W$ that $\widetilde{X}_W(f)$ is a $C^k$ map.\\ Fortunately, for any $p \in W$ we can find a $C^r$ bump function $\phi: U \to [0, 1]$ such that\newpage $\phi \equiv 1$ on an open neighborhood $\Omega$ of $p$ in $W$ and $\supp(\phi) \subseteq W$. Then importantly,\\ for all $q \in \Omega$ we have that $(\widetilde{X}(f))(q) = (X(q))(f) = (X(q))(\phi f) = (\widetilde{X}(\phi f))(q)$.\\ By part (b) though, we know that $\widetilde{X}(\phi f)$ is a $C^k$ map on $U$ though. So, this proves $f$\\ is a $C^k$ map on $\Omega$.\retTwo

	$(c \Longrightarrow a)$\\
	Let $(V, \varphi)$ be any smooth chart on $M$ such that $V \subseteq U$ and write the coordinates on $V$\\ as $\varphi = (y_1, \ldots, y_n)$. Like before, we can define a $C^{r-1}$ local trivialization $(\pi^{-1}(V), \Phi)$\\ on $TM$ by:
		
	{\centering$\Phi(p, \sum_{i=1}^n c_i \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial y_i}\right|_p) = (p, (c_1, \ldots, c_n))$.\retTwo\par}

	And now for each $1 \leq i \leq n$ we let $\sigma_i: V \to TM$ be the $C^{r-1}$ vector field defined by $\sigma_i(p) = \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial y_i}\right|_p$. Then $(\sigma_i)_{1 \leq i \leq n}$ is the frame associated with $\Phi$.\retTwo

	If we consider the component functions $X_1, \ldots, X_n : V \to \mathbb{R}$ such that:
	
	{\centering$X(p) = (p, \sum_{i=1}^n X_i(p) \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial y_i}\right|_p)$,\\ [4pt]\par}
	
	we can now say that $X$ is a $C^k$ vector field iff each $X_i$ is a $C^k$ map.\retTwo

	Yet also note that $y_j: V \to \mathbb{R}$ is a map in $C^r(V, \mathbb{R})$ for all $1 \leq j \leq n$. In turn, by assumption (c) we thus know that $\widetilde{X}(y_j) \in C^k(W, \mathbb{R})$. Yet also note that:

	{\centering $(\widetilde{X}(y_j))(p) = (X(p))(y_j) = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i(p) \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial y_i}\right|_p y_j = X_j(p)$ \retTwo\par}

	So, each $X_i$ is a $C^k$ map. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

Also observe the following about the function $\widetilde{X}: C^r(U, \mathbb{R}) \to \mathbb{R}^U$.\retTwo

\ul{Lemma:} Suppose $f \in C^r(U, \mathbb{R})$ and $p \in U$ satisfies that $\df f_p = 0$. Then $(\widetilde{X}(f))(p) = 0$.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Why?\\
	Note that $(\widetilde{X}(f))(p) = (X(p))(f) = (X(p))(\myId_\mathbb{R} \circ f) = \df f_p(X(p)) \myId_\mathbb{R} = 0$.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

Interestingly, I just realized I can also prove the following general result.\retTwo

\ul{Proposition:} Suppose $M$ is a $C^r$ manifold (with $r \geq 1$), $U \subseteq M$ is an open subset, and\\ $T: C^r(U, \mathbb{R}) \to \mathbb{R}^U$ is a linear map.
\begin{itemize}
	\item Suppose $T$ satisfies that if $p \in U$ and $f \in C^r(U, \mathbb{R})$ has $\df f_p = 0$ then $(T(f))(p) = 0$. Then we have that $T(fg) = fT(g) + gT(f)$ for all $f, g \in C^r(U, \mathbb{R})$.
	
	\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
		Proof:\\
		Given a fixed $p$ define $h = fg - g(p)f - f(p)g$. Then we can easily verify that\\ $\df h_p = 0$. In turn, by linearity and our starting assumption we have that:
		
		{\centering$0 = (T(h))(p) = (T(fg))(p) - g(p)(T(f))(p) - f(p)(T(g))(p)$.\retTwo\par}
		
		Or in other words, $(T(fg))(p) = g(p)(T(f))(p) + f(p)(T(g))(p)$. Since $p$ was arbitrary, this proves that $T(fg) = gT(f) + fT(g)$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	\item The converse claim holds if $r = \infty$.\newpage
	\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
		Proof:\\
		First I shall prove the easiest claim that if $f \equiv C$ on $U$ is a constant function then $T(f) \equiv 0$ on $U$.
		\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
			To see why, note that if $C = 0$ then $T(f) = 0T(f) \equiv 0$. Meanwhile, if $C \neq 0$ then

			{\centering $T(f) = \frac{1}{C}T(f^2) = \frac{1}{C}(2fT(f)) = 2T(f)$ \retTwo\par}
