			And now subtracting $T(f)$ from both sides we get that $T(f) = 0$.
		\end{myIndent}
		
		Secondly, I shall prove that if $p \in U$ and $f \in C^r(U, \mathbb{R})$ satisfies that $f$ is constant on a neighborhood $V$ of $p$ then $(T(f))(p) = 0$.
		\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
			To start off, without loss of generality we can assume $f(p) = 0$. After all, if not then by the previous claim we have that:
			
			{\centering$T(f) = T(f - f(p)) + T(f(p)) = T(f - f(p)) + 0$.\retTwo\par}

			Next, we can find a $C^r$ bump function $\omega: U \to [0, 1]$ such that $\omega \equiv 1$ on $\supp(f)$ and $\supp(\omega) \subseteq U - \{p\}$. Then $f = \omega f$ and in turn:

			{\centering $(T(f))(p) = (T(\omega f))(p) = \omega(p)(T(f))(p) + f(p)(T(\omega))(p) = 0 + 0 = 0$ \retTwo\par}
		\end{myIndent}

		Now I'm ready for proving the actual proposition's claim. Suppose $f \in C^r(U, \mathbb{R})$ and $p \in U$ is a  critical point of $f$. On a small enough smooth chart $(V, \varphi = (x_1, \ldots, x_n))$ on $M$ containing $p$ we can conclude that there are $C^\infty$ functions $h_i: V \to \mathbb{R}$ with $f|_V = f(p) + (x_i - x_i(p))h_i$ and $h_i(p) = 0$ for each $i$.\retTwo

		Next let $W \subseteq V$ be an open set containing $p$ and $\omega: U \to [0, 1]$ be a $C^r$ bump function such that $\omega \equiv 1$ on $W$ and $\supp(\omega) \subseteq V$. Notably, we also have that $\omega^2$ is a $C^r$ bump function with $\omega \equiv 1$ on $W$ and $\supp(\omega) \subseteq V$.\retTwo
		
		But now $\omega^2$ being constant on a neighborhood of $p$ means that:
		
		{\centering$T(\omega^2 f) = f(p)(T(\omega^2))(p) + \omega^2(p) (T(f))(p) = 0 + 1(T(f))(p)$.\retTwo\par}

		Yet also note that $\omega^2 f = f(p)\omega^2 + \sum_{i=1}^n [\omega (x_i - x_i(p)) \cdot \omega h_i]$.\retTwo
	
		Thus $T(\omega^2 f) = 0 + \sum_{i=1}^n [0T(\omega h_i) + 0T(\omega(x_i - x_i(p)))] = 0$. So,
		
		{\centering$T(f) = T(\omega^2 f) = 0$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo\par}
	\end{myIndent}
\end{itemize}

Based on the lemma before, we can now ask if we can go in reverse from what we've been doing. In other words\dots\retTwo

\ul{Theorem:} Let $M$ be a $C^r$ manifold, let $U \subseteq M$ be an open set, and let\\ $0 \leq k \leq r - 1$. Suppose we are given a linear map $\widetilde{Y}: C^r(U, \mathbb{R}) \to C^k(U, \mathbb{R})$\\ satisfying that if $f \in C^r(U, \mathbb{R})$ and $p \in U$ is such that $\df f_p = 0$ then $(\widetilde{Y}(f))(p) = 0$.\\ Then there is a unique rough local vector field $Y: U \to TM$ such that:

{\centering$(Y(p))(f) = (\widetilde{Y}(f))(p)$ for all $p \in U$ and $f \in C^r(U, \mathbb{R})$.\\ [4pt]\par}

Furthermore, $Y$ is a $C^k$ vector field.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Proof:\\
	To start off, we do have to exercise some caution for how we define $Y$. After all, for every $p \in U$ we want $Y(p)$ to be a linear map from $C^1(U, \mathbb{R})$. That said, if we were to simply\\ [-2pt] define $(Y(p))(f) = (\widetilde{Y}(f))(p)$ then we would only be defining $Y(p)$ on the domain $C^r(U, \mathbb{R})$. So, we need to be more subtle.\retTwo

	I'll first show for any $p \in U$ that there exists an open set $W \subseteq U$ containing $p$ as well as a  $C^k$ vector field $Y^{(W)}: W \to TM$ such that:
	
	{\centering$(\widetilde{Y}(f))(p) = (Y^{(W)}(p))(f)$ for all $f \in C^r(U, \mathbb{R})$ and $p \in W$.\\ [4pt]\par}

	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP	
		To start off, let $(V, \varphi)$ be a smooth chart on $M$ such that $p \in V \subseteq U$, and for all $q \in V$ write $\varphi(q) = (x_1(q), \ldots, x_n(q))$. Next, let $W \subseteq V$ be an open set containing $p$, and let $\omega: U \to [0, 1]$ be a $C^r$ bump function with $\omega \equiv 1$ on $W$ and $\supp(\omega) \subseteq V$.\retTwo

		Importantly, $\omega x_i: U \to \mathbb{R}$ is a well-defined $C^r$ map. Therefore, we can define a $C^k$ map $Y_i^{(W)} \coloneqq \widetilde{Y}(\omega x_i)$. And now we define the vector field $Y^{(W)}: W \to TM$ by:
		
		{\centering$Y^{(W)}(p) = \left(p, \sum_{i=1}^n Y_i^{(W)}(p) \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\right|_p\right)$\retTwo\par}

		All the component functions $Y_i^{(W)}$ being $C^k$ implies that $Y^{(W)}$ is a $C^k$ vector field. Also I claim that if $f \in C^r(U, \mathbb{R})$ and $p \in W$ then $(\widetilde{Y}(f))(p) = (Y(p))(f)$.
		\begin{myIndent}
			To see why, for every $i$ let $c_i = \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\right|_p f$.\retTwo
			
			We know that $g \coloneqq f - \sum_{i=1}^n c_i \omega x_i$ is a $C^r$ map on $U$ satisfying that\\ $\df g_p = 0$. Hence:

			{\centering $0 = (\widetilde{Y}(g))(p) = (\widetilde{Y}(f))(p) - \sum_{i=1}^n c_i Y_i^{(W)}(p)$ \retTwo\par}

			In other words:
			
			{\centering$(\widetilde{Y}(f))(p) = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i Y_i^{(W)}(p) = Y_i^{(W)}(p)\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\right|_p f = (Y^{(W)}(p))(f)$\retTwo\par}
		\end{myIndent}
	\end{myIndent}

	Secondly, I shall show that if $W$ and $\Omega$ are both open subsets of $U$ with $W \cap \Omega \neq \emptyset$,\\ and if $Y: W \to TM$ and $X: \Omega \to TM$ are both rough vector fields satisfying for\\ all $p \in W$, $q \in \Omega$, and $f \in C^r(U, \mathbb{R})$ that:
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item $(\widetilde{Y}(f))(p) = (Y(p))(f)$ for all $p \in W$,
		\item$(\widetilde{Y}(f))(q) = (X(q))(f)$ for all $q \in \Omega$,
	\end{enumerate}
	then $Y = X$ on $W \cap \Omega$.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		Again let $p \in W \cap \Omega$. Then we can pick a small enough smooth coordinate chart $(V, \varphi)$ on $M$ such that $p \in V \subseteq W \cap \Omega$. Also, we say $\varphi = (x_1, \ldots, x_n)$.\newpage

		Next, we can find an open set $V^\prime$ such that $p \in V^\prime \subseteq V$ as well a $C^r$ bump function $\omega: U \to [0, 1]$ with $\omega \equiv 1$ on $V^\prime$ and $\supp(\omega) \subseteq V$. Then, we write:
		
		{\centering$Y(p) = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\right|_p$ and $X(p) = \sum_{i=1}^n d_i \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\right|_p$.\retTwo\par}

		For any $1 \leq j \leq n$ we have that:

		{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
		$c_j = (X(p))(x_j) = (X(p))(\omega x_j)$\\ [4pt]
		$\phantom{c_j = (X(p))(x_j)} = (\widetilde{Y}(\omega x_j))(p) = (Y(p))(\omega x_j) = (Y(p))(x_j) = d_j$
		\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

		So, $X(p) = Y(p)$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Hopefully it is clear how the second claim proves the uniqueness part of the theorem\\ statement. Also importantly, the second claim let's us use the gluing lemma on a\\ covering of $C^k$ vector fields given by the first claim in order to get a single $C^k$ vector\\ field $Y: U \to TM$ doing exactly what we wanted. $\blacksquare$\retTwo 
\end{myIndent}

\mySepTwo

\hTwo Before moving on to the final topic I want to go over before starting the 250 homework, I'd like to say in what way the standard topology and $C^{r-1}$ structure on $TM$ (where $M$ is a $C^r$ manifold) is "natural" like I claimed without justification on \inLinkRap{Definition of the tangent bundle}{page 1132}.\retTwo

Note that if $(U, \varphi)$ is a smooth chart on a $C^r$ manifold $M$ and we write $\varphi = (x_1, \ldots, x_n)$, then for each $1 \leq i \leq n$ we have that $p \mapsto \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\right|_p$ defines a rough vector field over $U$. This vector field is called a \udefine{coordinate vector field}.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Proposition 10.24:} Let $M$ be a $C^r$ manifold. The topology and $C^{r-1}$ structure that $TM$ is equipped with are the unique such objects satisfying that $\pi: TM \to M$ is a $C^{r-1}$ vector bundle and every coordinate vector field is a $C^{r-1}$ vector field.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\ 
	Let $(U, \varphi)$ be a smooth chart on $M$ and write $\varphi = (x_1, \ldots, x_n)$. Then define\\ $\Phi: \pi^{-1}(U) \to U \times \mathbb{R}^k$ by $\Phi(p, \sum_{i=1}^n c_i \left. \frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\right|_p) = (p, (c_1, \ldots, c_n))$. Also for\\ [-3pt] every $1 \leq i \leq n$ let $\sigma_i : U \to TM$ be defined by $\sigma_i(p) = \left. \frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\right|_p$.\retTwo

	In the standard topology on $TM$, we know that $\Phi$ is a $C^{r-1}$ map and in turn $(\sigma_i)_{1 \leq i \leq n}$\\ is the local frame associated with $\Phi$. So, each $\sigma_i$ is a $C^{r-1}$ vector field like we wanted.\retTwo

	Meanwhile, suppose $TM$ is equipped with some alternate topology $\mathcal{T}$ and $C^{r-1}$ structure $\mathcal{A}$ such that $\pi: TM \to M$ is a $C^{r-1}$ vector bundle and every coordinate vector field is a $C^{r-1}$ vector field.\retTwo

	Then $(\sigma_i)_{1 \leq i \leq n}$ is a $C^r$ local frame for $(TM, \mathcal{T}, \mathcal{A})$ over $U$. Hence by corollary 10.21 on \inLinkRap{Corollary 10.21 page 1202}{page 1202}, we know that $(\pi^{-1}(U), \widetilde{\varphi})$ where $\widetilde{\varphi}(p, \sum_{i=1}^n c_i \left. \frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\right|_p) \coloneqq (\varphi(p), (c_1, \ldots, c_n))$ is a smooth chart on $(TM, \mathcal{T}, \mathcal{A})$. Yet $(\pi^{-1}(U), \widetilde{\varphi})$ is also a smooth chart in the original topology and $C^{r-1}$ structure on $TM$.\newpage

	Since such charts cover all of $TM$ we can now conclude by standard arguments (such as those in the middle of \inLinkRap{Page 1199 reference}{page 1199}) to conclude our new topology and $C^{r-1}$ structure are identical to our old objects. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo\mySepTwo

Given a $C^r$ manifold $M$, another $C^{r-1}$ vector bundle I want to define is $M$'s cotangent bundle $T^* M$.\retTwo

Let $p \in M$, let $U \subseteq M$ be an open set containing $p$, and let $f: U \to \mathbb{R}$ be a $C^1$ map. We can define a map in $T_p^* M \coloneqq (T_p M)^*$ by $v \mapsto \coloneqq v(f)$. Usually this map is denoted $\df f_p$ (and also called the \udefine{differential of $f$}). I'll briefly refer to this map though as $\widetilde{\df f_p}$ just to distinguish it from the typical differential.\retTwo

Next, given any $a \in \mathbb{R}$ we can identify $T_a \mathbb{R}$ with $\mathbb{R}$ by the linear map sending $\left.\frac{\df}{\df t}\right|_a$ to $1$. And this gives us a more direct way of considering the differential $\df f_p : T_p M \to T_{f(p)}\mathbb{R}$ as a dual vector.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Propositon:} $\df f_p = \widetilde{\df f_p}$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:

	{\centering$\widetilde{\df f_p}(v) = v(f) = v(\myId_{\mathbb{R}} \circ f) = \df f_p(v) \left.\frac{\df}{\df t}\right|_{f(p)} \myId_\mathbb{R} = \df f_p(v) \cdot 1$ $\blacksquare$\retTwo\par}
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo A big reason I wanted to show the prior equivalence is just because it shows that we\\ already know how to calculate a matrix representation of $\df f_p \in T_p^* M$. Namely, we can just compute the gradient of $f$ with respect to some local coordinates.\retTwo

Furthermore, we have the following corollary:\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Corollary:} Let $M$ be a $C^r$ manifold and suppose $f: U \to \mathbb{R}$ is a $C^1$ map. Then $f$ has a critical point at $p \in U$ iff $\df f_p = 0$ in $T_p^* M$.\retTwo

\begin{myIndent}\hTwo\mySepThree\end{myIndent}

\hTwo Given any $C^r$ manifold $M$ and $p \in M$, we can consider a smooth chart $(U, \varphi)$ on $M$ containing $p$. In particular, we write $\varphi(q) = (x_1(q), \ldots, x_n(q))$ for all $q \in U$. Then recall that $\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_1}\right|_p, \ldots, \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_n}\right|_p$ forms a basis for $T_p U$.\retTwo

In turn we can consider the dual basis $\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_1}\right|_p^*, \ldots, \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_n}\right|_p^*$ for $T_p^* M$.\retTwo

Also note that each $x_i : U \to \mathbb{R}$ is a $C^r$ map. So, we can consider the dual vector\\ $\df (x_i)_p \in T_p^* M$.\newpage

\exTwo\ul{Claim:} $\df (x_i)_p = \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\right|_p^*$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Let $v = \sum_{j=1}^n v_j \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_j}\right|_p$ be any vector in $T_p M$. Then:

	{\centering $\df (x_i)_p\left(\sum_{j=1}^n v_j \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_j}\right|_p\right) = \sum_{j=1}^n v_j \left(\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_j}\right|_p x_i\right) = v_i = \left(\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\right|_p^*\right)\left( \sum_{j=1}^n v_j \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_j}\right|_p \right)$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo\par}
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo Because of the prior claim, we just refer to the dual basis for $T_p^* M$ by $\df (x_1)_p, \ldots, \df (x_n)_p$.\retTwo

Next, suppose $(V, \psi)$ is another smooth chart on $M$ containing $p$ and write\\ $\psi(q) = (y_1(q), \ldots, y_n(q))$ for all $q \in V$. What is the matrix representing the\\ change of coordinates from $\df (x_1)_p, \ldots, \df (x_n)_p$ to $\df (y_1)_p, \ldots, \df (y_n)_p$?
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	The answer is incredibly straightforward. We already know the matrix representaion of the change from the coordinates $\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\right|_p$ to the coordinates $\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial y_i}\right|_p$ in the tangent space $T_p M$ is\\ [-4pt] simply given by:
	
	{\centering$\Df(\psi \circ \varphi^{-1})(\varphi(p))$.\retTwo\par}
	
	In turn, it is a well-known fact that the matrix representation of the change from the\\ coordinates $\df (y_i)_p$ to the coordinates $\df (x_i)_p$ is given by the matrix transpose\\ $\Df(\psi \circ \varphi^{-1})(\varphi(p))^*$. And finally, we can invert that to get the change of coordinates\\ going in the direction we want.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo Now let $T^* M = \coprod_{p \in M}T^*_p M$ and for any $(p, \omega) \in T^* M$ (i.e. $\omega \in T^*_p M)$ define\\ $\pi(p, \omega) = p$. Note that given any open $U \subseteq M$, and $C^1$ map $f: U \to \mathbb{R}$, we\\ have that $\df f: U \to T^* M$ defines a "rough" local section for $\pi: T^* M \to M$.
\begin{myIndent}\myComment
	The adjective "rough" here is just because we haven't equipped $T^* M$ with any topology for $f$ to be continuous with respect to yet.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\exTwo\ul{Proposition 11.9:} Let $M$ be a $C^r$ manifold (where $r \geq 1$). Then there is a unique topology (and $C^{r-1}$ structure if $r \geq 2$) on $T^* M$ such that $\pi: T^*M \to M$ is a $C^{r-1}$ vector bundle of rank $n = \dim(M)$ and for any local coordinates $(U, \varphi = (x_1, \ldots, x_n))$ on $M$ we have that each $\df x_i$ is a $C^{r-1}$ local section of $\pi$ (called a \udefine{coordinate covector field}).
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Given any smooth chart $(U, \varphi = (x_1, \ldots, x_n))$ on $M$ define the local trivialization
	
	{\centering$\Phi: \pi^{-1}(U) \to U \times \mathbb{R}^n$ by $\Phi(p, \sum_{i=1}^n \omega_i \df x_i) = (p, (\omega_1, \ldots, \omega_n))$.\retTwo\par}

	Also given another smooth chart $(V, \psi = (y_1, \ldots, y_n))$ on $M$ we can analogously define the local trivialization $\Psi: \pi^{-1}(V) \to V \times \mathbb{R}^n$. Then we can see that:
	
	{\centering $\Psi \circ \Phi^{-1}(p, \omega) = (p, \left(\left((\Df( \psi \circ \varphi^{-1}))(\varphi(p))\right)^*\right)^{-1}\omega)$. \retTwo\par}

	Importantly, $\left(\left((\Df( \psi \circ \varphi^{-1}))(\varphi(p))\right)^*\right)^{-1}$ is a $C^{r-1}$ map from $U$ to $\GL_n(\mathbb{R})$. So, we can conclude by lemma 10.6 on \inLinkRap{Lemma 10.6 page 1198}{page 1198} that there is a unique topology and $C^{r-1}$\\ structure on $T^* M$ such that all the $\Phi$ constructed priorly are $C^{r-1}$ local trivializations\\ and $\pi: T^*M \to M$ is a $C^{r-1}$ vector bundle.\retTwo

	The uniqueness of the topology and $C^{r-1}$ structure on $T^* M$ follows identically as in the proof of uniqueness in proposition 10.24 of the topology and $C^{r-1}$ structure on $TM$. $\blacksquare$\newpage
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo I'll briefly mention how to compute a \udefine{covector field} (i.e. section of $T^* M$) defined by a $C^{r}$ map $f: M \to \mathbb{R}$.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Let $(U, \varphi)$ be a smooth chart on $M$ and write $\varphi = (x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ Then we know there are functions $\tau_1, \ldots, \tau_n : U \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $\df f = \sum_{i=1}^n \tau_i \df x_i$. But now for any fixed $j$ we have that:

	{\centering $\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_j}(p) \coloneqq \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_j}\right|_p f = \df f(\left. \frac{\partial}{\partial x_j}\right|_p) = \sum_{i=1}^n \tau_i \df x_i(\left. \frac{\partial}{\partial x_j}\right|_p) = \tau_j(p)$ \retTwo\par}

	So, for each $1 \leq i \leq n$ we have that:
	
	{\centering$\tau_i(p) = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}(p) = \frac{\partial (f \circ \varphi^{-1})}{\partial x_i}(\varphi(p))$ for all $p \in U$.\retTwo\par}

	In other words, we have that $\df f(p) = \sum\limits_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}(p) \df x_i$ for all $p \in U$.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

The prior computation also now lets us conclude that if $f$ is a $C^r$ map then $\df f$ is a $C^{r - 1}$ covector field since each component function with respect to the frame $(\df x_i)_{1 \leq i \leq n}$ is a $C^{r-1}$ map.\retTwo

One other note is that a covector field is also called a \udefine{$1$ form}.\retTwo

\hTwo\mySepTwo

\Hstatement\blab{Set 2 Problem 2:} Let $M$ be a $C^2$ manifold, let $f: M \to \mathbb{R}$ be a $C^2$ map, and suppose $p \in M$ is a critical point of $f$. The \udefine{Hessian} at $p$ is the "symmetric bilinear form (i.e. symmetric $2$-tensor)" on $T_p M$ given with respect to any local coordinates $(U, \varphi = (x_1, \ldots, x_n))$ by:

{\centering$H_p(u, v) = \sum\limits_{i=1}^n \sum\limits_{j=1}^n \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_i \partial x_j}(p) u_i v_j$ where $u = \sum\limits_{i=1}^n u_i \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\right|_p$ and $v = \sum\limits_{j=1}^n v_j \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_j}\right|_p$.\retTwo\par}

{\color{BrickRed}(Here $\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_i \partial x_j}(p) \coloneqq \frac{\partial^2 (f \circ \varphi^{-1})}{\partial x_i \partial x_j}(\varphi(p))$.)} Show that this is well-defined independently of the local\\ coordinates chosen.\\ [-6pt]
\begin{myIndent}\HexOne
	The hard part is just showing that this is well-defined irrespective of which local coordinates are chosen. So, I'll let $(U, \varphi)$ and $(V, \psi)$ both be smooth charts on $M$ containing the critical point $p$, and also I'll write $\varphi = (x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ and $\psi = (y_1, \ldots, y_n)$.\retTwo

	Next I'll let $u$ and $v$ be vectors in $T_p M$. We can uniquely write:
	\begin{itemize}
		\item $u = \sum_{i=1}^n u_i \left. \frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\right|_p = \sum_{i=1}^n \overline{u_i} \left. \frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\right|_p$
		\item $v = \sum_{i=1}^n v_i \left. \frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\right|_p = \sum_{i=1}^n \overline{v_i} \left. \frac{\partial}{\partial y_i}\right|_p$.
	\end{itemize}

	And now, our task is to prove that:

	{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
	$\begin{bmatrix} u_1 & \cdots & u_n \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_1^2}(p) & \cdots &  \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_1 \partial x_n}(p) \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_n \partial x_1}(p) & \cdots &  \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_n^2}(p) \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} v_1 \\ \vdots \\ v_n \end{bmatrix}$\\ [30pt]
	$\phantom{aaaaaaaaa} = \begin{bmatrix} \overline{u_1} & \cdots & \overline{u_n} \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y_1^2}(p) & \cdots &  \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y_1 \partial y_n}(p) \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y_n \partial y_1}(p) & \cdots &  \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y_n^2}(p) \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} \overline{v_1} \\ \vdots \\ \overline{v_n} \end{bmatrix}$
	\end{tabular}\newpage\par}
	
	But now note that if $\sum_{i=1}^n c_i \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\right|_p = \sum_{i=1}^n \overline{c_i}\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial y_i}\right|_p$ then:

	{\centering $\begin{bmatrix}c_1 \\ \vdots \\ c_n\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{\partial x_1}{\partial y_1}(p) & \cdots & \frac{\partial x_1}{\partial y_n}(p) \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \frac{\partial x_n}{\partial y_1}(p) & \cdots & \frac{\partial x_n}{\partial y_n}(p) \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\overline{c_1} \\ \vdots \\ \overline{c_n}\end{bmatrix}$ \retTwo\par}

	Therefore, it suffices to prove that:

	{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
	$ \begin{bmatrix} \frac{\partial x_1}{\partial y_1}(p) & \cdots & \frac{\partial x_1}{\partial y_n}(p) \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \frac{\partial x_n}{\partial y_1}(p) & \cdots & \frac{\partial x_n}{\partial y_n}(p) \end{bmatrix}^{\trans}\begin{bmatrix} \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_1^2}(p) & \cdots &  \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_1 \partial x_n}(p) \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_n \partial x_1}(p) & \cdots &  \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_n^2}(p) \end{bmatrix}  \begin{bmatrix} \frac{\partial x_1}{\partial y_1}(p) & \cdots & \frac{\partial x_1}{\partial y_n}(p) \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \frac{\partial x_n}{\partial y_1}(p) & \cdots & \frac{\partial x_n}{\partial y_n}(p) \end{bmatrix}$\\ [30pt]
	$\phantom{aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y_1^2}(p) & \cdots &  \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y_1 \partial y_n}(p) \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y_n \partial y_1}(p) & \cdots &  \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y_n^2}(p) \end{bmatrix}$
	\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

	Or going component by component, we need to show for every $1 \leq i \leq n$ and\\ $1 \leq j \leq n$ that:

	{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
		$\frac{\partial^2 (f \circ \psi^{-1})}{\partial y_i \partial y_j}(\psi(p)) = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y_i \partial y_j}(p) = \sum\limits_{k=1}^n \sum\limits_{\ell = 1}^n \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_k \partial x_\ell}(p) \frac{\partial x_k}{\partial y_i}(p) \frac{\partial x_\ell}{\partial y_j}(p)$\\ [12pt]
		$\phantom{\frac{\partial^2 (f \circ \psi^{-1})}{\partial y_i \partial y_j}(\psi(p)) = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y_i \partial y_j}(p)} = \sum\limits_{k=1}^n \sum\limits_{\ell = 1}^n \frac{\partial^2 (f \circ \varphi^{-1})}{\partial x_k \partial x_\ell}(\varphi(p)) \frac{\partial (x_k \circ \psi^{-1})}{\partial y_i}(\psi(p)) \frac{\partial (x_\ell \circ \psi^{-1})}{\partial y_j}(\psi(p))$ 
	\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

	But now note by chain rule that:
	
	{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
		$\frac{\partial(f \circ \psi^{-1})}{\partial y_j}(\psi(p)) = \frac{\partial((f \circ \varphi^{-1}) \circ (\varphi \circ \psi^{-1}))}{\partial y_j}(\psi(p))$\\ [8pt]
		$\phantom{\frac{\partial(f \circ \psi^{-1})}{\partial y_i}(\psi(p))} = \sum\limits_{\ell=1}^n \frac{\partial (f \circ \varphi^{-1})}{\partial x_\ell}(\varphi(p))\frac{\partial(x_\ell \circ \psi^{-1})}{\partial y_j}(\psi(p))$\\ [12pt]
		$\phantom{\frac{\partial(f \circ \psi^{-1})}{\partial y_i}(\psi(p))} = \sum\limits_{\ell=1}^n \left(\frac{\partial (f \circ \varphi^{-1})}{\partial x_\ell} \circ (\varphi \circ \psi^{-1})\right)(\psi(p)) \cdot \frac{\partial(x_\ell \circ \psi^{-1})}{\partial y_j}(\psi(p))$.
	\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

	Next, we can apply both the chain and product rules again to get that:

	{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
		$\frac{\partial^2(f \circ \psi^{-1})}{\partial y_i\partial y_j}(\psi(p)) = \sum\limits_{\ell=1}^n \frac{\partial}{\partial y_i}\left[\left(\frac{\partial (f \circ \varphi^{-1})}{\partial x_\ell} \circ (\varphi \circ \psi^{-1})\right)(\psi(p)) \cdot \frac{\partial(x_\ell \circ \psi^{-1})}{\partial y_j}(\psi(p))\right]$\\ [12pt]
		$\phantom{\frac{\partial^2(f \circ \psi^{-1})}{\partial y_i\partial y_j}(\psi(p))} = \sum\limits_{\ell = 1}^n \sum\limits_{k = 1}^n \frac{\partial^2 (f \circ \varphi^{-1})}{\partial x_k \partial x_\ell}(\varphi(p)) \frac{\partial (x_k \circ \psi^{-1})}{\partial y_i}(\psi(p)) \frac{\partial (x_\ell \circ \psi^{-1})}{\partial y_j}(\psi(p))$\\ [8pt]
		$\phantom{\frac{\partial^2(f \circ \psi^{-1})}{\partial y_i\partial y_j}(\psi(p)) + aaaaaaaaaaaaaa} + \sum\limits_{\ell = 1}^n \frac{\partial (f \circ \varphi^{-1})}{\partial x_\ell}(\varphi(p)) \frac{\partial^2(x_\ell \circ \psi^{-1})}{\partial y_i \partial y_j}(\psi(p))$
	\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

	And finally, because $f$ has a critical point at $p$, we know that:
	
	{\centering$\frac{\partial (f \circ \varphi^{-1})}{\partial x_\ell}(\varphi(p)) = \left.\frac{\partial }{\partial x_\ell}\right| f = 0$ for all $\ell$.\retTwo\par}

	So the terms we don't want all cancel and finished proving coordinate-independence.\retTwo

	The fact that $H_p$ is a symmetric map (i.e. $H_p(u, v) = H_p(v, u)$) is because $f$ is $C^2$ and\\ so $\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_i \partial x_j}(p) = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_j \partial x_i}(p)$. Also, $H_p$ is clearly a bilinear map. $\blacksquare$\newpage
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo I'm short on time so I don't want to get into defining what a tensor product of bundles is / should be. However, the next question is about proving the existence of a Riemannian metric on a $C^r$ manifold. So, I ought to at least give some notes.\retTwo

If $M$ is a $C^r$ manifold, a \udefine{Riemannian metric} on $M$ is a "$C^{r-1}$ varying" choice of inner product $g_p : T_p M \times T_p M \to \mathbb{R}$ for every $p \in M$.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	As for what that definition means, I first need to give some observations about inner\\ products. So suppose $V$ is an $n$-dimensional real vector space and let $v_1, \ldots, v_n$ be a basis for $V$. Thus, we can uniquely write any vector $v \in V$ as $(c_1, \ldots, c_n) \coloneqq \sum_{i=1}^n c_i v_i$.\retTwo

	I'll write out this next reasoning in a way that generalizes to complex vector spaces. If $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ is an inner product and we interpret $\mVecAst{c} = (c_1, \ldots, c_n)$ as a column vector, we have that $\langle \mVecAst{c}, \mVecAst{d}\rangle = \mVecAst{d}^* \mathbf{A} \mVecAst{c}$ where $\mathbf{A}$ is the matrix:
	
	{\centering$\begin{bmatrix}\langle v_1, v_1\rangle & \cdots & \langle v_n, v_1\rangle \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \langle v_1, v_n\rangle & \cdots & \langle v_n, v_n\rangle\end{bmatrix}$.\retTwo\par}

	Note that $\mathbf{A}$ is a self-adjoint matrix, $\mVecAst{c}^* \mathbf{A} \mVecAst{c} \geq 0$ for all $\mVecAst{c}$, and $\mVecAst{c}^*\mathbf{A} \mVecAst{c} = 0$ iff $\mVecAst{c} = 0$. In other words, $\mathbf{A}$ is a \udefine{positive definite matrix}.\retTwo

	Conversely, suppose $\mathbf{B}$ is a self-adjoint positive definite matrix and define:
	
	{\centering$\langle \mVecAst{c}, \mVecAst{d}\rangle_{\mathrm{new}} = \mVecAst{d}^* \mathbf{B} \mVecAst{c}$.\retTwo\par}

	Note that:
	
	{\centering$\langle \mVecAst{d}, \mVecAst{c}\rangle_{\mathrm{new}} = \mVecAst{c}^* B \mVecAst{d} = \overline{\mVecAst{d}^* B^* \mVecAst{c}} = \overline{\mVecAst{d}^* B \mVecAst{c}} = \overline{\langle\mVecAst{c}, \mVecAst{d}\rangle_{\mathrm{new}}}$.\retTwo\par}

	Also it's easy to see that $\langle \mVecAst{c}, \mVecAst{d}\rangle_{\mathrm{new}}$ is linear with respect to the first argument $\mVecAst{c}$. And by positive definiteness we know that the last requirement for $\langle \cdot, \cdot\rangle_{\mathrm{new}}$ to be a well-defined inner product holds.
	\begin{myIndent}\myComment
		As a side note, in the real vector space and inner product case, all the prior reasoning holds just without any complex conjugates.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	\begin{myIndent}\mySepFour\end{myIndent}

	Focusing now on the case of a $C^r$ manifold $M$, let $(U, \varphi)$ be any smooth chart on $M$ and write $\varphi = (x_1, \ldots, x_n)$. Then by defining $\sigma_i : U \to TM$ by $\sigma_i(p) = \left. \frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\right|_p$, we get that\\ [-4pt] $(\sigma_i)_{1 \leq i \leq n}$ forms a $C^{r-1}$ frame for $TM$ over $U$.\retTwo
	
	It follows that if $\{g_p\}_{p \in M}$ is a Riemannian metric then there are coordinate functions\\ $A_{i,j}: U \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $p \in U$, if $u = \sum_{i=1}^n u_i \sigma_i(p)$ and $v = \sum_{i=1}^n v_i \sigma_i(p)$\\ are elements of $T_p M$ then:

	{\centering $g_p(u, v) = \begin{bmatrix} v_1 & \cdots & v_n\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} A_{1,1}(p) & \cdots & A_{1, n}(p) \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ A_{n,1}(p) & \cdots & A_{n,n}(p)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} u_1 \\ \vdots \\ u_n\end{bmatrix}$ \retTwo\par}

	In particular, $A_{i,j}(p) = g_p(\sigma_j(p), \sigma_i(p)) = g_p(\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_j}\right|_p, \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\right|_p)$.\newpage

	When we say that $g_p$ varies $C^{r-1}$-ly with $p$, what we mean is that there is an atlas of smooth charts $\{(U_\alpha, \varphi_\alpha)\}_{\alpha \in A}$ covering $M$ and satisfying that the coordinate functions $A_{i,j}$ induced by each smooth chart in our atlas are $C^{r-1}$ maps on $U$. Once I define what tensor bundles on $M$ are, it will become clear that this is equivalent to us having a $C^{r-1}$ "tensor field" (i.e. section) of a certain tensor bundle.\retTwo

	\begin{myIndent}\mySepFour\end{myIndent}

	\ul{Observation:} Suppose $\{g_p\}_{p \in M}$ is a Riemannian metric over a $C^r$ manifold $M$, and\\ let $(U, \varphi)$ and $(V, \psi)$ be overlapping smooth charts on $M$ (i.e. $U \cap V \neq \emptyset$). Write\\ $\varphi = (x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ and $\psi = (y_1, \ldots, y_n)$. Then for each $1 \leq i,j \leq n$ define:
	\begin{itemize}
		\item	$A_{i,j}: U \to \mathbb{R}$ by $A_{i,j}(p) = g_p(\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_j}\right|_p, \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\right|_p)$,
		\item $B_{i,j}: V \to \mathbb{R}$ by $B_{i,j}(p) = g_p(\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial y_j}\right|_p, \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial y_i}\right|_p)$.
	\end{itemize}

	If all the $A_{i,j}$ are $C^{r-1}$ maps then all the $B_{i,j}$ are $C^{r-1}$ maps on $U \cap V$.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		To see why, let $\mathbf{A}(p)$ and $\mathbf{B}(p)$ be the matrices with entries $A_{i,j}(p)$ and $B_{i,j}(p)$\\ respectively. Also let $\tau: \psi(U \cap V) \to \varphi(U \cap V)$ be the $C^{r}$ chart transition function. Then by doing a change of basis like in set 2 problem 2 two pages ago, we can get for all $p \in U \cap V$ that:

		{\centering $\mathbf{B}(p) = (\Df \tau(\psi(p)))^{\trans}\mathbf{A}(p) (\Df \tau(\psi(p)))$.\retTwo\par}

		Yet going component by component, this is equivalent to saying that:
		
		{\centering$B_{i,j}(p) = \sum\limits_{k=1}^n \sum\limits_{\ell = 1}^n \frac{\partial x_k}{\partial y_i}(p) \frac{\partial x_\ell}{\partial y_j}(p) A_{k,\ell}(p)$.\retTwo\par}

		So, each $B_{i,j}$ is a $C^{r-1}$ map on $U \cap V$ since the right hand side of the above\\ equation is $C^{r-1}$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
\end{myIndent}

A \udefine{Riemannian manifold} is a manifold equipped with a Riemannian metric. These manifolds are very important and in Math 250b during Winter quarter we will go way more in depth about them. The T.L.D.R. though for now is that a Riemannian metric allows one to talk about curvature or lengths or areas/volumes. Hopefully that is enough background to make the next question make sense.\retTwo

\Hstatement\blab{Set 2 Problem 3:} Show that if $M$ is a $C^r$ manifold (where $r \geq 1$) then $M$ admits a Riemannian metric.
\begin{myIndent}\HexOne
	\ul{Lemma:} Suppose $(U, \varphi)$ is a smooth chart on $M$. Then there is a well-defined Riemannian metric on $U$.
	\begin{myIndent}\HexTwoP
		Why?\\
		Write $\varphi = (x_1, \ldots, x_n)$. Then for all $p \in U$ define:
		
		{\centering$g_p(u, v) = \sum\limits_{i=1}^n \df x_i(u) \df x_i(v)$.\retTwo\par}

		Checking that this is an inner product is easy. Also all the coordinate functions with respect to the obvious frame are either the constant $0$ or constant $1$ functions.\newpage
	\end{myIndent}

	Now let $\{(U_\alpha, \varphi)\}_{\alpha \in A}$ be an open cover of $M$ with smooth charts. For each $\alpha \in A$ we can by the prior lemma find a Riemmanian metric $\{g_p^{(\alpha)}\}_{p \in U_\alpha}$ over  $U_\alpha$. Next, we can find a $C^{r}$ partition of unity $\{\phi_\alpha: M \to [0, 1]\}_{\alpha \in A}$ such that:
	\begin{itemize}
		\item $\sum_{\alpha \in A} \phi_\alpha = 1$ on $M$;
		\item $\supp(\phi_\alpha) \subseteq U_\alpha$ for all $\alpha \in A$;
		\item Every $p \in M$ has an open neighborhod $V \subseteq M$ such that only finitely many $\phi_\alpha$ are nonzero anywhere $V$.\retTwo
	\end{itemize} 

	Now set $h_p = \sum_{\alpha \in A}\phi_\alpha(p)g_p^{(\alpha)}$ for all $p \in M$. Note that this sum is well-defined because at the points $p$ where any $g_p^{(\alpha)}$ is not defined, we know $\phi_\alpha(p) = 0$ and so we can just ignore that term.\retTwo

	I claim that $\{h_p\}_{p \in M}$ is a Riemmanian metric.
	\begin{myIndent}\HexTwoP
		To see why $h_p : T_p M \times T_p M$ is a well-defined inner product, just note that finite\\ summing of inner product functions and scaling of inner product functions by positive real numbers gives us back a well-defined inner product function.\retTwo

		Meanwhile, to prove that $h^p$ varies $C^{r-1}$-ly over $M$, consider any $p \in M$ and let $V \subseteq M$ be an open neighborhood on which only finitely many $\phi_\alpha$ are nonzero. (In particular, say that the only nonzero $\phi_\alpha$ are $\phi_{\alpha_1}, \ldots, \phi_{\alpha_k}$). By shrinking $V$, we can further assume that $p \in \bigcap_{j=1}^k \supp(\phi_{\alpha_j})$. This has the added consequence that $p \in \bigcap_{j=1}^k U_{\alpha_j}$. So by shrinking $V$ again we can assume that $V \subseteq \bigcap_{j=1}^k U_{\alpha_j}$. And this is useful because it lets us say that $g_p^{(\alpha_j)}$ is well defined for all $p \in V$ and $1 \leq j \leq k$.\retTwo
		
		Now let $y_1, \ldots, y_n$ be smooth coordinates on $V$. Note that we have at least $k$ choices of such smooth coordinates to pick from. So, we don't need to restrict $V$ further to get those coordinates.\retTwo

		We denote the $(k, \ell)$th coordinate function for $\{g^{(\alpha_j)}_p\}_{p \in V}$ as:
		
		{\centering$A^{(\alpha_j)}_{k, \ell}(p) \coloneqq g_p^{(\alpha_j)}(\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial y_\ell}\right|_p, \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial y_k}\right|_p)$.\retTwo\par}

		And now the $(k, \ell)$th coordinate function for $\{h_p\}_{p \in V}$ is:

		{\centering $B_{k, \ell}(p) = \sum_{j=1}^k \phi_{\alpha_j}(p)A_{k, \ell}^{(\alpha_j)}(p)$ \retTwo\par}

		Thus the coordinate functions for $\{h_p\}_{p \in M}$ are $C^{r-1}$ maps. \HexOne  $\blacksquare$\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
\end{myIndent}

\blab{Set 2 Problem 7:} \hypertarget{Math 250A Set 2 Problem 7}{Let} $\alpha$ be an irrational number.
\begin{enumerate}
	\item[(i)] Show that for all integers $N > 0$ there exists integers $m, n$ with $1 \leq n \leq N$ such that $|n\alpha - m| < 1/N$.
	\begin{myIndent}\HexOne
		Proof:\\
		Let $\mathrm{frac}(x)$ denote the non-integer part of $x$. In particular, we will make it so that $\mathrm{frac}(x) \in [0, 1)$ by defining:

		{\centering $\mathrm{frac}(x) = \begin{cases} x - \lfloor x \rfloor & \text{ if } x \geq 0 \\ \lceil x \rceil - x & \text{ if } x < 0 \end{cases}$ \newpage\par}

		It suffices to show that there exists $n \in \{1, \ldots, N\}$ such that:
		
		{\centering$\mathrm{frac}(n\alpha) \in [0, \frac{1}{N}) \cup (\frac{N - 1}{N}, 1)$.\retTwo\par}

		Yet note by partitioning $[0, 1)$ into $N$ intervals of length $1/N$ and then considering the $N + 1$ many numbers $0, 1, \ldots, N$, we can conclude by the pigeonhole principle that there exists some $0 \leq k < n$ as well as distinct integers $i, j \in \{0, 1, \ldots, N\}$ with:
		
		{\centering$\frac{k}{N} \leq \mathrm{frac}(i\alpha), \mathrm{frac}(j\alpha) < \frac{k+1}{N}$.\retTwo\par}

		Without loss of generality suppose $i < j$. Then $n \coloneqq j - i \in \{1, \ldots, N\}$. Also, we will get that $\mathrm{frac}(n\alpha) \in [0, \frac{1}{N}) \cup (\frac{N - 1}{N}, 1)$ as we wanted.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	\item[(ii)] Let $\mathbb{T} = S^1 \times S^1$ denote the torus.
	\begin{myIndent}\pracOne
		Note that $\mathbb{T} = \Phi^{-1}((1, 1))$ where $\Phi: \mathbb{R}^4 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ is given by $\Phi(x, y, z, w) = (x^2 + y^2, z^2 + w^2)$. Also, $\Phi$ has full rank so long $(x, y) \neq 0$ and $(z, w) \neq 0$. It follows that $\mathbb{T}$ is a regular level set of $\Phi$. So, $\mathbb{T}$ is a $2$-dimensional embedded submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^4$ without a boundary.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
	We identify $\mathbb{R}^4 = \mathbb{R}^2 \times \mathbb{R}^2 \cong \mathbb{C} \times \mathbb{C}$. Now let $\gamma: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{T}$ be given by $\gamma(t) = (e^{2\pi i t}, e^{2\pi i \alpha t})$. Then show $\gamma$ is an injective immersion.
	\begin{myIndent}\HexOne
		Injectivity is the hardest to show. So suppose $\gamma(t_1) = \gamma(t_2)$. Then we must have that there exists integers $n, m$ such that:
		
		{\centering$2\pi t_1 = 2\pi t_2 + 2n\pi$ and $2\pi \alpha t_1 = 2\pi \alpha t_2 + 2m\pi$.\retTwo\par}

		Dividing by $2\pi$ we equivalently need:

		{\centering$t_1 =  t_2 + n$ and $\alpha t_1 = \alpha t_2 + m$.\retTwo\par}

		But then $\alpha t_2 + \alpha n = \alpha t_2 + m$. In other words, $\alpha n = m$. And finally, because $\alpha$ is irrational, the only integer sollutions to this are if $m = 0$ and $n = 0$. So, $t_1 = t_2 + 0$ and we've proven injectivity.\retTwo

		To show $\gamma$ is an immersion into $\mathbb{T}$, it suffices to show that $\gamma$ is an immersion into\\ the ambient manifold $\mathbb{R}^4 \cong \mathbb{C} \times \mathbb{C}$. This is easy though. Just observe that\\ $\gamma^\prime(t) = (2\pi i e^{2\pi i t}, 2\pi i \alpha e^{2\pi i \alpha t})$. Yet neither complex coordinate of $\gamma^\prime(t)$ ever equals\\ $0$. So, $\gamma^\prime(t) \neq 0$ for all $t \in \mathbb{R}$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	\item[(iii)] Show for all $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists an integer $n > 0$ such that $|\gamma(n) - \gamma(0)| < \varepsilon$.
	\begin{myIndent}\pracOne
		Here, we set $|(z, w) - (z^\prime, w^\prime)| \coloneqq |z - z^\prime| + |w - w^\prime|$ for all $z, z^\prime, w, w^\prime \in \mathbb{C}$. This metric generates the product topology on $\mathbb{C} \times \mathbb{C}$ which is identical to the Euclidean topology of $\mathbb{R}^4$. So, this metric induces the topology on $\mathbb{T}$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	\begin{myIndent}\HexOne
		We know the map $t \mapsto e^{2\pi i t}$ is a uniformly continuous function from $\mathbb{R}$ to $S^1$. So, for any $\varepsilon > 0$ we can find $\delta > 0$ such that $|t_1 - t_2| < \delta$ implies that $|e^{2\pi i t_1} - e^{2\pi i t_2}| < \varepsilon$.\newpage

		Next, pick a positive integer $N$ such that $1 / N < \delta$. Then from part (i) we know that there exist integers $m, n$ with $1 \leq n \leq N$ such that $|n\alpha - m| < 1 / N < \delta$. In turn, we have that:

		{\centering$|\gamma(n) - \gamma(0)| = |1 - 1| + |e^{2\pi i \alpha n} - 1| = |e^{2 \pi i \alpha n} - e^{2 \pi i m}| < \varepsilon$.\retTwo\par}
	\end{myIndent}

	\item[(iv)] Show that $\gamma$ is not a homeomorphism onto its image. So, $\gamma(\mathbb{R})$ is not an embedded\\ submanifold of $\mathbb{T}$.
	\begin{myIndent}\HexOne
		If $\gamma$ were a homeomorphism then there would exist a continuous inverse function $\gamma^{-1}: \gamma(\mathbb{R}) \to \mathbb{R}$ (where $\gamma(\mathbb{R})$ is equipped with the subspace topology). And now if $(z_k, w_k) \to (1, 1) \in \gamma(\mathbb{R})$, we ought to have $\gamma^{-1}(z_k, w_k) \to \gamma^{-1}(1, 1) = 0$ in $\mathbb{R}$.\retTwo

		Yet by (iii) we know there is a sequence $\{n_k\}_{k \in \mathbb{N}} \subseteq \mathbb{Z}_{> 0}$ with $\gamma(n_k) \to \gamma(0) = (1, 1)$. And now we have a contradiction as $n_k = \gamma^{-1}(\gamma(n_k))$ does not converge to\\ $0 = \gamma^{-1}(\gamma(0))$ as $k \to \infty$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	\item[(v)] Show that $\gamma(\mathbb{R})$ is a dense subset of $\mathbb{T}$.
	\begin{myIndent}\HexOne
		Given any point $(z, w) \in \mathbb{T}$, we can write it as $(e^{2\pi i A}, e^{2\pi i B})$ for some real numbers $A$ and $B$.\retTwo
		
		But now note for any integer $n$ that:

		{\centering $\gamma(A + n) = (e^{2\pi i A}, e^{2\pi i \alpha (A + n)})$. \retTwo\par}

		Thus, to show $(z, w) \in \overline{\gamma(\mathbb{R})}$ it suffices to show there exists a sequence of\\ integers $\{n_k\}_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that $e^{2\pi i \alpha A}e^{2\pi i \alpha n_k} \to e^{2\pi i B}$. Or equivalently, upon letting\\ $C = B - \alpha A$, we need to find a sequence of integers $\{n_k\}_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that:
		
		{\centering$e^{2\pi i (\alpha n - C)} \to 1$\retTwo\par}

		By the continuity of the map $t \mapsto e^{2\pi i t}$, in order to prove such a sequence exists\\ it suffices to prove for any $\varepsilon > 0$ that there exists integers $n$ and $m$ such that\\ $|\alpha n - C - m| < \varepsilon$. One more simplifying assumption is that if $C = 0$ then we\\ are already done by part (i). Otherwise, by moving integers over onto $m$, we can\\ assume without loss of generality that $C \in (0, 1)$.\retTwo

		Pick $N > 0$ with $\frac{1}{N} < \varepsilon$. Then we know from part (i) that there exists integers $n$ and $m$ with $|n\alpha - m| < \frac{1}{N}$. By negating $n$ and $m$ potentially, we can guarentee that:
		
		{\centering$0 < n\alpha - m < \frac{1}{N} < \varepsilon$.\retTwo\par}

		Let $K$ be the unique integer such that $(K - 1)(n\alpha - m) \leq C < K(n\alpha - m)$. Then we know that $0 < Kn\alpha - C - Km \leq n\alpha - m < \varepsilon$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
\end{enumerate}

\hTwo\mySepTwo\newpage

\dispDate{10/17/2026}

\blect{Math 231A Lecture Notes:}\\

I have a few more notes about harmonic functions to take and then I will move on to talking about the heat equation. To start off, the following is useful for bounding harmonic functions. (Also once again I'll just be assuming $n \geq 2$ always.)\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Harnack's Inequality:} Suppose $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is an open set and $K$ is a connected compact set contained in $U$. Then there exists a constant $C > 0$ such that:

{\centering$\max_{x \in K}(u) \leq C \min_{x \in K}(u)$\\[4pt]\par}

for all harmonic functions $u: U \to \mathbb{R}^n$ with $u \geq 0$ on $U$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	\begin{myIndent}\myComment
		Note that $C$ does not depend on the function $u$ at all.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Proof:\\
	Set $r = \frac{1}{4}d(K, \partial U) \coloneqq \frac{1}{4}\inf\{|x - y| : x \in K, y \in \partial U\}$. Since $K$ and $\partial U$ are disjoint closed sets with $K$ compact, we know $r > 0$.\retTwo

	Now for any $x \in K$ and $y \in \overline{B_r(x)}$ we know by the mean value theorem plus the fact that $u$ is nonnegative that:
	
	{\centering$u(x) = \frac{1}{(2r)^n \alpha(n)}\int_{B_{2r}(x)}u \geq \frac{1}{(2r)^n\alpha(n)}\int_{B_{r}(y)}u = \frac{r^n \alpha(n)}{(2r)^n \alpha(n)}u(y) = \frac{1}{2^n}u(y)$\retTwo\par}

	But now observe that because $K$ is compact, we can cover cover $K$ with a finite number $N$ of balls: $B^{(1)}, \ldots, B^{(N)}$, each with radius $r/2$ and centered at a point in $K$. Next, I claim that because $K$ is connected, we can for any $x, y \in K$ always find $z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_\ell \in K$ (where $\ell \leq 2N - 2$) such that $|x - z_1| \leq r$, $|z_i - z_{i+1}| \leq r$ for all $i$, and $|z_\ell - y| \leq r$. In fact, I'll even prove a slightly more general lemma.\retTwo

	\ul{Lemma:} Suppose $(X, d)$ is any metric space, $A \subseteq X$ is a connected set, and there exists finitely many sets $E_1, \ldots, E_N$ of diameter at most $r$ covering $A$. Given any $x, y \in A$ we can always find points $z_1, \ldots, z_\ell \in A$ (where $\ell \leq 2N - 2)$ such that $d(x, z_1) \leq r$, $d(z_i, z_{i+1}) \leq r$ for each $i$, and $d(z_\ell, y) \leq r$.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		Proof:\\
		It suffices to fix $x \in A$. Now to start off, I shall disregard getting an upper bound for $\ell$ and just show that for any $y \in A$ there even exists points $z_1, \ldots, z_\ell \in A$ such that $d(x, z_1) \leq r$, $d(z_i, z_{i+1}) \leq r$ for each $i$, and $d(z_\ell, y) < r$. To do this, I shall let $C \subseteq A$ be the set of all $y \in A$ such that this is possible. Note that $C$ is nonempty because trivially $x \in C$. Also, we can easily verify both $C$ and $A - C$ are open subsets of $A$. Since $A$ is connected, this thus proves that $C = A$.\retTwo

		Now fixing $y \in A$, we've shown that there are $z_1, \ldots, z_{\ell} \in A$ with $d(x, z_1) \leq r$, $d(z_i, z_{i+1}) \leq r$ for each $i$, and $d(z_\ell, y)\leq r$. For ease of notation, I'll let $z_0 \coloneqq x$ and $z_{\ell + 1} \coloneqq y$.\newpage

		If $\ell > 2N - 2$ then we know by the pigeonhole principle that there are integers $0 \leq i_1 < i_2 < i_3 \leq \ell + 1$ with $z_{i_1}, z_{i_2}, z_{i_3}$ all in the same set $E_j$. Then as $E_j$ has diameter at most $r$, we know $d(z_{i_1}, z_{i_3}) \leq r$. So, we can disregard each of the $z_j$ with $i_1 < j < i_3$ to get another collection of points satisfying our lemma. In particular, this collection has at least one less element because we disregarded $z_{i_2}$.\retTwo

		By repeating the prior reasoning finitely many times, we will eventually get that\\ $\ell \leq 2N - 2$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Based on the prior lemma, we can now see for any nonnegative harmonic function\\ $u: U \to \mathbb{R}$ and any $x, y \in K$ that:

	{\centering $ u(x) \geq \left(\frac{1}{2^n}\right)^{2N - 1}u(y)$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo\par}
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo I also want to motivate why we'd care about {\color{OliveGreen}Green's functions}.\retTwo

\pracOne\mySepTwo
Firstly, I want to briefly go over how the textbook (see \inLinkRap{Citation 16}{citation 16}) that my 231 class is\\ loosely based on defines what it means for an open set to have a $C^r$ boundary (where $r \geq 1$).\retTwo

Let $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be an open set and let $k \geq 1$. Evans (the author of that textbook) says that\\ $U$ has a \udefine{$C^k$ boundary} if for each $x^{(0)} \in \partial U$ there exists $r > 0$ and a $C^k$ function\\ $\gamma: \mathbb{R}^{n-1} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that upon relabeling and reorienting the coordinate axes if necessary, we have that:

{\centering $U \cap B(x^{(0)}, r) = \{x \in B(x^{(0)}, r) : x_n < \gamma(x_1, \ldots, x_{n-1})\}$ \retTwo\par}

\textit{I} claim that this happens if and only if $U$ is the interior of a regular domain $D$ without\\ corners and whose boundary is $\partial U$.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	$(\Longleftarrow)$\\
	Hopefully it is obvious how this direction is an easy result of the theorem on\\ \inLinkRap{Theorem page 1170}{pages 1170-1171}.\retTwo

	$(\Longrightarrow)$\\
	We know $D = U \cup \partial U$ is a closed subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$. So if it were a submanifold it would be properly embedded. Also it's clear that $U$ is a $C^r$ submanifold of codimension $0$. At the same time, if $p \in \partial U$ and we let $\gamma$ and $B(x^{(0)}, r)$ be as described in the above definition, then we can apply a change of coordinates:

	{\centering $(x_1, \ldots, x_n) \mapsto (x_1, \ldots, x_{n-1}, \gamma(x_1, \ldots, x_{n-1}) - x_n)$ \retTwo\par}

	in order to get an $n$-dimensional half slice chart for $D$ centered at $p$.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}
\mySepTwo

\hTwo Now suppose $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a bounded open set with a $C^1$ boundary. At any point $p \in \partial U$ we let $v(p)$ denote the outward pointing unit normal vector. Also let $\Phi: \mathbb{R}^n - \{0\} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the fundamental solution of $-\triangle$. (See \inLinkRap{Fundamental Solution of $-\triangle$}{page 1181}). And let $\tau_x f(y) \coloneqq f(y - x)$.\newpage

\exTwo\ul{Observation:} Let $u \in C^2(\overline{U})$ be an arbitrary function. Then for any $x \in U$:
$$u(x) = \int_{\partial U} \Phi(y - x)\frac{\partial u}{\partial v}(y) - u(y)\frac{\partial (\tau_x\Phi)}{\partial v}(y)\df S(y) - \int_U \Phi(y - x)\triangle u(y)\df y$$
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Proof:\\
	Fix any $x \in U$ and let $\varepsilon > 0$ be small enough so that $\overline{B_\varepsilon(x)} \subseteq U$. Then let $V_\varepsilon = U - B_\varepsilon$.\retTwo

	We have by {\color{OliveGreen}Green's $2$nd identity} that:

	{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
		$\int_{V_\varepsilon} \Phi(y - x)\triangle u(y) \df y = \int_{\partial V_\varepsilon} \Phi(y - x) \frac{\partial u}{\partial v}(y) - u(y)\frac{\partial (\tau_x\Phi)}{\partial v}(y)\df S(y)$\\ [8pt]
		$\phantom{\int_U \Phi(y - x)\triangle u(y) \df y} = \int_{\partial U} \Phi(y - x) \frac{\partial u}{\partial v}(y) - u(y)\frac{\partial (\tau_x\Phi)}{\partial v}(y)\df S(y)$\\ [2pt]
		$\phantom{aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa} - \int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(x)} \Phi(y-x) \frac{\partial u}{\partial v}(y) - u(y)\frac{\partial (\tau_x\Phi)}{\partial v}(y)\df S(y)$
	\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

	But now $\left|\int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(x)} \Phi(y - x) \frac{\partial u}{\partial v}(y)\df S(y)\right| = \int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(x)} |\Phi(y - x)| \cdot |\nabla u(y)|\df S(y)$. For\\ small enough $\varepsilon$ we can guarentee that there is some $C > 0$ with $|\nabla u(y)| \leq C$ for\\ all $y \in B_\varepsilon(x)$. And thus:

	{\centering $\left|\int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(x)} \Phi(y - x) \frac{\partial u}{\partial v}(y)\df S(y)\right| \leq C\varepsilon^{n-1} n\alpha(n) \max_{y \in \partial B_\varepsilon(0)}|\Phi(y)|$ \retTwo\par}

	If $n = 2$ then $\varepsilon \ln(\varepsilon) \to 0$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$. In other words $\ln(\varepsilon) = o(\varepsilon^{-1})$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$.\\ Similarly, if $n \geq 3$ then $\varepsilon^{2-n} = o(\varepsilon^{1 - n})$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$. So in general, we can conclude:

	{\centering $C\varepsilon^{n-1} n\alpha(n) \max_{y \in \partial B_\varepsilon(0)}|\Phi(y)| = \varepsilon^{n-1}o(1 - n) = o(1)$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$. \retTwo\par}
	
	Meanwhile, note that if $n = 2$ and $y \neq 0$ then $\nabla \Phi(y) \cdot \frac{y}{|y|} = \frac{-1}{2\pi|y|}$. Similarly, if $n \geq 3$ then $\nabla \Phi(y) \cdot \frac{y}{|y|} = \frac{-1}{n\alpha(n)|y|^{n-1}}$. So, we can say that:

	{\center$\int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(x)}  u(y)\frac{\partial (\tau_x\Phi)}{\partial v}(y)\df S(y) = \frac{-1}{n\alpha(n)\varepsilon^{n-1}}\int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(x)}u(y)\df S(y) \to -u(x)$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$. \retTwo\par}

	And thus we've proven that by taking $\varepsilon \to 0$, we have that:

	{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
		$\int_{V_\varepsilon} \Phi(y - x)\triangle u(y) \df y = \int_{\partial V_\varepsilon} \Phi(y - x) \frac{\partial u}{\partial v}(y) - u(y)\frac{\partial (\tau_x\Phi)}{\partial v}(y)\df S(y)$\\ [8pt]
		$\phantom{\int_U \Phi(y - x)\triangle u(y) \df y} = \int_{\partial U} \Phi(y - x) \frac{\partial u}{\partial v}(y) - u(y)\frac{\partial (\tau_x\Phi)}{\partial v}(y)\df S(y) - u(x)$. $\blacksquare$
	\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo Based on the prior observation, we can thus say that $u$ is uniquely determined on $U$ by $u$ and $\frac{\partial u}{\partial v}$ on $\partial U$ as well as $\triangle u$ on $U$. That said though, our PDE is actually over-determined if we give boundary conditions for both $u$ and $\frac{\partial u}{\partial v}$ on $\partial U$.\retTwo

We focus on the Dirichlet problem (i.e. where we don't control for $\frac{\partial u}{\partial v}$ at all). So, we need to cancel out the integral $\int_{\partial U} \Phi(y - x)\frac{\partial u}{\partial v}(y)\df S(y)$. To do this, we shall assume there exists a corrector function $\phi: U \times \overline{U} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that:
\begin{itemize}
	\item $\triangle_y \phi(x, y) = 0$ for all $x, y \in U$
	\item $\phi(x, y) = \Phi(y - x)$ for all $x \in U$ and $y \in \partial U$.
	\item $\phi^x(y) \coloneqq \phi(x, y)$ satisfies that $\phi^x \in C^2(\overline{U})$.
\end{itemize}
\begin{myIndent}\myComment
	(Don't worry for now about if $\phi$ exists. It will be our goal later to prove it exists and calculate it in the cases we are interested in.)\newpage
\end{myIndent}

By {\color{OliveGreen}Green's $2$nd identity} we have that:
$$-\int_U \phi^x(y)\triangle u(y) \df y = \int_{\partial U}u(y)\frac{\partial \phi^x}{\partial v}(y) - \Phi(y - x) \frac{\partial u}{\partial v}(y) \df S(y)\text{.}$$

\phantom{.}\\And by combining that with our prior observation we get that:
$$u(x) = \int_{\partial U} u(y)\left[\frac{\partial \phi^x}{\partial v}(y) - \frac{\partial (\tau_x\Phi)}{\partial v}(y)\right]\df S(y) + \int_U \left[\phi^x(y) - \Phi(y - x)\right]\triangle u(y)\df y$$

\phantom{.}\\ Notably the prior expression writes $u$ purely in terms of $u|_{\partial U}$ and $\triangle u$ on $U$.\retTwo

We define {\color{OliveGreen}\udefine{Green's function}}\udefine{ associated to the domain $\overline{U}$} to be the map:

{\centering$G(x, y) \coloneqq \Phi(y - x) - \phi^x(y)$.\retTwo\par}

And by the prior reasoning, we can conclude the following theorem:\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Theorem:} Suppose $u \in C^2(\overline{U})$ satisfies that $-\triangle u = f$ on $U$ and $u = g$ on $\partial U$ (where\\ $f$ and $g$ are continuous). Then:
$$u(x) = -\int_{\partial U}u(y)\frac{\partial G}{\partial v}(x, y)\df S(y) + \int_U f(y) G(x, y)\df y\text{.}$$
\begin{myIndent}\myComment
	(Here $\frac{\partial G}{\partial v}(x, y) = \nabla_y G(x, y) \cdot v$.)\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo\begin{myIndent}
	\mySepFour
\end{myIndent}

Given an open set $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ with a $C^1$ boundary, another way we can interpret {\color{OliveGreen}Green's\\ function} associated to $\overline{U}$ is that it is the map satisfying that $-\triangle_y G(x, y) = \delta_x$ for all\\ $x, y \in U$ and $G(x, y) = 0$ for all $x \in U$ and $y \in \partial U$.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Theorem:} For all $x, y \in U$ with $x \neq y$ we have that $G(x, y) = G(y, x)$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Fix $x, y \in U$ and define $w_1(z) \coloneqq G(x, z)$ and $w_2(z) \coloneqq G(y, z)$. Then $\triangle w_1(z) = 0$ for\\ all $z \in U - \{x\}$, $\triangle w_2(z) = 0$ for all $z \in U - \{y\}$, and $w_1(z) = w_2(z) = 0$ if $z \in \partial U$. Now let $\varepsilon > 0$ be such that $B_{2\varepsilon}(x) \cap B_{2\varepsilon}(y) = \emptyset$ and $B_{2\varepsilon}(x) \cup B_{2\varepsilon}(y) \subseteq U$.\retTwo
	
	By {\color{OliveGreen}Green's 2nd Identity} applied to the domain $V = U - (B_{\varepsilon}(x) \cup B_{\varepsilon}(y))$ we have that:

	{\centering $0 = -\int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(x) \cup \partial B_\varepsilon(y)} w_1 \frac{\partial w_2}{\partial v} - w_2 \frac{\partial w_1}{\partial v}\df S$. \retTwo\par}

	Or after some rearranging, we can equivalently say that:

	{\centering $ \int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(y)}w_1 \frac{\partial w_2}{\partial v}\df S - \int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(y)}  w_2 \frac{\partial w_1}{\partial v}\df S =  \int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(x)} w_2 \frac{\partial w_1}{\partial v}\df S - \int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(x)} w_1 \frac{\partial w_2}{\partial v} \df S$ \retTwo\par}

	But now observe the following:
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		$w_1$ is a smooth function on $B_\varepsilon(y)$ (since it is harmonic on $U - \{x\}$). So, we can find a constant $C > 0$ with $|\nabla w_1| \leq C$ on $\overline{B_\varepsilon(y)}$. And then:

		{\centering $\left|\int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(y)}  w_2 \frac{\partial w_1}{\partial v}\df S\right| \leq C\int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(y)} |w_2|\df S \leq C\varepsilon^{n-1} n\alpha(n) \max\limits_{z \in \partial B_\varepsilon(y)}|w_2(z)|$ \retTwo\par}

		Next, $w_2(z) = \Phi(z - y) - \phi^y(z)$. But $\phi^y$ is a smooth (since it is harmonic) function around $y$. So there exists a constant $D > 0$ with $|\phi^y(z)| \leq D$ for all $z \in \overline{B_\varepsilon(y)}$.\newpage And now:

		{\centering $ C\varepsilon^{n-1} n\alpha(n) \max\limits_{z \in \partial B_\varepsilon(y)}|w_2(z)| \leq CD\varepsilon^{n-1} n \alpha(n) + o(1)$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$ \retTwo\par}

		This finishes proving that $\int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(y)}  w_2 \frac{\partial w_1}{\partial v}\df S \to 0$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Analogous reasoning as in the prior observation shows that $\int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(x)} w_1 \frac{\partial w_2}{\partial v} \df S \to 0$ as\\ $\varepsilon \to 0$. And so, we can conclude that:

	{\centering $\lim\limits_{\varepsilon \to 0^+}\int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(y)}w_1 \frac{\partial w_2}{\partial v}\df S = \lim\limits_{\varepsilon \to 0^+} \int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(x)} w_2 \frac{\partial w_1}{\partial v}\df S$ \retTwo\par}

	Finally, we just have to compute these two limits.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		Note that:
		
		{\centering$\int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(y)}w_1 \frac{\partial w_2}{\partial v}\df S = -\frac{1}{n\alpha(n)\varepsilon^{n-1}}\int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(y)}w_1 \df S + \int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(y)} w_1 \frac{\partial \phi^y}{\partial v} \df S$.\retTwo\par}

		As $\varepsilon \to 0$ we have that $-\frac{1}{n\alpha(n)\varepsilon^{n-1}}\int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(y)}w_1 \df S \to -w_1(y)$.\retTwo

		Meanwhile, because $w_1$ and $\phi^y$ are smooth on $\overline{B_\varepsilon(y)}$ (since they are harmonic), we can find a constant $C$ such that $|w_1 \nabla \phi^y| \leq C$ on $\overline{B_\varepsilon(y)}$. And now:

		{\centering $\left|\int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(y)} w_1 \frac{\partial \phi^y}{\partial v} \df S\right|  \leq C\varepsilon^{n-1}\alpha(n) n \to 0$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$.
		\retTwo\par}

		This finishes showing that $\lim\limits_{\varepsilon \to 0^+}\int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(y)}w_1 \frac{\partial w_2}{\partial v}\df S = -w_1(y)$.\retTwo

		Analogous computations show $\lim\limits_{\varepsilon \to 0^+} \int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(x)} w_2 \frac{\partial w_1}{\partial v}\df S = -w_2(x)$\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	So, we've shown that $-G(x, y) = -w_1(y) = -w_2(x) = -G(y, x)$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo\begin{myIndent}\mySepFour\end{myIndent}

Right now I don't have the tools to prove when a {\color{OliveGreen}Green's function} does or does not\\ exist. However, I'll at least construct {\color{OliveGreen}Green's function} explicitely for the domain $\overline{B_1(0)}$.\\ [-8pt]
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	First I'll find the correction function $\phi^x$ when $x \neq 0$.\retTwo

	Given any $x \in \mathbb{R}^n - \{0\}$ let us denote $\widetilde{x} = \frac{x}{|x|^2}$. Importantly, if $x \in B_1(0)$ then\\ $|\widetilde{x}| > 1$. In turn, we know that $|x|(y - \widetilde{x}) \neq 0$ for all $y \in \overline{B}_1(0)$. And in turn, upon\\ [2pt] letting $\phi^x(y) = \Phi(|x|(y - \widetilde{x}))$, we have that:

	{\center$\triangle \phi^x(y) = |x|^2\triangle \Phi(|x|(y - \widetilde{x})) = |x|^2 \cdot 0 = 0$ for all $y \in B_1(0)$.\retTwo\par}

	Also note that if $|y| = 1$ then:

	{\centering $|x|^2|y - \widetilde{x}|^2 = |y|^2|x|^2 - 2x \cdot y + 1 = 1|x|^2 - 2x \cdot y + |y|^2 = |y - x|^2$ \retTwo\par}

	So $|x||y - \widetilde{x}| = |y - x|$ and this proves that $\phi^x(y) = \Phi(|x|(y - \widetilde{x})) = \Phi(y - x)$\\ for all $y \in \partial B_1(0)$.\retTwo

	Meanwhile, if $x = 0$ then just set the correction function equal to:

	{\centering $\phi^0 \equiv \begin{cases} 0 & \text{ if } n = 2\\ \frac{1}{n(n-2)\alpha(n)} & \text{ if } n = 3\text{.}\end{cases}$\newpage\par}

	Constant functions are trivially harmonic and we know $\phi^0(y) = \Phi(y)$ trivially when\\ $|y| = 1$.

	\mySepFour 

	With that, we are basically done. In the case that $n \geq 3$ we have that:
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		If $x \neq 0$ then:
		
		{\centering$G(x, y) = \Phi(y - x) - \Phi(|x|(y - \widetilde{x})) = \frac{1}{n(n - 2)\alpha(n)}\left(\frac{1}{|y - x|^{n-2}} - \frac{1}{|x|^{n-2}|y - \widetilde{x}|^{n-2}}\right)$\retTwo\par}

		Meanwhile, $G(0, y) = \Phi(y) - \frac{1}{n(n - 2)\alpha(n)} = \frac{1}{n(n - 2)\alpha(n)}\left(\frac{1}{|y|^{n-2}} - 1\right)$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	As for the case $n = 2$, we have that:
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		If $x \neq 0$ then:
		
		{\centering$G(x, y) = \Phi(y - x) - \Phi(|x|(y - \widetilde{x})) = \frac{-1}{2\pi}\left(\ln|y - x| - \ln(|x| \cdot |y - \widetilde{x}|)\right)$\retTwo\par}

		Meanwhile, $G(0, y) = \Phi(y) - 0 = \frac{-1}{2\pi}\ln|y|$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo I'd like to use this computation to find an analog of the Poisson integral formula on \inLinkRap{Math 220c Poisson Integral Formula}{page 808}.\\ [-8pt]
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	For all $n \geq 2$ and $1 \leq i \leq n$ we can calculate that $\frac{\partial}{\partial y_i}\left(\Phi(y - x)\right) = \frac{x_i - y_i}{n\alpha(n)|x - y|^n}$.\retTwo

	In a similar vein, if $x \neq 0$ and $n \geq 2$ then:
	
	{\centering$\frac{\partial}{\partial y_i}\left(\Phi(|x|(y - \widetilde{x}))\right) = \frac{1}{n\alpha(n)|x|^{n-1}|y - \widetilde{x}|^{n-1}} \cdot \frac{|x|}{2|y - \widetilde{x}|} \cdot 2(y_i - \frac{x_i}{|x|^2}) = \frac{1}{n\alpha(n)} \cdot \frac{x_i - y_i|x|^2}{|x|^n |y - \widetilde{x}|^n}$\retTwo\par}

	In particular, if $|y| = 1$ then $|x|^n |y - \widetilde{x}|^n = |y - x|^n$.\retTwo

	Therefore, we get for all $n \geq 2$, $1 \leq i \leq n$, $x \in B_1(0) - \{0\}$, and $y \in \partial B_1(0)$ that:

	{\centering$\frac{\partial}{\partial y_i}G(x, y) = \frac{-1}{n\alpha(n)} \cdot \frac{1 - |x|^2}{|x - y|^n} \cdot y_i$\retTwo\par}

	Also, the prior result extends to when $x = 0$. After all,  because the correction term is constant we know that:

	{\centering$\frac{\partial}{\partial y_i}G(x, y) = \frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial y_i}(y) = \frac{-1}{n\alpha(n)} \cdot \frac{1}{|y|^n} \cdot y_i = \frac{-1}{n\alpha(n)} \cdot \frac{1 - |x|^2}{|x - y|^n} \cdot y_i$\retTwo\par}

	And finally, we can now compute that $\frac{\partial G}{\partial v}(x, y) = \frac{-1}{n\alpha(n)} \cdot \frac{1 - |x|^2}{|x - y|^n} \cdot |y|^2 = \frac{-1}{n\alpha(n)} \cdot \frac{1 - |x|^2}{|x - y|^n}$.\retTwo

	With that, we can now conclude the following corollary:\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\exTwo\ul{Theorem:} Suppose $u \in C^2(\overline{B_1(0)})$ satisfies that $\triangle u = 0$ on $B_1(0)$ and $u|_{\partial B_1(0)} = g$. Then for all $x \in B_1(0)$ we have that:

{\centering $u(x) = \frac{(1 - |x|^2)}{n\alpha(n)}\int_{\partial B_1(0)} \frac{g(y)}{|x - y|^n} \df S(y)$ \retTwo\par}

\hTwo\mySepTwo

I need to move onto other topics. So, its time to talk about the heat equation.\newpage

All exercises for this class are from the Evan's PDE book (see \inLinkRap{Citation 16}{citation 16}). Also as a reminder, $\triangle$ and $\nabla$ and $\partial/\partial v$ are always assumed to be derivative operators on only the spatial variables.\retTwo

\Hstatement\blab{Exercise 2.10:} Suppose $u$ is smooth and satisfies $u_t - \triangle u = 0$ on $\mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R}_{> 0}$.
\begin{enumerate}
	\item[(a)] Show that $w(x, t) \coloneqq u(\lambda x, \lambda^2 t)$ also satisfies that $w_t - \triangle w = 0$ on $\mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R}_{> 0}$ for\\ every $\lambda \in \mathbb{R} - \{0\}$.
	\begin{myIndent}\HexOne
		Proof:\\
		So long as $\lambda \neq 0$ we know that $\lambda^2 t \in \mathbb{R}_{>0}$ for all $t \in \mathbb{R}_{> 0}$. Hence, $w$ is well-defined for all $\lambda \in \mathbb{R} - \{0\}$.\retTwo

		Next, note for any $1 \leq i \leq n$ that $\frac{\partial w}{\partial x_i} (x, t) = \lambda \frac{\partial u}{\partial x_i}(\lambda x, \lambda^2 t)$. In turn:
		
		{\centering$\frac{\partial^2 w}{\partial x_i^2} (x, t) = \lambda^2 \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial^2 x_i}(\lambda x, \lambda^2 t)$ and $\triangle w(x, t) = \lambda^2 \triangle u(\lambda x, \lambda^2 t)$.\retTwo\par}

		Similarly, we get that $w_t(x, t) = \lambda^2 u_t(\lambda x, \lambda^2 t)$. And now we can compute that:

		{\centering $w_t(x, t) - \triangle w(x, t) = \lambda^2(u_t(\lambda x, \lambda^2 t) - \triangle u(\lambda x, \lambda^2 t)) = \lambda^2 \cdot 0 = 0$. \retTwo\par}
	\end{myIndent}

	\item[(b)] Show that $w(x, t) \coloneqq x \cdot \nabla u(x, t) + 2t u_t(x, t)$ satisfies that $w_t - \triangle w = 0$ on\\ $\mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R}_{>0}$.
	\begin{myIndent}\HexOne
		Proof:\\
		Note that due to the product rule plus the fact that derivatives commute with each other, we know for any $1 \leq i \leq n$ that:

		{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
			$\partial_{x_i} w(x, t) = e_i \cdot \nabla u(x, t) + x \cdot \frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\nabla u(x, t) + 2t\partial_{x_i} u_t$\\ [4pt]
			$\phantom{\partial_{x_i} w(x, t)} = u_{x_i}(x, t) + x \cdot \nabla u_{x_i}(x, t) + 2t(u_{x_i})_t(x, t)$.
		\end{tabular} \retTwo\par}

		We can similarly take another partial derivative and get that:

		{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
			$\partial_{x_i}^2 w(x, t) = u_{x_i, x_i}(x, t) + e_i \cdot \nabla u_{x_i}(x, t) + x \cdot \frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\nabla u_{x_i}(x, t) + 2t\partial_{x_i}(u_{x_i})_t(x, t)$\\ [4pt]
			$\phantom{\partial_{x_i}^2 w(x, t)} = 2u_{x_i, x_i}(x, t) + x \cdot \nabla u_{x_i, x_i}(x, t) + 2t(u_{x_i, x_i})_t(x, t)$.
		\end{tabular} \retTwo\par}

		And now we can conclude that:
		
		{\centering$\triangle w(x, t) = 2\triangle u(x, t) + x \cdot \nabla \triangle u(x ,t) + 2t \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\triangle u(x, t)$\retTwo\par}

		Similarly, we can calculate that:

		{\centering $w_t(x, t) = x \cdot \nabla u_t(x, t) + 2u_t(x, t) + 2t \frac{\partial}{\partial t}u_{t}(x, t)$ \retTwo\par}

		And now we get that:
		
		{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
			$w_t(x, t) - \triangle w(x, t)$\\
			$\phantom{aaaaaaa} = 2(u_t(x, t) - \triangle u(x, t)) + x \cdot \nabla (u_t - \triangle u)(x, t) + 2t \frac{\partial}{\partial t}(u_t - \triangle u)(x, t)$\\ [10pt]
			$\phantom{aaaaaaa} = 2(0) + x \cdot 0 + 2t (0) = 0$. $\blacksquare$
		\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}
	\end{myIndent}
\end{enumerate}

\hTwo Now recall from \inLinkRap{Page 921 Fundamental Solution}{page 921} what the fundamental solution to the equation $u_t - \triangle u = 0$ on $\mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R}_{> 0}$ is. In math 148 we denoted it $S^{(n)}$. In math 231 we will denote it $\Phi$.\newpage

The last thing I will probably get to take notes on before returning to differential geometry is finally addressing the incomplete proof \hypertarget{idk reference 3}{on} \inLinkRap{incomplete proof page 925}{pages 924-925}. For the sake of completeness I will not assume a normalized constant of heat transport when I'm showing the following.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Proposition:} Let $\Phi(x, t) = \frac{1}{(2\pi \kappa t)^{n/2}} e^{\frac{-|x|^2}{4\kappa t}}$. Also suppose $f \in C^{2,1}(\mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0})$ with $f$ and all its derivatives bounded by a constant. Then:

{\centering$u(x, t) \coloneqq \int_0^t \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(y, s)\Phi(x - y, t - s)\df y\df s$\\ [4pt]\par}

satisfies that:

{\centering$\lim\limits_{\substack{t \to 0 \\ x^\prime \to x}}u(x^\prime, t) = 0$, that $u \in C^{2,1}(\mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R}_{>0})$, and $u_t - \kappa \triangle u = f$.\retTwo\par}

\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	See the work on \inLinkRap{incomplete proof page 925}{pages 924-925} for why $\lim\limits_{\substack{t \to 0 \\ x^\prime \to x}}u(x^\prime, t) = 0$.\retTwo
	
	Now we just need to show the other claims. To do this, I will first change variables and write $u(x, t) = \int_0^t \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(x - y, t - s)\Phi(y, s) \df y \df s$.\retTwo

	We'll in particular write $G(x, t, s) \coloneqq \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(x - y, t - s)\Phi(y, s)\df y$.\retTwo

	Note that $G_t, G_{x_i}$, and $G_{x_i, x_j}$ all exist, equal what they should equal, and are continuous on $\{(x, t, s) : x \in \mathbb{R}^n, t > 0, \text{ and } 0 < s < t\}$.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		I'll only show this for the $t$th partial derivative. Note that if $0 < s_0 < s < t < s_1$ then:
		
		{\centering$|f_t(x - y, t - s)\Phi(y, s)| \leq \|f_t\|_u\frac{1}{\sqrt{4 \pi \kappa s_0}} e^{\frac{-|y|^2}{4\kappa s_1}}$ where the latter is integrable.\retTwo\par}

		Thus by Leibniz' rule applied to a properly chosen neighborhood containing any $(x, t, s)$ we are interested in, we can conclude that:
		
		{\centering$G_t(x, t, s) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f_t(x - y, t - s)\Phi(y, s)\df y$.\retTwo\par}
		
		Also as $f_t(x - y, t - s)\Phi(y, s)$ is continuous, the same bound from before shows that $G_t$ is continuous.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	I'll furthermore point out that $f$ can be uniquely extended continuously to $\mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ via a result I am about to prove in a tangent, and then nonuniquely extended to a continuous bounded function on all of $\mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R}$ via the Tietz extension theorem. We shall choose such an extension and it doesn't matter which we pick since for the computations of $u_t$ and $\triangle u$ we will only access the value of $f$ on $\mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$.
\end{myIndent}
\pracOne\mySepTwo
I'll actually prove a slightly stronger statement in this tangent because why not?\retTwo

\ul{Proposition:} Suppose $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is an embedded $C^1$ submanifold of codimension $0$ with a nonempty boundary. If $f: D^\circ \to \mathbb{R}$ is a $C^1$ map with  $|\nabla f|$ bounded on $D^\circ$, then for all $x \in \partial D$ we have that $\lim_{x^\prime \to x} f(x^\prime)$ exists.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo 
	Proof:\\
	Let $(V, \varphi)$ be a smooth chart on $D$ containing $x$. Then let $\widehat{V} = \varphi(V)$ and $\widehat{x} = \varphi(x)$. Note\newpage that $(V, \varphi)$ must be a boundary chart as $x \in \partial D$. Hence, without loss of generality we can assume that $\widehat{x} \in \partial \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^n$ and $f \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is defined on $\widehat{V} \cap (\mathbb{R}_{>0}^n)$. Furthermore, because $\varphi$ is a homeomorphism, we know that $\lim_{x^\prime \to x} f(x^\prime)$ exists iff $\lim_{\widehat{x^\prime} \to \widehat{x}} f \circ \varphi^{-1}(\widehat{x^\prime})$ exists. And finally, if we restrict $V$ to the interior of a compact subneighborhood of $x$, we can guarentee that $\|Df \varphi^{-1}\|_{\opnorm}$ is bounded on $\widehat{V}$. In turn, we will get that $|\nabla (f \circ \varphi^{-1})|$ is also bounded on $D^\circ$.\retTwo

	Based on the prior reasoning, it thus suffices to assume $D$ is an open subset of $[0, \infty)^n$\\ and $f \in C^1(D \cap (0, \infty)^n, \mathbb{R})$ with $|\nabla f|$ bounded by some constant. Also, upon\\ writing $x = (x_1, \ldots, x_n)$, we know at least one $x_i$ is zero. By permuting our\\ coordinates if necessary we can always make it so that specifically $x_n = 0$.\retTwo

	Pick $R > 0$ such that $B_R(x) \cap [0, \infty)^n \subseteq D$. Then make the key observation that\\ $B_R(x) \cap (0, \infty)^n$ is convex. As a result, if $|\nabla f(y)| \leq C$ for all $y \in D$, we have that:

	{\centering $|f(y_1) - f(y_2)| \leq C|y_2 - y_1|$ for all $y_1, y_2 \in B_R(x) \cap (0, \infty)^n$. \retTwo\par}

	This lets us conclude that if $\{x_k\}_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ is \textit{any} sequence in $D$ converging to $x$, then\\ $\{f(x_k)\}_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ is a Cauchy sequence (and thus converges).
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		Why?\\
		For any $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $N$ with $|x_m - x_n| < \varepsilon / C$ for all $m, n \geq N$. In turn, $|f(x_m) - f(x_n)| < \varepsilon$ for all $m, n \geq N$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Also, if $\{x_k\}_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ and $\{y_k\}_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ are differing sequences in $D$ converging to $x$ then $\{f(x_k)\}_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ and $\{f(y_k)\}_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ must converge to the same thing.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		Why?\\
		Suppose to the contrary that they don't and then construct a new sequence by\\ $z_{2k - 1} = x_k$ and $z_{2k} = y_k$ for all $k$. Then $\{f(z_k)\}_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ will have two distinct\\ subsequential limits (and thus not converge). Yet we also know $\{z_k\}_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ converges to $x$ in $D$. This contradicts our prior observation. \pracTwo $\blacksquare$
	\end{myIndent}
\end{myIndent}
\mySepTwo\hTwo

\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Continuing where I left off, if $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $t \in \mathbb{R}$, and  $0 < s_0 < s < s_1$ then:
	
	{\centering$|f(x - y, t - s) \Phi(y, s)| \leq \|f\|_u\frac{1}{\sqrt{4 \pi \kappa s_0}} e^{\frac{-|y|^2}{4\kappa s_1}}$\retTwo\par}

	So by Leibniz' rule, we know that $G$ is a well-defined continuous function on the\\ set $\{(x, t, s) \in \mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R} \times (0, \infty)\}$.\retTwo

	Now, we're ready to define $H(x, t, a) \coloneqq \int_0^a G(x, t, s)\df s$ on $\mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R} \times (0, \infty)$.\\ Importantly, $\|G\|_u \leq \|f\|_u$ for all $(x, t, s) \in \mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R} \times (0, \infty)$. So, $H$ is well-defined\\ and continuous. Plus, by the fundamental theorem of calculus we have that:
	
	{\centering$\frac{\partial H}{\partial a}(x, t, a) = G(x, t, a)$ for all $(x, t, a) \in \mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R} \times (0, \infty)$.\retTwo\par}

	Next note that $|G_t(x, t, s)| \leq \|f_t\|_u$ for all:
	
	{\centering$(x, t, s) \in \{(x, t, s) : x \in \mathbb{R}^n, t > 0, \text{ and } 0 < s < t\}$.\retTwo\par}

	This is enough to show by Leibniz's rule that for any $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $t > 0$, and $0 < a \leq t$ that $\frac{\partial H}{\partial t}(x, t, a)$ exists and equals $\int_0^a G_t(x, t, s)\df s$.\newpage

	Now, we can apply chain rule to get that if $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $t > 0$ then:

	{\centering\begin{tabular}{l} 
		$u_t(x, t) = \frac{\partial H(x, t, t)}{\partial t} = \int_0^t G_t(x, t, s)\df s + G(x, t, t)$\\ [4pt]
		$\phantom{u_t(x, t) = \frac{\partial H(x, t, t)}{\partial t}} = \int_0^t \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f_t(x - y, t - s)\Phi(y, s)\df y \df s + \int_{\mathbb{R}^n}f(x - y, 0)\Phi(y, t)$
	\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

	Meanwhile, because $|G_{x_i}(x, t, s) \leq \|f_{x_i}\|_u$ and $|G_{x_i, x_j}(x, t, s)| \leq \|f_{x_i, x_j}\|_u$ for all:

	{\centering$(x, t, s) \in \{(x, t, s) : x \in \mathbb{R}^n, t > 0, \text{ and } 0 < s < t\}$,\\ [4pt]\par}

	we can analogously apply Leibniz's rule to get that:
	
	{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
	$u_{x_i, x_i}(x, t) = \frac{\partial^2 H}{\partial x_i^2}(x, t, t) = \int_{0}^t G_{x_i, x_i}(x, t, s)\df s$\\ [4pt]
	$\phantom{u_{x_i, x_i}(x, t) = \frac{\partial^2 H}{\partial x_i^2}(x, t, t)} = \int_0^t \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f_{x_i, x_i}(x - y, t- s)\Phi(y, s)\df y \df s$.
	\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

	And with that the hard part is now done because we have successfully moved the derivative operators inside our integral expression and proven that:

	{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
		$(\partial_t - \triangle)u(x, t)$\\ [2pt]
		$\phantom{aaaaaa} = \int_0^t \int_{\mathbb{R}^n}(\partial_t - \triangle)f(x - y, t - s)\Phi(y, s)\df y \df s + \int_{\mathbb{R}^n}f(x - y, 0)\Phi(y, t)\df y$.
	\end{tabular} \retTwo\par}

	\mySepThree 

	Now we still need to actually show for any fixed $(x, t) \in \mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R}_{>0}$ that our awful integral expression evaluates to $f(x, t)$. To do this, we consider any fixed $0 < \varepsilon < t$ and then we set:
	\begin{itemize}
		\item $I_\varepsilon \coloneqq \int_\varepsilon^t \int_{\mathbb{R}^n}(\partial_t - \triangle)f(x - y, t - s)\Phi(y, s)\df y \df s$
		\item $J_\varepsilon \coloneqq \int_0^\varepsilon \int_{\mathbb{R}^n}(\partial_t - \triangle)f(x - y, t - s)\Phi(y, s)\df y \df s$
		\item $K \coloneqq \int_{\mathbb{R}^n}f(x - y, 0)\Phi(y, t)\df y$.\retTwo
	\end{itemize}

	Note that $(\partial_t - \triangle)u(x, t) = I_\varepsilon + J_\varepsilon + K$.\retTwo

	\ul{Claim 1:} $J_\varepsilon \to 0$ as $\varepsilon \to 0^+$.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		Why?\\
		We know from our assumptions on $f$ that $\|f_t - \triangle f\|_u < \infty$. In turn, we have that:
		
		{\centering$|J_\varepsilon| \leq \varepsilon \|f_t - \triangle f\|_u \to 0$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$\retTwo\par}
	\end{myIndent}

	\ul{Claim 2:} $I_\varepsilon \to f(x, t) - K$ as $\varepsilon \to 0^+$.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		Why?\\
		Observe that:

		{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
			$\int_\varepsilon^t \int_{\mathbb{R}^n}f_t(x - y, t - s)\Phi(y, s)\df y \df s$\\ [4pt]
			$\phantom{aaaaaaaaaa} = \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \int_\varepsilon^t f_t(x - y, t - s)\Phi(y, s) \df s \df y$ {\color{red}(by Fubini)}\\ [4pt]
			$\phantom{aaaaaaaaaa} = -\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \int_\varepsilon^t \frac{\partial f(x - y, t - s)}{\partial s}\Phi(y, s) \df s \df y$\\ [4pt]
			$\phantom{aaaaaaaaaa} = -\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(x - y, 0)\Phi(y, t)\df y + \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(x - y, t - \varepsilon)\Phi(y, \varepsilon) \df y$\\
			$\phantom{aaaaaaaaaa = -\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(x - y, 0)\Phi(y, t)\df y} + \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \int_\varepsilon^t f(x - y, t - s)\Phi_t(y, s) \df s \df y$\\
			$\phantom{aaaaaaaaaaaaaaa = -\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(x - y, 0)\Phi(y, t)\df y}$ {\color{red}(by integration by parts)}\\ [4pt]
			$\phantom{aaaaaaaaaa} = -K + \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(x - y, t - \varepsilon)\Phi(y, \varepsilon) \df y$\\
			$\phantom{aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa - K} + \int_\varepsilon^t\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(x - y, t - s)\Phi_t(y, s) \df y \df s$ {\color{red}(by Fubini)}.
		\end{tabular}\newpage\par}

		Meanwhile, because $\Phi$ and all its derivatives vanish at infinity, we can conclude via integration by parts that for any $1 \leq i \leq n$ and fixed $\varepsilon \leq s \leq t$ that:

		{\center\begin{tabular}{l}
			$\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f_{x_i, x_i}(x - y, t - s)\Phi(y, s)\df y = -\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}\frac{\partial(f_{x_i}(x - y, t - s))}{\partial y_i} \Phi(y, s) \df y$\\ [4pt]
			$\phantom{\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f_{x_i, x_i}(x - y, t - s)\Phi(y, s)\df y} = \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f_{x_i}(x - y, t - s)\Phi_{y_i}(y, s) \df y$\\ [4pt]
			$\phantom{\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f_{x_i, x_i}(x - y, t - s)\Phi(y, s)\df y} = -\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \frac{\partial f(x - y, t - s)}{\partial y_i}\Phi_{y_i}(y, s) \df y$\\ [4pt]
			$\phantom{\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f_{x_i, x_i}(x - y, t - s)\Phi(y, s)\df y} = \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(x - y, t - s)\Phi_{y_i, y_i}(y, s) \df y$.\\ [4pt]
		\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

		So in conclusion, we get that:

		{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
			$I_\varepsilon = -K + \int_{\mathbb{R}^n}f(x - y, t - \varepsilon)\Phi(y, \varepsilon)\df y + \int_\varepsilon^t \int_{\mathbb{R}^n}f(x - y, t - s)(\Phi_t - \triangle \Phi)(y, s)\df y \df s$
		\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

		But now $\Phi$ satisfies the (homogeneous) heat equation. So the last integral cancels and we are left with:

		{\centering$I_\varepsilon = \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(x - y, t - \varepsilon)\Phi(y, \varepsilon)\df y - K$.\retTwo\par}

		Now note that:
		
		{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
			$\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(x - y, t - \varepsilon)\Phi(y, \varepsilon)\df y$\\ [4pt]
			$\phantom{aaaaaaa} = \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \left[f(x - y, t - \varepsilon) - f(x - y, t)\right]\Phi(y, \varepsilon)\df y + \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(x - y, t)\Phi(y, \varepsilon)\df y$
		\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

		I claim that $\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \left[f(x - y, t - \varepsilon) - f(x - y, t)\right]\Phi(y, \varepsilon)\df y \to 0$ as $\varepsilon \to 0^+$.\\ [-8pt]
		\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
			After all, since $f$ is continuous (and thus in particular uniformly continuous on a compact ball containing $(x, t)$) we can for any $\kappa > 0$ pick some $\delta > 0$ such that $|f(x - y, t - \varepsilon) - f(x - y, t)| < \kappa$ for all $y \in \overline{B_\delta}(x)$ and $\varepsilon < \delta$. In turn for $\varepsilon < \delta$ we have that:

			{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
				$\left|\int_{\overline{B_\delta(x)}} \left[f(x - y, t - \varepsilon) - f(x - y, t)\right]\Phi(y, \varepsilon)\df y\right|$\\ [8pt]
				$\phantom{aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa} \leq \kappa\int_{\overline{B_\delta(x)}}\Phi(y, \varepsilon)\df y \leq \kappa \int_{\mathbb{R}^n}\Phi(y, \varepsilon) \df y = \kappa$.
			\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}
			
			Yet simultaneously, because $|f(x - y, t - \varepsilon) - f(x - y, t)|$ is bounded by $2\|f\|_u$, it is an easy to establish fact that:

			{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
				$\lim\limits_{\varepsilon \to 0^+}\int_{B_\delta(x)^\comp} \left[f(x - y, t - \varepsilon) - f(x - y, t)\right]\Phi(y, \varepsilon)\df y \to 0$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$
			\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

			Therefore:
			
			{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
				$\limsup\limits_{\varepsilon \to 0^+}\left|\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \left[f(x - y, t - \varepsilon) - f(x - y, t)\right]\Phi(y, \varepsilon)\df y\right|$\\ [8pt]
				$\phantom{aaaaaaaaaaaa} = \limsup\limits_{\varepsilon \to 0^+}\left|\int_{\overline{B_\delta(x)}} \left[f(x - y, t - \varepsilon) - f(x - y, t)\right]\Phi(y, \varepsilon)\df y\right| \leq \kappa$
			\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}
