			And since $\kappa$ was arbitrary, we can take $\kappa \to 0$ to finish showing this claim.\retTwo
		\end{myIndent}

		Meanwhile, note that $w(x, \varepsilon) \coloneqq \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(x - y, t)\Phi(y, \varepsilon)\df y$ is just the solution\\ to the (homogeneous) heat equation $w_t - \triangle w = 0$ with an initial value of\\ $w(x, 0) = f(x, t)$. So we can already identify from the proof on \inLinkRap{Heat Equation Homogeneous Solution page 921}{pages 921-922}\\ that $\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(x - y, t)\Phi(y, \varepsilon)\df y \to f(x, t)$ as $\varepsilon \to 0^+$.\retTwo

		This finishes showing that $I_\varepsilon \to f(x, t) - K$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	And now adding together the limits we just proved finishes showing that:
	
	{\centering$u_t(x, t) - \triangle u(x, t) = f(x, t)$. $\blacksquare$\newpage\par}
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo\dispDate{10/23/2026}

\blect{Math 250A Lecture Notes:}\\
Today and maybe tomorrow I need to take lecture notes for this class and also do\\ homework. Once I've dealt with that, I can go back to taking PDE notes.\retTwo

To start off, I want to give an actual atlas for $S^n \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$. Note that this is in fact\\ an embedded submanifold as it is the regular zero set of $\Phi: \mathbb{R}^{n+1} \to \mathbb{R}$ given by\\ $\Phi(x) = |x|^2 - 1$. Note that all the following reasoning is heavily inspired by work on\\ \inLinkRap{placeholder}{page 241} showing that $\mathbb{C}_\infty$ is homeomorphic to $S^2$.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Let $U_1 = S^n - \{(0, \ldots, 0, 1)\}$ and let $\widehat{U}_1 = \mathbb{R}^n$. We define:
	\begin{itemize}
		\item $\varphi_1 : \mathbb{R}^{n+1} - \{(0, \ldots, 0, 1)\} \to \widehat{U}_1$ by:
		
		{\centering$\varphi_1(x_1, \ldots, x_n, x_{n+1}) \coloneqq (\frac{x_1}{1 - x_{n+1}}, \ldots, \frac{x_n}{1 - x_{n+1}})$\retTwo\par}

		\item $\psi_1 : \widehat{U}_1 \to \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ by $\psi_1(x_1, \ldots, x_n) \coloneqq (\frac{2x_1}{1 + |x|^2}, \ldots, \frac{2x_n}{1 + |x|^2}, \frac{|x|^2 - 1}{1 + |x|^2})$.\retTwo
	\end{itemize}

	Note that $\varphi_1$ is a smooth map. It follows that it's restriction to $U_1$ will still be a smooth\\ map with respect to the smooth structure on the open submanifold $U_1 \subseteq S^n \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$.\retTwo

	Meanwhile, note that $\psi_1$ is a smooth map. Furthermore:
	
	{\centering$|\psi_1(x)|^2 = \frac{1}{(1 + |x|^2)^2}(4|x|^2 + (|x|^2 - 1)^2) =  \frac{1}{(1 + |x|^2)^2}(|x|^4 + 2|x|^2 + 1) = 1$.\retTwo\par}

	So, $\psi_1$ maps into $S^n$. \retTwo

	We can further note that $(0, \ldots, 0, 1) \notin \psi_1(\widehat{U}_1)$. And since $U_1 \subseteq S^n \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ is an \textit{embedded} submanifold, we can thus conclude that restricting the codomain of $\psi_1$ does not change that $\psi_1$ is a smooth map.\retTwo

	With that, we've proven that $\varphi_1: U_1 \to \widehat{U}_1$ and $\psi_1: \widehat{U}_1 \to U_1$ are both smooth maps. Finally, I claim that $\psi_1 \circ \varphi_1 = \myId_{U_1}$ and $\varphi_1 \circ \psi_1 = \myId_{\widehat{U}_1}$.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		You do this computation yourself. There's no fancy ideas.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	And with that, we've proven that $(U_1, \varphi_1)$ is a smooth chart on $S^n$.\retTwo

	\mySepThree

	In a similar vein, if $U_2 = S^{n} - \{(0, \ldots, 0, -1)\}$ then we can define another smooth chart $(U_2, \varphi_2)$ on $S^{n}$ by:

	\begin{itemize}
		\item $\varphi_2(x_1, \ldots, x_{n+1}) = (\frac{x_1}{1 + x_{n+1}}, \ldots, \frac{x_n}{1 + x_{n+1}})$,
		\item $\varphi_2^{-1}(x_1, \ldots, x_n) = (\frac{2x_1}{1 + |x|^2}, \ldots, \frac{2x_n}{1 + |x|^2}, \frac{1 - |x|^2}{1 + |x|^2})$.\retTwo
	\end{itemize}
\end{myIndent}

The prior two charts $(U_1, \varphi_1)$ and $(U_2, \varphi_2)$ are called the \udefine{stereographic projections} and\\ they let you cover $S^n$ with the fewest possible charts.
\begin{myIndent}\myComment
	(We can't cover $S^n$ with just a single chart (smooth or not) because that would imply the compact set $S^n$ is homeomorphic to an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ (since $S^n$ has no boundary). But that's impossible.)\newpage
\end{myIndent}

Sometimes, we want to use a smooth graph chart instead though. I'll construct that here.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Let $U = \{(x_1, \ldots, x_{n+1}) \in S^{n} : x_{n+1} > 0\}$. Next set $\widehat{U} = B_1(0) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$. And finally, define the maps:
	\begin{itemize}
		\item $\varphi: \mathbb{R}^{n+1} \to \mathbb{R}^n$ by $\varphi(x_1, \ldots, x_n, x_{n+1}) \coloneqq (x_1, \ldots, x_n)$,
		\item $\psi: \widehat{U} \to \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ by $\psi(x_1, \ldots, x_n) = (x_1, \ldots, x_n, \sqrt{1 - x_1^2 - \ldots - x_n^2})$.\retTwo
	\end{itemize}

	By identical reasoning as before, these become smooth maps from $U$ to $\widehat{U}$ and $\widehat{U} \to U$ respectively. And identically to before, we can prove that $\psi \circ \varphi = \myId_U$ and $\varphi \circ \psi = \myId_{\widehat{U}}$.\retTwo

	This finishes showing that $(U, \varphi|_{U})$ is a smooth chart on $S^{n}$.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

In the prior construction, we can also obviously make the dependent variable in\\ our graph any $x_i$ instead of just $x_{n+1}$. Also, instead of considering the open set\\ $\{(x_1, \ldots, x_{n+1}) \in S^{n} : x_{n+1} > 0\}$ we can insetad consider the open set\\ $\{(x_1, \ldots, x_{n+1}) \in S^{n} : x_{n+1} < 0\}$. And then we just have to negate $\sqrt{1 - x_1^2 - \ldots - x_n^2}$ in our expression for the inverse map.\retTwo

\Hstatement\blab{Set 3 Problem 1:} Note that Oprea writes $\mSpan((x_1, \ldots, x_{n+1})) \in \mathbb{RP}^n$ as $[x_1 : \cdots : x_{n+1}]$.
\begin{enumerate}
	\item[(i)] Show that the map $q: S^2 \to \mathbb{RP}^2$ given by $q(x, y, z) = [x : y : z]$ is a smooth local diffeomorphism.
	\begin{myIndent}\HexOne
		Given any $(x_0, y_0, z_0) \in S^2$ we know at least one coordinate is nonzero. Without loss of generality, I will assume $z_0 > 0$. After all, the argument remains basically identical if $z_0 < 0$. And if $z_0 = 0$ then we can just rename our coordinates and do the exact same proof on our renamed coordinates.\retTwo

		Let $U = \{(x, y, z) \in S^2 : z > 0\}$. Then we have a smooth parametrization\\ $X: B_1(0) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2 \to U$ given by $X(x, y) = (x, y, \sqrt{1 - x^2 - y^2})$. In other\\ words, $(U, X^{-1})$ is a smooth chart on $S^2$ containing $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$.\retTwo

		Meanwhile, recall that $V = \{[x:y:z] \in \mathbb{RP}^2 : z \neq 0\}$ and $\psi: V \to \mathbb{R}^2$ given by $\psi([x:y:z]) = (\frac{x}{z}, \frac{y}{z})$ define a smooth chart on $\mathbb{RP}^2$. In particular, we have that $q(U) \subseteq V$.\retTwo

		To check that $q$ is smooth and a local diffeomorphism, it suffices to show that $q$ is smooth with respect to the local coordinates $(U, X^{-1})$ and $(V, \psi)$, and also that\\ $\Df(\psi \circ q \circ X)$ is invertible on $B_1(0)$. Fortunately, this is easy.
		\begin{myIndent}\HexTwoP
			Note that $\widehat{q} \coloneqq \psi \circ q \circ X: B_1(0) \to \mathbb{R}^2$ is given by:
			
			{\centering$\widehat{q}(x, y) = (\frac{x}{\sqrt{1 - x^2 - y^2}}, \frac{y}{\sqrt{1 - x^2 - y^2}})$.\retTwo\par}

			This is a smooth map on $B_1(0)$. Also:
			$$\Df \widehat{q}(x, y) = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1 - y^2}{(1 - x^2 - y^2)^{3/2}} & \frac{xy}{(1 - x^2 - y^2)^{3/2}} \\ \frac{xy}{(1 - x^2 - y^2)^{3/2}} & \frac{1 - x^2}{(1 - x^2 - y^2)^{3/2}}\end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{(1 - x^2 - y^2)^{3/2}}\begin{bmatrix} 1 - y^2 & xy \\ xy & 1 - x^2\end{bmatrix}$$\newpage

			Since $\frac{1}{(1 - x^2 - y^2)^{3/2}} \neq 0$ ever, we can thus conclude that $\Df \widehat{q}(x, y)$ is singular iff:
			
			{\centering$\begin{bmatrix} 1 - y^2 & xy \\ xy & 1 - x^2\end{bmatrix}$ is singular.\retTwo\par}

			This happens iff $0 = (1 - y^2)(1 - x^2) - x^2 y^2 = 1 - x^2 - y^2$. Yet the latter never happens for all $(x, y) \in B_1(0)$.\retTwo
		\end{myIndent}
	\end{myIndent}

	\item[(ii)] Let $f: S^2 \to \mathbb{R}^4$ be given by $f(x, y, z) = (x^2 - y^2, xy, xz, yz)$. Show that $f$ is a smooth immersion.
	\begin{myIndent}\HexOne
		To start off, let $\iota: S^2 \hookrightarrow \mathbb{R}^3$ be the embedding map. Also let $F: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^4$ be defined by $F(x, y, z) =(x^2 - y^2, xy, xz, yz)$. Then we have that $f = F \circ \iota$. Note that because $F$ an $\iota$ are both smooth, we trivially have that $f$ is smooth. The harder part is showing that $f$ is an immersion.\retTwo

		Now $\Df F(x, y, z) = \begin{bmatrix} 2x & -2y & 0 \\ y & x & 0 \\ z & 0 & x \\ 0 & z & y\end{bmatrix}$.\retTwo

		Based on the above expression, we can now conclude that $\Df F$ is full rank at most points of $S^2$. After all:
		\begin{itemize}
			\item If $x \neq 0$, $y \neq 0$, and $z \neq 0$, then the determinant of the bottom three rows\\ is $-2xyz \neq 0$. 
			\item If $z = 0$ then our matrix simplifies and we can show that $\Df F(x, y, z)$ has full\\ rank if and only if either $x \neq 0$ or $y \neq 0$.
			\item If $x = 0$ and $y \neq 0$ and $z \neq 0$ then we can also simplify our matrix and show\\ that $\Df F(x, y, z)$ has full rank.
			\item And if $y = 0$ and $x \neq 0$ and $z \neq 0$, then we similarly can show that\\ $\Df F(x, y, z)$ has full rank.\retTwo
		\end{itemize}

		In other words, the only points of $S^2$ where $\Df F$ is not full rank are $(0, 0, 1)$\\ and $(0, 0, -1)$. Since a composition of injective linear maps is injective, we can\\ thus conclude that $\df f_p$ is injective for all $p \in S^2 - \{(0, 0, 1), (0, 0, -1)\}$.\retTwo

		As for showing that $\df f_{(0, 0, \pm 1)}$ is injective, we need to show that:
		
		{\centering$T_{(0, 0, \pm 1)} S^2 \cap \ker(\df F_{(0, 0, \pm 1)}) = \{0\}$.\retTwo\par}

		Fortunately, $S^2$ is regular zero set of $\Phi: \mathbb{R}^{3} \to \mathbb{R}$ given by $\Phi(x) = |x|^2 - 1$. Therefore:

		{\centering $T_{(0, 0, \pm 1)} S^2 = \ker(\Df \Phi(0, 0, \pm 1)) = \ker(\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & \pm 2\end{bmatrix}) = \mathbb{R}^2 \times \{0\}$ \retTwo\par}

		Meanwhile, $\ker(\df F_{(0, 0, \pm 1)}) = \ker\left(\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ \pm 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \pm 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\right) = \{(0, 0)\} \times \mathbb{R}$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	\item[(c)] Deduce there exists an embedding $g: \mathbb{RP}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^4$ such that $g \circ q = f$.\newpage
	\begin{myIndent}\HexOne
		From part (a) we know that $q$ is a smooth submersion from $S^2$ to $\mathbb{RP}^2$. Its pretty trivial that $q$ is also surjective. Thirdly, note that the fibers of $q$ are precisely the sets $\{\mVecAst{x}, -\mVecAst{x}\}$ for any $\mVecAst{x} \in S^2$. This is notable because we in turn can see that $f$ is constant on each of the fibers of $q$.\retTwo

		By corollary 4.30 on \inLinkRap{Corollary 4.30 page 1109}{pages 1108-1109}, we thus know there is a unique smooth map $g: \mathbb{RP}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^4$ satisfying that $g \circ q = f$.\retTwo
		
		Now to show that $g$ is an immersion, note for any $[x] \in \mathbb{RP}^2$ that we can pick $x \in S^2$ with $q(x) = [x]$. Then $\df g_{[x]} \circ \df q_x = \df f_x$. Yet because $q$ is a local diffeomorphism, we know  $\df q_x$ is invertible. So, $\df g_{[x]} = \df f_x \circ (\df q_x)^{-1}$ is the composition of two injective linear maps and is thus injective.\retTwo

		Next, to prove that $g$ is an injection it suffices to show that if $f(x_1, y_1, z_1) = f(x_2, y_2, z_2)$ then $(x_1, y_1, z_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2, z_2)$ are in the same fiber of $p$.
		\begin{myIndent}\HexTwoP
			In other words, we need to show that $(x_2, y_2, z_2) = \pm(x_1, y_1, z_1)$.\retTwo

			To do this, recall from math 220 that the map $s(x, y) \coloneqq (x^2 - y^2, 2xy)$ acts homeomorphically (and in fact biholomorphically) from:
			\begin{itemize}
				\item $\mathbb{R} \times (0, \infty) \to \mathbb{R}^2 - \{(x, 0) : x \geq 0\}$,
				\item $\mathbb{R} \times (-\infty, 0) \to \mathbb{R}^2 - \{(x, 0) : x \geq 0\}$.\retTwo
			\end{itemize}

			Scaling the $y$ axis afterwards doesn't modify the codomain. So, the fiber of any $(x^\prime, y^\prime) \in \mathbb{R}^2 - \{(x, 0) : x \geq 0\}$ intersects $\mathbb{R}^2 - \{\mathbb{R} \times \{0\}\}$ at exactly two points.\retTwo

			Meanwhile, if $y = 0$ then we know $(x^2 - y^2, xy) = (x^2, 0) \in (0, \infty) \times \{0\}$. So, none of the $(x, 0)$ contribute any points to the fibers in the prior paragraph. Also, the fiber of every $(x^\prime, 0) \in \mathbb{R}^2 - \{(x, 0) : x > 0\}$ has exactly two points. Meanwhile, the fiber of $(0, 0)$ is just $\{(0, 0)\}$.\retTwo

			With that, we've shown that if $h: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ is given by $h(x, y) = (x^2 - y^2, xy)$ then $h^{-1}(\{(x^\prime, y^\prime)\})$ has exactly two points unless $(x^\prime, y^\prime) = (0, 0)$.\retTwo

			Finally, note that $h(x, y) = h(-x, -y)$ for all $(x, y) \in \mathbb{R}^2$. Hence, we've proven that if $h(x_1, y_1) = a = h(x_2, y_2)$ then $(x_1, y_1) = \pm (x_2, y_2)$.

			\mySepFour

			Now the prior reasoning was relevant because if $f(x_1, y_1, z_1) = f(x_2, y_2, z_2)$ then automatically $h(x_1, y_1) = h(x_2, y_2)$. So,  there exists $\kappa \in \{-1, +1\}$ with $x_2 = \kappa x_1$ and $y_2 = \kappa y_1$.\retTwo

			Now suppose $x_1 \neq 0$. Then $x_1 z_1 = x_2 z_2 = \kappa x_1 z_2 \implies z_1 = \kappa z_2$. But $\kappa = \kappa^{-1}$. So, we can conclude $z_2 = \kappa z_1$ as well.\retTwo

			Similarly, if $y_1 \neq 0$ then we can conclude that $z_2 = \kappa z_1$.\newpage
			
			Finally, suppose that $x_1 = y_1 = 0$. Then we know $z_1, z_2 \in \{-1, +1\}$ since\\ otherwise $(x_i, y_i, z_i) \notin S^2$. And thus, the claim becomes trivial that\\ $(x_1, y_1, z_1) = \pm (x_2, y_2, z_2)$.\retTwo
		\end{myIndent}

		Finally, since $g$ is a smooth injective immersion from the manifold $\mathbb{RP}^2$ which happens to be compact, we can conclude by \inLinkRap{Problem 5-3 page 1136}{problem 5-3} that $g$ is a smooth embedding. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
\end{enumerate}

\hTwo The next exercise will be important to proving a theorem in class.\retTwo

\Hstatement\blab{Set 3 Problem 5:} Let $M$ be a $C^r$ manifold (where $r \geq 1$) and let $\delta: M \to (0, \infty)$ be\\ a continuous function. Suppose $f: M \to \mathbb{R}^k$ is another continuous function. Then there\\ [2pt] is a $C^r$ map $F: M \to \mathbb{R}^k$ such that $|F(x) - f(x)| < \delta(x)$ for all $x \in M$.
\begin{myIndent}\HexOne
	Proof:\\
	Firstly, I shall find a sequence of points $\{a_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ and open sets $\{U_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that:
	
	{\centering$\bigcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}}U_n = M$, $a_n \in U_n$ for all $n$, and $|f(x) - f(a_n)| < \delta(x)$ for all $x \in U_n$.\\ [6pt]\par}

	\begin{myIndent}\HexTwoP
		Note that if $a \in M$ then we know that $\delta(a) > 0$. And now as $\delta$ is continuous, for any $0 < r < \delta(a)$ we can find an open set $V_a$ containing $a$ with $\delta(x) > r$ for all $x \in V_a$. Next, because $f$ is continuous at $a$, we can find an open set $U_a \subseteq V_a$ containing $a$ such that $|f(x) - f(a)| < r$ for all $x \in U_a$. In turn, $|f(x) - f(a)| < \delta(x)$ for all $x \in U_a$.\retTwo

		The prior paragraph shows us how to give an open covering of $M$ consisting of open sets $\{U_a\}_{a \in M}$ satisfying that $a \in U_a$ for all $a$ and $|f(x) - f(a)| < \delta(x)$ for all $x \in U_a$. Now we just use the second countability of $M$ in order to take a countable subcover.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Now that I have the prior sequence, I'm going to construct a $C^r$ partition of unity $\{\phi_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ subordinate to the open sets $U_n$. Then, I'm going to define $F: M \to \mathbb{R}^k$ by:
	
	{\center$F(x) = \sum_{n = 0}^\infty \phi_n(x)f(a_n)$.\retTwo\par}

	Note that since any $x \in M$ has a neighborhood on which only finitely many $\phi_n$ are\\ nonzero, we can say that locally $F$ is a linear combination of $C^r$ maps. Hence, $F$ is also\\ a $C^r$ map.\retTwo

	Also for any fixed $x \in X$, let $n_1, \ldots, n_k$ be the finitely many integers such that $\phi_{n_i}(x) \neq 0$. Then we have that:

	{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
		$|F(x) - f(x)| = \left|\sum_{i=1}^k \phi_{n_i}(x) \cdot [f(a_n) - f(x)]\right|$\\ [8pt]
		$\phantom{|F(x) - f(x)|} \leq \sum_{i=1}^k \phi_{n_i}(x) |f(x) - f(a_n)| < \sum_{i=1}^k \phi_{n_i}(x) \delta(x) = \delta(x)$. $\blacksquare$
	\end{tabular} \retTwo\par}
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo The final exercises on the homework all are about introducing Lie groups. Since 251 and not 250 is the Lie groups class, I don't think these will come up again in my differential geometry class. I'll still take notes on this though.\retTwo

Let $G$ be a group (written multiplicatively). We let $m: G \times G \to G$ denote the\\ multiplication map and $i: G \to G$ denote the inverse map. Also let $e$ denote the identity of $G$. If $G$ is also a smooth manifold and $m$ and $i$ are $C^\infty$ functions, we say $G$ is a \udefine{Lie group}.
\begin{myIndent}\myComment
	Note in particular that all Lie groups are topological groups.\newpage
\end{myIndent}

\hypertarget{Page 1233 Reference}{A} special property of a Lie group $G$ is that the group of $C^\infty$ diffeo-automorphisms on $G$ acts transitively on $G$. After all, given any $g \in G$ we define $L_g : G \to G$ and $R_g : G \to G$ by:

{\centering$L_g(h) \coloneqq gh$ and $R_g(h) \coloneqq hg$.\retTwo\par}

\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Note that $L_g$ is the composition of the smooth map $h  \mapsto (g, h)$ and the smooth map $m$. So, $L_g$ is a smooth map. We similarly can show that $R_g$ is a smooth map. Also, both $L_g$ and $R_g$ are diffeomorphisms since they have smooth inverses given by $L_{g^{-1}}$ and $R_{g^{-1}}$.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

Now if we consider the obvious action of diffeo-automorphisms of $G$ on $G$, we can see for any $g \in G$ that $L_g(e) = g$ for all $g$. This proves that the orbit of $e$ is all of $G$.\retTwo 


\exTwo\ul{Corollary:} Lie groups have no boundary.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Let $g$ be an interior point of $G$ and then suppose $h$ is any other point in $G$. We know there is a diffeomorphism $F: G \to G$ satisfying that $f(h) = g$. Yet diffeomorphisms must map interior points to interior points (see exercise 4-2 on \inLinkRap{Exercise 4-2 page 1057}{page 1057}). So, we know $h$ is an interior point of $G$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo A homomorphism $f: G \to H$ of Lie groups is a group homomorphism that is also a smooth map. An isomorphism of Lie groups is similarly a group isomorphism which is also a smooth diffeomorphism.\retTwo

A \udefine{Lie subgroup} $H$ of $G$ is a subgroup of $G$ endowed with a smooth structure making $H$ into a Lie group and an immersed submanifold of $G$.\retTwo

\Hstatement\blab{Set 3 Problem 2:} Let $G$ be a Lie group.
\begin{enumerate}
	\item[(i)] Show that if $H$ is a weakly embedded smooth submanifold of $G$ that is also a subgroup of $G$, then $H$ is a Lie subgroup of $G$.
	\begin{myIndent}\HexOne
		\ul{Lemma:} Suppose $M_1, M_2, N_1, N_2$ are $C^r$ manifolds. If $F: M_1 \to N_1$ and\\ $G: M_2 \to N_2$ are both $C^r$ immersions, then $F \times G: M_1 \times M_2 \to N_1 \times N_2$ is\\ also a $C^r$ immersion.
		\begin{myIndent}\HexTwoP
			Proof:\\
			Let $(p, q) \in M_1 \times M_2$ and recall that there are standard identifications:
			\begin{itemize}
				\item $T_{(p, q)} (M_1 \times M_2) \cong T_p M_1 \oplus T_q M_2$,
				\item $T_{(F(p), G(q))} (N_1 \times N_2) \cong T_{F(p)} N_1 \oplus T_{G(q)} N_2$.\retTwo
			\end{itemize}

			For each $i$ let $\pi_i : M_1 \times M_2 \to M_i$ and $\widetilde{\pi}_{i} : N_1 \times N_2 \to N_i$ be the\\ projection maps. Then importantly we have that $F \circ \pi_1 = \widetilde{\pi}_1 \circ (F \times G)$ and $G \circ \pi_2 = \widetilde{\pi}_2 \circ (F \times G)$. As a result for any $v \in T_{(p, q)} (M_1 \times M_2)$ we have that:\\ [-6pt]

			\hspace{-6em}\begin{tabular}{l}
				$\df (F \times G)_{(p, q)}(v) = \left(\df(\widetilde{\pi}_1)_{(F(p), G(p))} \circ \df (F \times G)_{(p, q)}(v), \phantom{a}\df(\widetilde{\pi}_2)_{(F(p), G(p))} \circ \df (F \times G)_{(p, q)}(v)\right)$\\ [6pt]
				$\phantom{\df (F \times G)_{(p, q)}(v)} = \left(\df(\widetilde{\pi}_1 \circ (F \times G))_{(p, q)}(v), \phantom{a}\df(\widetilde{\pi}_2 \circ (F \times G))_{(p, q)}(v)\right)$\\ [6pt]
				$\phantom{\df (F \times G)_{(p, q)}(v)} = \left(\df(F \circ \pi_1)_{(p, q)}(v), \phantom{a}\df(G \circ \pi_2)_{(p, q)}(v)\right)$\\ [6pt]
				$\phantom{\df (F \times G)_{(p, q)}(v)} = \left(\df F_p \circ \df (\pi_1)_{(p, q)}(v), \phantom{a}\df G_q \circ \df (\pi_2)_{(p, q)}(v)\right)$.
			\end{tabular}\newpage

			In other words, according to the standard identifications we have that:
			
			{\centering$\df (F \times G)_{(p, q)}(v_1, v_2) = (\df F_p(v_1), \df G_q(v_2))$.\retTwo\par}

			Even more succinctly, this means $\df (F \times G)_{(p, q)} = \df F_p \times \df G_q$ under this\\ identication. Finally, note that:
			
			{\centering$\ker(\df F_p \times \df G_q) = \ker(\df F_p) \oplus \ker(\df G_q) = \{0\} \oplus \{0\} = \{0\}$.\retTwo\par}
			
			So, we've finished showing that $\df (F \times G)_{(p, q)}$ is injective.\retTwo
		\end{myIndent}

		I went to the effort of showing the prior lemma because we can now use it to conclude that $H \times H$ is an immersed submanifold of $G \times G$. In turn, if $m: G \times G \to G$ is a smooth map then so is $m|_{H \times H} : H \times H \to G$.\retTwo

		Next, as $H$ is a subgroup of $G$, we know that the image of $m|_{H \times H}$ is contained in $H$. Therefore, as $H$ is weakly embedded we know that we can restrict the codomain of $m|_{H \times H}$ in order to get that $m|_{H \times H}: H \times H \to H$ is a smooth map.\retTwo

		We can use analogous reasoning to show that the inversion map $i$ is smooth from $H$ into $H$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	\item[(b)] Give an example of a dense immersed Lie subgroup of the torus $\mathbb{T} \coloneqq S^1 \times S^1$.
	\begin{myIndent}\HexOne
		Let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R} - \mathbb{Q}$ and then define $\gamma: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{T}$ by $\gamma(t) = (e^{2\pi i t}, e^{2\pi i \alpha t})$. We know\\ from set 2 problem 7 on \inLinkRap{Math 250A Set 2 Problem 7}{pages 1214-1216} that $\gamma$ is an injective immersion\\ whose image is dense in $\mathbb{T}$. Therefore, $H \coloneqq \gamma(\mathbb{R})$ is an immersed submanifold\\ of $\mathbb{T}$ that is dense in $S^1 \times S^1$.\retTwo

		Next, note that $\mathbb{T}$ is a Lie group under pointwise complex multiplication. 
		\begin{myIndent}\HexTwoP
			I don't feel like proving it since it seems obvious to me.\retTwo
		\end{myIndent}

		Furthermore, note that $\mathbb{R}$ is a Lie group under addition. Plus, $\gamma: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{T}$ is a group homomorphism. Thus, $H$ is automatically a subgroup of $\mathbb{T}$. And by definition we have that $\gamma$ is a smooth diffeomorphism from $\mathbb{R}$ to $H$.\retTwo

		It follows that multiplication and inversion are continuous with respect to the topology on $H$ because addition and negation is smooth with respect to the topology on $\mathbb{R}$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	\item[(c)] If $G$ is a Lie group, show that the connected component $G^0$ of the identity element $e$\\ is a Lie subgroup. Furthermore, every other connected component of $G$ is diffeomorphic\\ to $G^0$.
	\begin{myIndent}\HexOne
		To start off, because $G$ is locally connected (because it is a manifold), we know that every connected component of $G$ is an open set. Thus, $G^0$ is an open embedded submanifold of $G^0$.\retTwo

		Next, I claim that if $g \in G^0$ then so is $g^{-1}$. To see why, note that $i: G \to G$ is in particular a homeomorphism. So, it must permute the connected components of $G$. Yet also note that $e \in G^0$ and $i(e) = e$. So $i$ must map $G^0$ back to $G^0$.\newpage

		In a similar vein, I claim that if $g, h \in G^0$ then $gh \in G^0$ as well. After all, consider any fixed $g \in G^0$ and let $L_g: G \to G$ be the map $L_g(h) = gh$. Then $L_g$ is in particular a homeomorphism. So, it also must permute the connected components of $G$. Yet $e \in G^0$ and $L_g(e) = g \in G^0$. So, $L_g$ must map $G^0$ back to $G^0$. So, in particular, if $h \in G^0$ then $gh \in G^0$.\retTwo

		With that, we can now conclude by part (a) that $G^0$ is a Lie subgroup of $G$.\retTwo

		Finally, suppose $G^1$ is another connected component of $G$ and let $g^\prime \in G^1$. Then define $L_{g^\prime}: G \to G$ by $L_{g^\prime}(h) = g^\prime h$. Because $L_{g^\prime}$ is a homeomorphism, it must permute the connected components of $G$. Yet $e \in G^0$ and $L_{g^\prime}(e) = g^\prime \in G^1$. So, $L_{g^\prime}(G^0) = G^1$. And now by restricting the domain and codomain of $L_{g^\prime}$, we get that $L_{g^\prime}$ is a smooth diffeomorphism from $G^0$ to $G^1$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
\end{enumerate}

\hTwo Let $G$ be a Lie group and $X$ a $C^r$ manifold. We say $G$ acts on $X$ (on the left) if we have a $C^r$ map $G \times X \to X$ written as $(g, x) \mapsto gx$ satisfying the standard group action axioms.\retTwo

If $X, Y$ are two $C^r$ manifolds being acted on by a Lie group $G$ and $f: X \to Y$ is any map, we say $f$ is \udefine{$G$-equivariant} if $f(gx) = gf(x)$ for all $x \in X$ and $g \in G$.\retTwo

\Hstatement\blab{Set 3 Problem 3:}
\begin{itemize}
	\item[(i)] Suppose $G$ is a Lie group acting on a $C^r$ manifold $X$. Show that the maps $\mu_g: X \to X$ giveny by $\mu_g(x) = gx$ are all $C^r$-diffeomorphisms.
	\begin{myIndent}\HexOne
		To see that $\mu_g$ is $C^r$ for any fixed $g$, first note that $\iota_g : X \to G \times X$ given by\\ $x \mapsto (g, x)$ is a $C^r$ map. Then if $a: G \times X \to X$ is the group action, we know\\ that $\mu_g = a \circ \iota_g$ is a composition of two $C^r$ functions. So, $\mu_g$ is itself $C^r$.\retTwo

		Also note that $\mu_g$ is a diffeomorphism because it has the inverse function $\mu_{g^{-1}}$ which is a $C^r$ map by identical reasoning.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	\item[(ii)] As an example, show that the Lie group $G$ acts on itself via the conjugation action\\ $\mu_g(h) = ghg^{-1}$.
	\begin{myIndent}\HexOne
		We define the $a: G \times G \to G$ by $(g, h) \mapsto \mu_g(h) = ghg^{-1}$. Then, we just need to show that the map $a$ is smooth.\retTwo

		Fortunately, we know that the multiplication map $m: G \times G \to G$ given by\\ $m(g, h) = gh$ is a smooth map. Meanwhile, if we let $\pi_1: G \times G \to G$ be the\\ map $\pi_1(g, h) = g$, then we know that function is smooth. Then by composing\\ $\pi_1$ with the inverting function $i: G \to G$ which is also smooth, we get that\\ $i \circ \pi_1: G \times G \to G$ is a smooth map.\retTwo

		By the universal property of product manifolds, we now know that:
		
		{\centering$(g, h) \mapsto (m(g, h), i \circ \pi_1(g, h)) = (gh, g^{-1})$\\ [4pt]\par}

		is a smooth map from $G \times G$ to $G \times G$. And now we just compose that with the multiplication map $m$ one more time to get that $a(g, h) = ghg^{-1}$ is a smooth map.\newpage
	\end{myIndent}

	\item[(iii)] Show that if $f: G \to H$ is a Lie group homomorphism then $f$ has constant rank.
	\begin{myIndent}\HexOne
		Note for any fixed $g \in G$ that:
		
		{\centering$f(h) = f(g)f(g^{-1} h) = (L^\prime \circ f \circ L)(h)$.\\ [4pt]\par}

		where $L^\prime: H \to H$ is the diffeomorphism given by the left multiplication of $f(g)$\\ and $L : G \to G$ is the diffeomorphism given by the left multiplication of $g^{-1}$.\retTwo

		But now in particular, if $h = g$ then we can see that:

		{\centering $\df f_g = \df (L^\prime \circ f \circ L)_g  = \df L^\prime_{e} \circ \df f_e \circ \df  L_g$. \retTwo\par}

		Since both $\df L^\prime_{e}$ and $\df  L_g$ are bijective linear maps, we can thus say that $\df f_g$ has the same rank as $\df f_e$. And since $g$ was arbitrary, we've proven that $f$ has constant rank equal to whatever the rank of $\df f_e$ is.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	\item[(iv)] Suppose $X, Y$ are two $C^r$ manifolds both being acted on by a Lie group and $f:X \to Y$\\ is a $G$-equivariant $C^1$ map. If the action of $G$ on $X$ is transitive then $f$ has constant rank.
	\begin{myIndent}\HexOne
		Proof:\\
		Fix any $x_0 \in X$. Then consider any other $x_1 \in X$. Because $G$ acts on $X$ transitively, we know there exists $g \in G$ such that $gx_0 = x_1$. And now we let $\mu_g: X \to X$ and $\widetilde{\mu}_g{Y \to Y}$ respectively be the maps $x \mapsto gx$ and $y \mapsto gy$.\retTwo
		
		Because $\mu_g$ is a diffeomorphism, we can say that:

		{\centering \begin{tabular}{l}
			$\df f_{x_1} = \df f_{x_1} \circ \myId_{T_{x_1} X}= \df f_{x_1} \circ \df (\mu_g)_{x_0} \circ (\df (\mu_g)_{x_0})^{-1} = \df (f \circ \mu_g)_{x_0} \circ (\df (\mu_g)_{x_0})^{-1}$
		\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

		Yet then because $f$ is $G$-equivariant, we know $f \circ \mu_g = \widetilde{\mu}_g \circ f$. In turn, we know that:

		{\centering \begin{tabular}{l}
			$\df (f \circ \mu_g)_{x_0} = \df (\widetilde{\mu}_g \circ f)_{x_0} = \df (\widetilde{\mu}_g)_{f(x_0)} \circ \df f_{x_0}$
		\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

		So to summarize, $\df f_{x_1} = \df (\widetilde{\mu}_g)_{f(x_0)} \circ \df f_{x_0} \circ (\df (\mu_g)_{x_0})^{-1}$. Since $\df (\widetilde{\mu}_g)_{f(x_0)}$ and $(\df (\mu_g)_{x_0})^{-1}$ are both bijective linear maps, we can conclude that the rank of $\df f_{x_1}$ equals the rank of $\df f_{x_0}$. And since $x_1$ was arbitrary, we are done. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}
\end{itemize}

\hTwo The next bit of stuff is a tangent I don't have time to do but I want to do anyways. My goal is just to illustrate that Lie groups have stronger topological properties than mere topological groups.\retTwo

To start off, we have the following corollary to part (iii) of the prior problem.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Corollary:} Suppose $f: G \to H$ is a Lie group homomorphism. Then $f$ is a Lie group isomorphism if and only if $f$ is a bijection.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	The forwards implication is trivial. As for the backwards implication, note by part (iii) of the prior problem that $f$ has constant rank. Therefore, if $f$ is also bijective then we know from the corollary on \inLinkRap{page 1066 corollary}{page 1066} that $f$ is a smooth diffeomorphism. And hence, $f$ is a Lie group isomorphism. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo Note though that we don't have an analogous result for topological groups. After all,\\ we can give two topological groups $G$ and $H$ as a well as a bijective topological group homomorphism $f: G \to H$ that is not a topological group isomorphism (i.e. a group\\ homomorphism as well as a homeomorphism).
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Let $\mathbb{R}_d$ denote the real numbers with the discrete topology and let $\mathbb{R}$ denote the real\\ numbers with the standard Euclidean topology. Both $\mathbb{R}$ and $\mathbb{R}_d$ are topological groups under addition.\retTwo

	Consider the map $f: \mathbb{R}_d \to \mathbb{R}$ given by $f(x) = x$. This is a bijective group homomrphism. Furthermore, $f$ is trivially continuous. That said, $f^{-1}$ is not continuous.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

Another interesting result concerns when we know a group equipped with a topology and perhaps a smooth structure is a topological group or Lie group. But first we need a\\ smaller result.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Lemma:} Suppose $G$ is a group equipped with a topology. Let $m: G \times G \to G$ and $i: G \to G$ denote the multiplication and inversion operations. Then $G$ is a topological group if and only if the map $s: G \times G \to G$ given by $s(g, h) = gh^{-1}$ is continuous. 
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	For $i = 1, 2$ we let $\pi_i: G \times G \to G$ be the projection $(g_1, g_2) \mapsto g_i$. Both of these are continuous maps by the definition of the product topology.\retTwo

	$(\Longrightarrow)$\\
	If $G$ is a topological group then $s = m \circ (\pi_1, i \circ \pi_2)$ is a composition of continuous\\ maps and is thus continuous.\retTwo

	$(\Longleftarrow)$\\
	To start off, note that the map $\iota_e: G \to G \times G$ given by $\iota_e(g) = (e, g)$ is continuous. Also, $i = s \circ \iota_e$. So, $i$ is a continuous map. Next, note that $m = s \circ (\pi_1, i \circ \pi_2)$ is a composition of two continuous functions and is thus continuous.\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

Furthermore, if $G$ is a smoth manifold then $G$ is a Lie group if and only if the map\\ $s: G \times G \to G$ given by $s(g, h) = gh^{-1}$ is smooth.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	The proof is literally identical to before. Just swap out the word "continuous" with the word "smooth". $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo I also thought I needed the next result (which is an exercise from John Lee).\retTwo

\Hstatement\blab{Problem 7-1:} Suppose $G$ is a group that is also a smooth manifold. Also suppose the group\\ map $m: G \times G \to G$ given by $m(g, h) = gh$ is smooth. Then $m$ is a submersion.
\begin{myIndent}\HexOne
	Proof:\\
	To start off, we only need the smoothness of $m$ to prove that the map $R_g(h) = gh$ is a $C^\infty$ diffeo-automorphisms for all $g \in G$. And thus by identical reasoning as on \inLinkRap{Page 1233 Reference}{page 1233}, we can conclude that $G$ will have no boundary. This also in turn means that $G \times G$ has no boundary. And now in order to prove that $m$ is a submersion it is equivalent due the local section theorem on \inLinkRap{Local Section Theorem page 1106}{pages 1106-1107} to show that for any fixed $(g_1, g_2) \in G \times G$ there exists an open set $U \subseteq G$ containing $g_1g_2$ and a smooth map $\sigma: U \to G \times G$ such that $\sigma(g_1g_2) = (g_1, g_2)$.\newpage

	This is easy though and the $\sigma$ we will construct is even a \textit{global} section. Just define\\ $\sigma: G \to G \times G$ by $\sigma(g) = (gg_2^{-1}, g_2)$ Then $\sigma$ is smooth, $\sigma(g_1g_2) = (g_1, g_2)$,\\ and $m \circ \sigma(g) = g$ for all $g \in G$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo Now we're ready for the actual interesting result (which is also an exercise from John Lee).\retTwo

\Hstatement\blab{Problem 7-3:} Suppose that $G$ is a group that is also a smooth manifold. Also, let $m: G \times G \to G$ and $s: G \times G \to G$ be the maps $m(g, h) = gh$ and $s(g, h) = gh^{-1}$. If $m$ is a smooth map then so is $s$. Then consequently by our prior lemma, we know $G$ is a Lie group. 
\begin{myIndent}\HexOne
	Proof:\\
	Define $F: G \times G \to G \times G$ by $F(g, h) = (g, hg)$. Also for $i = 1, 2$ let $\pi_i: G \times G \to G$ be the map $(g_1, g_2) \mapsto g_i$.\retTwo
	
	My first obervation is that $F$ is a smooth map.
	\begin{myIndent}\HexTwoP
		After all, $F$ can be written as $F = (\pi_1,\phantom{a} m \circ (\pi_2, \pi_1))$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Secondly, I claim that $F$ is a local diffeomorphism.
	\begin{myIndent}\HexTwoP
		Since $G$ and thus $G \times G$ has no boundary (see my proof of the last problem), it\\ suffices by the inverse function theorem to prove that $\df F_(g, h)$ has full rank at all\\ $(g, h) \in G \times G$. The easiest way to go about this is to prove that $\df F_{(g, h)}$ is injective for all $(g, h) \in G \times G$.\retTwo
		
		We start by making the standard identification $T_{(g, h)}(G \times G) \cong T_g G \oplus T_h G$.\\ Then note for any $(v, w) \in T_g G \oplus T_h G$ that:

		{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
			$\df F_{(g, h)}(v, w) = (\df (\pi_1)_{(g, h)}(v, w), \phantom{a} \df (m \circ (\pi_2, \pi_1))_{(g, h)}(v, w))$\\ [4pt]
			$\phantom{\df F_{(g, h)}(v, w)} = \left(v, \phantom{a} \df m_{(h, g)}\left(\df (\pi_2)_{(g, h)}(v, w),\phantom{.} \df (\pi_1)_{(g, h)}(v, w)\right)\right)$\\ [4pt]
			$\phantom{\df F_{(g, h)}(v, w)} = \left(v, \phantom{a} \df m_{(h, g)}\left(w, v\right)\right)$.
		\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

		It easily follows that $(v, w) \in \ker(\df m_{(g, h)})$ if and only if $v = 0$ and\\ $(w, 0) \in \ker(\df m_{(h, g)})$\retTwo

		Next let $R_g: G \to G$ be the map $R_g(h) = hg$. We know that $R_g$ is a\\ diffeomorphism (see the prior problem). Also note that $R_g = m \circ (\myId_G, C_g)$\\ where $C_g: G \to G$ is the constant map sending everything to $g$. As a result,\\ for any $w \in T_h G$ we have that:

		{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
			$\df (R_g)_h w = \df m_{(h, g)}(\df (\myId_G)_h w, \phantom{.} \df (C_g)_g w) = \df m_{(h, g)}(w, 0)$.
		\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

		But because $R_g$ is a diffeomorphism, we know that $\df (R_g)_h w = 0$ if and only if\\ $w = 0$. So, $(w, 0) \in \ker(\df m_{(h, g)})$ implies that $w = 0$. And with that, we've finished proving that the kernel of $\df F_{(g, h)}$ is trivial.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Thirdly I observe that $F$ is a bijection whose inverse function is $F^{-1}(g, h) = (g, hg^{-1})$.\retTwo

	The three prior facts combined let us conclude that $F$ is a smooth diffeomorphism from $G \times G$ to $G \times G$. In other words, we now know that $F^{-1}$ is a smooth function.\retTwo

	Finally, we can now conclude that $s$ is smooth since:

	{\centering $s = \pi_2 \circ F^{-1} \circ (\pi_2, \pi_1)$. $\blacksquare$ \retTwo\par}
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo There is not an analogous result when we are only working with topological groups.
\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	For example, let $\mathbb{R}_l$ be the set of real numbers equipped with the lower limit topology\newpage (i.e. the topology generated by the basis of all half intervals $[a, b)$). We can consider $\mathbb{R}_l$\\ a group under addition.\retTwo

	I shall first show that the map $a: \mathbb{R}_l \times \mathbb{R}_l \to \mathbb{R}_l$ given by $a(x, y) \coloneqq x + y$ is continuous.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		It suffices to show for any $(x, y) \in \mathbb{R}_l \to \mathbb{R}_l$ and open set $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}_l$ cotaining $x + y$ we have that there is an open set $V \subseteq \mathbb{R}_l \times \mathbb{R}_l$ containing $(x, y)$ with $a(V) \subseteq U$.  Fortunately, by shrinking $U$ we can always without loss of generality assume\\ $U = [x + y, x + y + 2\varepsilon)$ for some $\varepsilon > 0$. And now we just set:
		
		{\centering$V = [x, x + \varepsilon) \times [y, y + \varepsilon)$.\retTwo\par}
	\end{myIndent}

	That said, also observe for any sequence $\{x_k\}_{k \in \mathbb{N}} \subseteq \mathbb{R}_l$ that $x_k \to x$ in $\mathbb{R}_l$ iff $x_k \to x$ in the standard Euclidean topology and there exists $K \in \mathbb{N}$ such that for all $k \geq K$ we have that $x_k \geq x$. Using this fact, we can easily show that the negation map $n: \mathbb{R}_l \to \mathbb{R}_l$ given by $n(x) = -x$ is \textit{not} continuous.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		To see why, note that $\frac{1}{k} \to 0$ in $\mathbb{R}_\ell$ by $n(\frac{1}{k}) = \frac{-1}{k} \not\to 0$ in $\mathbb{R}_\ell$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Therefore, $\mathbb{R}_l$ is \textit{not} a topological group even though its addition operation is\\ continuous.
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo\mySepTwo

\hypertarget{idk reference 9}{The} next notes finally return to what I was doing on \inLinkRap{Page 1157 reference}{page 1157}.\retTwo

My end goal before getting distracted by singular homology was to show that most $C^r$ manifolds we would care about can be embedded into Euclidean space if they weren't at first, and in fact if $M$ is $n$-dimensional then it can be embedded into $\mathbb{R}^{2n + 1}$. To accomplish this goal, it suffices to show that:
\begin{enumerate}
	\item[1.] We can embed $M$ into $\mathbb{R}^N$ for just some $N$.
	\item[2.] Given an $n$ dimensional embedded submanifold $M \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$ where $N > 2n + 1$, there is an embedding of $M$ into $\mathbb{R}^{N - 1}$.\retTwo
\end{enumerate}

Lemma 6.13 on \inLinkRap{Lemma 6.13 page 1156}{pages 1156-1157} takes a step towards addressing the second task, albeit the lemma only gives us an immersion and not an embedding of $M$. At least in the case though that $M$ is compact, then proposition 4.22 on \inLinkRap{Proposition 4.22 page 1104}{page 1104} tells us that our injective immersion is automatically an embedding. So for compact manifolds we are half done.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Lemma:} Suppose $M$ is a compact $n$-dimensional $C^r$ manifold (where $r \geq 1$). Then there exists $N \in \mathbb{N}$ and a $C^r$ embedding $f: M \hookrightarrow \mathbb{R}^N$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	For every $p \in M$ we can pick a smooth chart $(U_p, \varphi_p)$ such that $p \in U_p$. And then we can pick two more open sets $W_p$ and $V_p$ such that $p \in W_p \subseteq \overline{W_p} \subseteq V_p \subseteq \overline{V_p} \subseteq U_p$. But now as $M$ is compact, we know  there are finitely many $p_1, \ldots, p_\ell$ such that $M \subseteq \bigcup_{i=1}^\ell W_{p_i}$.\retTwo

	For each $i$ let $b_i: M \to [0, 1]$ be a $C^r$ bump function with $b_i \equiv 1$ on $\overline{W_{p_i}}$ and $b_i \equiv 0$\\ on $M - V_{p_i}$. Then by pasting lemma, we can guarentee that the product $b_i \varphi_{p_i}$ defines\\ a $C^r$ map from $M$ to $\mathbb{R}^n$ for each $i$ (where the product equals $0$ at all points outside the\newpage domain of the chart $(U_{p_i}, \varphi_{p_i})$). So, we now define the map $f: M \to \mathbb{R}^{(n + 1)\ell}$ by:

	{\centering $f(p) \coloneqq \left(b_1(p), \ldots, b_\ell(p), (b_1\varphi_1)(p), \ldots, (b_\ell\varphi_\ell)(p)\right)$\retTwo\par}

	Because $M$ is compact, in order to prove that $f$ is a $C^r$ embedding we just need to explain why $f$ is a $C^r$ injective immersion.\retTwo

	Fortunately, because every component function of $f$ is a $C^r$ map, we automatically have that $f$ is a $C^r$ map as well.\retTwo
	
	Also suppose $f(p) = f(q)$. Since $M \subseteq \bigcup_{i=1}^\ell W_{p_i}$ we know that $p \in W_{p_i}$ for some $i$. In turn $b_i(p) = 1$, and since $f(p) = f(q)$ this also guarentees that $b_i(q) = 1$. So, both $p, q$ are covered by the chart $(U_{p_i}, \varphi_{p_i})$ and $\varphi_i(p) = (b_i \varphi_i)(p) = (b_i \varphi_i)(q) = \varphi_i(q)$. Finally, since $\varphi_{p_i}$ is injective on $U_{p_i}$ and $p, q \in U_{p_i}$, we can conclude that $p = q$. So, we have shown that $f$ is injective.\retTwo

	Finally, to prove that $f$ is an immersion, consider any $p \in M$ and then pick $i$ with $p \in W_{p_i}$. Importantly, $b_i \equiv 1$ on a neighborhood of $p$. And now upon identifying:
	
	{\centering$T_{f(p)}\mathbb{R}^{(n + 1)\ell} \cong \left(\bigoplus_{i=1}^\ell T_{b_i(p)}\mathbb{R}\right) \oplus \left(\bigoplus_{i=1}^\ell T_{(b_i\varphi_i) (p)}\mathbb{R}^n\right)$\\ [4pt]\par}
	
	we have that:
	
	{\centering\begin{tabular}{l}
		$\df f_p = (\df b_1, \ldots, \df b_\ell, \df (b_1 \varphi_{p_1})_p, \ldots, \df (b_{i-1} \varphi_{p_{i-1}})_p, \df (\varphi_i)_p, \df (b_{i+1} \varphi_{p_{i+1}})_p, \ldots, (b_\ell \varphi_{p_\ell})_p)$.
	\end{tabular}\retTwo\par}

	Yet $\df (\varphi_i)_p : T_p M \to T_{\varphi_i(p)}\mathbb{R}^n$ is a linear bijection (and thus has rank $n = \dim(M)$). It then follows that $\df (f)_p$ must also have rank at least $n = \dim(M)$. So, $\df f_p$ is full rank and thus injective. And since $p$ was arbitrary, we've finished proving that $f$ is an immersion. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\exTwo\ul{Corollary (Whitney embedding theorem for compact manifolds):} Suppose $M$ is a compact $n$-dimensional $C^r$ manifold (where $r \geq 1$). Then there exists $N \in \mathbb{N}$ and a $C^r$ embedding $f: M \hookrightarrow \mathbb{R}^N$. If in addition we assume $r \geq 2$, then we can specifically choose $N$ to be equal to $2n + 1$.\retTwo

\hTwo\begin{myIndent}\mySepThree\end{myIndent}

The case of noncompact $C^r$ manifolds is more delicate and in fact Oprea skips going over this case in lecture. I don't want to skip this though.\retTwo

To start off, suppose $X$ is a topological space. We say a function $f: X \to \mathbb{R}$ is an\\ \udefine{exhaustion function} if for every $c \in \mathbb{R}$ the set $f^{-1}((-\infty, c])$ is compact.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Theorem 2.28:} Suppose $M$ is a $C^r$ manifold (where $r \geq 1$). Then $M$ admits a postive $C^r$ exhaustion function $f: M \to (0, \infty)$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	If $M$ is already compact, then we can just pick $f$ to be a constant function. So without loss of generality we will now assume $M$ is not compact.\newpage

	Using the fact that $M$ is second countable as well as an LCH space, we can find a sequence $\{U_k\}_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ of precompact open sets on $M$ such that $M \subseteq \bigcup_{k=1}^\infty U_k$. Next, we can pick $C^r$ partition of unity $\{\phi_k\}_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ subordinate to the sets $U_k$. In other words, $\phi_k$ is positive and $C^r$ for all $k$, $\supp(\phi_k) \subseteq U_k$ for all $k$, $\sum_{k=1}^\infty \phi_k = 1$, and every $p \in M$ has a neighborhood on which only finitely many $\phi_k$ are ever nonzero.\retTwo
	
	Finally, we define $f \coloneqq \sum_{k = 1}^\infty k \phi_k$. Note that $f$ is a $C^r$ map because locally around any $p \in M$ we have that $f$ is just a linear combination of finitely many of the $\phi_K$. Also note that $f(p) > 0$ for all $p \in M$. After all, $\phi_{k^\prime}(p) > 0$ for some $k^\prime$. And then since all the summands are nonnegative, we can conclude that $f(p) > k^\prime \phi_{k^\prime}(p) > 0$.\retTwo

	As for showing that $f$ is an exhaustion function, consider any $c \in \mathbb{R}$. We can pick a positive integer $N > c$. And now if $p \notin \bigcup_{i=1}^N U_{p_i}$ we know that:
	
	{\centering$\phi_1(p) =  \phi_2(p) = \cdots = \phi_N(p) = 0$.\\ [4pt]\par}

	As a result: $f(p) =\hspace{-0.3em} \sum\limits_{k = N + 1}^\infty\hspace{-0.1em} k\phi_k(p) > N\hspace{-0.1em} \sum\limits_{k = N + 1}^\infty\hspace{-0.1em} \phi_k(p) = N \cdot 1$.\retTwo
	
	This proves that $f^{-1}((-\infty, c]) \subseteq f^{-1}((-\infty, N]) \subseteq \bigcup_{i=1}^N U_{p_i} \subseteq \bigcup_{i=1}^N \overline{U_{p_i}}$. Since the right most set is a union of compact sets and thus compact itself, and also because $f^{-1}((-\infty, c])$ is a closed subset of $M$ due to $f$ being continuous, we can thus conclude that $f^{-1}((-\infty, c])$ is compact. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo Let $\lambda(k)$ denote the number of time continuously differentiable we need a function\\ $f: \mathbb{R}^{n + k} \to \mathbb{R}^n$ to be to prove that Sard's theorem holds for $f$.
\begin{myIndent}\myComment
	See \inLinkRap{Page 1154 reference}{page 1154} to recall what's up with $\lambda(k)$. (Namely, $\lambda(k) = k + 1$ for all $k \geq 0$. That said, the lower bound which \textit{I} managed to prove on $\lambda(k)$ is weaker.)\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

Recall from two pages ago the two tasks we need to accomplish. We'll accomplish the first task for a noncompact manifold by using a $C^r$ exhaustion function, Sard's theorem, and the Whitney embedding theorem for compact manifolds that we already proved.\retTwo

\exTwo\ul{Theorem 6.15:} Suppose $M$ is a noncompact $n$-dimensional $C^r$ manifold and that\\ $r \geq \max(2, \lambda(n - 1))$ {\color{red}(which equals $\max(2, n)$)}. Then there is a $C^r$ embedding\\ $F: M \hookrightarrow \mathbb{R}^{4n + 3}$.
\begin{myIndent}\exThreeP
	Proof:\\
	Let $f: M \to (0, \infty)$ be a $C^r$ exhaustion function. Because $r \geq \lambda(n - 1)$, we know that the set of critical values of $f$ in $(0, \infty)$ has measure zero. Hence, for every nonnegative integer $i$ we can pick real numbers $i < a_i < b_i < i + 1$ such that $a_i$ and $b_i$ are regular values of $f$.\retTwo
	
	Now define:
	\begin{itemize}
		\item $D_0 \coloneqq f^{-1}((-\infty, 1])$ and $E_0 \coloneqq  f^{-1}((-\infty, a_1])$,
		\item $D_i \coloneqq f^{-1}([i, i+1])$, and $E_i \coloneqq f^{-1}([b_{i-1}, a_{i+1}])$ for all $i \geq 1$.
	\end{itemize}

	By proposition 5.47 on \inLinkRap{Proposition 5.47 page 1127}{pages 1127-1128}, we can conclude that each $E_i$ is a compact\\ regular domain of $M$ for all $i \geq 0$. Furthermore, each $D_i$ will be a compact subset\\ of $M$ contained within the interior of each $E_i$.\newpage

	For all $i \geq 0$ we let $\phi_i: M \to [0, 1]$ be a $C^r$ bump function such that $\phi_i \equiv 1$ on a neighborhood of $D_i$ and $\supp(\phi_i) \subseteq E_i^\circ$. Also, for all $i \geq 0$ we let $g_i: E_i \hookrightarrow \mathbb{R}^{2n + 1}$ be a $C^r$ embedding.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		We know such an embedding exists due to Whitney's embedding theorem for\\ compact manifolds as well as the fact that $r \geq 2$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Importantly, the product $\phi_i g_i$ then defines a $C^r$ map on all of $M$ (where $(\phi_i g_i)(p) = 0$ if $p \notin E_i$.) Also observe that every point $p \in M$ has a neighborhood $U$ intersecting at most two of the $E_i$. In fact, we can even even say that $U$ intersects $E_i$ and $E_{i+1}$ for some $i$.
	\begin{myIndent}\exPPP
		To see, why note that $f^{-1}((-\infty, a_1))$ intersects only $E_0$ and $E_1$. Also, for any\\ $i \geq 0$ we have that $f^{-1}((a_i, a_{i+1}))$ and $f^{-1}((b_i, b_{i+1}))$ intersect only $E_i$ and $E_{i+1}$ on a neighborhood of $p$.\retTwo
	\end{myIndent}

	Now we define $F: M \to \mathbb{R}^{4n + 3} \cong \mathbb{R}^{2n + 1} \times \mathbb{R}^{2n + 1} \times \mathbb{R}$ by:
	
	{\centering$F(p) \coloneqq \left(\sum\limits_{i \text{ even}}(\phi_i g_i)(p),\phantom{a} \sum\limits_{i \text{ odd}}(\phi_i g_i)(p), \phantom{a} f(p)\right)$\retTwo\par}

	Note that $F$ is a $C^r$ map because every $p \in M$ has a neighborhood on which only one\\ summand from each of the sums in the definition of $F$ is nonzero. In a similar vein, to see that $F$ is an immersion, note for any $p \in M$ that there exists $i$ with $p \in D_i$. In turn, $(\phi_i g_i) = g_i$ on a neighborhood of $p$. Then combining the fact that $\df (g_i)_p$ is injective with the observation of what the formula for $F$ locally looks like will prove $\df F_p$ is injective.\retTwo

	As for showing that $F$ is injective, note that if $F(p) = F(q)$ then we know that\\ $f(p) = f(q)$. In particular, this means that if $p \in D_i$ then $q \in D_i$ also. So,\\ $\phi_i(p) = 1 = \phi_i(q)$. Next note that $F(p) = F(q)$ implies that:

	{\centering $g_i(p) = (\phi_i g_i)(p) = (\phi_i g_i)(q) = g_i(q)$.\retTwo\par}

	Yet $p, q \in D_i$ implies that $p, q \in E_i$ as well. And since $g_i$ is injective on $E_i$, we can\\ conclude that $p = q$.\retTwo

	Finally, I claim that $F$ is a proper map. To see why, suppose $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{4n + 3}$ is any compact set. Then in particular, there must exist $A, B \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{2n + 2} \times [A, B]$. Hence, $F^{-1}(K) \subseteq f^{-1}([A, B])$. Yet now note that $F^{-1}(K)$ is a closed set. Meanwhile, $f$ being an exhaustion function means that $f^{-1}([A, B])$ is a compact set. It follows that $F^{-1}(K)$ is compact.\retTwo

	By proposition 4.22 on \inLinkRap{Proposition 4.22 page 1104}{page 1104}, we can conclude that $F$ is a $C^r$ embedding. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
\end{myIndent}

\hTwo As for accomplishing the second task we first define for any $1$-dimensional linear subspace $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$ and any $R > 0$ the \udefine{tube with axis $S$ and radius $R$} given by:

{\centering$T_R(S) \coloneqq \{x \in \mathbb{R}^N : |x - y| < R \text{ for some } y \in S\}$.\retTwo\par}

\begin{myIndent}\pracTwo
	Note that if $S = \mSpan(v)$ then $\min\limits_{y \in S} |x - y| = \left|x - \frac{x\cdot v}{|v|^2}v\right|$.\retTwo
	
	Importantly, the map $x \mapsto \left|x - \frac{x\cdot v}{|v|^2}v\right|$ is a continuous function and so we can conclude that $T_R(S)$ is an open set.\newpage
\end{myIndent}

But now by the prior reasoning, we know that every ideal of $A/\langle x\rangle$ is principal. Hence, $I/\langle x\rangle$ is generated by $y + \langle x\rangle$ for some $y \in A$. And now $I = \langle x, y\rangle$. $\blacksquare$\retTwo
% 	\end{myIndent}
% \end{enumerate}
